This slide sets up the 3D genome units and the motif-strand question in the exercise. GM12878 has about 44 000 CTCF peaks in the file we use.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Transcription factors






A TF has a DNA-binding domain (DBD) that reads a short motif, and effector domains that recruit co-activators or co-repressors.
Humans have about 1600 TFs, classified by DBD family; half are C2H2 zinc fingers. Members of one family bind similar motifs.
About a quarter still have no known motif.


Numbers from Lambert et al. 2018, a manually curated census (1639 TFs; the counts in the figure are from its database). Each DBD family has a typical motif shape: bHLH factors bind the E-box CANNTG as dimers, bZIP factors palindromes, homeodomains TAAT cores, ETS factors GGAA cores (PU.1 is an ETS factor), forkheads TGTTTAC. Many paralogues share nearly identical motifs, so a motif match rarely tells you which family member binds: an ETS motif in a peak could be PU.1, ETS1, ELF1 or FLI1. Activation domains are mostly intrinsically disordered, acidic or rich in glutamine or proline. The KRAB zinc fingers (344 in the database) mostly silence transposable elements by recruiting KAP1/TRIM28 and SETDB1, which writes H3K9me3; this is the H3K9me3 at ZNF clusters seen in What is epigenetics?.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
A motif as a matrix






Align known binding sites, count each base at each position, add a pseudocount, divide to get frequencies \(p_{b,j}\).
The log-odds weight of base \(b\) at position \(j\) against a background \(q_b\): \(\;w_{b,j} = \log_2 \dfrac{p_{b,j}}{q_b}\). Positive: preferred; negative: disfavoured.
The pseudocount keeps unseen bases from getting \(-\infty\): with only 8 sites, “never seen” does not mean “impossible”.


This is the position weight matrix (PWM), the standard representation of a TF motif (Stormo 2000; Wasserman and Sandelin 2004). The example is an ETS-type site with the GGAA core that PU.1 binds. Walk through one column: column 1 has 6 G, 1 A, 1 C, 0 T. With a pseudocount of 1 per base and 8 sites the frequencies are 7/12, 2/12, 2/12 and 1/12; against a uniform background of 0.25, G scores log2(0.583/0.25) = +1.2 and T scores log2(0.083/0.25) = −1.6. Pseudocount choices vary (JASPAR tools use 0.8 in total, others 1 per base or a fraction proportional to the background); the more sites, the less it matters. A real background is not uniform: the human genome is 41% GC, so q(G) = q(C) ≈ 0.2 and q(A) = q(T) ≈ 0.3. The exercise builds a matrix like this by hand.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Scanning a sequence






The score of a window is the sum of the weights of its bases. Slide the window along the sequence, on both strands (the reverse complement).
A score above a threshold is a match (a predicted site). Tools set the threshold from a \(p\)-value: the chance that a random window scores as high.
Summing log-odds assumes the positions contribute independently. Usually a good approximation; dinucleotide models and neural networks relax it.


The second match in the figure only appears on the minus strand: the top strand reads ACTTCC, whose reverse complement is GGAAGT. A scanner reports it with strand “−”, and the motif then points to the left on the genome; this matters for CTCF orientation. The best possible score is the sum of the column maxima (8.4 here); the worst is the sum of the minima. Tools such as FIMO (MEME suite), HOMER, motifmatchr and Biostrings::matchPWM compute an exact p-value per score from the matrix and the background. With p < 1e-4 per window and strand, about 200 windows per Mb pass the threshold by chance, which is the topic of the next slides. The independence assumption fails for some TFs (e.g. flexible spacing in dimers); this is part of why convolutional neural networks, which learn motifs from data, outperform PWMs (machine-learning units).

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Information content and sequence logos






Information content of a column (uniform background): \(\;IC_j = 2 + \sum_b p_{b,j} \log_2 p_{b,j}\) bits. 2 bits: one base only; 0 bits: all four equally likely.
A sequence logo draws each column as a stack of height \(IC_j\), each letter scaled by its frequency.
CTCF (JASPAR MA0139.2, from 913 ChIP-seq sites): 15 positions, 16.1 bits in total; the core CCA·…AGGGGGC carries most of it.


Information content is the reduction in uncertainty compared with a random base (2 bits for DNA). Column 3 of CTCF (C in 903 of 913 sites) has 1.9 bits; column 1 only 0.34. The total information content gives a rule of thumb for how often a motif occurs by chance: roughly once every 2^IC bp per strand, so 2^16 ≈ 70 000 bp for a high-scoring CTCF match. JASPAR is the open database of curated TF matrices (2024 release: Rauluseviciute et al.); CIS-BP, HOCOMOCO and the HOMER and MEME collections are alternatives. Logo made with universalmotif in make-generegulation-figs.R. Note that this matrix was derived from ChIP-seq peaks, so it describes in vivo binding sites, including bias from the experiment; other matrices come from in vitro assays (SELEX, protein-binding microarrays).

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
How many matches by chance?






At a \(p\)-value threshold \(p\), a sequence of length \(L\) has about \(\;2 L p\;\) matches by chance (two strands).
chr21 (40 Mb of sequence): 8583 CTCF matches at \(p < 10^{-4}\), close to the 8018 expected by chance. Genome-wide, about 600 000 are expected.
GM12878 has 44 217 CTCF peaks. Even a long, informative motif has far more matches than bound sites.


Log scale on the y axis. This is the point of the slide: motif matches are cheap. A 6-bp exact word occurs once every 4^6 = 4096 bp per strand, about 500 times per Mb on both strands; a typical TF motif with 10–12 bits of information occurs thousands of times per Mb at usual thresholds. The observed counts are close to the expectation because the expectation is computed from the matrix itself with a uniform background, and chr21 is not uniform (41% GC); at stricter thresholds the observed count exceeds the expected one, partly because real CTCF sites are enriched (there are a few hundred bound sites on chr21) and partly because of base composition and repeats. Numbers computed in make-generegulation-figs.R with motifmatchr (exercise R7).

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Real data: CTCF peaks contain the CTCF motif
text:
Real data: CTCF peaks contain the CTCF motif






Of 200 bp around each CTCF summit, 78% contain a match (\(p < 10^{-4}\)), against 8% of GC-matched genomic windows and 9% of the same sequences shuffled.
The stronger the peak, the more likely the motif: 62% of the weakest quarter, 92% of the strongest.
Weak peaks without a motif: indirect binding, weaker motif variants, or noise.


Three backgrounds: random genomic windows (4%), windows matched to the GC content of the peaks (8%, because the CTCF motif is GC-rich and so occurs more often in GC-rich DNA), and the peak sequences shuffled so that each keeps its dinucleotide composition (9%). The GC-matched background is the fair one; a random-genome background would overstate the enrichment by a factor of two. This is exactly the issue of the null from the shuffle test in Genomic intervals: here the null must match sequence composition. HOMER uses GC-matched genomic background, MEME/SEA shuffled sequences. The strong dependence on peak strength is typical of ChIP-seq of a direct DNA binder and is a quality check: if the strongest peaks of your TF ChIP do not contain its motif, worry about the antibody.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Real data: the motif sits at the summit
text:
Real data: the motif sits at the summit






Position of the best CTCF match in 500 bp around each summit: a sharp peak at 0. 94% of best matches are within 50 bp of the summit (median distance 6 bp).
In GC-matched background windows the best matches are spread evenly.
Centrality is strong evidence that the motif is what the TF binds; tools such as CentriMo use it as a test.


The summit is the position with the most ChIP fragments, which pile up symmetrically around the protein’s binding position, so a directly bound motif should be at the summit within the precision of the experiment (tens of bp). A motif that is enriched in peaks but spread evenly over them suggests a partner factor or a sequence bias of the region, not the immunoprecipitated TF itself. The same plot centred on ATAC-seq summits is noisier, because an ATAC peak can contain several TFs. Only peaks with a match contribute (81% of peaks within ±250 bp; 17% of the 500-bp background windows have one). The exercise reproduces this histogram on 5000 peaks.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Most motif matches are not bound
text:
Most motif matches are not bound






Of the 8583 CTCF matches on chr21, only 369 (4.3%) lie in a GM12878 CTCF peak, although CTCF is one of the most motif-driven TFs.
Matches in accessible DNA (ATAC peaks) are bound 39% of the time, matches elsewhere 2%. The best-scoring quarter of matches is bound 12% of the time, the rest under 2%.
Conversely, 79% of chr21 CTCF peaks have a match: the motif is nearly necessary, far from sufficient.


This is the central quantitative message of the lecture. Accessibility and binding are not independent (CTCF binding itself creates an ATAC peak), so the 39% is not a causal estimate; but the asymmetry is the general pattern. For most TFs the fraction of bound matches is far lower than for CTCF, often well under 1%. The reasons are on the next slide. A consequence for analysis: predicting binding from sequence alone fails; combining sequence with accessibility (as chromVAR and many ML models do) works much better. Numbers from make-generegulation-figs.R; the exercise recomputes them (R7).

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Why a motif is bound or not
text:
Why a motif is bound or not






Nucleosomes: most TFs cannot bind a motif wrapped on a histone octamer. DNA methylation: some TFs, CTCF among them, do not bind a motif with a methylated CpG.
Cooperativity: TFs that bind next to each other stabilise each other, so a weak site is bound when a partner is there.
TF concentration and competition with other proteins set how many sites are occupied.


Each panel is a determinant that explains part of the gap on the previous slide. Nucleosomes: DNA on the octamer is bent and one face is blocked; access needs a pioneer factor or a remodeller (next slide). Methylation: the CTCF motif often contains CpGs (positions 13–14 of the JASPAR consensus GCCACCAGGGGGCGC); methylation there blocks binding, as at the H19 imprinting control region. Methyl-CpG can also increase binding for some TFs (the methyl-SELEX work of Yin et al. 2017). Cooperativity can be direct (protein–protein contacts, e.g. PU.1 with IRF4 or IRF8 on composite ETS–IRF elements in B cells) or indirect, through competition with the same nucleosome. TF concentration: a TF at higher levels occupies weaker sites; this is how dosage-sensitive TFs act.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Pioneer factors open closed chromatin






Pioneer factors bind their motif on nucleosomal DNA, recruit remodellers (SWI/SNF/BAF), and make the site accessible for other TFs.
Classic example: FOXA1/FOXA2 in liver; its forkhead domain resembles linker histone H1. In B cells PU.1 and EBF1 act as pioneers.
Pioneers set up competence: which enhancers can become active in a lineage. Signal-dependent TFs (NF-κB, steroid receptors) mostly bind where pioneers already opened the chromatin.


Zaret and Carroll 2011 is the review. FOXA binds its site on the nucleosome surface and can open compacted chromatin in vitro without ATP-dependent remodellers (Cirillo et al. 2002), though in cells it works with remodellers. Pioneering is a spectrum, not a binary class: many TFs can bind partial motifs on nucleosomes to some degree. The definition is operational: a TF that binds closed chromatin and is needed for its opening. PU.1 opens thousands of sites in macrophages and B cells (Heinz et al. 2010); EBF1 opens chromatin at B-cell genes during B-cell commitment (Boller et al. 2016). The steps in the figure map onto assays: step 1 has a ChIP peak but little ATAC; step 3 has ATAC, H3K27ac and other TFs. For the ML units: pioneers are exactly where sequence alone predicts accessibility best.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Combinatorial control: the B-cell example






B-cell identity rests on a few TFs: PU.1 and E2A induce EBF1, EBF1 and PAX5 activate each other and the B-cell programme, PAX5 represses other lineages.
An enhancer is active only with the right combination of TFs. PU.1 is in both B cells and macrophages, but binds different sites with different partners.
Combinations of ~1600 TFs give far more cell types than single TFs could.


The hierarchy is from mouse genetics: mice without E2A or EBF1 have no B cells, and Pax5-deficient pro-B cells can still become macrophages or T cells, so PAX5 is the commitment factor (Nutt et al. 1999). PAX5 targets include CD19 and CD79A (activated) and CSF1R (repressed). Heinz et al. 2010 is the key paper on the right panel: PU.1 binds tens of thousands of sites in macrophages and in B cells, but largely different ones, next to C/EBP motifs in macrophages and EBF/E2A/OCT motifs in B cells; collaboratively they choose which sites become enhancers. GM12878 is an Epstein–Barr-virus-transformed B cell, so in addition to the B-cell factors it has very active NF-κB and IRF4 (EBV activates them), relevant when you look at its motif enrichment.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Real data: B-cell motifs in GM12878 open chromatin
text:
Real data: B-cell motifs in GM12878 open chromatin






Distal ATAC peaks (summit more than 2 kb from a protein-coding TSS), 200 bp around the summit, against GC-matched genomic windows.
IRF4 (3.4×), CTCF (2.6×) and PU.1 (1.8×) motifs are the most enriched; OCT2, RUNX3 and EBF1 modestly (1.3–1.4×). Motifs of liver and erythroid TFs (HNF4A, FOXA1, GATA1) are not (≈1×).
The open chromatin of a cell type tells you its TFs: the basis of motif enrichment analysis and chromVAR.


Numbers next to the bars are the fraction of peaks with a match and the fraction of background windows with a match; 116 758 distal peaks of 155 151. Enrichments of 1.3–3-fold are typical: each motif occurs in only a minority of peaks, and many matches in either set are chance hits. IRF4 at the top fits an EBV-transformed B cell, where EBV drives IRF4; IRF and PU.1 motifs also occur together as composite ETS–IRF elements. Two honest caveats: PAX5’s JASPAR matrix is short (8 bp) and captures only part of its long bipartite site, so its enrichment is underestimated; and MEF2B, a germinal-centre B-cell TF, is depleted, a reminder that motif enrichment depends on the matrix, the background and the window, and that absence of enrichment does not mean absence of function. Formal motif enrichment (HOMER, MEME-SEA, chromVAR) and footprinting are taught in Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting; here the point is qualitative. Made with motifmatchr and JASPAR 2024 matrices in make-generegulation-figs.R.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Co-activators turn binding into activity






Activation domains recruit p300/CBP, which acetylates H3K27 (and TFs): the H3K27ac you map at active enhancers and promoters.
BRD4 reads acetyl-lysine with its bromodomains and, with Mediator, helps recruit and release RNA polymerase II.
Repressors recruit the opposite: HDACs, Polycomb, H3K9 methyltransferases.


This closes the loop with the writers/readers/erasers framing of What is epigenetics?: TF binding at a sequence leads to the writing of a mark (H3K27ac by p300/CBP), which is read by BRD4, which helps the transcription machinery. It also explains why H3K27ac is such a good marker of active enhancers, and why p300 ChIP-seq was one of the first ways enhancers were mapped (Visel et al. 2009). Drugs: BET inhibitors (JQ1) displace BRD4 and hit super-enhancer-driven oncogenes such as MYC; p300/CBP inhibitors and degraders are in development. Pol II often pauses about 50 bp downstream of the TSS; release requires P-TEFb, which BRD4 recruits. Repressive co-factors are the other half: HDAC-containing complexes, Polycomb (H3K27me3) and SETDB1 (H3K9me3).

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
From mechanism to assay






ATAC-seq finds the open, TF-bound cores of promoters, enhancers and CTCF sites. ChIP-seq of a TF finds its bound sites, motif at the summit.
Histone ChIP / CUT&Tag shows the marks on flanking nucleosomes. Hi-C shows the loops between CTCF sites and between enhancers and promoters.
Motif analysis links the peaks back to the TFs that explain them.


This is the map for the rest of the course. Each assay sees one layer of what we discussed: accessibility (a consequence of TF binding), the TF itself, the co-activator footprint as histone marks, and the 3D contacts. A useful exercise for students is to predict, for an element of their choice, what each track should look like, and then check it in the data. Note the bimodal histone signal: the marks are on the nucleosomes flanking the NDR, so a histone ChIP peak often has a dip where the ATAC peak is. Motif enrichment and footprinting have their own unit; the ML units train models that read the sequence directly.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Summary







idea
key fact




cis-regulatory elements
core promoter, enhancers, silencers, insulators: clusters of TF sites


core promoter
about −40 to +40; TATA, Inr, DPE; CpG-island (about half, broad, housekeeping) vs non-CpG (tissue-specific)


enhancer
activates at a distance (up to ~1 Mb), either orientation; often not the nearest gene


active enhancer
open core with TFs; H3K4me1 + H3K27ac on flanking nucleosomes; eRNAs


insulator
CTCF; loops between convergent CTCF sites by cohesin extrusion


TF
DNA-binding domain + effector domain; ~1600 in human


PWM
counts → frequencies (pseudocount) → log-odds \(\log_2(p/q)\); score = sum over positions


information content
\(2 + \sum p \log_2 p\) per column; logo; chance match ≈ every \(2^{IC}\) bp


binding
motif ≈ necessary, not sufficient: 4% of chr21 CTCF matches bound; accessibility, pioneers, partners


B cells
PU.1, E2A → EBF1 ↔︎ PAX5; combinations select enhancers




Students should be able to: build a PWM from a few aligned sites and score a sequence by hand; compute information content of a column; estimate the number of chance matches of a motif in a genome; explain why most matches are unbound; describe the marks of an active enhancer; and predict what ATAC-seq, TF ChIP-seq, histone ChIP-seq and Hi-C show at a promoter, an enhancer and a CTCF site. Next units: Genomic intervals (if not yet done), then the assay blocks, starting with ATAC-seq.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Banerji, Rusconi & Schaffner 1981, Cell. Expression of a β-globin gene is enhanced by remote SV40 DNA sequences. The discovery of enhancers.
Spitz & Furlong 2012, Nat Rev Genet. Transcription factors: from enhancer binding to developmental control. A clear review of enhancers, TF binding and combinatorial control.
Lambert et al. 2018, Cell. The human transcription factors. The census of ~1600 human TFs, their domains and motifs.
Wasserman & Sandelin 2004, Nat Rev Genet. Applied bioinformatics for the identification of regulatory elements. PWMs, information content and why most predicted sites are not functional (“the futility theorem”).
Zaret & Carroll 2011, Genes Dev. Pioneer transcription factors: establishing competence for gene expression. The pioneer factor concept.
Heinz et al. 2010, Mol Cell. Simple combinations of lineage-determining transcription factors prime cis-regulatory elements required for macrophage and B cell identities. PU.1 and its partners choose enhancers; also introduced HOMER.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Goal
After this exercise you will be able to:

Build a position weight matrix (PWM) from aligned binding sites with pseudocounts, and score sequences with it on both strands, by hand.
Compute the information content of a motif column and read a sequence logo.
Estimate how many chance matches a motif has in a region or a genome, and use that to judge claims about TF binding.
Fetch a matrix from JASPAR in R, scan peak sequences and backgrounds with motifmatchr, and measure enrichment, centrality and the fraction of bound matches.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Background
PWM. From \(N\) aligned sites, count each base \(b\) at each position \(j\) (\(n_{b,j}\)), add a pseudocount, and divide: \(p_{b,j} = (n_{b,j} + 1) / (N + 4)\) with a pseudocount of 1 per base. The log-odds weight against a background frequency \(q_b\) is \(w_{b,j} = \log_2 (p_{b,j} / q_b)\). The score of a sequence window is the sum of the weights of its bases. Scan both strands: the minus strand is the reverse complement.
Information content of column \(j\) against a uniform background: \(IC_j = 2 + \sum_b p_{b,j} \log_2 p_{b,j}\) bits, between 0 (no preference) and 2 (one base only). A logo stacks the letters of each column to height \(IC_j\).
Chance matches. An exact \(k\)-mer occurs with probability \(4^{-k}\) per position and strand in random sequence. For a PWM scanned at a \(p\)-value threshold \(p\), a sequence of length \(L\) has about \(2Lp\) matches by chance. Roughly, a motif with \(I\) bits of information is found about once every \(2^I\) bp per strand.
Bound or not. A TF binds only a small fraction of its motif matches: accessibility, nucleosomes, DNA methylation, partner TFs and TF concentration decide which.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Data
GM12878 CTCF peaks (ENCODE, IDR conservative, narrowPeak), GM12878 ATAC-seq peaks, the hg38 genome as a bgzipped, indexed FASTA (hg38.fa.bgz with .fai and .gzi, so that any region can be read without unpacking the whole file), the hg38 chromosome sizes and the ENCODE blacklist. From the course repository:
data/download.sh gene-regulation
mkdir -p ~/epi/generegulation && cd ~/epi/generegulation
D=/path/to/course/data                  # where download.sh put the files
You need samtools (1.10 or newer), bedtools and, in R, the Bioconductor packages JASPAR2024, TFBSTools, motifmatchr, universalmotif, Rsamtools, Biostrings, GenomicRanges and rtracklayer (see Install the software you need). The R part runs in about two minutes on a laptop.
Simplification: we use one matrix per TF and a single \(p\)-value threshold (\(10^{-4}\), uniform background). Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting does this properly, with motif databases, enrichment statistics and footprints.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
By hand
Do these on paper. A calculator for \(\log_2\) helps: \(\log_2 x = \ln x / \ln 2\); \(\log_2 3 = 1.585\), \(\log_2 (2/3) = -0.585\), \(\log_2 (1/3) = -1.585\).
B1. Build a PWM. Eight binding sites of a GATA-like factor, aligned:
AGATAA   TGATAA   AGATAG   AGATAA
TGATAG   AGATTA   AGATAA   CGATAA

Write the 4 × 6 count matrix (rows A, C, G, T).
Convert it to frequencies with a pseudocount of 1 per base. Why is a pseudocount needed here?
Compute the log-odds weights against a uniform background (\(q_b = 0.25\)). Write down the weight matrix; you will need it in B2.

B2. Score sequences. Using your weights from B1:

Score AGATAA, TGATAG, AGCTAA and GGGGGG. What are the highest and the lowest possible scores?
A sequence on the plus strand reads TTATCT. What does it score as written? What does it score on the minus strand? Where is the motif, and which way does it point?
With a threshold of 6 bits, which of the five sequences are matches?

B3. Information content.

Compute \(IC\) for column 1 and for column 2 of your PWM (with the pseudocounts).
What would \(IC\) of column 2 be without pseudocounts? Why does the pseudocount matter so much more with 8 sites than with 913 (the number of sites behind the JASPAR CTCF matrix)?
A column is 50% A and 50% G, never C or T. What is its \(IC\)? How tall is each letter in the logo?

B4. How many matches by chance? Take the human genome as \(3.1 \times 10^9\) bp of random sequence with equal base frequencies.

How often do you expect the exact 6-mer AGATAA per Mb (both strands)? In the whole genome?
Repeat for the E-box CACGTG. Why is the answer half of (a)? (Write out its reverse complement.)
A PWM is scanned with a threshold of \(p < 10^{-4}\) per position and strand. How many matches do you expect on chr21 (40 Mb of sequence) and in the genome? GM12878 has 44 217 CTCF peaks: what is the largest possible fraction of genome-wide CTCF matches that can be bound?
The CTCF matrix has 16.1 bits of information. Using the rule of thumb, about how often does a CTCF site of that quality occur by chance?

B5. Strand and orientation. A scan of chr1 with the CTCF matrix reports four matches (1-based start, strand):
site 1   1 000 001   +
site 2   1 180 001   −
site 3   1 400 001   −
site 4   1 650 001   +

The JASPAR consensus is GCCACCAGGGGGCGC. Write the plus-strand sequence of the genome at site 2 if it matched the consensus perfectly.
Draw the four sites as arrows. Which pairs are convergent? Loop extrusion by cohesin predicts loops between which sites?
Site 2 is deleted. Which loop do you now expect?

B6. Read a logo. Look at the CTCF logo on the Information content and sequence logos slide (JASPAR MA0139.2, 913 sites).

Which three positions carry the most information? About how many bits each?
Position 9 has G (566 sites) and A (333 sites). What does a mixed column mean for binding? Is a site with A at position 9 a “mutant” site?
Why are the end columns low?
A logo built from only 20 sites without pseudocounts looks “cleaner”, with taller columns. Is that motif more specific?

B7. Judge the claims.

“The CTCF motif is the main determinant of CTCF binding, so CTCF binds essentially every match to its motif.” Use your answer to B4c and the chr21 numbers from the lecture (8583 matches, 369 inside a CTCF peak) to judge the claim.
A paper reports: “TF X has 600 000 motif matches but only 12 000 ChIP-seq peaks. Therefore 98% of its sites are silenced by DNA methylation.” What else could explain the gap? What experiment would test the methylation claim?
A student finds the PU.1 motif in 22% of GM12878 ATAC peaks and concludes that PU.1 binds 22% of the open chromatin in B cells. What is missing from this reasoning? (In the lecture: 12% of GC-matched background windows also have a match.)

B8. Read the figure. You ChIP two TFs, Y and Z, and plot the position of the best match to each one’s motif relative to the summit, as on the centrality slide. Y gives a sharp peak at 0; Z gives a flat histogram, although Z’s motif is found in 40% of its peaks (15% in background). Give two explanations for Z.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
On the command line

C1 — Sequences around the CTCF summits
zcat $D/gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz \
  | awk -v OFS='\t' '{ s = $2 + $10; print $1, s - 100, s + 100, "peak" NR }' > ctcf_win.bed
head -2 ctcf_win.bed

grep -P '^chr([0-9]+|X)\t' $D/hg38.chrom.sizes > genome.txt
zcat $D/hg38_blacklist.bed.gz > blacklist.bed
bedtools shuffle -i ctcf_win.bed -g genome.txt -chrom -excl blacklist.bed -seed 1 > shuf_win.bed

for f in ctcf_win shuf_win; do
  awk '{ print $1 ":" $2 + 1 "-" $3 }' $f.bed > $f.regions
  samtools faidx -n 1000 -r $f.regions $D/hg38.fa.bgz | grep -v '>' | tr acgtn ACGTN > $f.txt
done
wc -l ctcf_win.txt shuf_win.txt
grep -c N shuf_win.txt

Explain the awk in the first command: which column is the summit, and why is the window s − 100 to s + 100? Why does the second awk add 1 to the start?
The genome file is soft-masked (repeats in lower case). What does tr acgtn ACGTN do, and what would go wrong without it?
How many shuffled windows contain an N, and why can that happen?



C2 — Counting words is not motif scanning
for f in ctcf_win shuf_win; do
  echo $f \
    $(grep -c -E 'CCCTC|GAGGG' $f.txt) \
    $(grep -c -E 'CCA[CG][CT]AG[AG][GT]GG|CC[AC][CT]CT[AG][CG]TGG' $f.txt) \
    $(awk '{ gc += gsub(/[GC]/, ""); n += 200 } END { printf "%.3f", gc / n }' $f.txt)
done

The columns are: windows containing CCCTC (on either strand), windows containing an 11-bp degenerate CTCF core (either strand), and GC content. Fill in a table and compute the fraction for each.
CTCF is named “CCCTC-binding factor”. Why is CCCTC a poor test for CTCF sites? Estimate how often a 5-mer occurs in 200 bp of random sequence (both strands).
Why do the shuffled windows have lower GC content than the peak windows, and why does that matter for (a)?

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
In R
library(JASPAR2024); library(TFBSTools); library(RSQLite)
library(GenomicRanges); library(rtracklayer); library(Rsamtools); library(Biostrings)
library(motifmatchr); library(universalmotif)
D <- "/path/to/course/data"

R1 — The CTCF matrix from JASPAR
jaspar <- dbConnect(SQLite(), db(JASPAR2024()))
ctcf_m <- getMatrixByID(jaspar, "MA0139.2")
ctcf_m
cnt <- Matrix(ctcf_m)            # counts: 4 rows (A, C, G, T) x 15 columns
cnt
colSums(cnt)                     # number of sites in each column

How many sites is the matrix built from, and from what kind of experiment? (Look at the type tag.)
Why are the column sums not all equal?



R2 — Frequencies, log-odds, information content and the logo
p   <- (cnt + 0.25) / colSums(cnt + 0.25)  # pseudocount 0.25 per base (1 per column)
lo  <- log2(p / 0.25)                       # log-odds against a uniform background
ic  <- 2 + colSums(p * log2(p))             # information content per column (bits)
round(lo, 2)
round(ic, 2); sum(ic)
consensus <- paste(rownames(cnt)[apply(cnt, 2, which.max)], collapse = "")
consensus
view_motifs(convert_motifs(ctcf_m, "universalmotif"), use.type = "ICM")

Which columns have the highest information content? Compare with your answers to B6.
What is the total information content, and what does the rule of thumb in B4d give?
What is the largest and the smallest weight in lo? Explain the smallest.



R3 — Sequences around the summits
ctcf <- import(file.path(D, "gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz"), format = "narrowPeak")
summit <- GRanges(seqnames(ctcf), IRanges(start(ctcf) + ctcf$peak, width = 1))
win <- resize(summit, width = 200, fix = "center")
genome <- FaFile(file.path(D, "hg38.fa.bgz"))
seqs <- getSeq(genome, win)
seqs
mean(letterFrequency(seqs, "GC", as.prob = TRUE))
Check that the summit computed here is the same base as in C1. (start() in R is 1-based; see Genomic intervals.)


R4 — Is the motif enriched in the peaks?
flank <- getSeq(genome, shift(win, 3000))                 # 3 kb to the right
shuf  <- shuffle_sequences(seqs, k = 2, rng.seed = 1)     # same dinucleotides, order destroyed
mean(letterFrequency(flank, "GC", as.prob = TRUE))
mean(letterFrequency(shuf,  "GC", as.prob = TRUE))
frac_with_match <- function(s)
  mean(motifMatches(matchMotifs(ctcf_m, s, p.cutoff = 1e-4, bg = "even"))[, 1])
c(peaks = frac_with_match(seqs), flank = frac_with_match(flank), shuffled = frac_with_match(shuf))

What fraction of peaks, flanking windows and shuffled peaks contain a match?
The two backgrounds control for different things. What does each keep from the peaks, and what does it lose? Which gives the more conservative enrichment, and why?
Compare with B4c: how many chance matches do you expect in a 200-bp window at \(p < 10^{-4}\)? Does that fit the backgrounds?



R5 — Strong and weak peaks
hit <- motifMatches(matchMotifs(ctcf_m, seqs, p.cutoff = 1e-4, bg = "even"))[, 1]
q <- cut(rank(ctcf$signalValue, ties.method = "first"), 4, labels = c("Q1 weakest", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4 strongest"))
tapply(hit, q, mean)
tapply(ctcf$signalValue, q, median)
What fraction of peaks has a match in each quarter? Give two reasons why a CTCF peak could lack a match.


R6 — Where in the peak is the motif?
Listing every match position is slow for 44 000 sequences, so take a random 5000 peaks and a 500-bp window:
set.seed(1)
pick <- sample(length(summit), 5000)
s500 <- getSeq(genome, resize(summit[pick], 500, fix = "center"))
pos  <- matchMotifs(ctcf_m, s500, p.cutoff = 1e-4, bg = "even", out = "positions")[[1]]
hits <- data.frame(seq = rep(seq_along(pos), lengths(pos)), start = unlist(start(pos)),
                   strand = unlist(lapply(pos, function(x) mcols(x)$strand)),
                   score = unlist(lapply(pos, function(x) mcols(x)$score)))
best <- hits[order(-hits$score), ]
best <- best[!duplicated(best$seq), ]                # best match per peak
best$centre <- best$start + 7 - 250.5                # motif centre relative to the summit
nrow(best) / 5000
mean(abs(best$centre) <= 50)
table(best$strand)
hist(best$centre, breaks = seq(-250, 250, 10), main = "CTCF motif position in peaks",
     xlab = "distance of the best match from the summit (bp)")

What fraction of the 5000 peaks has a match in ±250 bp, and what fraction of best matches lies within 50 bp of the summit?
Why + 7 and − 250.5? (The motif is 15 bp; the window positions run from 1 to 500.)
Are the matches mostly on one strand? What would you expect, and why does strand still matter for CTCF (B5)?



R7 — Most matches are not bound
chr21 <- getSeq(genome, GRanges("chr21", IRanges(1, seqlengths(genome)["chr21"])))
L <- sum(letterFrequency(chr21, "ACGT"))
m21 <- matchMotifs(ctcf_m, chr21, p.cutoff = 1e-4, bg = "even", out = "positions")[[1]][[1]]
length(m21); 2 * L * 1e-4                                # found vs expected by chance
sites21 <- GRanges("chr21", IRanges(start(m21), end(m21)))
atac <- import(file.path(D, "gm12878_atac_peaks.bed.gz"), format = "narrowPeak")
bound <- overlapsAny(sites21, ctcf)
open  <- overlapsAny(sites21, atac)
c(n = length(sites21), bound = sum(bound), frac_bound = mean(bound))
tapply(bound, open, mean)
c(peaks_chr21 = sum(seqnames(ctcf) == "chr21"),
  with_match = sum(overlapsAny(ctcf[seqnames(ctcf) == "chr21"], sites21)))

How many matches are on chr21, and how many did you expect (B4c)?
What fraction of matches lies in a CTCF peak? Among matches in ATAC peaks, and outside them?
What fraction of chr21 CTCF peaks contains a match? Write one sentence that states both (b) and (c): is the motif necessary, sufficient, both or neither?



R8 — Check your hand calculations
sites <- DNAStringSet(c("AGATAA", "TGATAA", "AGATAG", "AGATAA", "TGATAG", "AGATTA", "AGATAA", "CGATAA"))
pfm <- consensusMatrix(sites)[c("A", "C", "G", "T"), ]
pfm
lo8 <- log2(((pfm + 1) / (8 + 4)) / 0.25)
round(lo8, 2)
score <- function(x) sum(lo8[cbind(match(strsplit(x, "")[[1]], rownames(lo8)), 1:6)])
sapply(c("AGATAA", "TGATAG", "AGCTAA", "GGGGGG", "TTATCT"), score)
score(as.character(reverseComplement(DNAString("TTATCT"))))
Do the numbers agree with B1 and B2?

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — PWMs and logos (B1–B3, B6, R2)





Work column by column. With 8 sites and a pseudocount of 1 per base, every frequency is \((n + 1)/12\), so only four values occur: 1/12, 2/12, 3/12 … 9/12. For the information content, \(-p \log_2 p\) is 0.5 for \(p = 0.5\), 0.5 for \(p = 0.25\), 0.311 for \(p = 0.75\), 0.431 for \(p = 1/6\), 0.299 for \(p = 1/12\). The original papers: Stormo 2000 (PWMs), Schneider & Stephens 1990 (logos).









Hint 2 — chance matches and strands (B4, B5)





Expected count = (number of positions) × (strands) × (probability per position and strand). A palindromic word (equal to its own reverse complement) is the same match on both strands, so it should be counted once. A match on the − strand reads the motif on the reverse complement: write the consensus, then reverse it and complement each base. Convergent CTCF sites: a + site on the left and a − site on the right, pointing towards each other (see the CTCF loop-extrusion slide and Rao et al. 2014).









Hint 3 — command line (C1, C2)





Column 10 of a narrowPeak file is the summit offset from the start (format). samtools faidx reads regions written as chr:start-end (1-based, inclusive) from a bgzipped, indexed FASTA; -r takes them from a file and -n sets the line length. bedtools shuffle with -chrom -excl is the restricted shuffle of Genomic intervals. In a regular expression [CG] means C or G.









Hint 4 — JASPAR and motifmatchr (R1–R7)





JASPAR2024 is a database package; TFBSTools::getMatrixByID reads one matrix from it, and the matrix page is on the JASPAR website. motifmatchr::matchMotifs scans sequences: out = "matches" (default) gives TRUE/FALSE per sequence, out = "positions" the coordinates, strand and score of every match; bg = "even" uses a uniform background, p.cutoff the threshold. Rsamtools::FaFile and getSeq read sequences of a GRanges from an indexed FASTA. universalmotif has shuffle_sequences() (with k = 2 it keeps dinucleotide counts) and view_motifs(). Biostrings has letterFrequency(), consensusMatrix() and reverseComplement().









Hint 5 — judging claims (B7, B8)





Compare the number of matches with the number of peaks, and ask what else differs between bound and unbound matches: accessibility, nucleosomes, methylation, partners, TF level. For a causal claim about methylation, think of an experiment that changes methylation and measures binding (e.g. a DNMT inhibitor or DNMT knockout, or methylation-sensitive binding in vitro). For enrichment, always compare with a background with the same composition.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) Counts (columns 1–6):
A   5  0  8  0  7  6
C   1  0  0  0  0  0
G   0  8  0  0  0  2
T   2  0  0  8  1  0

\(p = (n + 1)/12\): column 1 is A 0.50, C 0.17, G 0.08, T 0.25; columns 2–4 have 0.75 for the consensus base and 0.08 for the others; column 5 is A 0.67, T 0.17, C and G 0.08; column 6 is A 0.58, G 0.25, C and T 0.08. Without a pseudocount every unseen base has frequency 0 and weight \(-\infty\), so a single unseen base would veto a site. Eight sites are far too few to call a base impossible.
Weights \(\log_2(p / 0.25)\):

A   1.00  -1.58   1.58  -1.58   1.42   1.22
C  -0.58  -1.58  -1.58  -1.58  -1.58  -1.58
G  -1.58   1.58  -1.58  -1.58  -1.58   0.00
T   0.00  -1.58  -1.58   1.58  -0.58  -1.58
B2. (a) AGATAA = 1.00 + 1.58 + 1.58 + 1.58 + 1.42 + 1.22 = 8.39 (the maximum: the best base in every column). TGATAG = 0 + 1.58 + 1.58 + 1.58 + 1.42 + 0 = 6.17. AGCTAA = 1.00 + 1.58 − 1.58 + 1.58 + 1.42 + 1.22 = 5.22. GGGGGG = −1.58 + 1.58 − 1.58 − 1.58 − 1.58 + 0 = −4.75. Minimum: −1.58 in every column = −9.51. (b) As written, TTATCT scores 0 − 1.58 + 1.58 − 1.58 − 0.58 − 1.58 = −1.58. Its reverse complement is AGATAA, which scores 8.39: the motif is on the minus strand, reading right to left on the genome. (c) AGATAA, TGATAG, and TTATCT on the minus strand pass 6 bits. AGCTAA (5.22) is a near miss: a single mismatch at a 1.58-bit position.
B3. (a) Column 1: \(p = (0.50, 0.17, 0.08, 0.25)\); \(\sum -p\log_2 p = 0.5 + 0.431 + 0.299 + 0.5 = 1.73\), so $IC = 2 - 1.73 = $ 0.27 bits. Column 2: \(p = (0.75, 0.08, 0.08, 0.08)\); \(0.311 + 3 \times 0.299 = 1.21\), $IC = $ 0.79 bits. (b) Without pseudocounts column 2 is 100% G: 2 bits. With 8 sites the pseudocount (4 extra “observations”) is a third of the data; with 913 sites it is 0.4%. CTCF’s column 3 (C in 903 of 913 sites) has 1.9 bits with or without it. (c) \(\sum -p\log_2 p = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1\), $IC = $ 1 bit. The stack is 1 bit tall; A and G are each 0.5 bit.
B4. (a) \(4^{-6} = 1/4096\) per position and strand. Per Mb: \(2 \times 10^6 / 4096 \approx\) 490. Genome: \(2 \times 3.1 \times 10^9 / 4096 \approx\) 1.5 million. (b) CACGTG is its own reverse complement (a palindrome): each occurrence is found on both strands but is one site, so about 245 per Mb and 760 000 per genome. (c) chr21: $2 ^6 ^{-4} = $ 8000 (8018 for the exact 40.1 Mb; 8583 found in R7). Genome: \(2 \times 3.1 \times 10^9 \times 10^{-4} \approx\) 620 000. Even if every one of the 44 217 peaks held a different match, at most \(44\,217 / 620\,000 \approx\) 7% of matches could be bound. (d) \(2^{16.1} \approx 70\,000\) bp per strand, so about one per 35 kb counting both strands: roughly 30 per Mb, 90 000 in the genome. Still twice the number of CTCF peaks.
B5. (a) A − strand match means the consensus reads on the reverse complement. The plus strand at site 2 reads the reverse complement of GCCACCAGGGGGCGC, which is GCGCCCCCTGGTGGC. (b) Sites: 1 →, 2 ←, 3 ←, 4 →. Convergent pairs (→ … ←): 1–2 and 1–3. Site 4 points away from all the others to its right (none). Cohesin extruding from between 1 and 2 stalls at 1 and 2: the loop is 1–2. 1–3 can form if cohesin passes site 2 (CTCF is not bound at every site in every cell). (c) Without site 2, cohesin stalls at 1 and 3: a larger loop 1–3. (Deleting or inverting CTCF sites re-wires loops in exactly this way.)
B6. (a) Positions 3 (C), 8 (G) and 11 (G), each about 1.9 bits (R2: 1.90, 1.91, 1.82). Position 7 (A, 1.55 bits) is next. (b) Both G and A are tolerated at position 9; G is preferred, but a site with A is a normal site with a slightly lower score, not a mutant. A logo shows a distribution of preferences, not one “correct” sequence. (c) The edges of the motif contact the protein less, and the alignment of sites is less precise at the edges. (d) No. With 20 sites and no pseudocount, unseen bases get frequency 0 and columns look like 2 bits by sampling alone. The apparent specificity is an artefact of the small sample.
B7. (a) The claim fails. On chr21 only 369 of 8583 matches (4.3%) are in a CTCF peak; genome-wide at most 7% could be (B4c). The motif is close to necessary (79% of peaks have a match, R7) but far from sufficient: accessibility, nucleosomes, methylation and the rest of the chromatin context decide. (b) Most matches are expected by chance (B4); most lie in closed chromatin or on nucleosomes; many are weak; X may need a partner; ChIP detects only sites occupied in many cells at once; and X’s concentration may limit occupancy. To test methylation: compare binding before and after removing DNA methylation (DNMT1/3A/3B knockout or a DNMT inhibitor) and check whether new peaks appear at matches that were methylated; or test methylated vs unmethylated DNA in vitro. (c) A background. 12% of GC-matched random windows also have a PU.1 match, so most of the 22% would be there by chance; the enrichment is 1.8×. A match is also not binding: PU.1 ChIP-seq is needed to say where PU.1 is bound.
B8. Z may bind DNA indirectly, through a partner whose motif is at the summit, while Z’s motif is enriched in the peaks because Z and its partner co-occur in the same regulatory regions. Or Z’s matrix is wrong or describes a related TF whose motif is common in such regions (e.g. a GC-rich motif in GC-rich peaks). An antibody problem (the ChIP pulls down another protein) gives the same picture.









Solutions — command line





C1. (a) $2 + $10 is the summit as a BED boundary (start + offset). s − 100 to s + 100 is 200 bases in BED, centred on the summit base (s to s + 1). samtools faidx regions are 1-based and inclusive, so the BED start needs + 1 (Genomic intervals). The first window is chr12 53676133 53676333. (b) It turns the lower-case (repeat-masked) bases into upper case. Without it, grep for CCCTC would miss every site in a repeat, and the GC count with [GC] would skip lower-case bases. (c) 1813 of 44 217 shuffled windows contain an N: the shuffle avoids the blacklist but not the assembly gaps (runs of N). Adding the gaps to the exclusion file would fix it.
C2. (a)




CCCTC/GAGGG
11-bp core
GC




CTCF peaks
25 506 (57.7%)
9635 (21.8%)
0.514


shuffled windows
12 176 (27.5%)
86 (0.19%)
0.396




A 5-mer has probability \(4^{-5} \approx 0.001\) per position and strand; 200 bp × 2 strands gives about 0.39 expected occurrences, so about a third of random windows contain one (\(1 - e^{-0.39} \approx 0.32\); observed 27.5%, lower because of the AT-rich background). Enrichment 2×, with a third of the background positive: useless for calling sites. The 11-bp core is much more specific but too strict: it misses many real sites that differ at one position. A PWM with a threshold sits between the two.
Peaks are in GC-rich, gene-dense DNA; the shuffled windows are anywhere in the genome (41% GC). A GC-rich word like CCCTC is more frequent in GC-rich DNA anyway, so part of the difference in (a) is composition. R4 uses backgrounds that control for this.










Solutions — R





R1. (a) 913 sites, from ChIP-seq (type: ChIP-seq), human. (b) Some sites in the alignment were shorter or did not cover the outer columns, so the sums fall from 913 to 908 towards the right end.
R2. (a) Columns 3 (1.90), 8 (1.91) and 11 (1.82); then 7 (1.55) and 2 (1.27). Columns 1 and 6 are weakest (0.34, 0.37). (b) Total 16.1 bits; consensus GCCACCAGGGGGCGC. \(2^{16.1} \approx 70\,000\) bp per strand (B4d). (c) Largest about +1.99 (C at position 3); smallest −9.83 (C at position 8, G at position 3, C at position 11): bases never seen get only the pseudocount: in column 8 (911 sites) \(p = 0.25/912\), and \(\log_2(p/0.25) = \log_2(1/912) \approx -9.8\). motifmatchr builds its own weights with a pseudocount of 0.8 in total, so its scores differ slightly from lo.
R3. 44 217 sequences of 200 bp, GC content 0.514 (the genome average is 0.41). The summit is start + peak in R because start() is already the file start + 1, the same base as C1’s BED s–s + 1.
R4. (a) Peaks 78.5%, flanking windows 5.4%, shuffled peaks 8.8%. (b) Flanks keep the regional context (same chromosome, nearby DNA) but not the composition: their GC is 0.445, lower than the peaks’ 0.514. Shuffling keeps the exact dinucleotide composition of each peak, including GC and CpG, but destroys any real sequence structure such as repeats. The shuffled background has more chance matches (8.8%) because the CTCF motif is GC-rich, so it gives the smaller, more conservative enrichment: about 9-fold against shuffled, 15-fold against flanks. (c) \(2 \times 186 \times 10^{-4} \approx 0.037\) expected matches per window (186 positions for a 15-bp motif), so about 4% of uniform random windows; GC-rich windows have more, as both backgrounds show.
R5. Q1 weakest 61.5%, Q2 74.1%, Q3 86.2%, Q4 strongest 92.1% (median signalValue 35, 81, 160, 256). Peaks without a match: CTCF bound indirectly or through a weaker or different variant of its motif (JASPAR has other CTCF matrices, e.g. with an upstream module); false-positive peaks among the weakest; or a motif just outside the 200-bp window.
R6. (a) 79.8% of the 5000 peaks have a match within ±250 bp; 94.3% of best matches are within 50 bp of the summit. (b) A 15-bp match starting at position start has its centre at start + 7; the summit lies between positions 250 and 251 of the 500-bp window (centre 250.5). (c) 2054 on + and 1936 on −: about half each, as expected because CTCF sites occur in both orientations in the genome. The strand still matters biologically: it gives the orientation of each site, which decides which loops can form (B5).
R7. (a) 8583 matches; 8018 expected by chance at a uniform background. (b) 369 (4.3%) in a CTCF peak. Of matches in ATAC peaks, 38.8% are bound; outside, 2.2%. (c) 320 of 405 chr21 CTCF peaks (79%) contain a match. “Four in five CTCF peaks contain a CTCF motif, but only one in twenty-three motif matches is bound: the motif is close to necessary but far from sufficient for binding.” (Necessary only approximately: a fifth of peaks lack a match at this threshold.)
R8. The count matrix, the weights and the scores agree with B1 and B2: 8.39, 6.17, 5.22, −4.75, −1.58, and 8.39 for the reverse complement of TTATCT.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Where this leads

The ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq blocks produce the peaks that we scanned here, from raw reads.
Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting turns R4 into a proper test over hundreds of matrices (HOMER, MEME-SEA, chromVAR) and looks for TF footprints in ATAC data.
The 3D genome units show the CTCF loops of B5 in Hi-C maps.
The machine-learning units train a network to tell CTCF peaks from GC-matched background: its first layer learns PWM-like filters.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined.

Stormo 2000, Bioinformatics. DNA binding sites: representation and discovery. PWMs, log-odds scores and information content, from the person who introduced them.
Schneider & Stephens 1990, Nucleic Acids Res. Sequence logos: a new way to display consensus sequences. The logo.
Wasserman & Sandelin 2004, Nat Rev Genet. Applied bioinformatics for the identification of regulatory elements. Why most predicted sites are not functional.
Rauluseviciute et al. 2024, Nucleic Acids Res. JASPAR 2024: 20th anniversary of the open-access database of transcription factor binding profiles. The matrix database used here.
Lambert et al. 2018, Cell. The human transcription factors. Which TFs exist, and which have known motifs.

Short questions on regulatory elements, transcription factors and motifs. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Banerji, Rusconi and Schaffner moved the SV40 72-bp element 3.3 kb downstream of the β-globin gene and flipped its orientation. Transcription stayed high. Which two properties of enhancers does this show, and what control showed that the element acts in cis?






Answer





Distance independence (it works kilobases away, upstream or downstream) and orientation independence. Acting in cis: the element had to be on the same DNA molecule as the gene; SV40 DNA supplied on a separate molecule did not enhance.




Q2. A gene’s promoter has a CpG observed/expected ratio of 0.9 and is marked by H3K4me3 in almost every tissue. A second gene’s promoter has a ratio of 0.2 and a TATA box. Which is more likely a housekeeping gene, and which a tissue-specific one?






Answer





The CpG-island promoter (o/e 0.9, marked everywhere) is typical of housekeeping (and developmental) genes; the CpG-poor promoter with a TATA box is typical of a tissue-specific gene, marked only where it is expressed.




Q3. An element 40 kb from gene A and 300 kb from gene B carries H3K4me1 and H3K27ac, has an ATAC-seq peak and produces short bidirectional RNAs. What is it, and which gene does it regulate?






Hint





Think of the ZRS and SHH.









Answer





An active enhancer (open core, H3K4me1 + H3K27ac, eRNAs). Its target cannot be read from these data: enhancers often skip the nearest gene. Use 3D contacts (Hi-C, Capture-C), correlation with expression across samples, or a perturbation (CRISPRi of the element) to find out.




Q4. From 10 aligned sites a column has 7 A, 1 C, 2 G and 0 T. With a pseudocount of 1 per base and a uniform background, what are the log-odds weights of A and T? Why not use zero for T?






Answer





\(p_A = 8/14 = 0.571\), \(w_A = \log_2(0.571/0.25) = +1.19\). \(p_T = 1/14 = 0.071\), \(w_T = \log_2(0.071/0.25) = -1.81\). Without a pseudocount \(p_T = 0\) and \(w_T = -\infty\): any site with T there would be rejected, although 10 sites cannot show that T is impossible.




Q5. What is the information content of a column with frequencies A 0.25, C 0.25, G 0.25, T 0.25? And of A 1.0? What does each look like in a sequence logo?






Answer





\(2 + 4 \times 0.25 \log_2 0.25 = 2 - 2 = 0\) bits: an empty column. A 1.0: \(2 + 1 \times \log_2 1 = 2\) bits: a single A of full height.




Q6. A TF motif is scanned with a threshold of \(p < 10^{-5}\) per position and strand. About how many matches do you expect by chance in 1 Mb? In a 3.1 Gb genome?






Answer





\(2 \times 10^6 \times 10^{-5} = 20\) per Mb; \(2 \times 3.1 \times 10^9 \times 10^{-5} = 62\,000\) in the genome. More than the number of peaks of most TF ChIP-seq experiments.




Q7. In GM12878, 78% of CTCF peaks contain a CTCF motif match, but only 4% of CTCF matches on chr21 lie in a CTCF peak. Give three reasons why a motif match may not be bound.






Answer





Any three of: the match is in closed chromatin or wrapped on a nucleosome; the CpG in the motif is methylated (CTCF is methylation-sensitive); the match is weak (low score); a needed partner TF is absent; the TF’s concentration only fills the best sites; many matches are chance hits in sequence the TF never samples. Matches in ATAC peaks were bound 39% of the time, matches outside 2%.




Q8. The plus strand of a region reads …TTGCGCCCCCTGGTGGCAA…. A CTCF scan reports a match on the minus strand. Write the matched site in the orientation of the JASPAR consensus (GCCACCAGGGGGCGC). Which way does it point on the chromosome?






Answer





The reverse complement of GCGCCCCCTGGTGGC is GCCACCAGGGGGCGC, the consensus. On a minus-strand match the motif reads right to left, so it points towards lower coordinates (←). It forms loops with + sites (→) to its left: convergent pairs.




Q9. A pioneer factor binds a site in closed chromatin in progenitor cells. Which assays would show (a) binding before opening, (b) opening, (c) activation of the enhancer?






Answer






ChIP-seq or CUT&RUN of the pioneer TF gives a peak where ATAC-seq has none (yet). (b) ATAC-seq peak appears; nucleosomes are moved (MNase-seq). (c) H3K27ac (p300/CBP) and other TFs arrive; eRNAs; the target gene’s expression rises.





Q10. A paper lists 900 “super-enhancers” in a lymphoma line and claims they form a distinct class of regulatory elements. What is the main criticism?






Answer





The cutoff is drawn on a continuous ranking of stitched H3K27ac (or Mediator) signal; there is no gap that separates a class. When super-enhancers are dissected genetically, their parts often act like ordinary enhancers whose effects add up. The ranking is useful (it highlights identity genes and oncogenes), but “a distinct class” needs functional evidence.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
About this lecture





ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq and CUT&Tag measure different things, but they all hand you the same raw material: DNA fragments from enriched regions, read by a sequencer. This lecture is the shared processing that turns those reads into a signal track you can trust.

Reads: FASTQ, base qualities, adapters, trimming.
Alignment: bowtie2, SAM/BAM, FLAGs, MAPQ and multi-mapping reads.
Filtering: duplicates, the blacklist, chrM, the order of the steps.
Coverage: read extension, CPM and RPGC, fold change over input, with deepTools.
Real data throughout: GM12878 CTCF ChIP-seq and its input, chr21.


Students have done RNA-seq, so FASTQ and BAM are not new; what is new is everything that comes after alignment when there is no gene annotation to count on. The running example is the ENCODE CTCF ChIP-seq experiment ENCSR000DZN (replicate 1) and its input control, restricted to chr21 so that every command runs in seconds; students run exactly this chain in the exercise. The same chain, with a few assay-specific additions (Tn5 shift, fragment sizes, chrM), is reused in the ATAC-seq and CUT&Tag units. Peak calling is not here: it has its own units. At the end we compare our home-made track with the one ENCODE made from the same data.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Three assays, one kind of data
text:
Three assays, one kind of data






ChIP: crosslink, shear, pull down with an antibody. ATAC: Tn5 cuts open DNA. CUT&Tag: an antibody tethers Tn5 to the target.
Each gives fragments, more of them at the target than elsewhere. We sequence one end (single-end) or both ends (paired-end) of each fragment.
Processing: find where each fragment came from, keep the trustworthy ones, count how many cover each position, compare with the background.


This is the key abstraction of the unit: the biology differs, the data have the same shape. In RNA-seq, reads come from transcripts, and the question is how many per gene. Here, reads come from fragments of genomic DNA, and the question is where in the genome they pile up more than expected. The “background” fragments are important: in ChIP they come from non-specific pull-down and open chromatin; in ATAC from Tn5 cutting anywhere accessible. Everything in this lecture is about separating enrichment from background and artefacts. The details of each assay come in the ATAC, ChIP and CUT&Tag units.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
FASTQ and base quality






Four lines per read: name, sequence, +, quality. Each quality character encodes Q = −10 log10(perror).
Q20 = 1 error in 100, Q30 = 1 in 1000. To decode: ASCII code − offset (33 today, 64 in old Illumina files like this one).


Work through the example on the slide: the character e has ASCII code 101; this 2011 file uses the old Phred+64 encoding, so Q = 37 and the error probability is 10 to the minus 3.7, about 2 in 10 000. The L near the end is Q12, about 6% error. Always check the encoding of old public data: if you read a +64 file as +33, every base looks like Q60–70, which is impossible, and a tool may silently accept it. In the exercise students convert the file to +33 with a one-line Perl tr before trimming. fastp has a –phred64 option, but with fastp 0.23.4 we got different filter counts from run to run with it, so we convert explicitly: one more reason to look at the data rather than trust flags. Modern Illumina instruments also bin qualities into a few values (e.g. 2, 12, 23, 37), so do not expect a smooth spectrum.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Real data: quality along the read
text:
Real data: quality along the read






CTCF ChIP (36 bp, 2011): median Q38, mean Q37 at the start, Q35 at the last base. Input (28 bp, 2009): mean Q27 falling to Q24; at the last base 16% of bases are below Q20.
Quality falls along the read: the sequencing chemistry loses phase cycle by cycle. A few bad bases are tolerated by the aligner; bad tails are trimmed.


These plots come from the first 100 000 reads of each FASTQ file (make-enrichalign-figs.R), the same thing fastp and FastQC show in their reports. The input library is older (2009, Illumina GA) and clearly worse: shorter and lower quality. That matters later: 28 bp reads are less often unique in the genome. A caveat that applies to all course data: these reads were selected because ENCODE could align them to chr21 or chrM, so reads too bad to align are already missing. Real raw data look a bit worse than this.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Adapters and read-through






If the fragment is shorter than the read, the sequencer reads on into the adapter. The adapter part matches nothing in the genome.
Common in ATAC and CUT&Tag (fragments under 100 bp), rare in sonicated ChIP with short reads: fastp found no adapter in our 36 bp CTCF reads.
fastp detects adapters (from the data, or from the overlap of paired reads) and trims them, removes low-quality and too-short reads (tail trimming on request: --cut_right), and writes an HTML report.

fastp -w 8 -i chip.fastq.gz -o chip.trim.fastq.gz -h chip.fastp.html -j chip.fastp.json

In paired-end data the read-through is easy to detect without knowing the adapter: when the fragment is shorter than the read length, read 1 and read 2 overlap completely and each runs into the other’s adapter. fastp uses that overlap. For the CTCF ChIP, fastp found no adapter, and filtered 9514 of 390 097 reads (2.4%) as low quality (by default: more than 40% of bases below Q15) and 13 for too many Ns. For the input, only 348 reads were removed. Trimming matters more with end-to-end alignment (next slides): an untrimmed adapter tail forces mismatches. In the ATAC-seq unit, with 2×100 bp reads of fragments often under 100 bp, the effect is large. Other trimmers: Trim Galore (cutadapt), Trimmomatic; nf-core uses Trim Galore.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Aligning DNA is simpler than aligning RNA
text:
Aligning DNA is simpler than aligning RNA






No splicing: a read from genomic DNA aligns contiguously, with at most a few mismatches and small indels. bowtie2 or BWA-MEM, not STAR.
No annotation: every position of the genome is a possible target. The regions come from the data (peaks), not from a GTF.


Students used STAR or HISAT2, which search for split alignments across introns, or salmon, which skips alignment to the genome altogether. Neither is right here: spliced alignment would invent “introns” in DNA reads, and pseudo-alignment needs a list of transcripts. bowtie2 is the standard for short ChIP, ATAC and CUT&Tag reads; BWA-MEM is common for longer reads and is the default in nf-core/chipseq. You could use STAR with splicing switched off, but there is no reason to. What carries over from RNA-seq: the BAM format, sorting and indexing, MAPQ, samtools.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: How bowtie2 finds a position: seed and extend
text:
How bowtie2 finds a position: seed and extend






Step 1: the genome is indexed once (bowtie2-build, an FM index based on the Burrows–Wheeler transform; 27 s for chr21+chrM with 8 threads, an hour or more for the whole human genome). Short substrings of the read, the seeds, are looked up exactly in the index; this is fast because the index makes exact-match lookups cheap. Step 2: each candidate locus is aligned in full with dynamic programming, scoring mismatches (penalty up to 6, less at low-quality bases) and gaps. Step 3: the best alignment is reported, and the gap between best and second best becomes MAPQ. End-to-end mode (the default) is strict: every base must align, so trim first. Local mode soft-clips ends that do not match (S in the CIGAR); it is forgiving, which is why it is popular for CUT&Tag, but it can also hide adapter problems. You do not need the algorithm for the exam; you need to know why a read in a repeat gets a low MAPQ and what soft-clipping is.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
bowtie2 on the command line
# once per genome: build the index (chr21 + chrM in this course; 27 s with 8 threads)
bowtie2-build --threads 8 hg38_chr21_chrM.fa hg38_chr21_chrM

# align, and sort by position on the way out (3 s for 380 000 reads)
bowtie2 -p 8 -x hg38_chr21_chrM -U chip.trim.fastq.gz 2> chip.bowtie2.log \
  | samtools sort -@ 4 -o chip.sorted.bam -
samtools index chip.sorted.bam          # .bai: jump to any region
samtools flagstat chip.sorted.bam       # how many mapped, paired, duplicates ...
samtools idxstats chip.sorted.bam       # reads per chromosome
380570 reads; of these: 2014 (0.53%) aligned 0 times
                        291310 (76.55%) aligned exactly 1 time
                        87246 (22.93%) aligned >1 times

Paired-end: -1 R1.fastq.gz -2 R2.fastq.gz instead of -U. The pipe avoids writing a large unsorted SAM file. “Aligned >1 times” means bowtie2 found more than one valid alignment and reported one of them: these become the low-MAPQ reads. 23% of the ChIP reads on chr21+chrM are multi-mapping; that is not a failure of the experiment, it is what 36 bp reads in a genome full of repeats look like. Only 0.5% did not align at all, much lower than in real data, because the course reads were preselected (slide on the shortcut). The 2014 unaligned reads are mostly reads that ENCODE aligned after cropping them to 28 bp, and whose last bases do not match. For whole-genome indexes, download a prebuilt one (iGenomes, the bowtie2 website) instead of building it.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
The SAM record






A real read from the ChIP BAM. Columns students must be able to read on paper: FLAG, RNAME, POS (1-based leftmost base), MAPQ and CIGAR; and for paired-end data, the mate columns and TLEN. The tags are aligner-specific: AS is this alignment’s score, XS the score of the second-best alignment (only present when there is one), NM the edit distance, MD where the mismatches are. The second tag line is an Alu read (its sequence starts with the classic Alu motif): AS = XS = −5, a tie, so MAPQ 1. A reverse-strand read is stored as the reverse complement of what the sequencer read, and POS is still the leftmost base: the read’s own 5’ end, where the fragment starts, is at POS + length − 1. That matters for extending reads and for Tn5 shifts in ATAC.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Decoding the FLAG by hand






Exam material. FLAG is a sum of powers of two, so each value decodes uniquely: subtract the largest bit that fits, repeat. 99 = 64 + 32 + 2 + 1: read 1, mate on the reverse strand, proper pair, paired. Its mate is 147 = 128 + 16 + 2 + 1. 83 and 163 are the same pair the other way round. Single-end reads: 0 or 16 when mapped, 4 when unmapped. With samtools: -f keeps reads with all the given bits set, -F drops reads with any of them set. -F 1804 (4 + 8 + 256 + 512 + 1024) is the ENCODE filter: drop unmapped reads, reads whose mate is unmapped, secondary alignments, QC failures and duplicates. samtools flags 1804 decodes it for you; so does the Picard “explain flags” web page.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
MAPQ and reads in repeats






About half of the human genome is repeat-derived (transposons, segmental duplications, satellites). A short read there fits several places equally well.
bowtie2 reports one of them at random, with MAPQ 0 or 1. Keep only MAPQ ≥ 30 (or ≥ 10–20 in some pipelines) for coverage tracks.


MAPQ is phred-scaled like base quality: in principle MAPQ 30 means 1 in 1000 that the position is wrong. Each aligner computes it differently: bowtie2 tops out at 42, BWA at 60, STAR uses 255 for unique. Removing multi-mappers has a cost: repeats become blind spots, with no signal at all. That is no information, not evidence of no binding. Some marks, especially H3K9me3 in heterochromatin, live mostly in repeats; there, people keep multi-mappers or distribute them with an EM algorithm. Mappability tracks (e.g. from GenMap or Umap) give, for each position and read length, whether a read starting there is unique. Longer and paired reads raise mappability.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Real data: MAPQ on chr21






Two peaks: MAPQ 0–1 (22% of ChIP reads, 25% of input reads) and MAPQ 42. Little in between.
Filtering at MAPQ ≥ 30 keeps 76% (ChIP, 36 bp) and 74% (input, 28 bp) of the reads on chr21. Shorter reads are unique less often.


The distribution is strongly bimodal: a read is either unique or not. The intermediate values are reads whose second-best alignment is somewhat worse, e.g. two copies of a repeat that differ by a few bases. The threshold therefore matters less than one might fear: 10, 20 or 30 remove almost the same reads. The input has slightly more multi-mappers on chr21 than the ChIP, partly because its reads are 8 bases shorter and partly because the ChIP reads are enriched at CTCF sites, which are mostly in unique sequence. Overall the input looks more “unique” (91% MAPQ ≥ 30 of all reads) only because two thirds of its reads are on chrM, which is unique in this reference. Keep that in mind when comparing summary numbers between libraries.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Paired-end reads and the fragment






A proper pair: the two reads face each other on opposite strands, at a plausible distance. TLEN = rightmost end − leftmost start + 1 = the fragment length.
Single-end data know only one end: the fragment length must be estimated and the reads extended.


Work through the numbers: read 1 starts at 1001, read 2 (36 bp) ends at 1200, so TLEN = 1200 − 1001 + 1 = 200, positive on the leftmost read and negative on its mate. Paired-end sequencing is now standard for ATAC and CUT&Tag because the fragment length itself is information: the ATAC nucleosome ladder, the CUT&Tag sub-nucleosomal fragments. It also helps mapping: a read in a repeat can be placed by its uniquely mapped mate. Our CTCF data are single-end, as most ChIP-seq before about 2015 was, so we estimate the fragment length later in the lecture. Filtering paired data: -f 2 keeps proper pairs; remove reads whose mate failed filtering, otherwise you get orphan reads (samtools fixmate -m and -F 1804 take care of most of this).

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
PCR and optical duplicates






Library preparation includes PCR, so each original molecule can be sequenced many times. Duplicates are defined by position: same start and strand for single-end reads, same both ends for paired-end reads. Optical duplicates are a different artefact: one cluster read as two on the flow cell, recognised by being physically close. samtools markdup (or Picard MarkDuplicates) sets bit 1024 and keeps the copy with the best base qualities; with -r it removes them instead. The paired-end recipe needs name-collated input and samtools fixmate -m first: collate → fixmate -m → sort → markdup. For single-end reads, sort → markdup is enough. Why not in RNA-seq? A highly expressed gene saturates the possible start positions, so many identical starts are real; removing them would compress expression. In ChIP and ATAC, a position is covered by few independent fragments, so identical starts are mostly PCR copies, which would create fake peaks. The duplicate rate also measures library complexity: a high rate means few unique molecules (little input DNA, too many PCR cycles), discussed in Experimental design and QC.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Real data: the blacklist and chrM
text:
Real data: the blacklist and chrM






Blacklist (ENCODE exclusion list): regions with extreme signal in every experiment, input included: satellite repeats, rDNA, centromeres. 910 regions in GRCh38, 24 on chr21. Remove reads there.
chrM: many copies per cell, no nucleosomes. 14% of ChIP reads but 66% of input reads here; in ATAC often 20–80%. Remove before normalising.


Left: input reads pile up in a 520 bp blacklisted region at chr21:10.01 Mb: 451 reads where about 2 are expected from the input’s depth, and 72 ChIP reads. Here 448 of the 451 have MAPQ 1, so the MAPQ filter already removes them; elsewhere it does not: after MAPQ and duplicate filtering, the 3 kb blacklisted region at chr21:6.37 Mb still has 24 times the average input density. The blacklist catches what the other filters miss. Such regions are usually unassembled or collapsed repeats: in the reference there is one copy, in the cell there are many, so reads from all copies land on it, with high MAPQ. They produce “peaks” in every experiment and would dominate any genome-wide ranking. Amemiya, Kundaje and Boyle derived the list from large collections of input (and DNase) data, so it is assay-independent. Right: the share of aligned reads on chrM. Mitochondrial DNA is present in hundreds of copies per cell; in ATAC, Tn5 attacks it eagerly because it is not packed into nucleosomes. For a nuclear chromatin assay, chrM reads are not informative: drop them before computing CPM, otherwise a library with more chrM looks shallower. Also note NUMTs: nuclear copies of mitochondrial sequence pull mitochondrial reads into the nuclear genome, one more reason for the MAPQ filter and the blacklist.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: The filtering chain, step by step
text:
The filtering chain, step by step





samtools view -b -q 30 -F 1804 -o chip.q30.bam chip.sorted.bam        # unique, mapped, primary
samtools markdup -s chip.q30.bam chip.markdup.bam                     # flag duplicates (1024)
samtools view -b -F 1024 -o chip.dedup.bam chip.markdup.bam chr21     # drop them, and chrM
bedtools intersect -v -abam chip.dedup.bam -b blacklist.bed > chip.final.bam

The real read counts from the exercise. ChIP: 390 097 raw → 197 587 final reads (51%). Input: 476 372 → 116 397 (24%), because most of its reads are chrM duplicates. Order matters. MAPQ and flag filters first, so that duplicates are judged among reads we trust. Duplicates before taking chr21: it makes no difference here, but marking on the whole BAM is the norm. Blacklist last (or any time), because it removes positions, not reads with problems. For paired-end data add -f 2 to the first step, and mark duplicates on pairs (fixmate -m first). A note on duplicates at strong peaks: in the ChIP, 49% of the reads inside the 405 chr21 CTCF peaks were flagged as duplicates, against 4% outside peaks. With single-end 36 bp reads, a 200 bp peak has only a few hundred possible start positions per strand, so at very strong peaks some “duplicates” are real independent fragments. Dedup compresses the strongest peaks; it is still the standard, because PCR copies are the bigger danger.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Single-end reads need extending






A fragment covers the binding site, but a 36 bp read covers only its first 36 bases. Fragments from the + strand are read from their left end, so their reads sit to the left of the site; fragments from the − strand are read from the right end. The result is two humps, about one fragment length apart, with the site itself in the gap. Extending each read in its own direction to the fragment length rebuilds the fragment and gives one peak on the site. For paired-end data there is nothing to estimate: deepTools uses the real fragment between the mates. The fragment length is estimated from the strand shift: MACS3 predictd pairs + and − strand peaks; the strand cross-correlation used in ENCODE QC computes the correlation of the two strands at every shift. For ATAC, the cut sites are the signal, so ATAC tracks are often built from the Tn5 insertion points (read 5’ ends, shifted), discussed in the ATAC units.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Real data: the two strands around CTCF sites
text:
Real data: the two strands around CTCF sites






Left: 5’ ends of + strand reads peak about 50 bp left of the CTCF summits, − strand reads about 50 bp right. Median distance between them: ≈ 100 bp = the typical fragment.
macs3 predictd estimates the same: 100 bp. Right: reads extended to 100 bp give one peak, centred on the summits.


These are the 405 ENCODE CTCF peak summits on chr21, with the filtered ChIP reads summed around them (make-enrichalign-figs.R). The medians of the 5’ end positions are −50 bp for + strand reads and +48 bp for − strand reads. The sharp inner edges at about ±18 bp are a footprint: CTCF itself protects about 20–40 bp of DNA, and fragment ends cannot fall inside the protein. 100 bp is shorter than the 150–300 bp a sonicated library usually shows on a gel; for TF ChIP the strand-shift estimate is often shorter than the gel size, because it measures the fragments that actually carry the bound protein. We therefore use –extendReads 100 in the exercise. ENCODE ran its own estimate on the full data set.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Coverage and normalisation: CPM and RPGC
text:
Coverage and normalisation: CPM and RPGC






Raw counts scale with sequencing depth. CPM divides by the number of reads (in millions): the same as CPM in RNA-seq.
RPGC (1× normalisation) scales so the genome average is 1: a value of 38.7 means 38.7 times the average coverage.
Both assume the total amount of signal is comparable between samples. A global change (a drug that removes a mark everywhere) breaks them: spike-ins, in Experimental design and QC.


In deepTools: bamCoverage –normalizeUsing CPM, BPM (like TPM: per bin, then scaled to a million), RPKM, or RPGC with –effectiveGenomeSize. CPM per bin depends on the bin size, because it is a count of reads overlapping a bin; RPGC is a per-base coverage and does not. Effective genome size: the mappable part of the genome, about 2.7–2.9 Gb for human depending on read length (deepTools documents values); in the exercise we use the non-N length of chr21, 40.1 Mb, because our BAM contains chr21 only. Exam-style calculation: 15 million reads of 200 bp fragments over 2.9 Gb gives an average depth of 1.03; a base covered by 40 fragments has RPGC 38.7. These are the RNA-seq ideas students know, with the same weakness: normalising to the total assumes most of the genome does not change. The differential-accessibility unit returns to this.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Fold change over the input






The input (same chromatin, no antibody) shows local background: copy number, open chromatin, mappability, GC bias. Dividing by it removes what ChIP and input share.
bamCompare scales both to the same depth, then reports ratio or log2 ratio per bin, with a pseudocount to avoid dividing by zero.


Background is not flat. Amplified regions, open chromatin (sheared more easily) and repeats all give more reads in the input as well as in the ChIP. Dividing by the input corrects for these. Pseudocount: with 0 input reads, the ratio is infinite; adding 1 to both counts gives log2(5/1) = 2.3 for a bin with 4 ChIP reads, and 0 for an empty bin. The pseudocount shrinks ratios of small counts towards 0, which is what you want for noisy bins. Bin size: a 10 bp bin with 0 or 1 input read gives a meaningless ratio, so ratios use larger bins (50 bp here) or smoothed input. Peak callers like MACS3 do the smarter version: a local background estimated from the input over 1 kb and 10 kb windows. That is in the peak-calling unit.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Coverage tracks with deepTools
# ChIP and input, each normalised to counts per million, reads extended to 100 bp
bamCoverage -b chip.final.bam  -o chip.cpm.bw  --normalizeUsing CPM --extendReads 100 --binSize 10 -p 8
bamCoverage -b input.final.bam -o input.cpm.bw --normalizeUsing CPM --extendReads 100 --binSize 10 -p 8

# the same ChIP track as "times the average coverage" (RPGC; chr21 only, so chr21's size)
bamCoverage -b chip.final.bam -o chip.rpgc.bw --normalizeUsing RPGC \
  --effectiveGenomeSize 40088619 --extendReads 100 --binSize 10 -p 8

# ChIP over input: depth-scaled, log2 ratio in 50 bp bins, pseudocount 1
bamCompare -b1 chip.final.bam -b2 input.final.bam -o chip_vs_input.log2.bw \
  --operation log2 --scaleFactorsMethod readCount --pseudocount 1 \
  --extendReads 100 --binSize 50 -p 8

Each command takes 2–5 seconds on the chr21 BAMs; on a full human ChIP-seq BAM of 30 million reads, a few minutes. –extendReads without a number uses the mate for paired-end data. –ignoreForNormalization chrX chrM is common when the BAM still contains them. bamCompare –operation ratio gives the plain ratio, comparable with ENCODE’s fold-change track; subtract gives a difference. The output is bigWig, the indexed format from Genomic intervals, so it opens instantly in IGV. Alternatives: MACS3 writes fold-enrichment bedGraphs as part of peak calling (that is what ENCODE’s track is), and nf-core uses bedtools genomecov scaled to one million reads.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Real data: our tracks at a locus
text:
