From the ENCODE data standards pages (ChIP-seq TF, histone, ATAC-seq; current at the time of writing) and Landt et al. 2012. Thresholds are guides for flagging, not laws: a factor with few sites can have a low FRiP and be fine, broad marks have flat cross-correlation curves, and complexity metrics depend on depth. ENCODE itself marks data with coloured audit flags rather than rejecting them outright. The value of the table is as a reference point when you look at your own numbers or at a paper’s supplementary QC table. TSS enrichment thresholds depend on the TSS annotation and the exact method, so compare like with like.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Red flags in published data






No input for a ChIP-seq, or the same input reused for unrelated cell types. n = 1 with claims about differences between conditions.
FRiP of 1–2% for a histone mark, a fingerprint that looks like the input, duplication above 50% with no comment, fewer reads than the standard.
A global change (inhibitor, knockout of a writer) normalised by read depth. Conditions processed on different days. No antibody catalogue or lot number.


A checklist for reading methods sections and supplementary tables, and the core of the “judge the design” exam questions. Each flag is not automatically fatal, but each should be explained. Where to find the information: GEO entries often list the controls and the number of replicates; supplementary tables sometimes give FRiP and duplication. If the raw data are public, you can compute all of these metrics yourself in an hour, which is what the exercise does for an ENCODE dataset. Good practice to point out: ENCODE and the nf-core pipelines report all of these metrics by default, and the ENCODE portal flags experiments that fail them.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Summary

≥ 2 biological (ENCODE), ≥ 3 per condition for differential tests; pseudoreplicates are not replicates

input for ChIP (shearing, copy number, mappability); IgG often too little DNA; ATAC has none

one main band, a second line of evidence, knockout loses the signal


global changes
depth normalisation hides them; spike-in chromatin, scale by \(1/N_\text{spike}\)


batches
never confound with condition; model ~ batch + condition

NRF, PBC1 = \(M_1/M_\text{distinct}\), PBC2 = \(M_1/M_2\); computed before duplicate removal


enrichment
FRiP; fingerprint (input on the diagonal, ChIP bends); NSC, RSC from strand cross-correlation


reproducibility
correlation of binned counts; IDR on ranked peaks


ATAC
fragment-size ladder, TSS enrichment, mitochondrial fraction




Students should leave able to compute NRF, PBC1, PBC2 and FRiP from counts, read a fingerprint and a cross-correlation plot, explain what an input corrects and why spike-ins are needed for global changes, and critique a study design. Next: the ATAC-seq block, where TSS enrichment and fragment sizes are covered properly, and the ChIP-seq block, where the input enters the peak caller.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Landt et al. 2012, Genome Res. ChIP-seq guidelines and practices of the ENCODE and modENCODE consortia. Where most of the metrics and thresholds in this lecture come from.
Kharchenko, Tolstorukov & Park 2008, Nat Biotechnol. Design and analysis of ChIP-seq experiments for DNA-binding proteins. Strand cross-correlation and the SPP peak caller.
Li, Brown, Huang & Bickel 2011, Ann Appl Stat. Measuring reproducibility of high-throughput experiments. The IDR method.
Orlando et al. 2014, Cell Rep. Quantitative ChIP-Seq normalization reveals global modulation of the epigenome. ChIP-Rx spike-in normalisation.
Diaz, Park, Lim & Song 2012, Stat Appl Genet Mol Biol. Normalization, bias correction, and peak calling for ChIP-seq. CHANCE and the fingerprint plot.
Ewels, Magnusson, Lundin & Käller 2016, Bioinformatics. MultiQC: summarize analysis results for multiple tools and samples in a single report.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Goal
After this exercise you will be able to:

Compute the library-complexity metrics NRF, PBC1 and PBC2 and the FRiP by hand and from a BAM file, and judge them against the ENCODE standards.
Read a fingerprint plot and a strand cross-correlation curve, and compute NSC and RSC.
Do a spike-in normalisation by hand, and explain why read-depth normalisation hides a global change.
Critique the design of an epigenomic study: replicates, controls, batches, normalisation.
Run the QC of a real ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq experiment on the command line (samtools, bedtools, deepTools) and in R (GenomicAlignments), and compare your numbers with ENCODE’s.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Background
Library complexity. Count the filtered reads (MAPQ ≥ 30, primary; duplicates not yet removed) by position: for single-end reads the 5’ end and strand, for paired-end reads the fragment’s start and end. With \(N\) reads, \(M_\text{distinct}\) distinct positions, \(M_1\) positions with exactly one read and \(M_2\) with exactly two:
\[\text{NRF} = \frac{M_\text{distinct}}{N}, \qquad \text{PBC1} = \frac{M_1}{M_\text{distinct}}, \qquad \text{PBC2} = \frac{M_1}{M_2}\]
ENCODE ChIP-seq: NRF > 0.9, PBC1 > 0.9, PBC2 > 10 is ideal; 0.8–0.9 (NRF “compliant”, PBC1 “mild”), PBC2 3–10 (“mild”); NRF or PBC1 below 0.5 or PBC2 below 1 is severe. ATAC-seq preferred values: NRF > 0.9, PBC1 > 0.9, PBC2 > 3.
FRiP = reads overlapping peaks / all filtered reads. ENCODE scrutinises TF ChIP-seq with FRiP below 1% (Landt et al. 2012); ATAC-seq should have FRiP > 0.3 (> 0.2 acceptable).
Fingerprint. Count reads in bins, sort the bins, plot the cumulative fraction of reads against the fraction of bins. Input ≈ diagonal; an enriched sample bends towards the lower right.
Strand cross-correlation \(CC(k)\): the correlation between + strand read 5’ ends at \(x\) and − strand read 5’ ends at \(x + k\). It peaks at the fragment length, with a “phantom” peak at the read length.
\[\text{NSC} = \frac{CC(\text{fragment})}{\min CC}, \qquad \text{RSC} = \frac{CC(\text{fragment}) - \min CC}{CC(\text{read length}) - \min CC}\]
ENCODE repeats experiments with NSC < 1.05 and RSC < 0.8.
Spike-in (ChIP-Rx). A fixed amount of fly chromatin is added to each sample before the IP. With \(N_\text{fly}\) the reads (in millions) on the fly genome, multiply the human signal by \(\alpha = 1/N_\text{fly}\).

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Data
The CTCF ChIP-seq of GM12878 (ENCODE ENCSR000DZN, replicate 1, single-end 36 bp, 2008-era Illumina reads with phred+64 qualities) and its input control (ENCSR000EYX, single-end 27–28 bp), and ATAC-seq of GM12878 in two biological replicates (ENCSR095QNB, paired-end 2 × 100 bp). For each library you get the original, untrimmed reads that ENCODE aligned to chr21 or chrM, plus a Bowtie2 index of chr21 + chrM, the ENCODE peaks (CTCF and ATAC, IDR-thresholded), the blacklist and the GENCODE annotation.
data/download.sh epigenomics-design      # about 1.5 GB
mkdir -p ~/epi/design && cd ~/epi/design
D=/path/to/course/data                   # where download.sh put the files
T=8                                      # threads
You need fastp, bowtie2, samtools (1.12 or newer), bedtools, deepTools and R with GenomicAlignments (see Install the software you need). The ChIP part runs in a minute; aligning the ATAC-seq reads takes about 10 minutes with 8 threads, so run it as a batch job on the cluster (wrap the alignment block in an sbatch script) and do the by-hand part meanwhile.






A shortcut to be aware of



The reads were selected because ENCODE aligned them to chr21 or chrM. Two consequences: the alignment rate is close to 100% (the reads that would not align were never selected), and the chrM fraction is hugely inflated (all mitochondrial reads were kept, but only 1/60 of the nuclear ones). We therefore compute every metric on chr21 only, where the reads are a faithful sample of the full library. The ENCODE values for the whole genome are given in the solutions for comparison.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
By hand
Do these on paper.
B1. Library complexity. Two ChIP-seq libraries were each sequenced to 10 million uniquely mapped reads (before duplicate removal).

Compute NRF, PBC1 and PBC2 for both, and classify each with the ENCODE ChIP-seq table.
What fraction of library 2’s reads would samtools markdup -r remove? How many usable reads are left?
Library 2 is sequenced again, to 40 M reads. Will NRF go up, stay the same or go down? Will the number of usable reads go up four-fold? Why?
Why must these metrics be computed before duplicate removal?

B2. FRiP. A CTCF ChIP-seq has 18 M filtered reads, of which 540 000 overlap the 45 000 called peaks. The peaks are on average 300 bp wide; the mappable genome is 2.7 Gb.

Compute FRiP. Does it pass the ENCODE guideline?
What FRiP would you expect if the reads were spread uniformly over the mappable genome? How many times more reads are in the peaks than expected?
The input of the same experiment has a FRiP of 0.4% in the same peaks. Why is that higher than your answer in (b)?
An ATAC-seq library has FRiP 0.15. What does ENCODE say? Name two things that could have gone wrong in the experiment.

B3. Read a fingerprint plot. The figure shows four samples, A–D, each with 1-kb bins over the genome.






Which curve is most likely an input? Which is a TF ChIP-seq with strong, sharp peaks? Which is a broad histone mark such as H3K27me3?
For curve B, read off the fraction of reads in the top 10% of bins.
Curve D follows the input until the last 1% of bins, which hold almost 30% of the reads. Is this a good ChIP? What could produce such a curve? (Think about the blacklist and about PCR.)

B4. Strand cross-correlation. Two single-end (36 bp) ChIP-seq experiments give these cross-correlation values:

What is the fragment length of experiment X? Why does the curve have a peak at 36 bp at all?
Experiment Y is an H3K36me3 ChIP-seq. Is a low RSC enough to reject it? Which other metric would you look at?

Normalise the HOXA counts per million human reads. What do you conclude?
Normalise with the spike-in factor \(\alpha = 1/N_\text{fly}\). What do you conclude now? By how much did H3K27me3 change at HOXA?
Why did the fly share of the library go up in the treated sample?
The treated sample accidentally received twice as many human cells as the control (same amount of fly chromatin). How would that bias the result, and which measurement would reveal the mistake?

B6. Judge the design. For each study, list the problems and propose a better design within a similar budget.

“We performed H3K27ac ChIP-seq on a tumour and on adjacent normal tissue from one patient. Peaks were called with MACS2 (no control). We identify 5214 tumour-specific enhancers.”
“ATAC-seq was performed on livers of three Tet2-knockout and three wild-type mice. Knockout livers were collected and processed in week 1 and sequenced on flow cell 1; wild-type livers in week 2 on flow cell 2. Differential accessibility was tested with DESeq2 (~ genotype).”
“CUT&RUN for H3K27me3 in three replicates of DMSO- and EZH2-inhibitor-treated cells. Tracks were normalised to counts per million. H3K27me3 is unchanged at most domains, so we conclude that the inhibitor does not reduce H3K27me3 at Polycomb targets.”

B7. How many reads? You plan a TF ChIP-seq and want 20 M usable fragments per replicate (ENCODE). A pilot run gave: 92% of reads aligned, 80% of the aligned reads have MAPQ ≥ 30, and 15% of those are duplicates.

What fraction of sequenced reads is usable? How many reads must you sequence per replicate?
The duplicate rate was measured at pilot depth (2 M reads). Will it be the same at full depth? What does that mean for your estimate?
The pilot FRiP is 5% and you expect about 20 000 binding sites. On average, how many reads fall into one peak at 20 M usable reads? And at FRiP 0.5%?

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
On the command line

C1 — Produce the filtered BAM files
This is the alignment chain from From reads to coverage: trim with fastp, align with Bowtie2, keep primary alignments with MAPQ ≥ 30 (and proper pairs for paired-end), mark and remove duplicates, keep chr21 and drop blacklisted regions. We keep the intermediate files: filt.bam (filtered, duplicates still in) is what complexity is computed on, final.bam is what everything else uses.
# single-end CTCF ChIP and input (old reads: phred+64 qualities)
for s in ctcf_chip ctcf_input; do
  fastp --phred64 -w $T -i $D/gm12878_$s.fastq.gz -o $s.trim.fq.gz \
        -j $s.fastp.json -h $s.fastp.html 2> $s.fastp.log
  bowtie2 -p $T -x $D/bowtie2/hg38_chr21_chrM -U $s.trim.fq.gz 2> $s.bowtie2.log \
    | samtools view -u -q 30 -F 0x904 - \
    | samtools sort -@ $T -o $s.filt.bam -
  samtools index $s.filt.bam
  samtools markdup -r -s $s.filt.bam $s.dedup.bam 2> $s.markdup.txt
  samtools index $s.dedup.bam
  samtools view -b $s.dedup.bam chr21 \
    | bedtools intersect -v -abam - -b $D/hg38_blacklist.bed.gz > $s.final.bam
  samtools index $s.final.bam
done

# paired-end ATAC-seq, two replicates
for r in rep1 rep2; do
  s=atac_$r
  fastp -w $T -i $D/gm12878_atac_${r}_R1.fastq.gz -I $D/gm12878_atac_${r}_R2.fastq.gz \
        -o $s.R1.fq.gz -O $s.R2.fq.gz -j $s.fastp.json -h $s.fastp.html 2> $s.fastp.log
  bowtie2 -p $T -X 2000 -x $D/bowtie2/hg38_chr21_chrM \
          -1 $s.R1.fq.gz -2 $s.R2.fq.gz 2> $s.bowtie2.log \
    | samtools view -u -q 30 -f 2 -F 0x904 - \
    | samtools sort -n -u -@ $T - \
    | samtools fixmate -m -u - - \
    | samtools view -u -f 2 - \
    | samtools sort -@ $T -o $s.filt.bam -
  samtools index $s.filt.bam
  samtools markdup -r -s $s.filt.bam $s.dedup.bam 2> $s.markdup.txt
  samtools index $s.dedup.bam
  samtools view -b $s.dedup.bam chr21 \
    | bedtools intersect -v -abam - -b $D/hg38_blacklist.bed.gz > $s.final.bam
  samtools index $s.final.bam
done
Then count what is left at each stage:
grep overall *.bowtie2.log
for s in ctcf_chip ctcf_input atac_rep1 atac_rep2; do
  echo $s $(samtools view -c $s.filt.bam) $(samtools view -c $s.filt.bam chrM) \
       $(samtools view -c $s.filt.bam chr21) $(samtools view -c $s.dedup.bam chr21) $(samtools view -c $s.final.bam)
done

Make a table: filtered reads, of which chrM, of which chr21; chr21 reads after duplicate removal; final reads. Why are the ATAC numbers dominated by chrM, and why must you not quote this chrM fraction as the library’s (see the warning above)?
What fraction of the chr21 reads were duplicates in each library? Which library is the least complex?
Why does the ATAC loop filter on -f 2 twice, before and after samtools fixmate?



C2 — Library complexity with awk
Single-end: one line per read with chromosome, 5’ end and strand; count identical lines.
for s in ctcf_chip ctcf_input; do
  samtools view -b $s.filt.bam chr21 | bedtools bamtobed -i - \
    | awk -v OFS='\t' '{ print $1, ($6 == "+" ? $2 : $3), $6 }' \
    | sort | uniq -c \
    | awk -v s=$s '{ n += $1; m++; if ($1 == 1) m1++; if ($1 == 2) m2++ }
        END { printf "%s reads %d distinct %d M1 %d M2 %d NRF %.3f PBC1 %.3f PBC2 %.2f\n",
              s, n, m, m1, m2, m/n, m1/m, m1/m2 }'
done
Paired-end: one line per fragment (both mates), from a name-sorted BAM.
for s in atac_rep1 atac_rep2; do
  samtools view -b $s.filt.bam chr21 | samtools sort -n - | bedtools bamtobed -bedpe -i - \
    | awk -v OFS='\t' '{ st = ($2 < $5 ? $2 : $5); en = ($3 > $6 ? $3 : $6); print $1, st, en }' \
    | sort | uniq -c \
    | awk -v s=$s '{ n += $1; m++; if ($1 == 1) m1++; if ($1 == 2) m2++ }
        END { printf "%s fragments %d distinct %d M1 %d M2 %d NRF %.3f PBC1 %.3f PBC2 %.2f\n",
              s, n, m, m1, m2, m/n, m1/m, m1/m2 }'
done

Explain the first awk: why is the position of a − strand read its end ($3) and not its start?
Classify the four libraries with the ENCODE tables (ChIP-seq table for ChIP and input, ATAC table for ATAC).
Compare with the genome-wide values that ENCODE reports for the same libraries (in the solutions). Is chr21 a fair sample?



C3 — FRiP
zcat $D/gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz > ctcf_peaks.bed
zcat $D/gm12878_atac_peaks.bed.gz > atac_peaks.bed
for s in ctcf_chip ctcf_input; do
  echo $s CTCF-peaks $(samtools view -c -L ctcf_peaks.bed $s.final.bam) $(samtools view -c $s.final.bam)
done
for s in atac_rep1 atac_rep2 ctcf_input; do
  echo $s ATAC-peaks $(samtools view -c -L atac_peaks.bed $s.final.bam) $(samtools view -c $s.final.bam)
done
# bases of chr21 inside peaks (overlapping peaks merged)
for p in ctcf atac; do
  awk '$1 == "chr21"' ${p}_peaks.bed | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n | bedtools merge | awk -v p=$p '{ s += $3 - $2 } END { print p, NR, s }'
done

Compute the FRiP of each sample. Do the ChIP and the ATAC-seq pass the guidelines?
The assembled part of chr21 is about 40.1 Mb. What FRiP would uniformly spread reads have in each peak set? How many times higher is the input’s FRiP than that? What does this tell you about the input (lecture: the background is not flat)?
We used ENCODE’s peaks, called on the full data of both replicates. Why does that make the FRiPs of the two ATAC replicates comparable? What would change if each replicate’s FRiP were computed with its own peaks?



C4 — Fingerprint
plotFingerprint -b ctcf_chip.final.bam ctcf_input.final.bam atac_rep1.final.bam \
  --labels CTCF input ATAC --region chr21 --binSize 1000 --numberOfSamples 50000 -p $T \
  --JSDsample ctcf_input.final.bam --outQualityMetrics fingerprint_metrics.txt \
  --outRawCounts fingerprint_counts.tab -o fingerprint.png
cut -f1-3,6-8 fingerprint_metrics.txt | column -t -s $'\t'

Open fingerprint.png. Which curve is the input, and how far is it from the diagonal? Which sample is most enriched?
All three curves stay at zero up to about 0.3 on the x axis. Why? (What is on the first 5–10 Mb of chr21?)
The metrics file gives the “elbow point” and the “synthetic” values: what a perfectly uniform sample of the same depth would give. Compare the input with its synthetic value.



C5 — Replicate concordance
for b in 10000 1000; do
  multiBamSummary bins -b atac_rep1.final.bam atac_rep2.final.bam ctcf_chip.final.bam ctcf_input.final.bam \
    --labels ATAC1 ATAC2 CTCF input --region chr21 --binSize $b -p $T \
    -o bins$b.npz --outRawCounts bins$b.tab
  plotCorrelation -in bins$b.npz --corMethod spearman --whatToPlot heatmap --plotNumbers \
    --skipZeros -o cor$b.png --outFileCorMatrix cor$b.txt
done
plotCorrelation -in bins10000.npz --corMethod pearson --log1p --whatToPlot scatterplot \
  --skipZeros -o scatter10k.png
cat cor10000.txt cor1000.txt

What is the Spearman correlation between the ATAC replicates in 10 kb and in 1 kb bins? Why is it lower in smaller bins?
Is CTCF closer to its input or to ATAC? Why is a high correlation between ChIP and input not a good sign?
A correlation of 0.9 between replicates sounds excellent. Why is it not enough to show that the peaks are reproducible? (Lecture: IDR.)

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
In R
You need GenomicAlignments and ggplot2. Work in the same folder:
library(GenomicAlignments); library(ggplot2)
setwd("~/epi/design")

R1 — Strand cross-correlation of CTCF
The function counts the 5’ ends of + and − strand reads at each base of chr21 and computes the Pearson correlation between the + strand counts at \(x\) and the − strand counts at \(x + k\). Only positions with a + strand read contribute to the sum of products, which makes it fast.
strand_cc <- function(bam, shifts = 0:1000, len = 46709983) {
  r <- readGAlignments(bam)
  plus <- as.character(strand(r)) == "+"
  fwd <- tabulate(start(r)[plus], len)          # 5' ends of + strand reads
  rev <- tabulate(end(r)[!plus], len)           # 5' ends of - strand reads
  p <- which(fwd > 0)
  m <- mean(fwd) * mean(rev); s <- sd(fwd) * sd(rev)
  sapply(shifts, function(k) {                  # correlation of fwd(x) and rev(x + k)
    q <- p + k; ok <- q <= len
    (sum(fwd[p[ok]] * rev[q[ok]]) / len - m) / s
  })
}
k <- 0:1000
cc_chip  <- strand_cc("ctcf_chip.final.bam")
cc_input <- strand_cc("ctcf_input.final.bam")
frag <- k[k > 50][which.max(cc_chip[k > 50])]
c(fragment = frag, cc_frag = max(cc_chip[k > 50]), cc_read = cc_chip[k == 36], min = min(cc_chip))
d <- rbind(data.frame(k, cc = cc_chip, sample = "CTCF"), data.frame(k, cc = cc_input, sample = "input"))
ggplot(d[d$k <= 500, ], aes(k, cc)) + geom_line() + facet_wrap(~sample, scales = "free_y") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(36, frag), linetype = 2) + labs(x = "strand shift (bp)", y = "cross-correlation")

What is the fragment length? Compute NSC and RSC for the CTCF ChIP (read length 36). Does it pass?
Describe the input curve. Is there a fragment-length peak?
ENCODE reports, for the same replicate genome-wide, RSC 1.69 and NSC 4.9 (phantompeakqualtools). Which of your two numbers agrees, and which does not? (Hint: what decides the minimum of the curve?)



R2 — Replicate concordance in R
b10 <- read.delim("bins10000.tab", check.names = FALSE)
names(b10) <- c("chr", "start", "end", "ATAC1", "ATAC2", "CTCF", "input")
b10 <- b10[rowSums(b10[, c("ATAC1", "ATAC2")]) > 0, ]
c(pearson_raw = cor(b10$ATAC1, b10$ATAC2),
  pearson_log = cor(log1p(b10$ATAC1), log1p(b10$ATAC2)),
  spearman    = cor(b10$ATAC1, b10$ATAC2, method = "spearman"))
ggplot(b10, aes(ATAC1 + 1, ATAC2 + 1)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() + coord_equal()
b10$M <- log2((b10$ATAC2 + 1) / sum(b10$ATAC2)) - log2((b10$ATAC1 + 1) / sum(b10$ATAC1))
b10$A <- (log2(b10$ATAC1 + 1) + log2(b10$ATAC2 + 1)) / 2
ggplot(b10, aes(A, M)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.3) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "red")

Why is the Pearson correlation of raw counts different from that of log counts? Which would you report?
The MA plot (as for RNA-seq): where is the spread largest, and why?



R3 — Why depth normalisation hides a global change
Simulate 500 H3K27me3 domains and 5000 background bins. The inhibitor removes 75% of H3K27me3 everywhere; the background (unspecific DNA) is unchanged. Both libraries are sequenced to the same depth, and each sample has the same amount of fly spike-in chromatin.
set.seed(1)
true_ctrl <- c(rgamma(500, shape = 4, rate = 0.02), rep(20, 5000))  # domains, then background
true_trt  <- c(0.25 * true_ctrl[1:500], rep(20, 5000))
spike     <- 2000                                                    # fly signal, same in both
depth     <- 2e6
lib <- function(true) {                                              # sequencing = sampling to fixed depth
  p <- c(true, spike) / sum(true, spike)
  as.vector(rmultinom(1, depth, p))
}
ctrl <- lib(true_ctrl); trt <- lib(true_trt)
fly  <- c(ctrl = tail(ctrl, 1), trt = tail(trt, 1))
ctrl <- head(ctrl, -1); trt <- head(trt, -1)
dom <- 1:500
cpm <- function(x) x / sum(x) * 1e6
c(cpm_ratio   = median(cpm(trt)[dom] / cpm(ctrl)[dom]),
  spike_ratio = median((trt[dom] / fly["trt"]) / (ctrl[dom] / fly["ctrl"])))

What are the two median ratios (treated / control at the domains)? Which one recovers the true 0.25?
Why is the CPM ratio not 1, as in the toy example of the lecture, but somewhat below? (Hint: what fraction of the library is background in each sample?)
Set true_trt <- true_ctrl (no change) and rerun. Do both methods give about 1?

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — complexity (B1, C2)





NRF is a fraction of reads, PBC1 a fraction of positions, PBC2 a ratio of counts of positions. Duplicates removed = \(N - M_\text{distinct}\). A library contains a fixed number of distinct molecules: sequencing deeper samples the same molecules again. The ENCODE definitions are on the ENCODE data standards terms page. bedtools bamtobed writes one BED line per read (-bedpe: per pair; needs a name-sorted BAM, samtools sort -n). samtools markdup needs samtools fixmate -m for paired-end data.









Hint 2 — FRiP (B2, C3)





Expected FRiP for uniform reads = fraction of the (mappable) genome covered by peaks. samtools view -c -L file.bed counts the reads that overlap any region of the BED file; bedtools merge collapses overlapping peaks. FRiP is described in Landt et al. 2012.









Hint 3 — fingerprint and cross-correlation (B3, B4, C4, R1)





Read the fingerprint from the right: the top 10% of bins are \(x\) from 0.9 to 1, and they hold \(1 - y(0.9)\) of the reads. See the plotFingerprint manual, including the description of its quality metrics. For NSC and RSC, plug the three numbers into the formulas in Background. The phantom peak and its explanation are in Landt et al. 2012 (Fig. 4) and Kharchenko et al. 2008. readGAlignments reads a BAM file; tabulate counts integers.









Hint 4 — spike-ins and design (B5, B6, R3)





CPM: divide by the human reads in millions. Spike-in: multiply by \(1/N_\text{fly}\) (millions). The method is Orlando et al. 2014. For the design questions go through: biological replicates per condition, control, antibody, batches vs condition, normalisation under a global change. rmultinom draws a fixed total of reads from the given proportions, like a sequencer.









Hint 5 — deepTools and depth (B7, C5, R2)





Usable fraction = product of the fractions kept at each step. multiBamSummary bins counts reads in bins; plotCorrelation plots and writes the correlation matrix. Spearman correlation uses ranks; Pearson on raw counts is dominated by the largest bins.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) Library 1: NRF \(8.2/10 = 0.82\), PBC1 \(7.0/8.2 = 0.85\), PBC2 \(7.0/0.9 = 7.8\): NRF compliant (0.8–0.9), mild bottlenecking by PBC1 and PBC2: acceptable. Library 2: NRF \(0.30\), PBC1 \(1.2/3.0 = 0.40\), PBC2 \(1.2/0.6 = 2.0\): NRF concerning, PBC1 severe, PBC2 moderate: a strongly bottlenecked library. (b) \(1 - 0.30 = 70\%\) of the reads are duplicates; 3.0 M usable reads remain. (c) NRF goes down: the library holds a limited number of distinct molecules (judging from PBC2, not many more than the 3 M already seen), so most new reads are copies of molecules already sequenced. The usable reads grow far less than four-fold. More sequencing cannot rescue a library that was amplified from too little DNA; make a new one. (d) After duplicate removal every position has exactly one read, so NRF = PBC1 = 1 by definition; the information is in how many copies there were.
B2. (a) \(540\,000 / 18\,000\,000 = 3\%\): above 1%, passes. (b) Peaks cover \(45\,000 \times 300 = 13.5\) Mb, \(13.5 / 2700 = 0.5\%\) of the mappable genome; expected FRiP 0.5%, so the ChIP has 6 times more reads in peaks than uniform. (c) The input is not uniform: CTCF sites are often in open chromatin, which shears more easily, and they are in mappable, GC-rich DNA. (In the course data the input’s FRiP in CTCF peaks is about 8 times the uniform expectation, C3.) (d) Below 0.2: not acceptable. Possible causes: too few cells or too much Tn5 for the cell number (over-tagmentation, more background), dead or dying cells (fragmented chromatin), poor nuclei isolation, many mitochondrial reads (these are removed but signal the problem), or a library dominated by background after too many PCR cycles.
B3. (a) A is the input (close to the diagonal). B is the sharp TF: flat for 90% of the bins, then a steep rise. C, a smooth curve bending away from the diagonal over the whole range, is the broad mark. (b) At \(x = 0.9\), \(y \approx 0.23\), so the top 10% of bins hold about 77% of the reads. (c) No: 99% of the genome looks like an input. A few bins with huge counts produce the jump: artefact regions such as satellite repeats, rDNA or the mitochondrial genome (blacklisted regions), or a few PCR jackpots. Check what those bins are; remove the blacklist and duplicates and replot.
B4. (a) X: NSC \(0.32 / 0.15 = 2.13\), RSC \((0.32 - 0.15)/(0.21 - 0.15) = 2.83\): passes both. Y: NSC \(0.26/0.25 = 1.04\), RSC \((0.26 - 0.25)/(0.30 - 0.25) = 0.2\): fails both (NSC < 1.05, RSC < 0.8). (b) About 180 bp: the shift where + and − strand reads correlate best. The read-length (phantom) peak comes from mappability: a position that can be mapped on the + strand can also be mapped on the − strand one read length further, so the two strands correlate at that shift in any library, even an input. (c) No. Broad marks spread over whole gene bodies have flat cross-correlation curves even when the ChIP works. Look at the fingerprint (and FRiP in broad domains), the browser, and the replicate agreement.
B5. (a) Human reads: 23.75 M and 21.25 M. HOXA: \(600/23.75 = 25.3\) and \(450/21.25 = 21.2\) reads per million human reads, a 16% drop: “a mild decrease”. (b) \(\alpha = 1/1.25 = 0.8\) and \(1/3.75 = 0.267\); scaled counts \(600 \times 0.8 = 480\) and \(450 \times 0.267 = 120\): a 4-fold drop (75% loss). (c) The same amount of fly H3K27me3 went into each IP, but the treated cells had much less human H3K27me3 to pull down, so the fly chromatin made up a larger share of the immunoprecipitated DNA (and of the reads). (d) Twice as much human chromatin per fly chromatin makes the fly share smaller, \(\alpha\) larger, and the treated sample looks too high: the loss is underestimated. The input (sequenced without IP) shows the actual human:fly ratio in each sample; ChIP-Rx-type normalisations correct by it.
B6. (a) n = 1 per condition (no biological replicates: no estimate of variability, any difference could be between two people); no input (copy-number changes in the tumour create “tumour-specific peaks”); tumour vs normal adjacent tissue also differ in cell-type composition. Better: tumours and matched normals from at least 3 (better 5+) patients, an input for each sample, the patient as a blocking factor (~ patient + tissue), and peaks called against the input. (b) Genotype is completely confounded with week and flow cell: the design matrix cannot separate them, and ~ genotype attributes every batch effect to the knockout. Better: process and sequence knockout and wild-type livers together (e.g. one KO and one WT per day, all on one flow cell or spread evenly), and include the batch in the model. (c) CPM normalisation assumes the total amount of H3K27me3 is unchanged, which is exactly what an EZH2 inhibitor violates: after normalisation the remaining signal is scaled up and domains look unchanged. Use a spike-in (e.g. Drosophila chromatin or the E. coli DNA carried over in CUT&RUN), or check global levels by western blot / mass spectrometry. The conclusion as written is not supported.
B7. (a) \(0.92 \times 0.80 \times 0.85 = 0.626\); \(20 / 0.626 \approx 32\) M reads per replicate. (b) No: the duplicate rate rises with depth because the library has a limited number of distinct molecules. Expect more than 15% duplicates at 32 M, so sequence more, or (better) check the complexity first (e.g. with a library-complexity extrapolation such as preseq). (c) \(20 \text{ M} \times 0.05 = 1\) M reads in peaks, about 50 reads per peak; at FRiP 0.5%, about 5 reads per peak: too few to call most peaks reliably.









Solutions — command line





Runtimes on a shared (busy) 40-core server with T=8: the alignment block 11 min (ChIP and input 20 s, the rest ATAC, mostly Bowtie2); counting 13 s; complexity 2 s (SE) and 21 s (PE); FRiP 2 s; plotFingerprint 30 s; the two multiBamSummary runs 8 s. In R: R1 12 s, R2 and R3 under a second. Your numbers may differ by a few hundred reads, about 0.1% (Bowtie2 breaks ties between equally good alignments at random).

Bowtie2 aligned 98.9% (ChIP), 100% (input) and 99.4% (both ATAC) of the reads: high because of the read selection. The ATAC subset is ~94% chrM because the selection kept every mitochondrial read but only the nuclear reads from chr21 (1.5% of the genome). ENCODE’s genome-wide numbers are 13.9% (rep1) and 10.3% (rep2) mitochondrial reads: still substantial, typical of ATAC-seq without a mitochondria-depleting protocol (Omni-ATAC). (b) Duplicates on chr21: CTCF 19.9%, input 1.4%, ATAC rep1 20.2%, rep2 11.2%. ATAC rep1 is the least complex, closely followed by the CTCF ChIP. (c) Filtering on MAPQ removes one mate of some pairs; the first -f 2 keeps reads flagged as proper pairs, but an orphaned mate still carries that flag. fixmate rewrites the flags from the mates actually present, and the second -f 2 drops the orphans, which markdup would otherwise choke on.

ENCODE, genome-wide (all reads of the replicate): CTCF rep1 NRF 0.75, PBC1 0.84, PBC2 9.9 (29.5 M reads); ATAC rep1 NRF 0.79–0.80, PBC1 0.80, PBC2 5.1–5.2; rep2 NRF 0.88–0.89, PBC1 0.89, PBC2 9.2–9.6. The ATAC values agree almost exactly; the ChIP values are close (ENCODE also counts reads in repeats and pericentromeres on other chromosomes, which add duplicates). chr21 is a fair sample of the library.

C3. (a) CTCF ChIP: 44 914 / 200 297 = 22.4%, far above 1%. Input: 1690 / 107 975 = 1.6%. ATAC rep1: 283 347 / 482 022 = 58.8%; rep2: 247 495 / 495 353 = 50.0%, both well above 0.3. (ENCODE genome-wide: 54–60% for rep1 and 46–52% for rep2 with their peak sets.) (b) 405 CTCF peaks on chr21 cover 74 287 bp, 0.19% of 40.1 Mb; the 1784 ATAC peaks on chr21 merge into 821 regions covering 620 kb, 1.5% (ENCODE’s IDR peaks list a region once per summit, so many overlap). The input has 1.6% of its reads in CTCF peaks (8 times the uniform expectation) and 8.3% in ATAC peaks (5 times): input DNA is enriched in open chromatin, which is why the ChIP must be compared with the input, not with a flat background. (c) Same peaks for both replicates means the same denominator of “where signal can be”: the FRiP then compares only the signal-to-noise of the libraries. With each replicate’s own peaks, the deeper or better replicate also gets more peaks, which raises its FRiP further; FRiP and peak number are not independent.
C4. (a) The input is the curve closest to the diagonal, but still clearly below it; ATAC is the most enriched (top 1% of 1-kb bins hold about 52% of the ATAC reads, 30% of CTCF reads, 8% of input reads). (b) About 28–40% of the 1-kb bins have no reads in any sample: the short arm of chr21 (0–~5 Mb, unassembled), the centromere (~11–13 Mb) and other gaps and repeats, where nothing can map. With the blacklist and these gaps the “genome” is smaller than the chromosome. (c) Elbow points: CTCF 0.74, input 0.62, ATAC 0.90; the synthetic (perfectly uniform) values are all about 0.51. Even the input is far from its synthetic value: it is not uniform, partly because of the unmappable bins, partly the open-chromatin bias seen in C3. The Jensen–Shannon distance to the input is 0.26 for CTCF and 0.49 for ATAC.
C5. (a) Spearman ATAC1–ATAC2: 0.90 in 10 kb bins, 0.59 in 1 kb bins (bins with reads in at least one sample). Small bins have few reads each, so Poisson counting noise is a larger part of the variation. (b) In 10 kb bins CTCF correlates about equally with its input (0.64) and with ATAC (0.65), and the input correlates even better with ATAC (0.75–0.76) than with CTCF. At this scale all libraries share the same background: mappability, GC content and open chromatin (C3). A ChIP that correlates highly with its input has little specific signal; here CTCF’s signal is in a few hundred narrow peaks, which hardly move a 10 kb-bin correlation. (c) Correlation over bins is dominated by the many background bins and by large-scale coverage variation that both replicates share; it says little about whether the same peaks, in the same order, are found. IDR answers that question.









Solutions — R





R1. (a) Fragment length 93 bp (ENCODE: 90–95). \(CC(93) = 0.147\), \(CC(36) = 0.091\), minimum (at ~1 kb) \(0.0032\): NSC \(= 0.147 / 0.0032 \approx 47\), RSC \(= (0.147 - 0.0032)/(0.091 - 0.0032) = 1.65\). Passes both thresholds easily. Note that the phantom peak at 36 bp is hidden on the rising flank of the fragment peak: CTCF fragments here are short. Runtime: about 12 s for both BAM files. (b) The input curve is low and noisy (0.001–0.0025), slowly decreasing with the shift, without a clear fragment-length peak: no enrichment. (c) RSC agrees (1.65 vs 1.69); NSC does not (47 vs 4.9). RSC is a ratio of two differences above the minimum and is robust. NSC divides by the minimum of the curve, the background correlation, which depends on how the background is estimated: per base or in bins, which chromosomes and regions are included (pericentromeric repeats, artefacts), the range of shifts. Compare NSC only between datasets computed the same way.
R2. Pearson of raw counts 0.97, of log counts 0.94, Spearman 0.89 (the 3580 10-kb bins with ATAC reads). (a) Raw counts are dominated by the few bins with very high counts (strong peaks), which inflates the Pearson correlation; log counts or ranks weigh all bins more equally. Report Spearman or Pearson on log counts, and say which. In ENCODE ATAC peaks (the counts used for differential accessibility), the log correlation is 0.99. (b) The spread is largest at low A (few reads): Poisson noise is relatively largest when counts are small, the same funnel shape as an MA plot in RNA-seq.
R3. (a) The CPM ratio is 0.40, the spike-in ratio 0.25: only the spike-in recovers the true 4-fold loss. (b) The domains hold about 100 000 units of signal in the control (500 × a mean of 200) and 25 000 after treatment; the background is 100 000 units in both. So the background is half of the control library but 80% of the treated one, and normalising both to the same total scales the treated sample up by \(200\,000 / 125\,000 = 1.6\): \(0.25 \times 1.6 = 0.40\). The domains seem to lose 60% instead of 75%. Real ChIP data behave in the same way: how much the global change is hidden depends on the share of background in the library. (c) Both give 1.00.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Where this leads

ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder explains the fragment-size distribution and TSS enrichment of these two replicates.
Peak calling calls the CTCF peaks with MACS3 against the input you aligned here, and runs IDR on replicates.
Differential accessibility and Annotation and differential binding use the replicate structure, batches and (for global changes) spike-in factors.
In practice, nf-core/chipseq and nf-core/atacseq compute all of these metrics and collect them in a MultiQC report.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined.

Landt et al. 2012, Genome Res. ChIP-seq guidelines and practices of the ENCODE and modENCODE consortia.
Kharchenko, Tolstorukov & Park 2008, Nat Biotechnol. Design and analysis of ChIP-seq experiments for DNA-binding proteins.
Li, Brown, Huang & Bickel 2011, Ann Appl Stat. Measuring reproducibility of high-throughput experiments.
Orlando et al. 2014, Cell Rep. Quantitative ChIP-Seq normalization reveals global modulation of the epigenome.
Diaz, Park, Lim & Song 2012, Stat Appl Genet Mol Biol. Normalization, bias correction, and peak calling for ChIP-seq.
Ewels, Magnusson, Lundin & Käller 2016, Bioinformatics. MultiQC: summarize analysis results for multiple tools and samples in a single report.

Short questions on replicates, controls, normalisation and QC metrics. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A ChIP-seq library has 20 M uniquely mapped reads (before duplicate removal) at 15 M distinct positions; 12 M positions have exactly one read and 2 M have exactly two. Compute NRF, PBC1 and PBC2. Is the library acceptable by the ENCODE standards?






Hint





NRF = distinct / reads; PBC1 = one-read positions / distinct; PBC2 = one-read / two-read positions. ENCODE ideal: > 0.9, > 0.9, > 10.









Answer





NRF \(= 15/20 = 0.75\), PBC1 \(= 12/15 = 0.80\), PBC2 \(= 12/2 = 6\). NRF is “acceptable” (0.5–0.8), PBC1 and PBC2 indicate mild bottlenecking (0.8–0.9 and 3–10). Usable, but sequencing deeper will mostly add duplicates.




Q2. A TF ChIP-seq has 25 M filtered reads, 200 000 of which fall in peaks. What is the FRiP? What would you check before deciding that the experiment failed?






Answer





FRiP \(= 0.2 / 25 = 0.8\%\), below ENCODE’s 1% guideline. Before rejecting it: how many peaks are there (a factor with few genuine sites can have a low FRiP and still be good), the fingerprint against the input, the cross-correlation (RSC), the replicate agreement, and whether the expected motif is enriched at the peak summits.




Q3. Name three sources of reads that are present in a ChIP-seq library but have nothing to do with the antibody’s target. Which of them does an input control correct for, and which does it not?






Answer





Open chromatin shears more easily (more fragments at promoters); copy-number gains (more DNA, more reads); mappability and repeats (no reads, or pile-ups in collapsed repeats); GC and PCR bias. The input, made from the same sheared chromatin without an antibody, shows all of these. It does not model DNA that binds non-specifically to the antibody or the beads: an IgG control does, but it often yields too little DNA for a good library.




Q4. In a fingerprint plot, sample S1 lies almost on the diagonal, and sample S2 stays near 0 until \(x = 0.8\) and then rises to 1. At \(x = 0.9\), S2 is at 0.35. What are S1 and S2 likely to be? What fraction of S2’s reads are in the top 10% of bins?






Answer





S1 is an input (or a failed ChIP): reads spread evenly over the bins. S2 is an enriched ChIP. The top 10% of bins (from 0.9 to 1) hold \(1 - 0.35 = 65\%\) of S2’s reads.




Q5. A single-end 50 bp ChIP-seq has strand cross-correlation 0.12 at 50 bp, 0.10 at its maximum (220 bp), and a minimum of 0.08. Compute NSC and RSC. What do the two peaks of the curve mean, and is this a good experiment?






Hint





NSC = CC(fragment) / min; RSC = (CC(fragment) − min) / (CC(read) − min).









Answer





NSC \(= 0.10/0.08 = 1.25\); RSC \(= 0.02/0.04 = 0.5\). The peak at 220 bp is the fragment length (enrichment around binding sites); the peak at 50 bp is the “phantom” read-length peak caused by mappability, present in every library. Here the phantom peak is higher than the fragment peak (RSC < 0.8): weak enrichment. ENCODE would repeat a TF ChIP like this; for a broad histone mark a flat curve is less worrying.




Q6. H3K79me2 ChIP-Rx with Drosophila spike-in. Control: 30 M reads, 1.5 M on the fly genome; DOT1L inhibitor: 30 M reads, 6 M on the fly genome. A gene body has 3000 reads in the control and 2400 after treatment. Compare the change with CPM normalisation and with spike-in normalisation.






Answer





CPM per human reads: \(3000/28.5 = 105\) and \(2400/24 = 100\): a 5% drop, “no real change”. Spike-in: \(\alpha = 1/1.5 = 0.67\) and \(1/6 = 0.167\); \(3000 \times 0.67 = 2000\) and \(2400 \times 0.167 = 400\): a 5-fold loss. The inhibitor removed most H3K79me2 everywhere; depth normalisation redistributes what is left and hides it.




Q7. Wild-type samples were sequenced in January and knockout samples in March, three of each. Why can DESeq2 not estimate the knockout effect with ~ batch + genotype? What would happen with ~ genotype?






Answer





Batch and genotype are perfectly confounded: the batch column of the design matrix equals the genotype column, so the two effects cannot be separated (the matrix is not of full rank and DESeq2 refuses to fit it). With ~ genotype the model fits, but every difference between January and March (reagents, antibody lot, sequencing run) is reported as an effect of the knockout. Only a new design helps: process both genotypes in each batch.




Q8. A paper reports peaks “reproducible in two pseudoreplicates” from a single ChIP-seq sample per condition and concludes that 3000 binding sites differ between conditions. What do pseudoreplicates show, and what do they not show?






Answer





Pseudoreplicates are random halves of the reads of one library. Agreement between them shows that a peak is supported by enough reads (counting noise is small). They share the same cells, chromatin, IP and library, so they say nothing about biological or experimental variability. With n = 1 per condition there is no estimate of that variability, and no valid test of differences between conditions.




Q9. ATAC-seq experiments usually have no input control, and nobody computes strand cross-correlation for them. Why is this acceptable, and which QC metrics take their place?






Answer





There is no natural control: Tn5 cutting of open chromatin is the signal, and the background is estimated from the sample itself (genome-wide and local rates in MACS). Paired-end reads measure every fragment length directly, so cross-correlation is not needed. ATAC-specific QC: TSS enrichment (signal to noise; ENCODE > 7 ideal for GRCh38), the fragment-size distribution (nucleosome-free peak and mono-nucleosome peak), the mitochondrial fraction, FRiP (> 0.3), library complexity, and agreement between biological replicates.




Q10. A collaborator wants to rescue a ChIP-seq library with 70% duplicates by sequencing it four times deeper. Will that work?






Answer





No. 70% duplicates means the library contains few distinct molecules (low complexity, typically from too little immunoprecipitated DNA and many PCR cycles). Deeper sequencing mostly reads the same molecules again: the duplicate rate rises further and the number of usable reads grows very little. Make a new library from more starting material (or pool IPs), with fewer PCR cycles.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
About this lecture
In What is epigenetics? we saw that active promoters and enhancers are nucleosome-depleted: the DNA there is open. ATAC-seq maps that open DNA genome-wide, from a few thousand cells, in an afternoon. It is the most used chromatin assay today, and its data carry more than peaks: the lengths of the fragments tell you where the nucleosomes are.

Why measure accessibility, and how it was done before ATAC-seq (DNase-seq, FAIRE, MNase-seq).
The Tn5 transposase: cutting and adding adapters in one step, and what that does to the library.
The fragment-length distribution and the nucleosome ladder, down to the 10-bp helical period.
ATAC-specific QC: mitochondrial reads, TSS enrichment, and what a bad library looks like.
Protocol variants and experimental design.


This is the first unit of the ATAC-seq block. Students already know nucleosomes, NDRs and the MNase ladder from What is epigenetics?, and the generic steps of alignment, duplicates and blacklists from From reads to coverage and Experimental design and QC. Here the focus is what is special about ATAC-seq: the enzyme, the fragments it makes, and the QC that follows from that. The following unit, ATAC-seq processing and peak calling, does the Tn5 shift in detail, peak calling and consensus peaks. All real-data figures in this lecture come from ENCODE GM12878 ATAC-seq replicate 1 (ENCSR095QNB), reads from chr21 and chrM, processed with exactly the commands of the exercise.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Open chromatin marks regulatory DNA






Promoters and enhancers that are in use have a nucleosome-depleted region where transcription factors bind. Elsewhere the DNA is wrapped in nucleosomes.
An enzyme added to nuclei cuts, or tags, mostly where it can reach the DNA. Count where it acted, and the pile-ups are the accessible regions.
Accessibility is mark-free: no antibody, no prior choice of protein. One assay finds promoters, enhancers and insulators (CTCF sites) at once.


The logic of every accessibility assay: use a large enzyme as a probe for access. Nucleosomes protect the DNA wrapped on them; linkers are partly accessible; NDRs are very accessible. A peak of accessibility does not tell you which factor is bound or whether the element is active or poised; that is what histone marks and TF ChIP add. But it is the best single map of “where the regulatory DNA of this cell type is”. About 1–3% of the genome is accessible in a given cell type; across all cell types studied by ENCODE, millions of distinct accessible sites have been found (Thurman et al. 2012). The weak cuts in linkers in the figure come back later: they make the nucleosome ladder.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Before ATAC-seq: four ways to find open DNA
text:
Before ATAC-seq: four ways to find open DNA






DNase I hypersensitive sites (1970s–80s, Southern blots): active genes are more sensitive to DNase I. DNase-seq (Boyle et al. 2008; Hesselberth et al. 2009) maps them genome-wide.
FAIRE: crosslink, shear, and keep the DNA that is not bound to proteins. MNase-seq does the opposite: digest everything unprotected and sequence the nucleosome cores.
ATAC-seq (Buenrostro et al. 2013) gives the DNase-seq answer, plus nucleosome positions, from far fewer cells.


DNase I hypersensitivity is the classic marker of regulatory DNA: Weintraub and Groudine showed in 1976 that active globin genes are more DNase-sensitive, and individual hypersensitive sites at enhancers and the beta-globin LCR were mapped by Southern blot in the 1980s. DNase-seq turned that into a genome-wide map and was the main ENCODE accessibility assay; Thurman et al. 2012 is the landmark paper. It needs millions of cells and careful titration of the enzyme. FAIRE (Giresi et al. 2007) is simple but has low signal-to-noise. MNase-seq gives a negative image: nucleosomes, with the NDR as a gap. ATAC-seq won because it is fast, works on 500–50 000 cells, and its fragments contain both kinds of information. DNase-seq is still used, and single-hit DNase protocols give very clean footprints.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
ATAC-seq in one picture






Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin: lyse cells gently, add the Tn5 transposase loaded with sequencing adapters to the nuclei, purify the DNA and amplify by PCR.
Tn5 inserts its adapters into accessible DNA in the nucleus, so the library is made where the chromatin is intact.
No size selection is needed, and the whole protocol takes about three hours.


The original protocol (Buenrostro et al. 2013) used 50 000 cells, a lysis buffer with NP-40, 30 minutes of transposition at 37 °C, a column cleanup and PCR with barcoded primers. The number of PCR cycles is chosen by qPCR on a small aliquot to avoid over-amplification. Because transposition and library construction are the same step, there is no fragmentation, end repair or ligation: this is why it needs so little material. The price is that the library structure is set by the enzyme, which is what the next slides are about.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Tn5: cut and paste in one step
text:
Tn5: cut and paste in one step






Tn5 is a bacterial transposase. A hyperactive mutant is loaded with two kinds of short DNA adapters, each ending in the 19-bp mosaic end it recognises.
A Tn5 dimer cuts both strands of the target DNA and joins an adapter to each new end: tagmentation (tagging + fragmentation).
The two cuts are 9 bp apart. Filling the gaps copies those 9 bp onto both fragments. Read ends must therefore be shifted (+4 / −5 bp) to mark the centre of the insertion; ATAC-seq processing and peak calling does this.


Adey et al. 2010 developed in vitro tagmentation with hyperactive Tn5 for making sequencing libraries (Nextera); Buenrostro’s insight was to do it on native chromatin. The transposase stays bound to the DNA after insertion and is removed during purification (SDS or the column). The 9-bp staggered cut leaves a 9-nt single-stranded gap on each fragment; the first step of the PCR (5 minutes at 72 °C) fills it. So the 9 bp next to every insertion appear on both neighbouring fragments. For peaks of hundreds of bp the shift does not matter; for footprinting and for the precise position of insertions it does. Here we only need to remember that each read’s 5’ end is (within a few bp) a Tn5 insertion.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Two adapters: only half the fragments can be sequenced
text:
Two adapters: only half the fragments can be sequenced






Tn5 is loaded with adapter A and adapter B at random. A fragment gets one adapter at each end: A–B, B–A, A–A or B–B, each with probability ¼.
The PCR uses one primer for A and one for B, and the sequencer reads from A (read 1) and B (read 2). Only A–B and B–A fragments are amplified and sequenced: \(2 \times \tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{1}{2} = 50\%\).
Fragments longer than about 1 kb are also lost: they amplify and cluster poorly. Reads come mostly from fragments shorter than ~600 bp.


This is a property of the Nextera chemistry. A–A and B–B fragments can only be copied linearly (one primer) and in addition fold back into hairpins (suppression PCR), so they are effectively absent. For bulk ATAC-seq this costs half the material but does not bias which regions are seen. It matters for single-cell ATAC-seq: each cell has two copies of each site, and losing half of the fragments is one reason scATAC data are so sparse. Long fragments are lost because two insertions far apart are needed, and long molecules amplify and form clusters less efficiently on the flow cell. This size limit is why ATAC is mostly blind to the inside of closed chromatin: fragments from there are too long.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: A read pair is a fragment, and a fragment is two insertions
text:
A read pair is a fragment, and a fragment is two insertions






Paired-end sequencing reads both ends of each fragment. The 5’ end of each read sits at a Tn5 insertion site.
The aligner reports the fragment length (template length, TLEN, column 9 of SAM): positive for the leftmost mate, negative for the other.
This is why ATAC-seq is sequenced paired-end: it gives two insertion sites and the length between them, and the length carries information.


Students met TLEN in From reads to coverage. Here it gets a meaning: it is the distance between two Tn5 insertions, and the distribution of these distances is the next slide. With 2×100 bp reads and fragments shorter than 100 bp, both reads run through the whole fragment into the adapter on the other side, which is why adapters must be trimmed before alignment (the read would otherwise not align end-to-end). In the exercise we trim with fastp. Single-end ATAC-seq exists but loses the fragment lengths and half the insertion sites.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Why fragment lengths come in steps
text:
Why fragment lengths come in steps






Two insertions in the same open region (or the same linker) give a short, nucleosome-free fragment, under ~100 bp.
Two insertions in linkers on either side of one nucleosome give a fragment of about 180–250 bp; around two nucleosomes ~350–450 bp, and so on.
So the fragment-length histogram is a nucleosome ladder, the same one as in the MNase experiment of What is epigenetics?


The key idea of the lecture. Tn5 cannot insert into DNA wrapped on a nucleosome (with a few exceptions at the edges), so any fragment that contains a nucleosome is at least 147 bp plus whatever linker on either side. The mono-nucleosome fragments are mostly from just outside open regions and from accessible linkers in otherwise ordinary chromatin. This is how one ATAC-seq library contains both maps: short fragments mark the open sites, nucleosome-sized fragments mark the positioned nucleosomes around them (NucleoATAC and similar tools exploit this). The repeat in human cells is about 190 bp.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Real data: the nucleosome ladder






GM12878, ENCODE ATAC-seq replicate 1, 252 213 fragments on chr21 after filtering.
A large nucleosome-free peak (mode 45 bp), then mono- (210 bp) and di-nucleosome (391 bp) peaks. On a log scale (inset) a weak tri-nucleosome shoulder near 550–600 bp is visible too.


This is the plot to make for every ATAC-seq library, first. 28.7% of the fragments are shorter than 100 bp, 16.1% are 180–250 bp. The step between the mono and di peaks, about 180 bp, is close to the nucleosome repeat length (~190 bp). The peaks are broad because linker lengths vary and Tn5 does not always cut in the middle of a linker. The spikes on the mono peak (e.g. 167, 177, 187 bp) are the same 10-bp periodicity as on the next slide, continuing into nucleosomal fragments; with only 250 000 fragments on one chromosome the curve is also noisy. The sharp drop below about 35 bp is not biology: the shortest fragments are lost in the cleanup, and reads that short fail the length filter after trimming. Notice the small ripples on the nucleosome-free peak: next slide. ENCODE requires that the nucleosome-free and mono-nucleosome peaks are both present.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
The 10.5-bp ripple: DNA’s helical turn











DNA on a nucleosome (and DNA lying on any surface) exposes its backbone once per helical turn, about 10.5 bp. Tn5 cuts where it can reach, so fragment lengths prefer steps of ~10.5 bp.
Bottom: fragment counts divided by a smooth trend. The peaks are 10.2 bp apart on average.


Buenrostro et al. 2013 showed this periodicity in the first ATAC-seq paper; it is a sign that the fragments really come from chromatinised DNA. The detrending is done in the figure script: divide the counts by a running mean over 31 bp so that only the short-range wiggle remains. The ripple is clearest between 40 and 200 bp. A library made from naked DNA (or a very over-tagmented one) loses both the ladder and the ripple. Not every pipeline checks the periodicity, but it is a nice sanity check that costs nothing.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Tn5 is not a perfectly random cutter
text:
Tn5 is not a perfectly random cutter






Base composition of the genome around 200 000 insertion sites (5’ ends of + strand reads, chr21). Random cutting would give flat lines at the genome average.
Tn5 has a weak, symmetric sequence preference centred on the 9-bp duplicated stretch, and prefers GC-rich DNA.
The bias is small per site but matters for footprinting and for comparing regions of different sequence. Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting corrects for it.


Every enzyme-based assay has a sequence bias: DNase I and MNase too (MNase strongly prefers AT-rich DNA). For Tn5 the preference is a palindromic, roughly symmetric pattern, because the enzyme acts as a dimer. In the figure, position 0 is the first base of the + strand read, so the 9-bp duplicated stretch runs from 0 to +8 and its centre is at +4; the pattern is mirror-symmetric around that centre, which is the reason for the +4 / −5 shift. For peak calling the bias averages out. For TF footprints, where you look for a dip of a few bp in the insertion profile, the enzyme’s preference alone can create or hide a “footprint”. Tools such as TOBIAS model and remove it.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Mitochondrial DNA soaks up Tn5






mtDNA is a 16.6-kb circle without nucleosomes, present in hundreds to thousands of copies per cell. All of it is accessible.
In the original protocol, often 20–50% of reads come from chrM. They cost sequencing but carry no information about nuclear chromatin.
Remove chrM reads before peak calling and before computing other QC metrics; report the chrM fraction as a QC number.


The arithmetic in the figure is an order-of-magnitude argument: about 130 Mb of open nuclear DNA against tens of Mb of naked mtDNA, so a large share of insertions can land in chrM if Tn5 gets into the mitochondria. The lysis detergent permeabilises the mitochondrial membranes as well. The fraction varies enormously by cell type: cells with many mitochondria (heart, muscle, liver) are worst. Omni-ATAC (Corces et al. 2017) changes the lysis and washes away much of the cytoplasm, which typically brings chrM down to a few percent. Note also that nuclear mitochondrial DNA segments (NUMTs) in the nuclear genome attract chrM-like reads; that is one reason blacklists exist.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Real data: the chrM fraction






In our chr21 + chrM read set, 90.7% of the aligned reads are on chrM. That number is not the library’s chrM fraction: chr21 is only 1.5% of the genome.
Scale chr21 up to the whole genome: chrM ≈ 12.8% of all reads. ENCODE’s own QC of the full library reports 13.9%.


An honest-simplification moment (principle 10). We only have reads that ENCODE aligned to chr21 or chrM, so the chrM share in our files is grossly inflated. The estimate: if chr21 holds about f = 1.5% of the nuclear reads (its share of the genome length, roughly), the whole library had chr21_reads / f nuclear reads, and chrM fraction = chrM / (chrM + chr21 / f). The estimate (12.8%) is close to ENCODE’s value computed from all reads (13.9%; 11.7 M of 83.7 M mapped reads), so the shortcut works. In the exercise students compute this with samtools idxstats. For a standard-protocol library from a cell line, 14% is good; Omni-ATAC libraries are often below 5%.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
The TSS enrichment score






Active promoters are the most reliably open sites in every cell type, so a good library has many insertions at TSSs relative to the DNA a few kb away.
ENCODE definition: aggregate insertions in ±2 kb around all TSSs, divide by the mean of the outer 100 bp at each end, and take the value at the centre (ENCODE’s pipeline: the maximum of the profile in 10-bp bins).
A signal-to-noise measure that needs no peak calling and works on any library, even a shallow one.


TSS enrichment has largely replaced FRiP as the headline QC number for ATAC-seq, because FRiP depends on the peak caller and the depth while TSS enrichment does not. The flanks at ±1.9–2 kb are mostly closed chromatin, so they measure background: insertions anywhere, from naked DNA of dead cells and from random tagmentation. Thresholds depend on the TSS annotation: ENCODE uses RefSeq TSSs, with < 5 concerning, 5–7 acceptable and > 7 ideal on GRCh38 (6 and 10 on hg19). Strand matters: each TSS window is flipped for − strand genes so downstream is always to the right. The ENCODE pipeline actually computes read coverage (not 5’ ends) in 400 bins of 10 bp, and reports the maximum of the mean profile; the exact numbers therefore differ a little between tools.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Real data: TSS enrichment






602 protein-coding TSSs on chr21 (GENCODE), insertions from 252 213 fragments. TSS enrichment = 34.0.
Far above ENCODE’s “ideal” threshold of 7. ENCODE’s genome-wide value for this library: 29.6.
The profile is asymmetric: the maximum is upstream of the TSS (around −140 to −90 bp), in the NDR; the sharp drop just downstream is the +1 nucleosome.


Our number uses protein-coding TSSs of chr21 only, GENCODE rather than RefSeq, and insertion sites rather than read coverage, so it is not identical to ENCODE’s; it should be in the same range. Many TSSs on chr21 are of genes not expressed in B cells, and they contribute flat profiles: the score is an average over active and inactive promoters. That is why the score also depends on the cell type and annotation, and why thresholds are rough. A score of 3 would mean the library is mostly background; a score of 30 means a very clean library.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Short and long fragments see different things
text:
Short and long fragments see different things






Split the fragments by length: nucleosome-free (< 100 bp) and mono-nucleosome (180–250 bp). Plot fragment centres around TSSs.
Nucleosome-free fragments pile up just upstream of the TSS (the NDR). Mono-nucleosome fragments dip at the TSS and peak on both sides: the +1 nucleosome at +124 bp, and upstream a peak at −91 bp.


This is the nucleosome map hidden in an ATAC-seq library, made with nothing more than a length filter. The +1 nucleosome (fragment centres peak at +124 bp here) is the best-positioned nucleosome of an active promoter. The upstream peak (−91 bp) is less clean: in a very accessible promoter, two insertions on either side of the whole NDR also give a 180–250 bp fragment, so not every ‘mono-nucleosome-sized’ fragment contains a nucleosome. The nucleosome-free fragments peak at about −100 bp, in the NDR just upstream of the TSS. Peak callers for ATAC usually use all fragments or just the nucleosome-free ones; the choice is part of the next unit. Each curve is divided by its own flank mean, so shapes are compared, not absolute numbers; with 600 TSSs on one chromosome the curves are noisy. Tools such as NucleoATAC do this properly genome-wide.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Real data: ATAC-seq next to histone marks
text:
Real data: ATAC-seq next to histone marks






GM12878 at ITGB2 (chr21), the β2 integrin (CD18) of white blood cells, strongly expressed in B-lymphoblastoid cells. Our ATAC coverage, ENCODE ATAC peaks, and ENCODE H3K4me3 and H3K27ac (fold change over input).
ATAC peaks sit at promoters (with H3K4me3) and enhancers (H3K27ac without H3K4me3). The ATAC peak is narrow, in the NDR; the histone marks are on the flanking nucleosomes.


ITGB2 is on the − strand, so it is transcribed right to left. Most of its GENCODE transcripts start at 44.921 Mb (strong H3K4me3, an ATAC peak in the middle of it); others start at an upstream promoter at 44.929 Mb, inside a broad H3K27ac region with several ATAC peaks (promoter plus candidate enhancers). The ATAC peaks in the gene body with H3K27ac but little H3K4me3 (44.91 Mb) are candidate intronic enhancers. On the left is the promoter of PTTG1IP, the strongest ATAC peak in the window. The ATAC track is coverage from our own chr21 alignment (fragments, counts per million), the histone tracks are ENCODE fold-change bigWigs from chromatin-intro. Point out that ATAC and H3K27ac do not have the same shape: the histone mark is on nucleosomes, so it is often highest on either side of the ATAC peak, with a dip where the nucleosomes are missing. Also point out the small ATAC peak at 44.893 Mb without either histone mark: it sits on a CTCF peak (ENCODE GM12878 CTCF), so accessibility finds insulators too.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: What a bad library looks like
text:
What a bad library looks like






Too much Tn5 per nucleus (too few cells): almost all fragments short, the ladder disappears, background rises. Too little (too many cells): long fragments dominate, the nucleosome-free peak is weak.
Dead or damaged cells: naked or degraded DNA is tagmented everywhere. The ladder may even look strong, but the TSS profile is flat.
Always look at both plots: the fragment lengths say how the reaction went, the TSS profile says whether the result has signal.


These are schematic curves, not real data, drawn to show the typical patterns (the Grandi et al. 2022 protocol paper has real examples). The Tn5-to-nuclei ratio is the main knob of the reaction, which is why cell counts matter. Dead cells are the most common problem with primary samples: apoptotic DNA is cleaved between nucleosomes and gives a strong ladder by itself, and necrotic DNA is accessible everywhere. Both reduce the TSS score. Remedies: dead-cell removal, DNase treatment of the culture before harvesting (Omni-ATAC), sorting live cells. A third failure: too much PCR, which shows up as a high duplicate rate (From reads to coverage).

text:
