view_motifs(convert_motifs(pfms[c("Spi1_MA0080.7", "SPIB_MA0081.3", "ETS1_MA0098.4")]))

How many motifs are there? Which TF families have the most motifs?
The CTCF matrix is a table of counts. How many binding sites was it built from? (Sum a column.)
Look at the three ETS logos. What do they share, and where do they differ?



R3 — Motif matches in all tested peaks
system.time(hit <- motifMatches(matchMotifs(pfms, tested, genome = genome, p.cutoff = 5e-5)))
dim(hit)
summary(colMeans(hit))
sort(colMeans(hit), decreasing = TRUE)[1:5]

What is the median fraction of peaks that match a motif? Compare with your answer to B1 for a 500-bp peak at \(p = 5 \times 10^{-5}\).
Which motifs match the most peaks? Why might short or low-information motifs match far more peaks than the median?



R4 — Enrichment in B-up and T-up peaks
First one motif with fisher.test, then all motifs at once with the hypergeometric distribution (identical to one-sided Fisher, but vectorised and on the log scale, so that p-values below \(10^{-308}\) do not become 0):
tab <- table(B_up = b_up, SPIB = hit[, "SPIB_MA0081.3"])
tab
fisher.test(tab, alternative = "greater")

enrich <- function(target, hit, bg = !target) {
  a <- colSums(hit[target, ]); b <- sum(target) - a
  c <- colSums(hit[bg, ]);     d <- sum(bg) - c
  lp <- phyper(a - 1, a + c, b + d, a + b, lower.tail = FALSE, log.p = TRUE) / log(10)
  data.frame(tf = sub("_MA.*", "", colnames(hit)), family = fam[colnames(hit)],
             frac_target = a / (a + b), frac_bg = c / (c + d), OR = (a * d) / (b * c),
             log10p = lp, padj = p.adjust(10^lp, "BH"))
}
eB <- enrich(b_up, hit); eT <- enrich(t_up, hit)
head(eB[order(eB$log10p), -2], 15)
head(eT[order(eT$log10p), -2], 15)
c(B = sum(eB$padj < 0.05 & eB$OR > 1), T = sum(eT$padj < 0.05 & eT$OR > 1))
sel <- c("EBF1_MA0154.5", "PAX5_MA0014.4", "PAX2_MA0067.3", "POU2F2_MA0507.3", "Runx1_MA0002.3",
         "TCF7_MA0769.3", "Gata3_MA0037.5", "ETS1_MA0098.4", "Spi1_MA0080.7", "CTCF_MA0139.2")
round(cbind(B = eB[sel, c("OR", "log10p")], T = eT[sel, c("OR", "log10p")]), 2)

From tab, compute the odds ratio by hand and compare with fisher.test. Why does fisher.test report \(p < 2.2 \times 10^{-16}\) while enrich() gives \(10^{-934}\)?
Which TF families dominate the top of each list? Do they match what you know about B and T cells?
How many motifs are significant at FDR 5%? Is that a useful number?
Look at EBF1, PAX5 and PAX2 in B-up peaks. What do you conclude about the B-cell master regulators EBF1 and PAX5, and about the PAX5 matrix?
CTCF has OR < 1 in both lists. Explain.



R5 — A GC-matched background
gc <- as.numeric(letterFrequency(getSeq(genome, tested), "GC") / 500)
tapply(gc, b_up, mean)
bin <- cut(gc, seq(0, 1, 0.02))
pool <- split(which(!b_up), bin[!b_up])
gcm <- unlist(lapply(split(which(b_up), bin[b_up]), function(i) {
  p <- pool[[as.character(bin[i[1]])]]
  if (length(p) == 0) integer(0) else p[sample.int(length(p), length(i), replace = length(p) < length(i))]
}))
mean(gc[gcm])
eB_gc <- enrich(b_up, hit, bg = seq_along(tested) %in% gcm)
sel2 <- c("SPIB_MA0081.3", "EBF1_MA0154.5", "SP1_MA0079.5", "KLF4_MA0039.5", "Nrf1_MA0506.3",
          "CTCF_MA0139.2")
data.frame(OR_all = eB[sel2, "OR"], OR_gc = eB_gc[sel2, "OR"], row.names = sel2)

Are B-up peaks more or less GC-rich than the other tested peaks?
Which motifs change most when the background is GC-matched, and in which direction? Explain using (a). (Note: the GC-matched set contains each background peak at most once per draw, but may repeat peaks; that is fine for this purpose.)



R6 — chromVAR across 13 cell types
grp <- paste(info$celltype, info$donor, sep = "_")                 # one column per donor x cell type
cm <- sapply(split(info$sample, grp), function(s) rowSums(cnt[, s, drop = FALSE]))
top <- order(rowSums(cm), decreasing = TRUE)[1:100000]              # the 100 000 most-read peaks
se <- SummarizedExperiment(assays = list(counts = cm[top, ]), rowRanges = peaks[top],
                           colData = DataFrame(celltype = sub("_.*", "", colnames(cm))))
se <- addGCBias(se, genome = genome)
mm <- matchMotifs(pfms, se, genome = genome, p.cutoff = 5e-5)
bg <- getBackgroundPeaks(se, niterations = 50)
system.time(dev <- computeDeviations(se, annotations = mm, background_peaks = bg))
z <- deviationScores(dev)
dim(z)
v <- computeVariability(dev)
head(v[order(-v$variability), c("name", "variability")], 15)

show <- c("GATA1::TAL1_MA0140.3", "Gata3_MA0037.5", "KLF1_MA0493.3", "CEBPA_MA0102.5",
          "Spi1_MA0080.7", "EBF1_MA0154.5", "TCF3_MA0522.4", "POU2F2_MA0507.3", "Runx1_MA0002.3",
          "TCF7_MA0769.3", "TBX21_MA0690.3", "CTCF_MA0139.2")
ord <- c("HSC", "MPP", "LMPP", "CMP", "GMP", "MEP", "Ery", "Mono", "CLP", "B", "CD4", "CD8", "NK")
zm <- sapply(ord, function(ct) rowMeans(z[show, dev$celltype == ct, drop = FALSE]))
round(zm)
pheatmap(pmax(pmin(zm, 15), -15), cluster_cols = FALSE,
         color = colorRampPalette(c("#2a6f97", "white", "#c0392b"))(101))

How many samples and cell types are there? Which motifs are the most variable?
Read the table zm: in which cell types is each motif most accessible? Do they fit the known regulators of each lineage (GATA1 and KLF1 for erythroid cells, C/EBPα for myeloid cells, PU.1, EBF1 and E2A (TCF3) for B cells, RUNX, TCF7 and T-bet (TBX21) for T and NK cells)?
Compare GATA1::TAL1 and Gata3. What does this tell you about naming a TF from a chromVAR result?
Some highly variable motifs have names like FIGLA, ASCL1 or TBR1, factors not expressed in blood. Look at their family in fam and suggest which blood TF they stand for.



R7 — Tn5 insertions and a CTCF footprint
ga <- readGAlignments("gm12878_atac_rep1.bam",
                      param = ScanBamParam(which = GRanges("chr21", IRanges(1, 46709983))))
ins <- GRanges("chr21", IRanges(ifelse(strand(ga) == "+", start(ga) + 4, end(ga) - 5), width = 1),
               seqinfo = Seqinfo("chr21", 46709983))
length(ins)
cov_ins <- coverage(ins)$chr21                     # insertions per base along chr21 (an Rle)

ctcf_pk <- import(file.path(D, "gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz"), format = "narrowPeak")
atac_pk <- import(file.path(D, "gm12878_atac_peaks.bed.gz"), format = "narrowPeak")
chr21 <- GRanges("chr21", IRanges(1, 46709983))
sites <- matchMotifs(pfms[["CTCF_MA0139.2"]], chr21, genome = genome,
                     out = "positions", p.cutoff = 1e-4)[[1]]
sites <- sites[!overlapsAny(sites, import(file.path(D, "hg38_blacklist.bed.gz")))]
grp <- ifelse(overlapsAny(sites, ctcf_pk), "bound (ChIP peak)",
       ifelse(overlapsAny(sites, atac_pk), "open, no ChIP peak", "closed, no ChIP peak"))
table(grp)
mean(overlapsAny(ctcf_pk[seqnames(ctcf_pk) == "chr21"], sites))   # ChIP peaks with a motif

profile <- function(s) {                                          # mean insertions, motif-oriented
  w <- promoters(resize(s, 1, fix = "center"), upstream = 100, downstream = 101)
  x <- as.matrix(Views(cov_ins, ranges(w)))
  minus <- as.logical(strand(w) == "-")
  x[minus, ] <- x[minus, ncol(x):1]
  colMeans(x)
}
fp <- data.frame(pos = rep(-100:100, 3), grp = rep(sort(unique(grp)), each = 201),
                 ins = unlist(lapply(sort(unique(grp)), function(g) profile(sites[grp == g]))))
ggplot(fp, aes(pos, ins, colour = grp)) + geom_line() +
  labs(x = "bp from CTCF motif centre", y = "Tn5 insertions per site")

b <- fp[fp$grp == "bound (ChIP peak)", ]
c(flank = mean(b$ins[abs(b$pos) >= 30 & abs(b$pos) <= 60]),
  centre = mean(b$ins[abs(b$pos) <= 10]), far = mean(b$ins[abs(b$pos) >= 90]))

How many insertions are there on chr21? How many CTCF motif sites, and what fraction of them lies in a CTCF ChIP peak? What fraction of the chr21 ChIP peaks contains a motif site?
Describe the three profiles. Compute centre/flank for the bound sites (compare with B7).
Why are the “open, no ChIP peak” sites so much lower than the bound sites, although they are in ATAC peaks?
Replace upstream = 100, downstream = 101 by a window that is not strand-aware (resize(s, 201, fix = "center") and no flipping). What happens to the profile, and why?



R8 — Tn5 sequence preference
k <- sample(length(ga), 200000)
st <- as.character(strand(ga))[k]
pos <- ifelse(st == "+", start(ga)[k] + 4, end(ga)[k] - 5)
win <- GRanges("chr21", IRanges(pos - 10, pos + 10), strand = st)
freq <- consensusMatrix(getSeq(genome, win), as.prob = TRUE)[c("A", "C", "G", "T"), ]
colnames(freq) <- -10:10
round(freq, 2)

chr21 is about 41% GC. At which positions near the insertion is the base composition clearly not random?
Why does this matter for footprints of a motif whose sequence is the same at every site?

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — chance matches and the 2×2 table (B1, B2, R3, R4)





Windows per peak ≈ \(2L\); expected matches \(\lambda = 2Lp\); \(P(\ge 1) = 1 - e^{-\lambda}\). Odds ratio \(ad/bc\); expected target matches \((a+b)(a+c)/N\). R: fisher.test, phyper with lower.tail = FALSE gives \(P(X > q)\), so use \(q = a - 1\) for \(P(X \ge a)\). matchMotifs returns a sparse peaks × motifs matrix via motifMatches().









Hint 2 — multiple testing (B3)





Bonferroni: \(p < \alpha / m\). BH: compare \(p_{(i)}\) with \(\alpha\, i / m\) and find the largest \(i\) that passes; all smaller p-values pass too. R: p.adjust.









Hint 3 — motif databases (R2, B5)





JASPAR 2024 (paper: Rauluseviciute et al. 2024); in R the JASPAR2024 package with TFBSTools::getMatrixSet. The family and class of each matrix are in tags(pfm). universalmotif::view_motifs draws and aligns logos. Other collections: CIS-BP, HOCOMOCO.









Hint 4 — chromVAR (B6, R6)





The chromVAR vignette explains addGCBias, getBackgroundPeaks, computeDeviations, deviationScores (z) and computeVariability; method in Schep et al. 2017. A negative z means the motif’s peaks are less accessible than expected in that sample, relative to matched background peaks; it says nothing about the mechanism.









Hint 5 — insertions and footprints (B7, R7, R8)





readGAlignments reads the BAM; start()/end() are the leftmost/rightmost aligned base, so the 5’ end of a − strand read is its end(). coverage of 1-bp ranges counts insertions per base; indexing an Rle with a GRanges and as.matrix gives one row per window. promoters builds strand-aware windows. Residence time and footprints: Sung et al. 2014; bias correction: TOBIAS (Bentsen et al. 2020).









Hint 6 — alignment (C1)





fastp detects and trims the Nextera adapters; bowtie2 -X 2000 allows fragments up to 2 kb; samtools fixmate -m adds the mate tags that samtools markdup needs; samtools idxstats gives reads per chromosome.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) About \(2 \times 300 = 600\) windows; \(\lambda = 600 \times 10^{-4} = 0.06\) chance matches per peak. (b) \(50\,000 \times 0.06 = 3000\). (c) \(1 - e^{-0.06} = 0.058\): about 6% of peaks contain a chance match. (d) What fraction of peaks would contain a GATA match by chance (the GATA motif is short, so at a lenient threshold this can be 10–20%), the match threshold and peak width, and above all a comparison with a background set of peaks. “25%” alone is not evidence of anything.
B2. (a)




with match
without
fraction




target
120
280
30%


background
1440
8160
15%




\(\mathrm{OR} = (120 \times 8160)/(280 \times 1440) = 979\,200 / 403\,200 = 2.43\). (c) \(400 \times 1560 / 10\,000 = 62.4\) expected; 120 observed, about twice as many. (d) \(2724 / 19\,439 = 14.0\%\) vs \(23\,440 / 192\,385 = 12.2\%\); \(\mathrm{OR} = (2724 \times 168\,945)/(16\,715 \times 23\,440) = 1.17\). Highly significant because the sets are large, but a weak effect: on this evidence EBF1 is not a major distinguishing motif. Before concluding, check a GC-matched background (EBF1’s motif is GC-rich and B-up peaks are AT-rich; with GC matching the OR rises to about 1.5, R5), the quality of the matrix, EBF1 expression, EBF1 ChIP-seq, and chromVAR (R6: the EBF1 motif is most accessible in lymphoid progenitors). EBF1 is in fact a B-cell master regulator; motif enrichment just measures it poorly here.

B3. (a) \(0.05 / 800 = 6.25 \times 10^{-5}\): four motifs pass (\(10^{-40}\), \(3 \times 10^{-12}\), \(2 \times 10^{-6}\), \(4 \times 10^{-5}\)). (b) BH thresholds \(0.05\,i/800 = 6.25 \times 10^{-5}\, i\): \(6.25 \times 10^{-5}\), \(1.25 \times 10^{-4}\), \(1.9 \times 10^{-4}\), \(2.5 \times 10^{-4}\), \(3.1 \times 10^{-4}\), \(3.75 \times 10^{-4}\), \(4.4 \times 10^{-4}\), \(5 \times 10^{-4}\). The 7th p-value (\(2.5 \times 10^{-4} \le 4.4 \times 10^{-4}\)) passes, the 8th (\(6 \times 10^{-4} > 5 \times 10^{-4}\)) does not: 7 motifs. (c) \(800 \times 0.05 = 40\). (d) Essentially one: all ETS motifs share the GGAA core, so they are 12 correlated tests of one signal (perhaps two, if PU.1-type and ETS1-type sites separate).
B4. (a) GC-rich and CpG-containing motifs: SP/KLF (GGGCGG), NRF1, E2F, ETS motifs typical of promoters (GABPA), CTCF. They are enriched in promoters against AT-rich random DNA because of composition and because promoters are open, not because they explain anything specific. (b) GC-matched peaks are also open chromatin with the same base composition, so a motif that remains enriched is more frequent in the target than composition and openness alone predict. (c) Report 0.93 (and say which background). The apparent depletion of SP1 against all peaks comes from the B-up peaks being AT-richer (distal elements) than the background, which contains many GC-rich promoters; with GC matched, SP1 is neither enriched nor depleted: no evidence for or against SP1.
B5. (a) No. SPIB, PU.1 and SPIC have nearly identical motifs (one family, one DNA-binding domain); the small differences in OR reflect the matrices, not which protein binds. (b) Expression (RNA-seq of B and T cells: PU.1 and SPIB are expressed in B cells; SPIC mainly in red-pulp macrophages), ChIP-seq or CUT&RUN for each candidate, and perturbation (knock-out or degradation followed by ATAC-seq). (c) The ETS core GGAA is shared, but the flanks differ: PU.1/SPIB prefer an A-rich 5’ flank (AAAGAGGAAGT), ETS1/GABPA prefer CCGGAAGT. T-cell-specific peaks contain ETS1-type sites, B-cell-specific peaks PU.1-type sites, and each matrix detects mostly its own subtype.
B6. (a) GATA1::TAL1: MEPs (and erythroblasts); SPI1: monocytes and B cells; CEBPA: monocytes; TCF7: CD4 T cells. (b) In monocytes, reads in peaks with a GATA motif are much less frequent than expected from the average sample and from matched background peaks: those peaks are relatively closed. It says nothing about repression: most likely no GATA factor is active in monocytes, and the peaks are open only in other cell types. (c) GATA1 and GATA3 bind the same WGATAR motif. chromVAR measures the motif, not the protein; in erythroid cells the GATA-motif peaks are open because of GATA1, whatever name the matrix carries. (d) Samples differ technically (GC bias of the library, fraction of reads in peaks); these shift all peaks with a given GC content or accessibility, motif or not. Background peaks matched on these properties move the same way, so the z-score keeps only the motif-specific part.
B7. (a) Two flanking maxima (≈ 0.7 at ±30–60 bp), a dip over the motif (≈ 0.25, the footprint), lower values further out (≈ 0.3 at ±100 bp). (b) \(0.25 / 0.70 \approx 0.36\). Without protection about 1 (a flat profile, apart from sequence bias). (c) Closed chromatin is inaccessible to Tn5 along the whole window, so there are almost no insertions (0.01 per base per site) and nothing to protect. No open region, no flanks, no dip. (d) The glucocorticoid receptor has a short residence time (about 10 s): it binds and leaves many times during tagmentation, so Tn5 mostly finds the site free. No footprint even though ChIP shows binding (Sung et al. 2014). (e) Tn5 sequence bias at the motif sequence: it is present whether or not the TF is there. Correct with a bias model (TOBIAS ATACorrect, chromBPNet), compare with naked-DNA Tn5 data, or compare bound with unbound sites of the same motif.
B8. (1) The background: random genomic regions are closed and AT-rich, so any set of open regions is enriched for the motifs of open chromatin; AP-1 is the classic motif of active enhancers. Compare with peaks that did not change (GC-matched). (2) The p-value: with thousands of peaks any small difference is significant; report the odds ratio and the fractions. (3) Causality and identity: enrichment is a correlation; the AP-1 family (FOS, JUN, ATF, BATF, …) has many members; to show that AP-1 opens the regions, measure binding (ChIP/CUT&RUN for the stimulated factor) and perturb it (inhibitor, knock-out) to see whether the peaks fail to open. chromVAR or footprinting changes are supportive, not proof.









Solutions — command line





C1. (a) 5 993 179 read pairs passed fastp; 99.65% aligned (94.5% concordantly once, 4.4% more than once). The rate is so high because the reads were selected as those ENCODE aligned to chr21 or chrM: a real full library would give a lower number, with reads from all chromosomes. After filtering (proper pairs, MAPQ ≥ 30) and duplicate removal: 504 974 reads on chr21 and 2 125 212 on chrM. (b) \(2\,125\,212 / 2\,630\,186 = 81\%\) of the filtered reads are mitochondrial. Mitochondrial DNA is not packed in nucleosomes, and a cell has hundreds of copies, so Tn5 cuts it eagerly (see ATAC-seq). Our subset exaggerates it (only chr21 of the nuclear genome is kept), but 20–50% chrM is common in full ATAC libraries. It does not matter here because we only look at insertions on chr21; it does waste sequencing depth. (c) markdup removed 8 720 088 of 11 350 274 reads (77%), most of them on the tiny chrM, where so many fragments share both ends by chance. On chr21, a PCR duplicate would count the same insertion twice: at single-base resolution this adds spikes that look like signal, so footprinting always uses deduplicated reads.









Solutions — R





R1. (a) B 4, CD4 5, CD8 5, CLP 5, CMP 8, Ery 8, GMP 7, HSC 7, LMPP 3, MEP 7, Mono 6, MPP 6, NK 6 samples (77 in all, counting technical replicates). 590 650 − 589 071 = 1579 peaks (0.3%) were lost or split in the liftOver. (b) 211 824 tested peaks; 19 439 B-up and 16 972 T-up. The block runs in about 2 minutes. Differential accessibility reports 19 404 and 16 897: the tested peaks are the same, but there the cut-off of 1 is applied to the apeglm-shrunk fold change, which pulls a few borderline peaks below it. Here we skip the shrinkage to save time.
R2. (a) 879 motifs. The largest families are zinc-finger proteins with more than 3 adjacent fingers (124), HOX (49), NK homeodomain (40), paired-related homeodomain (39), FOX (33), dispersed zinc fingers (32), Tal-related bHLH (32) and ETS (28). (b) Each column sums to 903: the matrix was built from 903 aligned sites. (c) All three have the GGAA core. PU.1 and SPIB add an A-rich 5’ flank (AAAGAGGAAGT), ETS1 prefers CC before the core (ACCGGAAGT).
R3. The matching takes about 3 minutes. (a) Median 6.4% of peaks (range 0.4–65%), close to the 5% expected by chance for a 500-bp peak at \(p = 5 \times 10^{-5}\) (\(2 \times 500 \times 5 \times 10^{-5} = 0.05\)). Most motifs are present in a few percent of peaks, real sites and chance matches together. (b) MEIS1 (65%), SP5 (55%), IKZF2 (53%), FIGLA and ZEB1 (41%). These are short matrices with little information (MEIS1: TGACAG; IKZF: GGGAA; E-box: CAGCTG). A short matrix has few distinct scores, so the score cut-off that corresponds to \(p < 5 \times 10^{-5}\) cannot be set precisely, and many windows reach it. Treat enrichment results for such motifs with extra care.
R4. (a) \(\mathrm{OR} = (8242 \times 153\,118)/(11\,197 \times 39\,267) = 2.87\), the same as fisher.test’s estimate (2.870; Fisher reports a conditional maximum-likelihood estimate, which is almost identical for large tables). fisher.test prints < 2.2e-16 because it reports p-values only down to machine precision; the true value is about \(10^{-934}\), which only the log-scale computation can represent. (b) B-up: ETS of the PU.1 type (SPIB, SPI1, SPIC), IRF/STAT (ETS–IRF composite elements and interferon-response elements), IKZF1, and POU/OCT (POU2F1/2/3, the OCT2 motif). T-up: BCL11B, ETS of the ETS1/ERG/GABPA type, IKZF3, RUNX (Runx1 OR 2.06, ETS1 OR 2.67), and further down TCF7/LEF (TCF7 OR 2.07). Both fit: PU.1, SPIB, OCT2, IRF4/8 and IKAROS are B-cell regulators; RUNX1/3, ETS1, TCF1 and BCL11B are T-cell regulators. (c) 474 (B-up) and 497 (T-up) of 879. Not useful by itself: half of all motifs, mostly redundant family members and composition effects. Rank by odds ratio and group by family. (d) B-up: EBF1 OR 1.17 (\(p \approx 10^{-13}\)), PAX5 OR 0.92 (not significant), PAX2 OR 1.92 (\(10^{-39}\)). Both are B-cell master regulators, so absence of enrichment is not absence of function. For EBF1 the effect is weak with this background (see R5); for PAX5 the JASPAR matrix MA0014.4 is short and matches only 1.8% of peaks, while the longer PAX2 matrix (same paired domain) detects the enrichment. A failed matrix, not failed biology. In T-up peaks EBF1 is clearly depleted (OR 0.50). (e) CTCF sites are open in nearly every cell type, so they are rarely differential: they are under-represented in any set of cell-type-specific peaks compared with all tested peaks (OR 0.52 and 0.63).
R5. (a) Less GC-rich: mean GC 0.476 vs 0.508 for the other tested peaks. The GC-matched set has 0.476. (b) GC-rich motifs move towards 1: SP1 0.60 → 0.94, KLF4 0.75 → 1.07, NRF1 0.39 → 0.73; their “depletion” was mostly composition. EBF1 (GC-rich motif) rises from 1.17 to 1.47. SPIB hardly changes (2.87 → 2.71) and CTCF stays depleted (0.52 → 0.58): those are not composition effects. (Exact values vary slightly with the random draw.)
R6. (a) dim(z) is 879 × 47: 47 donor × cell-type samples covering 13 cell types; computeDeviations takes about 25 s on 4 cores after the motif matching (whole block about 3 minutes). The most variable motifs are GATA (GATA1::TAL1 34, then GATA4, Gata3, GATA6, GATA2), the PU.1-type ETS motifs (SPIC, Spi1, SPIB, 14–16) and E-box motifs (ERF::FIGLA, FIGLA, ZEB1, 13–15). (b) GATA1::TAL1: MEP 77, Ery 50, CMP 37, MPP 12, negative in all lymphoid and myeloid cells. KLF1: weak (Mono 12, Ery 5): the KLF motif is GC-rich and shared with many KLF/SP factors. CEBPA: GMP 21, Mono 22. Spi1: LMPP 19, GMP 25, Mono 22, B 19; negative in MEP, Ery, T and NK. EBF1: CLP 20, B 6. TCF3 (E2A): CLP 27, LMPP 19, B 17, CD4 9. POU2F2: B 13. Runx1: LMPP 18. TCF7: CD4 11, CD8 8. TBX21: NK 21, CD8 15. CTCF: high only in GMPs (26), a pattern without an obvious biological explanation; worth checking for a technical batch. Overall, the known regulators of each lineage come out where expected. (c) Gata3 follows GATA1::TAL1 (MEP 46, Ery 27, CMP 36) and is negative in CD4 T cells (−17), where GATA3 is the active GATA factor. The motif cannot tell family members apart; in erythroid cells the open GATA sites are bound by GATA1. (d) fam["FIGLA_MA0820.2"] and BHLHE22 are “Tal-related” and ASCL1 “MyoD/ASC-related”: bHLH factors binding E-boxes (CANNTG). In blood the E-box factors are E2A (TCF3), HEB (TCF12) and E2-2 (TCF4) in lymphoid cells, and TAL1 with GATA1 in erythroid cells. TBR1 (“TBrain-related”) is a T-box motif: in blood it stands for T-bet (TBX21) and Eomes, high in NK and CD8 T cells.
R7. (a) 504 974 insertions on chr21. 15 684 CTCF motif matches at \(p < 10^{-4}\): 400 (2.6%) in a CTCF ChIP peak, 427 in an ATAC peak without ChIP peak, 14 857 in closed chromatin. 82% of the 405 chr21 ChIP peaks contain a motif match. (b) Bound sites: flanks rise to about 0.7 insertions per site at −23 and +33 bp (5-bp smoothed), a dip over the motif (about 0.2 on either side of the centre) with a narrow spike at the centre, and lower values far out. Averages: flank (30–60 bp) 0.48, centre (±10 bp) 0.34, far (≥ 90 bp) 0.20; centre/flank = 0.71 (the central spike raises the ±10-bp average; without it the dip is deeper). Open but unbound sites: flat at about 0.45, no flanks, no dip, but the same central spike. Closed sites: flat near 0.01. (c) Being in an ATAC peak only means the site lies somewhere in an open region, typically not at its centre and not bound: no protein protects it and no CTCF-positioned nucleosome-free region surrounds it. Without binding there is neither a footprint nor the flank pattern. (d) Without orientation, + and − strand sites are averaged in opposite directions: the profile becomes nearly symmetric (flank maxima at −32 and +32 instead of −23 and +33) and the dip slightly shallower (minimum 0.26 instead of 0.22). Real asymmetric features of the CTCF footprint are smeared out.
R8. (a) Positions −4 to +4 deviate most from the surroundings: C is enriched at −2 (0.37) and +3/+4 (0.34–0.35), G at +1 (0.37) and −5/−4 (0.35–0.36), A at 0 to +2 (0.28–0.30), while T is depleted at +1 (0.15) and A at −4 to −2 (0.15–0.17). Further out the composition settles at the GC-rich level of open chromatin (about 0.3 for each of C and G), above the chr21 average of 41% GC. (b) The sequence of a motif is nearly the same at every site, so Tn5’s preference for or against it repeats at every site. Averaged over thousands of sites this gives a reproducible spike or dip that has nothing to do with binding, as in the central spike of R7. Footprints must be compared with unbound sites of the same motif or corrected with a bias model.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Where this leads

HOMER and MEME do known and de novo motif enrichment from the command line: findMotifsGenome.pl b_up.bed hg38.fa out/ -size 200 -bg tested.bed, or sea --p b_up.fa --n tested.fa --m JASPAR2024.meme and streme (see the lecture).
TOBIAS corrects Tn5 bias and compares footprints between conditions: TOBIAS ATACorrect --bam atac.bam --genome hg38.fa --peaks peaks.bed, then ScoreBigwig and BINDetect --motifs JASPAR.meme.
chromVAR on single cells (ArchR, Signac) gives each cell a motif z-score; the same idea as R6 with cells as columns.
ChIP-seq, CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag measure the binding of one TF directly and give the ground truth that motifs and footprints only suggest.
How a CNN reads DNA shows that a convolutional filter is a motif scanner, and models like chromBPNet learn motifs and Tn5 bias from the sequence.

title: Quiz: motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined.

Heinz et al. 2010, Mol Cell. Simple combinations of lineage-determining transcription factors prime cis-regulatory elements required for macrophage and B cell identities.
Bailey et al. 2015, Nucleic Acids Res. The MEME Suite.
Rauluseviciute et al. 2024, Nucleic Acids Res. JASPAR 2024: 20th anniversary of the open-access database of transcription factor binding profiles.
Schep et al. 2017, Nat Methods. chromVAR: inferring transcription-factor-associated accessibility from single-cell epigenomic data.
Sung et al. 2014, Mol Cell. DNase footprint signatures are dictated by factor dynamics and DNA sequence.
Bentsen et al. 2020, Nat Commun. ATAC-seq footprinting unravels kinetics of transcription factor binding during zygotic genome activation.

Short questions on motif matches, enrichment, chromVAR and footprints. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. You scan 200-bp peaks for a motif at a match threshold of \(p = 10^{-4}\). How many chance matches do you expect per peak, and in 20 000 peaks?






Hint





Count the windows on both strands.









Answer





About \(2 \times 200 = 400\) windows per peak, so \(400 \times 10^{-4} = 0.04\) chance matches per peak, and about \(0.04 \times 20\,000 = 800\) in 20 000 peaks. A motif in 4% of peaks is therefore what chance alone gives.




Q2. 1000 target peaks, 200 with a match; 9000 background peaks, 900 with a match. Compute the odds ratio and the number of target matches expected under the null.






Hint





\(\mathrm{OR} = ad / bc\). Under the null the target is a random draw from all 10 000 peaks.









Answer





\(a = 200, b = 800, c = 900, d = 8100\). \(\mathrm{OR} = (200 \times 8100) / (800 \times 900) = 1\,620\,000 / 720\,000 = 2.25\). Expected: \(1000 \times 1100 / 10\,000 = 110\); observed 200, so the motif is enriched (20% vs 10%). The p-value comes from Fisher’s exact test, equivalently the hypergeometric distribution.




Q3. You test 900 motifs. What p-value threshold does Bonferroni give at 5%? Why is “612 motifs significant at FDR 5%” from 20 000 target peaks not a useful result on its own?






Answer





\(0.05 / 900 \approx 5.6 \times 10^{-5}\). With 20 000 target peaks, tiny differences in motif frequency become significant, and motifs of one family (and GC-rich or AT-rich motifs) are counted many times over. Rank by effect size (odds ratio, fractions with a match), group motifs by family, and check the background.




Q4. Peaks that gain accessibility after a treatment are compared with random genomic windows, and CTCF, SP1 and NRF1 motifs come out as highly enriched. Is the treatment acting through these TFs? What background would you use instead?






Answer





Probably not. These motifs are typical of open chromatin and GC-rich promoters in general; random genomic windows are mostly closed and AT-rich, so any set of peaks is “enriched” for them. Use peaks that did not change (all tested peaks) as background, ideally GC-matched. Then CTCF in particular usually comes out depleted, because its sites are open in every condition.




Q5. The top motifs in B-cell-specific peaks are SPIB, SPI1 (PU.1) and SPIC, all ETS factors with nearly the same motif. Which TF binds? How would you find out?






Answer





The motif cannot tell: family members share a DNA-binding domain and motif. Check which family members are expressed (RNA-seq of the same cells; in B cells both PU.1 and SPIB are), and measure binding directly (ChIP-seq or CUT&RUN for the candidates), or perturb them (knock-out, degradation) and see which peaks close.




Q6. In a chromVAR analysis the motif GATA1::TAL1 has z = +60 in erythroblasts and z = −20 in B cells. What does each value mean?






Answer





In erythroblasts, reads in peaks with the GATA motif are far more frequent than expected from the average sample and from background peaks with the same GC content and accessibility: GATA-motif peaks are specifically open, consistent with GATA1 activity. In B cells they are less accessible than expected relative to background peaks. A negative z says nothing about mechanism: it does not mean that a GATA factor represses those peaks in B cells, only that they are relatively closed.




Q7. Why does chromVAR compare each motif with background peaks matched for GC content and average accessibility?






Answer





Samples differ technically: one library may have more reads in GC-rich peaks (PCR) or in strong peaks (better signal-to-noise). These effects would change the reads in a motif’s peaks without any change in TF activity. Background peaks with the same GC and accessibility are affected in the same way, so standardising against them (the z-score) removes the technical part.




Q8. An aggregate ATAC-seq profile around 2000 bound CTCF motif sites shows about 0.8 insertions per site at ±30 bp, 0.3 over the motif, and 0.4 at ±100 bp. Sketch it and name the features. What would the profile look like at 2000 CTCF motif sites in closed chromatin?






Answer





Two flanking peaks at ±30 bp (open, nucleosome-free DNA next to the bound protein), a dip over the motif (the footprint: CTCF blocks Tn5), and a lower level further out (decreasing accessibility towards the nucleosomes). Centre/flank \(\approx 0.3/0.8 \approx 0.4\). At closed sites: flat and close to zero, because Tn5 hardly inserts in closed chromatin. There is no peak to have a footprint in.




Q9. A narrow 2-bp spike in the middle of a footprint is seen at bound sites and equally at unbound sites with the same motif. What is it, and how is it handled?






Answer





Tn5 sequence bias: Tn5 prefers to insert at certain sequences, and the motif has the same sequence at every site, so the preference repeats at every site and adds up in the aggregate. It is not caused by the protein. Correct by comparing with insertions expected from sequence alone (Tn5 on naked DNA, a k-mer bias model as in TOBIAS ATACorrect, or a learned bias model as in chromBPNet), or always compare bound with unbound sites of the same motif.




Q10. “ChIP-seq shows that the glucocorticoid receptor binds 5000 sites, but ATAC-seq shows no footprint at them, so the ChIP-seq peaks must be false.” Is the conclusion justified?






Answer





No. A footprint needs the TF to occupy the site for a large part of the tagmentation reaction. Factors with short residence times (seconds), such as the glucocorticoid receptor, bind and leave quickly, so Tn5 mostly finds the site free and no dip forms, although the TF binds and opens the region (Sung et al. 2014). Absence of a footprint is not evidence of absence of binding.

title: Gene regulation
text:
About this lecture
Chromatin marks tell you where the regulatory DNA is. This lecture is about what that DNA is and who reads it: short sequence elements (promoters, enhancers, silencers, insulators) and the sequence-specific transcription factors (TFs) that bind them.

The cis-regulatory code: core promoters, enhancers, silencers, insulators.
Transcription factors: DNA-binding domains, and motifs written as position weight matrices.
Why a TF binds only a small fraction of its motif matches: accessibility, pioneer factors, cooperation.
Combinatorial control: the B-cell TFs behind the GM12878 data.
How all of this shows up in ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq, Hi-C and motif analysis.


Students know transcription and “a TF binds a promoter” from their bachelor’s, and from What is epigenetics? they know the six histone marks and that open chromatin is nucleosome-depleted. This unit supplies the sequence side: what the regulatory elements are, how a TF recognises DNA, and how to write that down as a matrix one can scan a genome with. The running example is GM12878, the B-lymphoblastoid cell line used throughout the course: we look at its CTCF peaks, its ATAC peaks and an enhancer cluster at PAX5, the master regulator of B-cell identity. Every later assay unit measures one of the things introduced here.

title: Gene regulation
text:
The cis-regulatory code


A gene’s expression is set by short DNA elements in cis (on the same molecule): the core promoter, enhancers that activate, silencers that repress, and insulators that delimit their reach.
Each element is a cluster of TF binding sites, typically 6–20 bp each, in a stretch of a few hundred bp.
The proteins that read them (TFs, co-factors) act in trans: they are encoded elsewhere and diffuse to their sites.


The cis/trans distinction comes from genetics: a cis-acting mutation affects only the allele on the same chromosome, a trans-acting one (in a TF gene) affects both alleles. Most variants associated with disease in genome-wide association studies are non-coding and fall in enhancers, so this code matters for human genetics too. Scale: a promoter’s core is about 80 bp; an enhancer a few hundred bp; the regulatory domain of a gene can be up to a megabase, usually bounded by CTCF sites (insulators). ENCODE lists close to a million candidate cis-regulatory elements in the human genome, against about 20 000 protein-coding genes: most genes have several enhancers.

title: Gene regulation
text:
The first enhancer (1981)


A 72-bp repeat from the SV40 virus raised transcription of a β-globin gene on the same plasmid about 200-fold.
It worked in either orientation, upstream or downstream, and kilobases away from the start site (1.4 kb upstream, 3.3 kb downstream).
This defines an enhancer: a DNA element that activates transcription from a distance, independent of orientation.


Banerji, Rusconi and Schaffner transfected HeLa cells with a rabbit β-globin gene and measured correctly initiated transcripts by S1 mapping. On its own the plasmid gave barely detectable transcripts; with SV40 DNA in cis, 200 times more, and the activity mapped to the 72-bp repeat. The bars in the figure are schematic: the paper reports the 200-fold enhancement and that the element acted “in either orientation at many positions”. The key word is cis: SV40 DNA on a separate plasmid did nothing. The same year a polyoma virus element gave the same result, and within two years the first cellular enhancer was found in the immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus, in B cells, which fits our running example. Reporter assays like this one are still the standard functional test; today they are run in parallel on thousands of fragments (massively parallel reporter assays, STARR-seq).

title: Gene regulation
text:
The core promoter


The core promoter (about −40 to +40 around the transcription start site, TSS) is where RNA polymerase II and the general transcription factors assemble the pre-initiation complex.
Known elements: TATA box (about −30, bound by TBP), Initiator (Inr, at the TSS), DPE, BRE. Each promoter has only some of them; a minority have a TATA box.
The core promoter decides where transcription starts and in which direction. How often it starts is set mostly by TFs at proximal sites and enhancers.


The general transcription factors (TFIID, which contains the TATA-binding protein TBP and about 13 TAF subunits, plus TFIIA, B, E, F and H) are present in every cell; they are not what makes a gene cell-type specific. The core elements are short and degenerate, so you cannot find promoters by searching for TATA boxes: only a minority of human promoters (often quoted as 10–20%) have one, mostly highly regulated tissue-specific genes. Letters in the consensus sequences are IUPAC codes (W = A or T, R = A or G, Y = C or T, S = C or G). In practice, promoters are mapped from the data: 5’ ends of transcripts (CAGE), H3K4me3, and the GENCODE annotation you used in Genomic intervals. Review: Haberle and Stark 2018.

title: Gene regulation
text:
Two kinds of promoters


CpG observed/expected around all 19 989 protein-coding TSSs: two populations. About half are CpG-island promoters (52% by a strict cutoff), the rest are CpG-poor.
CpG-island promoters: housekeeping and developmental genes, broad TSS, rarely a TATA box, kept unmethylated. 78% carry H3K4me3 in GM12878.
Non-CpG promoters: often tissue-specific, sharper TSS, more TATA boxes. Only 31% are marked in a B-cell line.


CpG observed/expected is the number of CG dinucleotides divided by (number of C × number of G / length): about 0.2–0.25 in bulk human DNA because methylated CpGs mutate to TpG over evolution; near 1 in CpG islands, which escaped methylation in the germline. The cutoff (o/e > 0.6 and GC > 55%, over ±500 bp) is a strict version of the classic Gardiner-Garden and Frommer definition; looser definitions give 55–70% CGI promoters. The H3K4me3 colouring shows why the two classes matter for epigenomics: CpG-island promoters are marked in most cell types (CFP1 binds unmethylated CpG and recruits the H3K4 methyltransferase), while non-CpG promoters are marked only where the gene is used. Silencing differs too: CpG-island promoters of developmental genes are silenced by Polycomb (H3K27me3), and stably by DNA methylation in, for example, X inactivation and cancer. Made with make-generegulation-figs.R.

title: Gene regulation
text:
Promoters are bidirectional


A promoter’s nucleosome-depleted region usually contains two core promoters facing away from each other.
The sense transcript becomes the mRNA. The antisense transcript (PROMPT or upstream antisense RNA) is short, terminated early and degraded by the RNA exosome.
When both directions are productive you get a head-to-head gene pair sharing one promoter region.


Divergent transcription was found by sequencing nascent RNA (GRO-seq) and RNA in cells lacking the nuclear exosome (Preker et al. 2008). The asymmetry comes from sequence downstream of each TSS: the sense direction has 5’ splice sites (U1 snRNP binding suppresses early termination), the antisense direction has early polyadenylation signals. Relevance for the course: an ATAC-seq peak at a promoter is a single NDR, but it hosts two initiation sites, and H3K4me3 and H3K27ac are found on both sides of it (the bimodal shape in the next units). Enhancers show the same bidirectional initiation, which leads to the eRNAs a few slides on.

title: Gene regulation
section: Enhancers can act from far away
text:
Enhancers can act from far away


The ZRS controls SHH in the developing limb from about 1 Mb away, inside an intron of LMBR1, across a gene desert.
Single-base changes in the ZRS cause extra digits (preaxial polydactyly); deleting it in mice abolishes Shh expression in the limb: limbs without digits, an otherwise normal animal.
Lesson: the nearest gene is often not the target. Enhancers are tissue-specific modules; one gene can have many, each for one tissue or stage.


The ZRS (zone of polarising activity regulatory sequence) is the textbook long-range enhancer (Lettice et al. 2003; Sagai et al. 2005). It shows three features at once: distance (about 1 Mb in human), position inside another gene whose expression it does not control, and modularity: SHH has other enhancers for the brain, the gut and the notochord, and only the limb one is lost in these mutants, so the phenotype is restricted to the limbs. This is why “nearest gene” assignment of peaks, which students did in Genomic intervals, is only a first guess. Linking enhancers to genes properly uses 3D contacts (Hi-C, the 3D genome units), correlation across samples, and perturbation (CRISPRi), the topic of the integration unit. Coordinates in the figure are hg38 from GENCODE; the ZRS position is approximate.

title: Gene regulation
section: How an enhancer reaches its promoter
text:
How an enhancer reaches its promoter


The DNA between enhancer and promoter loops out, so that proteins bound at both meet in 3D.
TFs on the enhancer bind co-activators such as Mediator, which contacts RNA polymerase II at the promoter. Cohesin extrudes and holds loops.
Active enhancers are themselves transcribed: short, bidirectional enhancer RNAs (eRNAs), a sign of activity used to map enhancers.


The looping model is supported by chromosome conformation capture (3C, Hi-C, Micro-C) and microscopy, and by experiments where forcing a loop (tethering a protein that self-associates) activates a gene. It is not the whole story: imaging often shows enhancer and promoter several hundred nm apart even when the gene is on, and some models propose transcriptional “hubs” or condensates in which many TFs and co-activators are concentrated. Mediator is a complex of about 30 subunits; it binds activation domains of TFs and Pol II. eRNAs were found by Kim et al. 2010; FANTOM5 (Andersson et al. 2014) used bidirectional CAGE signal to define about 43 000 active enhancers across human cell types. Whether eRNAs have a function or are a by-product is debated; as a marker they are very useful. Loops and cohesin come back in the 3D genome units.

title: Gene regulation
text:
Enhancer states and their marks


Primed: H3K4me1, a pioneer TF may be bound, little accessibility. Active: open core with TFs, H3K4me1 and H3K27ac, eRNAs. Poised (in stem cells): H3K4me1 with H3K27me3.
The core is a nucleosome-depleted region of a few hundred bp; the marks sit on the flanking nucleosomes.
This is why “H3K27ac peak, distal to a TSS, no H3K4me3” is the standard working definition of an active enhancer.


This connects the marks table of What is epigenetics? to enhancer biology. Creyghton et al. 2010 and Rada-Iglesias et al. 2011 showed that H3K27ac separates active from primed or poised enhancers carrying H3K4me1. The poised state (H3K4me1 + H3K27me3) is mostly described in embryonic stem cells, at developmental enhancers that become active upon differentiation. The marks are correlates of activity, not proof of function (the cause-or-consequence slide in What is epigenetics?): only a fraction of H3K27ac-marked elements activate a reporter, and some functional enhancers carry little H3K27ac. The definition H3K27ac minus H3K4me3, away from TSSs, is the one students used to build an enhancer set in Genomic intervals. In the table, “weak” ATAC means accessible in some cells or partly: primed enhancers often give small peaks.

title: Gene regulation
section: Real data: an enhancer cluster at PAX5
text:
Real data: an enhancer cluster at PAX5


PAX5 is the master regulator of B-cell identity. In GM12878, 500 kb around PAX5 contain 91 ATAC peaks and 71 H3K27ac peaks, most of them far from any TSS, many inside the neighbouring gene ZCCHC7.
H3K4me1 is broad over the whole cluster; H3K27ac and ATAC mark the active cores; H3K4me3 marks the PAX5 promoter (and, weakly, some strong enhancers).


ENCODE fold-change tracks (500-bp bins, maximum per bin) and ATAC IDR peaks from GM12878, plotted by make-generegulation-figs.R. PAX5 is on the minus strand, so its promoter is at the right end of the gene, near 37.03 Mb; the gene extends to the left beyond the window. Many of the active elements lie inside ZCCHC7; which gene each one regulates cannot be read from these tracks (the problem of the ZRS slide again), it needs contact or perturbation data. CTCF peaks are few and sharp: they mark boundaries and loop anchors, not enhancers. Point out the scales: H3K27ac reaches 100-fold enrichment, H3K4me1 only 20-fold, because H3K4me1 is spread over many nucleosomes. Weak H3K4me3 at very active enhancers is normal; it is a reason not to define promoters by H3K4me3 alone.

title: Gene regulation
section: “Super-enhancers”: a useful ranking, a contested category
text:
“Super-enhancers”: a useful ranking, a contested category


Stitch distal H3K27ac peaks within 12.5 kb, rank by total signal, and cut where the curve turns up: 929 regions (6%) hold 45% of the signal in GM12878. They sit near B-cell genes (ETV6, PLCG2, BCL2, PAX5 …).
Whyte et al. 2013 called such regions super-enhancers and proposed they drive cell identity genes.
Critique: the cutoff is arbitrary on a continuous distribution, and dissected super-enhancers often behave as several ordinary enhancers adding up. Use the ranking, be careful with the category.


The method (ROSE) stitches enhancer peaks within 12.5 kb, excludes peaks near TSSs, ranks stitched regions by signal (originally Mediator or H3K27ac ChIP), and draws the cutoff where a line of slope 1 touches the normalised curve. Our version uses H3K27ac peaks and fold-change bigWig signal, so numbers differ from published lists. The biology behind it is real: genes with large, highly active enhancer clusters tend to be cell identity genes and oncogenes, and those clusters are sensitive to BET inhibitors (BRD4) and to loss of Mediator. The critique (Pott and Lieb 2015; Hay et al. 2016 on the α-globin locus) is that there is no evidence for a distinct class with emergent properties: the distribution has no gap, and deleting individual constituents mostly gives additive effects. Read “super-enhancer” as “the top of a ranking of enhancer clusters”.

title: Gene regulation
text:
Silencers and insulators


Silencers bind repressors that recruit co-repressors (HDACs, histone methyltransferases). Example: REST binds the RE1 element and silences neuronal genes in non-neuronal cells.
Insulators delimit where regulation acts: enhancer-blocking (an enhancer cannot activate a promoter on the other side) and barrier (heterochromatin cannot spread past).
In vertebrates most insulator activity depends on CTCF.


Silencers are much less catalogued than enhancers, partly because a loss of function is harder to measure than a gain; recent screens suggest some elements act as enhancers in one cell type and silencers in another. The classic vertebrate insulator is the chicken β-globin HS4 element: its enhancer-blocking activity needs a CTCF site (Bell, West and Felsenfeld 1999), its barrier activity other proteins. A beautiful human example combines CTCF and DNA methylation: at the H19/IGF2 imprinting control region CTCF binds only the unmethylated maternal allele and blocks the shared enhancers from reaching IGF2; on the methylated paternal allele CTCF cannot bind and IGF2 is expressed. We return to methylation-sensitive binding a few slides on.

title: Gene regulation
text:
CTCF and loop extrusion


Cohesin loads on DNA and extrudes a growing loop until it meets CTCF bound in the right orientation.
Loops form between convergent CTCF sites (motifs pointing towards each other): about 90% of loops with a CTCF motif at both anchors in high-resolution Hi-C. Flip one site and the loop is lost.
The result: insulated domains (TADs) in which enhancers find their promoters more easily than across the boundary.


CTCF has 11 zinc fingers and binds a long (about 20 bp) asymmetric motif, so each site has an orientation; the N-terminus of CTCF faces the loop and stops cohesin coming from that side. Rao et al. 2014 found that loop anchors are mostly convergent pairs of CTCF motifs; inverting a single CTCF site with CRISPR re-wires the loop (de Wit et al. 2015; Guo et al. 2015). Removing CTCF or cohesin acutely (degron experiments) erases most TADs and loops but changes the expression of surprisingly few genes in the short term, a reminder that boundaries are one layer among several. This slide sets up the 3D genome units and the motif-strand question in the exercise. GM12878 has about 44 000 CTCF peaks in the file we use.

title: Gene regulation
text:
Transcription factors


A TF has a DNA-binding domain (DBD) that reads a short motif, and effector domains that recruit co-activators or co-repressors.
Humans have about 1600 TFs, classified by DBD family; half are C2H2 zinc fingers. Members of one family bind similar motifs.
About a quarter still have no known motif.


Numbers from Lambert et al. 2018, a manually curated census (1639 TFs; the counts in the figure are from its database). Each DBD family has a typical motif shape: bHLH factors bind the E-box CANNTG as dimers, bZIP factors palindromes, homeodomains TAAT cores, ETS factors GGAA cores (PU.1 is an ETS factor), forkheads TGTTTAC. Many paralogues share nearly identical motifs, so a motif match rarely tells you which family member binds: an ETS motif in a peak could be PU.1, ETS1, ELF1 or FLI1. Activation domains are mostly intrinsically disordered, acidic or rich in glutamine or proline. The KRAB zinc fingers (344 in the database) mostly silence transposable elements by recruiting KAP1/TRIM28 and SETDB1, which writes H3K9me3; this is the H3K9me3 at ZNF clusters seen in What is epigenetics?.

title: Gene regulation
text:
A motif as a matrix


Align known binding sites, count each base at each position, add a pseudocount, divide to get frequencies p_{b,j}.
The log-odds weight of base b at position j against a background q_b: \;w_{b,j} = \log_2 \dfrac{p_{b,j}}{q_b}. Positive: preferred; negative: disfavoured.
The pseudocount keeps unseen bases from getting -\infty: with only 8 sites, “never seen” does not mean “impossible”.


This is the position weight matrix (PWM), the standard representation of a TF motif (Stormo 2000; Wasserman and Sandelin 2004). The example is an ETS-type site with the GGAA core that PU.1 binds. Walk through one column: column 1 has 6 G, 1 A, 1 C, 0 T. With a pseudocount of 1 per base and 8 sites the frequencies are 7/12, 2/12, 2/12 and 1/12; against a uniform background of 0.25, G scores log2(0.583/0.25) = +1.2 and T scores log2(0.083/0.25) = −1.6. Pseudocount choices vary (JASPAR tools use 0.8 in total, others 1 per base or a fraction proportional to the background); the more sites, the less it matters. A real background is not uniform: the human genome is 41% GC, so q(G) = q(C) ≈ 0.2 and q(A) = q(T) ≈ 0.3. The exercise builds a matrix like this by hand.

title: Gene regulation
text:
Scanning a sequence


The score of a window is the sum of the weights of its bases. Slide the window along the sequence, on both strands (the reverse complement).
A score above a threshold is a match (a predicted site). Tools set the threshold from a p-value: the chance that a random window scores as high.
Summing log-odds assumes the positions contribute independently. Usually a good approximation; dinucleotide models and neural networks relax it.


The second match in the figure only appears on the minus strand: the top strand reads ACTTCC, whose reverse complement is GGAAGT. A scanner reports it with strand “−”, and the motif then points to the left on the genome; this matters for CTCF orientation. The best possible score is the sum of the column maxima (8.4 here); the worst is the sum of the minima. Tools such as FIMO (MEME suite), HOMER, motifmatchr and Biostrings::matchPWM compute an exact p-value per score from the matrix and the background. With p < 1e-4 per window and strand, about 200 windows per Mb pass the threshold by chance, which is the topic of the next slides. The independence assumption fails for some TFs (e.g. flexible spacing in dimers); this is part of why convolutional neural networks, which learn motifs from data, outperform PWMs (machine-learning units).

title: Gene regulation
text:
Information content and sequence logos


Information content of a column (uniform background): \;IC_j = 2 + \sum_b p_{b,j} \log_2 p_{b,j} bits. 2 bits: one base only; 0 bits: all four equally likely.
A sequence logo draws each column as a stack of height IC_j, each letter scaled by its frequency.
CTCF (JASPAR MA0139.2, from 913 ChIP-seq sites): 15 positions, 16.1 bits in total; the core CCA·…AGGGGGC carries most of it.


Information content is the reduction in uncertainty compared with a random base (2 bits for DNA). Column 3 of CTCF (C in 903 of 913 sites) has 1.9 bits; column 1 only 0.34. The total information content gives a rule of thumb for how often a motif occurs by chance: roughly once every 2^IC bp per strand, so 2^16 ≈ 70 000 bp for a high-scoring CTCF match. JASPAR is the open database of curated TF matrices (2024 release: Rauluseviciute et al.); CIS-BP, HOCOMOCO and the HOMER and MEME collections are alternatives. Logo made with universalmotif in make-generegulation-figs.R. Note that this matrix was derived from ChIP-seq peaks, so it describes in vivo binding sites, including bias from the experiment; other matrices come from in vitro assays (SELEX, protein-binding microarrays).

title: Gene regulation
text:
How many matches by chance?


At a p-value threshold p, a sequence of length L has about \;2 L p\; matches by chance (two strands).
chr21 (40 Mb of sequence): 8583 CTCF matches at p < 10^{-4}, close to the 8018 expected by chance. Genome-wide, about 600 000 are expected.
GM12878 has 44 217 CTCF peaks. Even a long, informative motif has far more matches than bound sites.


Log scale on the y axis. This is the point of the slide: motif matches are cheap. A 6-bp exact word occurs once every 4^6 = 4096 bp per strand, about 500 times per Mb on both strands; a typical TF motif with 10–12 bits of information occurs thousands of times per Mb at usual thresholds. The observed counts are close to the expectation because the expectation is computed from the matrix itself with a uniform background, and chr21 is not uniform (41% GC); at stricter thresholds the observed count exceeds the expected one, partly because real CTCF sites are enriched (there are a few hundred bound sites on chr21) and partly because of base composition and repeats. Numbers computed in make-generegulation-figs.R with motifmatchr (exercise R7).

title: Gene regulation
section: Real data: CTCF peaks contain the CTCF motif
text:
Real data: CTCF peaks contain the CTCF motif


Of 200 bp around each CTCF summit, 78% contain a match (p < 10^{-4}), against 8% of GC-matched genomic windows and 9% of the same sequences shuffled.
The stronger the peak, the more likely the motif: 62% of the weakest quarter, 92% of the strongest.
Weak peaks without a motif: indirect binding, weaker motif variants, or noise.


Three backgrounds: random genomic windows (4%), windows matched to the GC content of the peaks (8%, because the CTCF motif is GC-rich and so occurs more often in GC-rich DNA), and the peak sequences shuffled so that each keeps its dinucleotide composition (9%). The GC-matched background is the fair one; a random-genome background would overstate the enrichment by a factor of two. This is exactly the issue of the null from the shuffle test in Genomic intervals: here the null must match sequence composition. HOMER uses GC-matched genomic background, MEME/SEA shuffled sequences. The strong dependence on peak strength is typical of ChIP-seq of a direct DNA binder and is a quality check: if the strongest peaks of your TF ChIP do not contain its motif, worry about the antibody.

title: Gene regulation
section: Real data: the motif sits at the summit
text:
Real data: the motif sits at the summit


Position of the best CTCF match in 500 bp around each summit: a sharp peak at 0. 94% of best matches are within 50 bp of the summit (median distance 6 bp).
In GC-matched background windows the best matches are spread evenly.
Centrality is strong evidence that the motif is what the TF binds; tools such as CentriMo use it as a test.


The summit is the position with the most ChIP fragments, which pile up symmetrically around the protein’s binding position, so a directly bound motif should be at the summit within the precision of the experiment (tens of bp). A motif that is enriched in peaks but spread evenly over them suggests a partner factor or a sequence bias of the region, not the immunoprecipitated TF itself. The same plot centred on ATAC-seq summits is noisier, because an ATAC peak can contain several TFs. Only peaks with a match contribute (81% of peaks within ±250 bp; 17% of the 500-bp background windows have one). The exercise reproduces this histogram on 5000 peaks.

title: Gene regulation
section: Most motif matches are not bound
text:
Most motif matches are not bound


Of the 8583 CTCF matches on chr21, only 369 (4.3%) lie in a GM12878 CTCF peak, although CTCF is one of the most motif-driven TFs.
Matches in accessible DNA (ATAC peaks) are bound 39% of the time, matches elsewhere 2%. The best-scoring quarter of matches is bound 12% of the time, the rest under 2%.
Conversely, 79% of chr21 CTCF peaks have a match: the motif is nearly necessary, far from sufficient.


This is the central quantitative message of the lecture. Accessibility and binding are not independent (CTCF binding itself creates an ATAC peak), so the 39% is not a causal estimate; but the asymmetry is the general pattern. For most TFs the fraction of bound matches is far lower than for CTCF, often well under 1%. The reasons are on the next slide. A consequence for analysis: predicting binding from sequence alone fails; combining sequence with accessibility (as chromVAR and many ML models do) works much better. Numbers from make-generegulation-figs.R; the exercise recomputes them (R7).

title: Gene regulation
section: Why a motif is bound or not
text:
Why a motif is bound or not


Nucleosomes: most TFs cannot bind a motif wrapped on a histone octamer. DNA methylation: some TFs, CTCF among them, do not bind a motif with a methylated CpG.
Cooperativity: TFs that bind next to each other stabilise each other, so a weak site is bound when a partner is there.
TF concentration and competition with other proteins set how many sites are occupied.


Each panel is a determinant that explains part of the gap on the previous slide. Nucleosomes: DNA on the octamer is bent and one face is blocked; access needs a pioneer factor or a remodeller (next slide). Methylation: the CTCF motif often contains CpGs (positions 13–14 of the JASPAR consensus GCCACCAGGGGGCGC); methylation there blocks binding, as at the H19 imprinting control region. Methyl-CpG can also increase binding for some TFs (the methyl-SELEX work of Yin et al. 2017). Cooperativity can be direct (protein–protein contacts, e.g. PU.1 with IRF4 or IRF8 on composite ETS–IRF elements in B cells) or indirect, through competition with the same nucleosome. TF concentration: a TF at higher levels occupies weaker sites; this is how dosage-sensitive TFs act.

title: Gene regulation
text:
Pioneer factors open closed chromatin


Pioneer factors bind their motif on nucleosomal DNA, recruit remodellers (SWI/SNF/BAF), and make the site accessible for other TFs.
Classic example: FOXA1/FOXA2 in liver; its forkhead domain resembles linker histone H1. In B cells PU.1 and EBF1 act as pioneers.
Pioneers set up competence: which enhancers can become active in a lineage. Signal-dependent TFs (NF-κB, steroid receptors) mostly bind where pioneers already opened the chromatin.


Zaret and Carroll 2011 is the review. FOXA binds its site on the nucleosome surface and can open compacted chromatin in vitro without ATP-dependent remodellers (Cirillo et al. 2002), though in cells it works with remodellers. Pioneering is a spectrum, not a binary class: many TFs can bind partial motifs on nucleosomes to some degree. The definition is operational: a TF that binds closed chromatin and is needed for its opening. PU.1 opens thousands of sites in macrophages and B cells (Heinz et al. 2010); EBF1 opens chromatin at B-cell genes during B-cell commitment (Boller et al. 2016). The steps in the figure map onto assays: step 1 has a ChIP peak but little ATAC; step 3 has ATAC, H3K27ac and other TFs. For the ML units: pioneers are exactly where sequence alone predicts accessibility best.

title: Gene regulation
text:
Combinatorial control: the B-cell example


B-cell identity rests on a few TFs: PU.1 and E2A induce EBF1, EBF1 and PAX5 activate each other and the B-cell programme, PAX5 represses other lineages.
An enhancer is active only with the right combination of TFs. PU.1 is in both B cells and macrophages, but binds different sites with different partners.
Combinations of ~1600 TFs give far more cell types than single TFs could.


The hierarchy is from mouse genetics: mice without E2A or EBF1 have no B cells, and Pax5-deficient pro-B cells can still become macrophages or T cells, so PAX5 is the commitment factor (Nutt et al. 1999). PAX5 targets include CD19 and CD79A (activated) and CSF1R (repressed). Heinz et al. 2010 is the key paper on the right panel: PU.1 binds tens of thousands of sites in macrophages and in B cells, but largely different ones, next to C/EBP motifs in macrophages and EBF/E2A/OCT motifs in B cells; collaboratively they choose which sites become enhancers. GM12878 is an Epstein–Barr-virus-transformed B cell, so in addition to the B-cell factors it has very active NF-κB and IRF4 (EBV activates them), relevant when you look at its motif enrichment.

title: Gene regulation
section: Real data: B-cell motifs in GM12878 open chromatin
text:
Real data: B-cell motifs in GM12878 open chromatin


Distal ATAC peaks (summit more than 2 kb from a protein-coding TSS), 200 bp around the summit, against GC-matched genomic windows.
IRF4 (3.4×), CTCF (2.6×) and PU.1 (1.8×) motifs are the most enriched; OCT2, RUNX3 and EBF1 modestly (1.3–1.4×). Motifs of liver and erythroid TFs (HNF4A, FOXA1, GATA1) are not (≈1×).
The open chromatin of a cell type tells you its TFs: the basis of motif enrichment analysis and chromVAR.


Numbers next to the bars are the fraction of peaks with a match and the fraction of background windows with a match; 116 758 distal peaks of 155 151. Enrichments of 1.3–3-fold are typical: each motif occurs in only a minority of peaks, and many matches in either set are chance hits. IRF4 at the top fits an EBV-transformed B cell, where EBV drives IRF4; IRF and PU.1 motifs also occur together as composite ETS–IRF elements. Two honest caveats: PAX5’s JASPAR matrix is short (8 bp) and captures only part of its long bipartite site, so its enrichment is underestimated; and MEF2B, a germinal-centre B-cell TF, is depleted, a reminder that motif enrichment depends on the matrix, the background and the window, and that absence of enrichment does not mean absence of function. Formal motif enrichment (HOMER, MEME-SEA, chromVAR) and footprinting are taught in Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting; here the point is qualitative. Made with motifmatchr and JASPAR 2024 matrices in make-generegulation-figs.R.

title: Gene regulation
text:
Co-activators turn binding into activity


Activation domains recruit p300/CBP, which acetylates H3K27 (and TFs): the H3K27ac you map at active enhancers and promoters.
BRD4 reads acetyl-lysine with its bromodomains and, with Mediator, helps recruit and release RNA polymerase II.
Repressors recruit the opposite: HDACs, Polycomb, H3K9 methyltransferases.


This closes the loop with the writers/readers/erasers framing of What is epigenetics?: TF binding at a sequence leads to the writing of a mark (H3K27ac by p300/CBP), which is read by BRD4, which helps the transcription machinery. It also explains why H3K27ac is such a good marker of active enhancers, and why p300 ChIP-seq was one of the first ways enhancers were mapped (Visel et al. 2009). Drugs: BET inhibitors (JQ1) displace BRD4 and hit super-enhancer-driven oncogenes such as MYC; p300/CBP inhibitors and degraders are in development. Pol II often pauses about 50 bp downstream of the TSS; release requires P-TEFb, which BRD4 recruits. Repressive co-factors are the other half: HDAC-containing complexes, Polycomb (H3K27me3) and SETDB1 (H3K9me3).

title: Gene regulation
text:
From mechanism to assay


ATAC-seq finds the open, TF-bound cores of promoters, enhancers and CTCF sites. ChIP-seq of a TF finds its bound sites, motif at the summit.
Histone ChIP / CUT&Tag shows the marks on flanking nucleosomes. Hi-C shows the loops between CTCF sites and between enhancers and promoters.
Motif analysis links the peaks back to the TFs that explain them.


This is the map for the rest of the course. Each assay sees one layer of what we discussed: accessibility (a consequence of TF binding), the TF itself, the co-activator footprint as histone marks, and the 3D contacts. A useful exercise for students is to predict, for an element of their choice, what each track should look like, and then check it in the data. Note the bimodal histone signal: the marks are on the nucleosomes flanking the NDR, so a histone ChIP peak often has a dip where the ATAC peak is. Motif enrichment and footprinting have their own unit; the ML units train models that read the sequence directly.

title: Gene regulation
text:
Summary







idea
key fact




cis-regulatory elements
core promoter, enhancers, silencers, insulators: clusters of TF sites


core promoter
about −40 to +40; TATA, Inr, DPE; CpG-island (about half, broad, housekeeping) vs non-CpG (tissue-specific)


enhancer
activates at a distance (up to ~1 Mb), either orientation; often not the nearest gene


active enhancer
open core with TFs; H3K4me1 + H3K27ac on flanking nucleosomes; eRNAs


insulator
CTCF; loops between convergent CTCF sites by cohesin extrusion


TF
DNA-binding domain + effector domain; ~1600 in human


PWM
counts → frequencies (pseudocount) → log-odds \log_2(p/q); score = sum over positions


information content
2 + \sum p \log_2 p per column; logo; chance match ≈ every 2^{IC} bp


binding
motif ≈ necessary, not sufficient: 4% of chr21 CTCF matches bound; accessibility, pioneers, partners


B cells
PU.1, E2A → EBF1 ↔︎ PAX5; combinations select enhancers




Students should be able to: build a PWM from a few aligned sites and score a sequence by hand; compute information content of a column; estimate the number of chance matches of a motif in a genome; explain why most matches are unbound; describe the marks of an active enhancer; and predict what ATAC-seq, TF ChIP-seq, histone ChIP-seq and Hi-C show at a promoter, an enhancer and a CTCF site. Next units: Genomic intervals (if not yet done), then the assay blocks, starting with ATAC-seq.

title: Gene regulation
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Banerji, Rusconi & Schaffner 1981, Cell. Expression of a β-globin gene is enhanced by remote SV40 DNA sequences. The discovery of enhancers.
Spitz & Furlong 2012, Nat Rev Genet. Transcription factors: from enhancer binding to developmental control. A clear review of enhancers, TF binding and combinatorial control.
Lambert et al. 2018, Cell. The human transcription factors. The census of ~1600 human TFs, their domains and motifs.
Wasserman & Sandelin 2004, Nat Rev Genet. Applied bioinformatics for the identification of regulatory elements. PWMs, information content and why most predicted sites are not functional (“the futility theorem”).
Zaret & Carroll 2011, Genes Dev. Pioneer transcription factors: establishing competence for gene expression. The pioneer factor concept.
Heinz et al. 2010, Mol Cell. Simple combinations of lineage-determining transcription factors prime cis-regulatory elements required for macrophage and B cell identities. PU.1 and its partners choose enhancers; also introduced HOMER.

title: Exercise: Gene regulation and TF motifs
text:
After this exercise you will be able to:

Build a position weight matrix (PWM) from aligned binding sites with pseudocounts, and score sequences with it on both strands, by hand.
Compute the information content of a motif column and read a sequence logo.
Estimate how many chance matches a motif has in a region or a genome, and use that to judge claims about TF binding.
Fetch a matrix from JASPAR in R, scan peak sequences and backgrounds with motifmatchr, and measure enrichment, centrality and the fraction of bound matches.

title: Exercise: Gene regulation and TF motifs
text:
After this exercise you will be able to:

Build a position weight matrix (PWM) from aligned binding sites with pseudocounts, and score sequences with it on both strands, by hand.
Compute the information content of a motif column and read a sequence logo.
Estimate how many chance matches a motif has in a region or a genome, and use that to judge claims about TF binding.
Fetch a matrix from JASPAR in R, scan peak sequences and backgrounds with motifmatchr, and measure enrichment, centrality and the fraction of bound matches.

title: Exercise: Gene regulation and TF motifs
text:
Background
PWM. From \(N\) aligned sites, count each base \(b\) at each position \(j\) (\(n_{b,j}\)), add a pseudocount, and divide: \(p_{b,j} = (n_{b,j} + 1) / (N + 4)\) with a pseudocount of 1 per base. The log-odds weight against a background frequency \(q_b\) is \(w_{b,j} = \log_2 (p_{b,j} / q_b)\). The score of a sequence window is the sum of the weights of its bases. Scan both strands: the minus strand is the reverse complement.
Information content of column \(j\) against a uniform background: \(IC_j = 2 + \sum_b p_{b,j} \log_2 p_{b,j}\) bits, between 0 (no preference) and 2 (one base only). A logo stacks the letters of each column to height \(IC_j\).
Chance matches. An exact \(k\)-mer occurs with probability \(4^{-k}\) per position and strand in random sequence. For a PWM scanned at a \(p\)-value threshold \(p\), a sequence of length \(L\) has about \(2Lp\) matches by chance. Roughly, a motif with \(I\) bits of information is found about once every \(2^I\) bp per strand.
Bound or not. A TF binds only a small fraction of its motif matches: accessibility, nucleosomes, DNA methylation, partner TFs and TF concentration decide which.

title: Exercise: Gene regulation and TF motifs
text:
Data
GM12878 CTCF peaks (ENCODE, IDR conservative, narrowPeak), GM12878 ATAC-seq peaks, the hg38 genome as a bgzipped, indexed FASTA (hg38.fa.bgz with .fai and .gzi, so that any region can be read without unpacking the whole file), the hg38 chromosome sizes and the ENCODE blacklist. From the course repository:
data/download.sh gene-regulation
mkdir -p ~/epi/generegulation && cd ~/epi/generegulation
D=/path/to/course/data                  # where download.sh put the files
You need samtools (1.10 or newer), bedtools and, in R, the Bioconductor packages JASPAR2024, TFBSTools, motifmatchr, universalmotif, Rsamtools, Biostrings, GenomicRanges and rtracklayer (see Install the software you need). The R part runs in about two minutes on a laptop.
Simplification: we use one matrix per TF and a single \(p\)-value threshold (\(10^{-4}\), uniform background). Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting does this properly, with motif databases, enrichment statistics and footprints.

title: Exercise: Gene regulation and TF motifs
text:
By hand
Do these on paper. A calculator for \(\log_2\) helps: \(\log_2 x = \ln x / \ln 2\); \(\log_2 3 = 1.585\), \(\log_2 (2/3) = -0.585\), \(\log_2 (1/3) = -1.585\).
B1. Build a PWM. Eight binding sites of a GATA-like factor, aligned:
AGATAA   TGATAA   AGATAG   AGATAA
TGATAG   AGATTA   AGATAA   CGATAA

Write the 4 × 6 count matrix (rows A, C, G, T).
Convert it to frequencies with a pseudocount of 1 per base. Why is a pseudocount needed here?
Compute the log-odds weights against a uniform background (\(q_b = 0.25\)). Write down the weight matrix; you will need it in B2.

B2. Score sequences. Using your weights from B1:

Score AGATAA, TGATAG, AGCTAA and GGGGGG. What are the highest and the lowest possible scores?
A sequence on the plus strand reads TTATCT. What does it score as written? What does it score on the minus strand? Where is the motif, and which way does it point?
With a threshold of 6 bits, which of the five sequences are matches?

B3. Information content.

Compute \(IC\) for column 1 and for column 2 of your PWM (with the pseudocounts).
What would \(IC\) of column 2 be without pseudocounts? Why does the pseudocount matter so much more with 8 sites than with 913 (the number of sites behind the JASPAR CTCF matrix)?
A column is 50% A and 50% G, never C or T. What is its \(IC\)? How tall is each letter in the logo?

B4. How many matches by chance? Take the human genome as \(3.1 \times 10^9\) bp of random sequence with equal base frequencies.

How often do you expect the exact 6-mer AGATAA per Mb (both strands)? In the whole genome?
Repeat for the E-box CACGTG. Why is the answer half of (a)? (Write out its reverse complement.)
A PWM is scanned with a threshold of \(p < 10^{-4}\) per position and strand. How many matches do you expect on chr21 (40 Mb of sequence) and in the genome? GM12878 has 44 217 CTCF peaks: what is the largest possible fraction of genome-wide CTCF matches that can be bound?
The CTCF matrix has 16.1 bits of information. Using the rule of thumb, about how often does a CTCF site of that quality occur by chance?

B5. Strand and orientation. A scan of chr1 with the CTCF matrix reports four matches (1-based start, strand):
site 1   1 000 001   +
site 2   1 180 001   −
site 3   1 400 001   −
site 4   1 650 001   +

The JASPAR consensus is GCCACCAGGGGGCGC. Write the plus-strand sequence of the genome at site 2 if it matched the consensus perfectly.
Draw the four sites as arrows. Which pairs are convergent? Loop extrusion by cohesin predicts loops between which sites?
Site 2 is deleted. Which loop do you now expect?

B6. Read a logo. Look at the CTCF logo on the Information content and sequence logos slide (JASPAR MA0139.2, 913 sites).

Which three positions carry the most information? About how many bits each?
Position 9 has G (566 sites) and A (333 sites). What does a mixed column mean for binding? Is a site with A at position 9 a “mutant” site?
Why are the end columns low?
A logo built from only 20 sites without pseudocounts looks “cleaner”, with taller columns. Is that motif more specific?

B7. Judge the claims.

“The CTCF motif is the main determinant of CTCF binding, so CTCF binds essentially every match to its motif.” Use your answer to B4c and the chr21 numbers from the lecture (8583 matches, 369 inside a CTCF peak) to judge the claim.
A paper reports: “TF X has 600 000 motif matches but only 12 000 ChIP-seq peaks. Therefore 98% of its sites are silenced by DNA methylation.” What else could explain the gap? What experiment would test the methylation claim?
A student finds the PU.1 motif in 22% of GM12878 ATAC peaks and concludes that PU.1 binds 22% of the open chromatin in B cells. What is missing from this reasoning? (In the lecture: 12% of GC-matched background windows also have a match.)

B8. Read the figure. You ChIP two TFs, Y and Z, and plot the position of the best match to each one’s motif relative to the summit, as on the centrality slide. Y gives a sharp peak at 0; Z gives a flat histogram, although Z’s motif is found in 40% of its peaks (15% in background). Give two explanations for Z.

title: Exercise: Gene regulation and TF motifs
text:
On the command line

C1 — Sequences around the CTCF summits
zcat $D/gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz \
  | awk -v OFS='\t' '{ s = $2 + $10; print $1, s - 100, s + 100, "peak" NR }' > ctcf_win.bed
head -2 ctcf_win.bed

grep -P '^chr([0-9]+|X)\t' $D/hg38.chrom.sizes > genome.txt
zcat $D/hg38_blacklist.bed.gz > blacklist.bed
bedtools shuffle -i ctcf_win.bed -g genome.txt -chrom -excl blacklist.bed -seed 1 > shuf_win.bed

for f in ctcf_win shuf_win; do
  awk '{ print $1 ":" $2 + 1 "-" $3 }' $f.bed > $f.regions
  samtools faidx -n 1000 -r $f.regions $D/hg38.fa.bgz | grep -v '>' | tr acgtn ACGTN > $f.txt
done
wc -l ctcf_win.txt shuf_win.txt
grep -c N shuf_win.txt

Explain the awk in the first command: which column is the summit, and why is the window s − 100 to s + 100? Why does the second awk add 1 to the start?
The genome file is soft-masked (repeats in lower case). What does tr acgtn ACGTN do, and what would go wrong without it?
How many shuffled windows contain an N, and why can that happen?



C2 — Counting words is not motif scanning
for f in ctcf_win shuf_win; do
  echo $f \
    $(grep -c -E 'CCCTC|GAGGG' $f.txt) \
    $(grep -c -E 'CCA[CG][CT]AG[AG][GT]GG|CC[AC][CT]CT[AG][CG]TGG' $f.txt) \
    $(awk '{ gc += gsub(/[GC]/, ""); n += 200 } END { printf "%.3f", gc / n }' $f.txt)
done

The columns are: windows containing CCCTC (on either strand), windows containing an 11-bp degenerate CTCF core (either strand), and GC content. Fill in a table and compute the fraction for each.
CTCF is named “CCCTC-binding factor”. Why is CCCTC a poor test for CTCF sites? Estimate how often a 5-mer occurs in 200 bp of random sequence (both strands).
Why do the shuffled windows have lower GC content than the peak windows, and why does that matter for (a)?

title: Exercise: Gene regulation and TF motifs
text:
In R
library(JASPAR2024); library(TFBSTools); library(RSQLite)
library(GenomicRanges); library(rtracklayer); library(Rsamtools); library(Biostrings)
library(motifmatchr); library(universalmotif)
D <- "/path/to/course/data"

R1 — The CTCF matrix from JASPAR
jaspar <- dbConnect(SQLite(), db(JASPAR2024()))
ctcf_m <- getMatrixByID(jaspar, "MA0139.2")
ctcf_m
cnt <- Matrix(ctcf_m)            # counts: 4 rows (A, C, G, T) x 15 columns
cnt
colSums(cnt)                     # number of sites in each column

How many sites is the matrix built from, and from what kind of experiment? (Look at the type tag.)
Why are the column sums not all equal?



R2 — Frequencies, log-odds, information content and the logo
p   <- (cnt + 0.25) / colSums(cnt + 0.25)  # pseudocount 0.25 per base (1 per column)
lo  <- log2(p / 0.25)                       # log-odds against a uniform background
ic  <- 2 + colSums(p * log2(p))             # information content per column (bits)
round(lo, 2)
round(ic, 2); sum(ic)
consensus <- paste(rownames(cnt)[apply(cnt, 2, which.max)], collapse = "")
consensus
