Compute ChIP / input and \(\log_2\)((ChIP + 1) / (input + 1)) for each bin.
Bins A and B have similar log2 ratios. Is B as convincing as A? What would you change to make bin B more reliable?

B7. Duplicates. Eight single-end reads on chr21 (POS, strand, CIGAR all 36M):
r1 1000 +    r2 1000 +    r3 1000 −    r4 1003 +
r5 1000 +    r6 1210 −    r7 1210 −    r8 1500 +

Which reads would samtools markdup flag as duplicates? What is the duplicate fraction?
Why are r1 and r3 not duplicates of each other, although they have the same POS?
In the real ChIP data, 49% of the reads inside CTCF peaks on chr21 were flagged as duplicates, but only 4% outside peaks. Give two explanations. Why does this happen with single-end reads more than with paired-end reads?

B8. The order of the steps.

Put these in a sensible order and give one reason for each position: blacklist removal, bamCoverage, adapter trimming, MAPQ/FLAG filter, alignment, duplicate marking, sorting.
In the input, 66% of the aligned reads are on chrM. A colleague makes the input’s CPM track from the BAM with the chrM reads. Is the input signal on chr21 too high or too low? By how much, roughly?
Another colleague makes the ChIP track from chip.sorted.bam (no filtering at all). Name two things that will look different in the track.

B9. Read the figures (lecture slides Real data: MAPQ on chr21 and Real data: the two strands around CTCF sites).

In the MAPQ histogram, almost no reads have MAPQ between 2 and 29. Why is the distribution bimodal, and what does that imply for the choice of threshold?
The 5’ ends of + strand reads peak about 50 bp to the left of the CTCF summits, those of − strand reads about 50 bp to the right. Estimate the fragment length. Why is there almost no read 5’ end within ±18 bp of the summits?
After MAPQ filtering, a 5 kb satellite repeat on chr21 has no reads at all. A colleague concludes that CTCF does not bind there. Comment.

title: Exercise: From reads to coverage
text:
On the command line

C1 — Look at the reads
zcat $D/gm12878_ctcf_chip.fastq.gz | head -8
zcat $D/gm12878_ctcf_input.fastq.gz | head -4
zcat $D/gm12878_ctcf_chip.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2 { n++; len[length($0)]++ } END { print n; for (l in len) print l, len[l] }'
zcat $D/gm12878_ctcf_chip.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 0' | head -100000 | fold -w1 | LC_ALL=C sort | uniq -c | head -5

How many reads are there, and how long are they? What do the read names tell you about the instrument?
Which characters occur in the quality lines (the last command lists the lowest ones)? Decide whether the file is Phred+33 or Phred+64 (B1b).



C2 — Convert the qualities and trim with fastp
Old Phred+64 files are best converted to Phred+33 before anything else. Each quality character moves down by 31 (@ → !, h → I):
for s in chip input; do
  zcat $D/gm12878_ctcf_$s.fastq.gz | perl -pe 'tr/@-~/!-_/ if $. % 4 == 0' | gzip > $s.fastq.gz
  fastp -w 8 -i $s.fastq.gz -o $s.trim.fastq.gz -h $s.fastp.html -j $s.fastp.json 2> $s.fastp.log
done
grep -A 7 "Filtering result" chip.fastp.log input.fastp.log

How many reads did fastp remove from each file, and why? Were any adapters found? Would you expect adapters in 36 bp reads from sonicated ChIP fragments?
Open chip.fastp.html in a browser. How does the quality change along the read? Compare with the input.



C3 — The genome index
The course data folder contains a prebuilt bowtie2 index for chr21 + chrM ($D/bowtie2/). This is how it was made (27 seconds with 8 threads; hours for the whole human genome, so for real work download a prebuilt one):
mkdir -p index
bowtie2-build --threads 8 $D/hg38_chr21_chrM.fa index/hg38_chr21_chrM > index/build.log
ls -lh index


C4 — Align, sort, index
for s in chip input; do
  bowtie2 -p 8 -x $D/bowtie2/hg38_chr21_chrM -U $s.trim.fastq.gz 2> $s.bowtie2.log \
    | samtools sort -@ 4 -o $s.sorted.bam -
  samtools index $s.sorted.bam
done
cat chip.bowtie2.log input.bowtie2.log
samtools flagstat chip.sorted.bam
samtools idxstats chip.sorted.bam
samtools idxstats input.sorted.bam
samtools view chip.sorted.bam | head -3

What fraction of each library aligned exactly once, more than once, not at all? Why is the unaligned fraction so low here (see the warning box under Data)?
What fraction of the aligned reads are on chrM in the ChIP and in the input? chrM is 16.6 kb, chr21 46.7 Mb: how many times more reads per kb does chrM get in the input?
Decode the FLAG, POS, MAPQ and CIGAR of the first three alignments.



C5 — Filter, mark duplicates, remove the blacklist
zcat $D/hg38_blacklist.bed.gz > blacklist.bed
for s in chip input; do
  samtools view -b -q 30 -F 1804 -o $s.q30.bam $s.sorted.bam            # unique, mapped, primary
  samtools markdup -s $s.q30.bam $s.markdup.bam 2> $s.markdup.txt       # flag duplicates (1024)
  samtools index $s.markdup.bam
  samtools view -b -F 1024 -o $s.dedup.bam $s.markdup.bam chr21         # drop duplicates and chrM
  bedtools intersect -v -abam $s.dedup.bam -b blacklist.bed > $s.final.bam
  samtools index $s.final.bam
done
grep -E "^READ|DUPLICATE SINGLE:" chip.markdup.txt input.markdup.txt
for s in chip input; do
  echo $s \
    $(zcat $s.fastq.gz | awk 'END { print NR / 4 }') \
    $(zcat $s.trim.fastq.gz | awk 'END { print NR / 4 }') \
    $(samtools view -c -F 4 $s.sorted.bam) \
    $(samtools view -c $s.q30.bam) \
    $(samtools view -c -F 1024 $s.markdup.bam) \
    $(samtools view -c $s.dedup.bam) \
    $(samtools view -c $s.final.bam)
done

Fill in the table: reads left after each step (raw, after fastp, aligned, MAPQ ≥ 30 and -F 1804, duplicates removed, chr21 only, blacklist removed), as numbers and as a percentage of the raw reads, for ChIP and input.
What is the duplicate rate of each library? Where are the input’s duplicates? (samtools view -c -f 1024 input.markdup.bam chrM and the same for chr21.)
How many reads did the blacklist remove? Which blacklisted regions on chr21 have the most input reads per kb, and how does that compare with the chr21 average (116 397 reads / 40 089 kb)?

bedtools intersect -c -a blacklist.bed -b input.dedup.bam \
  | awk -v OFS='\t' '$4 > 0 { print $0, $4 / ($3 - $2) * 1000 }' | sort -k5,5gr | head -3


C6 — How long are the fragments?
Our reads are single-end, so the fragment length must be estimated from the shift between the strands (lecture: Single-end reads need extending):
macs3 predictd -i chip.final.bam -f BAM -g 40088619 2>&1 | grep "predicted fragment length"
What fragment length does MACS3 predict? We use it for --extendReads below.


C7 — Coverage tracks
for s in chip input; do
  bamCoverage -b $s.final.bam -o $s.cpm.bw --normalizeUsing CPM --extendReads 100 --binSize 10 -p 8
done
bamCoverage -b chip.final.bam -o chip.rpgc.bw --normalizeUsing RPGC \
  --effectiveGenomeSize 40088619 --extendReads 100 --binSize 10 -p 8
bamCompare -b1 chip.final.bam -b2 input.final.bam -o chip_vs_input.log2.bw \
  --operation log2 --scaleFactorsMethod readCount --pseudocount 1 \
  --extendReads 100 --binSize 50 -p 8
bamCompare -b1 chip.final.bam -b2 input.final.bam -o chip_vs_input.ratio.bw \
  --operation ratio --scaleFactorsMethod readCount --pseudocount 1 \
  --extendReads 100 --binSize 50 -p 8
ls -lh *.bw

Why is --effectiveGenomeSize 40 088 619 and not the length of chr21 (46 709 983)? (Hint: grep -v ">" $D/hg38_chr21_chrM.fa | head -100000 | grep -c N and think about what N means.)
The RPGC and CPM tracks differ only by a constant factor. Compute it from B5 and check it in IGV at any peak.



C8 — Look at it in IGV
Open IGV, choose the genome hg38, and load chip.cpm.bw, input.cpm.bw, chip_vs_input.log2.bw, $D/gm12878_ctcf_fc.bigWig, $D/gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz and chip.final.bam. Go to chr21:43,775,000-43,825,000.

How many CTCF peaks are in the window? Do your ChIP track and ENCODE’s fold change agree on where they are?
Zoom in to the peak at about 43 789 450 until you see single reads in the BAM track. Colour the reads by strand (right click → Color alignments by → read strand). Where are the + strand reads, where the − strand reads?
Why is your log2 ratio track so much noisier than ENCODE’s fold change away from the peaks? (Count the input reads in the window: samtools view -c input.final.bam chr21:43775000-43825000.)

title: Exercise: From reads to coverage
text:
In R
You need GenomicAlignments (with Rsamtools), rtracklayer and GenomicRanges (see Install the software you need). Run R in the folder with your BAM files:
suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(GenomicAlignments); library(rtracklayer) })
D <- "/path/to/course/data"
setwd("~/epi/align")

R1 — Read the BAM and look at MAPQ
aln <- readGAlignments("chip.sorted.bam", param = ScanBamParam(what = c("flag", "mapq")))
aln
table(seqnames(aln))
mq <- mcols(aln[seqnames(aln) == "chr21"])$mapq
table(cut(mq, c(-1, 1, 10, 29, 41, 42)))
mean(mq >= 30)
hist(mq, breaks = 0:43 - 0.5, main = "ChIP, chr21", xlab = "MAPQ")

What fraction of the ChIP reads on chr21 have MAPQ 0 or 1, and what fraction MAPQ ≥ 30? Compare with samtools view -c -q 30 chip.sorted.bam chr21.
Repeat for input.sorted.bam. Which library has more multi-mappers on chr21, and why might that be (read length)?



R2 — Duplicates by hand
A single-end read is a duplicate of another if they have the same chromosome, strand and 5’ end.
q30 <- granges(readGAlignments("chip.q30.bam"))
five <- resize(q30, width = 1, fix = "start")       # the 5' end, strand-aware
key <- paste(seqnames(five), start(five), strand(five))
sum(duplicated(key)); mean(duplicated(key))
tapply(duplicated(key), as.character(seqnames(five)), mean)

How many duplicates do you find? Compare with DUPLICATE SINGLE in chip.markdup.txt.
Why is the duplicate rate on chrM so much higher than on chr21?



R3 — Coverage at a CTCF peak
fin <- granges(readGAlignments("chip.final.bam"))
ext <- resize(fin, width = 100, fix = "start")       # extend each read to 100 bp
cpm <- coverage(ext)$chr21 * 1e6 / length(fin)
bw  <- import("chip.cpm.bw", as = "RleList")$chr21
win <- 43789200:43789700
plot(win, as.numeric(cpm[win]), type = "l", lwd = 2, xlab = "chr21", ylab = "CPM")
lines(win, as.numeric(bw[win]), col = "red")
max(cpm[win]); max(bw[win])

Does your hand-made CPM agree with bamCoverage? Where do they differ, and why? (bamCoverage counts the reads that overlap each 10 bp bin, not the coverage of each base.)
Repeat with resize(fin, width = 36, fix = "start") (no extension). What happens to the peak?



R4 — Strands around the CTCF summits
pk <- import(file.path(D, "gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz"), format = "narrowPeak")
pk <- pk[seqnames(pk) == "chr21"]
summit <- GRanges("chr21", IRanges(start(pk) + pk$peak, width = 1))
five <- resize(fin, width = 1, fix = "start")
h <- findOverlaps(five, summit, maxgap = 300)
d <- start(five)[queryHits(h)] - start(summit)[subjectHits(h)]
s <- as.character(strand(five))[queryHits(h)]
tapply(d, s, median)
hist(d[s == "+"], breaks = 60, col = rgb(0.16, 0.44, 0.59, 0.5), main = "", xlab = "5' end - summit (bp)")
hist(d[s == "-"], breaks = 60, col = rgb(0.9, 0.5, 0.13, 0.5), add = TRUE)

What are the median offsets of the + and − strand 5’ ends? Estimate the fragment length and compare with C6.
What fraction of all filtered ChIP reads is within 300 bp of a chr21 summit? (length(unique(queryHits(h))) / length(fin).) This is close to the FRiP score of Experimental design and QC.



R5 — Your track against ENCODE’s
chr21 <- GRanges("chr21", IRanges(1, 46709983))
bins <- tileGenome(c(chr21 = 46709983), tilewidth = 1000, cut.last.tile.in.chrom = TRUE)
enc  <- import(file.path(D, "gm12878_ctcf_fc.bigWig"), which = chr21, as = "RleList")
mine <- import("chip_vs_input.ratio.bw", as = "RleList")
e <- binnedAverage(bins, enc["chr21"], "v")$v
m <- binnedAverage(bins, mine["chr21"], "v")$v
bl <- import(file.path(D, "hg38_blacklist.bed.gz"))
ok <- !overlapsAny(bins, bl) & e > 0 & m > 0
inpk <- overlapsAny(bins, pk)
c(bins = sum(ok), all = cor(log2(e[ok]), log2(m[ok])), peaks = cor(log2(e[ok & inpk]), log2(m[ok & inpk])))
plot(log2(e[ok]), log2(m[ok]), pch = ".", col = ifelse(inpk[ok], "red", "grey50"),
     xlab = "log2 ENCODE fold change", ylab = "log2 our ChIP / input")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2)

How well do the two tracks agree over all 1-kb bins, and over the bins with a peak?
List three differences between the way you and ENCODE made the tracks that could explain the disagreement in the background.

title: Exercise: From reads to coverage
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — qualities (B1, C1, C2)





\(Q\) = ASCII code − offset; I = 73, 5 = 53, # = 35, e = 101, L = 76 (see an ASCII table and the FASTQ format page). Phred+33 qualities rarely go above Q41 (J). The probability of no error in \(n\) bases is \((1-p)^n\). In the conversion, Perl’s tr/@-~/!-_/ maps the character range @…~ (ASCII 64–126) onto !…_ (33–95), only on every fourth line ($. % 4 == 0). fastp’s options are documented in its README; by default it removes reads with more than 40% of bases below Q15, reads with more than 5 N, and reads shorter than 15 bases after trimming.









Hint 2 — FLAG, POS, TLEN (B2–B4, C4)





Subtract the largest power of two that fits, repeat. The SAM specification (section 1.4) defines every column; the Picard explain-flags page and samtools flags 99 decode FLAGs for you. A − strand read is stored reverse-complemented: its 5’ end is its rightmost base, POS + length − 1. -F removes reads with any of the bits, -f keeps reads with all of them (samtools view).









Hint 3 — normalisation (B5, B6, C7)





CPM per bin = reads overlapping the bin × 106 / reads in the BAM. RPGC = coverage / (reads × fragment length / effective genome size). The deepTools pages for bamCoverage, bamCompare and effective genome size give the formulas and the defaults. bamCompare --scaleFactorsMethod readCount scales the larger library down to the smaller one before adding the pseudocount.









Hint 4 — duplicates, blacklist, order (B7, B8, C5)





samtools markdup compares the 5’ end and strand (single-end) or both ends (paired-end), and keeps the copy with the highest base qualities; -s prints statistics. For paired-end reads it needs samtools fixmate -m on name-collated reads first. The blacklist is described in Amemiya et al. 2019; bedtools intersect -v -abam writes the reads that overlap no blacklisted region (docs). For B8b: CPM divides by all reads in the BAM.









Hint 5 — fragment length and IGV (B9, C6, C8)





macs3 predictd pairs strong + strand and − strand peaks and reports the most common distance between them; -g is the effective genome size. In IGV, bigWig and BED files load with File → Load from File; a BAM needs its .bai index next to it.









Hint 6 — R (R1–R5)





readGAlignments with a ScanBamParam reads extra columns such as mapq and flag. granges() turns alignments into ranges; resize(..., fix = "start") is strand-aware, so the “start” of a − strand read is its right end. coverage returns an RleList per chromosome. tileGenome and binnedAverage make bins and average a signal over them; import with as = "RleList" reads a bigWig.

title: Exercise: From reads to coverage
text:
Solutions
All numbers below come from running the commands exactly as written (fastp 0.23.4, bowtie2 2.4.4, samtools 1.21, bedtools 2.30, deepTools 3.5.1, MACS3 3.1.0).






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) I = 73 − 33 = Q40, \(p = 10^{-4} = 0.0001\); 5 = Q20, \(p = 0.01\); # = Q2, \(p = 10^{-0.2} = 0.63\) (a “this base is useless” marker). (b) As +33, e would be 101 − 33 = Q68, far above anything a sequencer reports (+33 data top out around Q41). As +64: e = 101 − 64 = Q37 (\(p = 2 \times 10^{-4}\)), L = 76 − 64 = Q12 (\(p = 0.063\)). (c) \(36 \times 0.001 = 0.036\) errors per read at Q30; \(36 \times 0.01 = 0.36\) at Q20. The probability of at least one error at Q30 is \(1 - 0.999^{36} = 0.035\), so about 13 400 of 380 000 reads. Aligners tolerate this with mismatches.
B2. 99 = 64 + 32 + 2 + 1: read 1, mate reverse, proper pair. 147 = 128 + 16 + 2 + 1: read 2, reverse strand, proper pair. 83 = 64 + 16 + 2 + 1: read 1, reverse strand, proper pair. 163 = 128 + 32 + 2 + 1: read 2, mate reverse, proper pair (so read 2 is forward). 0: single-end, mapped, + strand. 16: single-end, − strand. 4: unmapped. 1123 = 1024 + 64 + 32 + 2 + 1: like 99, but flagged as a duplicate. (a) 99 and 147 are a pair (read 1 forward on the left, read 2 reverse on the right); 83 and 163 are a pair (read 2 forward on the left, read 1 reverse on the right). (b) -F 1804 removes 4 (unmapped) and 1123 (duplicate). -f 2 removes 0, 16, 4 (not proper pairs: single-end) and keeps the four proper-pair reads and 1123.
B3. (a) Read 2 ends at 10 181 + 36 − 1 = 10 216. Fragment = 10 216 − 10 001 + 1 = 216 bp; TLEN = +216 for read 1, −216 for read 2. (b) The mate (POS 5 140) is leftmost; the FLAG-83 read ends at 5 300 + 50 − 1 = 5 349. Fragment = 5 349 − 5 140 + 1 = 210 bp; TLEN is −210 in the FLAG-83 line and +210 in its mate’s line.
B4. (a) The − strand: the read covers 2 000–2 035, and its 5’ end (where sequencing started, the end of the fragment) is at 2 035. (b) Extending towards smaller coordinates: 1 936–2 035.
B5. (a) \(120 \times 10^6 / 197\,587 = 607\) CPM. (b) Average coverage \(197\,587 \times 100 / 40\,088\,619 = 0.493\); RPGC \(= 120 / 0.493 = 243\). (c) The same: \(240 \times 10^6 / 395\,174 = 607\) CPM, and the average coverage doubles to 0.986, so RPGC 243. Both remove the effect of depth. The ratio RPGC / CPM = genome size / (fragment length × \(10^6\)) \(= 40\,088\,619 / 10^8 = 0.40\), the same for every position (C7b).
B6. (a) A: 60/12 = 5, log2(61/13) = 2.23. B: 3/0 = ∞, log2(4/1) = 2.0. C: 0/2 = 0, log2(1/3) = −1.58. D: 0/0 undefined, log2(1/1) = 0. (b) No. Bin A rests on 72 reads, bin B on 3: one read more or less changes B’s ratio a lot (2 reads would give 1.58, 4 reads 2.32). Use larger bins, a deeper or smoothed input (MACS-style local background over 1–10 kb), or require a minimum count. The pseudocount already pulls B down from ∞ to 2.
B7. (a) r2 and r5 are duplicates of r1 (same 5’ end 1000, + strand). r7 duplicates r6 (− strand; both have 5’ end 1 245). r4 starts 3 bp later: not a duplicate. Three duplicates out of 8: 37.5% (markdup keeps the copy with the best qualities and flags the others). (b) r3 is on the − strand: its 5’ end is at 1 035 and it came from a different fragment, extending to the left. Duplicates must match position and strand. (c) PCR duplicates are concentrated where the reads are, but there is also a real effect: with single-end 36 bp reads, a ~200 bp peak offers only about 200 possible start positions per strand. With tens of thousands of fragments in a strong peak, independent fragments often share a start by chance (saturation), so dedup also removes real signal at the strongest peaks. With paired-end reads, two fragments must share both ends to be called duplicates, which is much rarer by chance.
B8. (a) Trimming (before alignment, so adapters do not force mismatches) → alignment → sorting (markdup, indexing and region access need positions in order) → MAPQ/FLAG filter (judge duplicates only among reads you trust) → duplicate marking → blacklist removal (positional; can be anywhere after alignment, but before computing totals for normalisation) → bamCoverage (last, so the CPM denominator counts only the reads that are kept). (b) Too low: CPM divides by all reads in the BAM, including the chrM reads. With 66% on chrM, the chr21 signal is divided by about three times too many reads, so it is about 3× too low (1/0.34 = 2.9), and a ChIP/input ratio is about 3× too high. (c) Multi-mapping reads pile up in repeats (signal where it cannot be trusted, and reads randomly placed between copies); duplicates inflate some positions into spikes; blacklisted regions show huge artefact peaks (e.g. 451 input reads at chr21:10.01 Mb); and the CPM denominator includes chrM and unmapped-to-chr21 reads, so all values are scaled differently.
B9. (a) A read is either unique (MAPQ 42 when the second-best alignment is much worse) or has several equally good places (MAPQ 0–1). Intermediate values need a second-best alignment that is a little worse, which is rarer. So any threshold between about 5 and 30 removes almost the same reads. (b) About 50 + 50 = 100 bp (the medians are −50 and +48). The protein occupies the DNA around the motif: fragment ends cannot fall where CTCF sits, so there is a footprint of about ±18 bp with almost no 5’ ends. (c) No information is not evidence of absence: with MAPQ ≥ 30, reads in a repeat with several identical copies are removed, so the region is blind. To ask about binding there, you need longer or paired reads, multi-mapper-aware methods, or a different assay.









Solutions — command line





C1. (a) 390 097 ChIP reads of 36 bp; 476 372 input reads of 28 bp. The names (MAGNUM:8:1:1064:11147#0/1, FC200NVAA_41408:7:1:760:865) are old Illumina names: instrument, lane, tile, x and y position of the cluster, index (#0) and read number (/1). (b) The lowest characters are B (10 555 times in 100 000 reads), then C, D, E, F; the most common is f. There is no !, # or digit. B = 66: as Phred+64 that is Q2, the Illumina 1.5+ marker for an unusable read tail. The file is Phred+64.
C2. (a) ChIP: 380 570 of 390 097 reads pass (9 514 removed as low quality, 13 for too many N); input: 476 024 of 476 372 pass (348 low quality). No adapters were detected or trimmed: the fragments (about 100–300 bp) are much longer than 28–36 bp reads, so read-through is very rare. In ATAC-seq with 2 × 100 bp reads it is common. Runtime: about 2 s per file with 8 threads. (b) ChIP: mean quality about Q37 at the start, Q35 at base 36; input: Q27 falling to Q24, and at the last base 16% of the input’s bases are below Q20. (If you run fastp with --phred64 on the original file instead of converting first, the filtering counts change from run to run with fastp 0.23.4, and the report shows qualities that are 31 too high. Converting explicitly avoids both.)
C3. Six .bt2 files, about 63 MB in total; 22–27 s with 8 threads.
C4. (a) ChIP: 76.6% exactly once, 22.9% more than once, 0.53% (2 014) not at all. Input: 88.9% exactly once, 11.1% more than once, 0.00% not aligned. In real data 5–20% fail to align (contamination, adapter dimers, unplaced sequence); here the reads were preselected because ENCODE aligned them. Alignment took about 3 s per library. (b) ChIP: 52 343 of 378 556 aligned reads (13.8%) on chrM; input: 315 745 of 476 024 (66.3%). Reads per kb: input chrM \(315\,745 / 16.6 = 19\,060\), chr21 \(160\,279 / 46\,710 = 3.4\): about 5 600 times more per kb on chrM. (c) All three are FLAG 0 (single-end, + strand, mapped) at chr21:5 010 117–5 010 694, CIGAR 36M (36 aligned bases), with MAPQ 1, 0 and 1: AS equals XS, so each has an equally good second place. The start of chr21’s long arm is full of segmental duplications. The second read also has 4 mismatches (NM:i:4, AS:i:-20).

The whole of C5 takes about 10 s. (b) ChIP: 77 450 of 299 649 (25.8%); input: 283 747 of 433 306 (65.5%). The input’s duplicates are almost all on chrM: 281 873 of 314 048 chrM reads (90%) against 1 874 of 119 258 chr21 reads (1.6%). The chrM is covered thousands of times over, so most possible start positions are taken many times: saturation, not just PCR. On chr21 the ChIP has 19.7% duplicates, concentrated in the peaks (B7c). (c) 1 117 ChIP and 987 input reads. Highest density: chr21 8234456 8234568 (12 reads in 112 bp, 107 per kb) and chr21 6369257 6372342 (215 reads in 3.1 kb, 70 per kb), against an average of 2.9 input reads per kb on chr21: 24–37 times too many, after MAPQ and duplicate filtering. (The 520 bp region at 10.01 Mb in the lecture figure had 451 input reads before filtering, but 448 of them had MAPQ 1: there the MAPQ filter already did the work.)
C6. predicted fragment length is 100 bps (from 359 paired + and − strand peaks; about 1 s).
C7. Each command takes 2–5 s. (a) The effective genome size is the part of the genome where reads can align. chr21 has 46 709 983 bases, of which 6 621 364 are N (unsequenced gaps, mostly the short arm and the centromere); 40 088 619 are A, C, G or T. A stricter value would also subtract unmappable repeats; deepTools lists such values for whole genomes and several read lengths. (b) RPGC / CPM = \(40\,088\,619 / (100 \times 10^6) = 0.40\) (B5c); at the summit of the peak at chr21:43 789 481 the CPM track reads 1063 and the RPGC track 426.
C8. (a) Three ENCODE peaks, at about 43.789, 43.811 and 43.817 Mb, each with a peak in both tracks. (b) + strand reads are piled up to the left of the summit, − strand reads to the right, about 100 bp apart (the lecture figure Real data: the two strands around CTCF sites). (c) The input has only 116 397 reads on all of chr21, about 3 per kb, and 377 reads in this 50 kb window: most 50 bp bins have 0 or 1 input read, so the ratio jumps between bins. ENCODE’s fold change (MACS2) uses a local background from the input averaged over 1 kb and 10 kb, never lower than the genome-wide average, and pools two replicates.









Solutions — R





R1. (a) 326 213 ChIP reads on chr21; MAPQ 0–1: 72 811 (22.3%); MAPQ ≥ 30: 75.9% (247 580 reads, the same as samtools view -c -q 30 chip.sorted.bam chr21). Reading the BAM takes about 2 s. (b) Input on chr21: 25.1% MAPQ 0–1, 74.4% ≥ 30: slightly more multi-mappers than the ChIP. The input reads are 28 bp, the ChIP reads 36 bp; a shorter read is unique in fewer places. (The ChIP is also enriched at CTCF sites, which are mostly in unique sequence.)
R2. (a) 77 450 duplicates (25.8%): exactly the number samtools markdup reported. (b) chrM: 54.9% of the ChIP’s chrM reads are duplicates, chr21: 19.7%. chrM is 16.6 kb with 52 069 filtered reads, about 3 per base: nearly every possible (start, strand) is used several times, even without PCR.
R3. (a) The shapes agree, but bamCoverage’s values are a little higher: at the summit (chr21:43 789 481) 194 extended reads cover the base, 194 × 106 / 197 587 = 982 CPM, while the bamCoverage track reads 1063. bamCoverage counts every read that overlaps a 10 bp bin, even by one base, so a bin collects a few more reads than any single base in it. (b) Without extension the peak splits into two humps about 100 bp apart, with a dip at the summit (the + and − strand reads on either side), as in the lecture figure.
R4. (a) Median offsets −50 bp (+ strand) and +48 bp (− strand): a fragment of about 98 bp, in agreement with MACS3’s 100 bp. (Reading the BAMs and the R steps take a few seconds each.) (b) 54 003 of 197 587 reads (27.3%) have their 5’ end within 300 bp of one of the 405 summits on chr21. For a TF ChIP this is a good value (ENCODE’s guidelines treat FRiP below 1% as a warning sign).
R5. (a) 33 287 bins are used (not blacklisted, non-zero in both). Pearson correlation of the log2 values: 0.63 over all bins, 0.91 over the 466 bins that contain an ENCODE peak. The tracks agree on the peaks and much less on the background. (b) ENCODE pooled two replicates, we used one; ENCODE’s MACS2 fold change uses a local background from the input smoothed over 1–10 kb (and a genome-wide floor), we divided 50 bp bins with a pseudocount of 1; ENCODE estimated its own fragment length and cropped the ChIP reads to 28 bp; and ENCODE used the whole genome, so some reads are placed differently.

title: Exercise: From reads to coverage
text:
Where this leads

Experimental design and QC turns the numbers in your C5 table into QC metrics: library complexity from duplicates, FRiP (R4b), fingerprints and strand cross-correlation.
ChIP-seq peak calling starts from chip.final.bam and input.final.bam and replaces the noisy per-bin ratio with MACS3’s local Poisson background.
ATAC-seq processing and peak calling uses the same chain with paired-end reads, adapter trimming that really matters, chrM removal and the Tn5 shift.
The production version of all of this is nf-core/chipseq or nf-core/atacseq.

title: Exercise: From reads to coverage
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined.

Langmead & Salzberg 2012, Nat Methods. Fast gapped-read alignment with Bowtie 2.
Li et al. 2009, Bioinformatics. The Sequence Alignment/Map format and SAMtools.
Chen et al. 2018, Bioinformatics. fastp: an ultra-fast all-in-one FASTQ preprocessor.
Ramírez et al. 2016, Nucleic Acids Res. deepTools2: a next generation web server for deep-sequencing data analysis.
Amemiya, Kundaje & Boyle 2019, Sci Rep. The ENCODE Blacklist: identification of problematic regions of the genome.
Robinson et al. 2011, Nat Biotechnol. Integrative genomics viewer.

title: Quiz: from reads to coverage
text:
Short questions on reads, alignment, filtering and coverage tracks. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A base in a Phred+33 FASTQ file has the quality character + (ASCII 43). What is its Q, and the probability that the base call is wrong? What would the same character mean in a Phred+64 file?






Hint





Q = ASCII − offset, and \(p = 10^{-Q/10}\).









Answer





Phred+33: Q = 43 − 33 = 10, \(p = 10^{-1} = 0.1\), one error in ten. In Phred+64, ASCII 43 would be Q = −21, which is impossible: Phred+64 qualities start at @ (ASCII 64). Seeing characters below ; in a file tells you it is Phred+33.




Q2. Decode the FLAGs 163 and 1040. What kind of read is each, and would samtools view -F 1804 keep it?






Hint





Subtract the largest power of two that fits, and repeat. 1804 = 1024 + 512 + 256 + 8 + 4.









Answer





163 = 128 + 32 + 2 + 1: read 2 of a properly paired fragment, on the forward strand, mate on the reverse strand. Kept. 1040 = 1024 + 16: a single-end read on the reverse strand, marked as a duplicate. Removed by -F 1804, because 1804 contains the 1024 bit.




Q3. A proper pair of 50 bp reads: read 1 has FLAG 99 and POS 20 001, read 2 has FLAG 147 and POS 20 251. How long is the fragment, and what is TLEN in each line?






Answer





Read 2 ends at 20 251 + 50 − 1 = 20 300. Fragment = 20 300 − 20 001 + 1 = 300 bp. TLEN = +300 for read 1 (the leftmost), −300 for read 2.




Q4. A read aligned with MAPQ 1 and the tags AS:i:-6 XS:i:-6. What does this tell you about the read, and should it go into a coverage track?






Answer





The best alignment score (AS) equals the second-best (XS): the read fits at least two places equally well, typically copies of a repeat, and bowtie2 reported one of them at random. MAPQ 1 means the position is very likely wrong. Remove it (MAPQ ≥ 30): otherwise its signal is spread at random over the copies. The repeat then has no signal at all, which means no information, not no binding.




Q5. Why are duplicates usually removed in ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq but usually kept in RNA-seq? When can removing them in ChIP-seq hurt?






Answer





In RNA-seq a highly expressed gene produces so many fragments that many share a start position by chance: removing them would compress the expression of the most expressed genes. In ChIP and ATAC, each position is covered by few independent fragments from a small amount of DNA, so identical start positions are mostly PCR copies, and an amplified fragment would look like a peak. Removing them can hurt at very strong, narrow peaks with single-end reads: there are only a few hundred possible start positions per strand, so independent fragments collide (saturation). In the CTCF data, 49% of reads inside peaks were flagged as duplicates against 4% outside.




Q6. 60% of the aligned reads of an ATAC-seq library are on chrM. You make a CPM track of the nuclear genome without removing the chrM reads. Compared with a track made after removing them, are the nuclear values too high or too low, and by what factor?






Answer





Too low, by a factor of 2.5. CPM divides by all reads in the BAM. Only 40% of the reads are nuclear, so the denominator is 1/0.4 = 2.5 times too large. Two libraries with different chrM fractions would look different even if their nuclear signal were the same.




Q7. A ChIP library has 20 million filtered reads, extended to 200 bp; the effective genome size is 2.7 × 109 bp. A base is covered by 45 fragments. What is its RPGC value? What is the CPM of a bin overlapped by 45 reads?






Hint





Average coverage = reads × fragment length / genome size.









Answer





Average coverage \(= 2 \times 10^7 \times 200 / 2.7 \times 10^9 = 1.48\). RPGC \(= 45 / 1.48 = 30.4\): 30 times the genome average. CPM \(= 45 \times 10^6 / (2 \times 10^7) = 2.25\).




Q8. After depth scaling, a 50 bp bin has 9 ChIP reads and 1 input read; another has 1 ChIP read and 0 input reads. Compute \(\log_2\)((ChIP + 1) / (input + 1)) for both. Why add 1?






Answer





log2(10/2) = 2.32 and log2(2/1) = 1.0. Without the pseudocount the second bin would be 1/0 = ∞, the most “enriched” bin in the genome on the strength of a single read. Adding 1 to both counts makes the ratio of small counts shrink towards 0 (no change), while large counts are hardly affected.




Q9. In a single-end ChIP-seq experiment, the coverage of the reads themselves (not extended) shows two humps about 180 bp apart around each binding site, with a dip in between. Explain the pattern. What should you do before making a coverage track?






Answer





Each read is one end of a fragment that spans the site. Fragments sequenced from the + strand put their reads to the left of the site, those from the − strand to the right, so the reads form two humps about one fragment length apart, and the site itself is between them. The distance (here about 180 bp) estimates the fragment length. Extend every read in its own direction to that length (bamCoverage --extendReads 180): the extended reads overlap on the site and give one peak. (Paired-end data give each fragment directly.)




Q10. To save time, a student aligns whole-genome ChIP-seq reads to a reference that contains only chr21. Most reads align, many with MAPQ 42. Explain what has gone wrong, and why the high MAPQ is no reassurance.






Answer





Reads from the other chromosomes were forced onto chr21 wherever the sequence was most similar (repeats, paralogues, processed pseudogenes), creating false signal. MAPQ only compares the places the aligner can see: if the true origin is not in the reference, a read can look unique on chr21 and get MAPQ 42. Align to the whole genome and select chr21 afterwards. (The course data avoid this by including only reads that ENCODE placed on chr21 or chrM against the whole genome.)

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
About this lecture
You can align reads and make a coverage track (From reads to coverage). Whether that track means anything depends on decisions made before the first read was sequenced, and on a handful of numbers you should check before the first peak is called.

Design: biological replicates, controls (input, IgG, none), antibodies, spike-ins for global changes, batches.
QC metrics shared by ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq and CUT&Tag: library complexity, duplicates, FRiP, fingerprint, strand cross-correlation, replicate concordance, and for ATAC TSS enrichment and fragment sizes.
What each metric looks like on good and bad data, and the ENCODE thresholds.
Real numbers from the course data: GM12878 CTCF ChIP-seq with its input, and ATAC-seq in two replicates, on chr21.
How to read a methods section, and the red flags in published data.


This unit sits between the alignment unit and the assay blocks. Everything here is reused in the ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq, CUT&Tag and differential-analysis units, so it is taught once. The tone is practical: what can go wrong in an epigenomic experiment, how you would see it in the data, and how you decide whether to trust a dataset, your own or a published one. Students know design matrices and normalisation from RNA-seq; we reuse that, and spend the time on what is specific to enrichment assays: controls, enrichment metrics, and global changes. All real-data figures are made with make-design-figs.R from the same reads the students align in the exercise.

title: Experimental design and QC
section: What makes an epigenomic experiment interpretable?
text:
What makes an epigenomic experiment interpretable?


Each step from cells to peaks can fail silently: the pipeline still produces a BAM, a bigWig and a peak list.
Each failure leaves a fingerprint in the data that a QC metric is designed to catch.
Two failures cannot be repaired afterwards: no replicates and no control. Plan them before the experiment.


Walk along the chain. Samples: if conditions and batches are confounded, no analysis can separate them. Chromatin: sonication shears open chromatin more easily, so even DNA with no antibody shows “peaks” at promoters; amplified regions give more reads everywhere. IP: an antibody that binds weakly or cross-reacts gives a low signal-to-noise ratio. Library: if the IP returned very little DNA, PCR copies a few molecules many times. Sequencing: too few reads and weak sites are missed. Analysis: standard normalisation assumes the total amount of the mark is the same in all samples. The rest of the lecture goes through these in order: design first (the part you cannot fix), then the metrics. Point out that a pipeline never fails on bad data; it produces confident-looking output either way.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Replicates: biological, technical and pseudo


Biological replicates (independent cultures, animals, patients) are what a claim about biology needs. ENCODE requires at least two; for differential analysis use at least three per condition, as in RNA-seq.
Technical replicates only measure the noise of the protocol. Pseudoreplicates (random halves of one library) only measure counting noise: a stand-in when there is a single sample, never evidence of reproducibility.


The same logic as in RNA-seq: the variance you need to estimate for a test is the variance between independent biological units. Two growths of a cell line on different days are the minimum for a cell line; for tissues, different animals or donors. Technical replicates (the same chromatin split into two IPs) are useful when developing a protocol, but adding them does not increase n. ENCODE’s consortium decision (Landt et al. 2012) was two biological replicates per ChIP-seq experiment; more replicates did not add many sites. For differential binding or accessibility, power depends on replicates far more than on depth: three per condition is the usual minimum, more when the effect is subtle or the samples are primary tissue. Pseudoreplicates: ENCODE’s pipeline splits the pooled reads at random into two halves and calls peaks on each half; this tells you whether a peak is supported by enough reads, not whether the experiment would replicate. Students should be suspicious of “n = 1, peaks called on pseudoreplicates” in a paper that makes biological claims.

title: Experimental design and QC
section: Why a control? The background is not flat
text:
Why a control? The background is not flat


Reads pile up where nothing is bound: open chromatin shears more easily, amplified regions have more DNA, repeats get no unique reads, GC-rich fragments amplify better.
An input library (sheared chromatin, no antibody) shows exactly these biases. Peak callers compare the ChIP to it locally, not to a flat average.


The schematic has the four common causes. Open promoters: sonication preferentially fragments open, nucleosome-free DNA, so input DNA has small bumps at active promoters, which a naive caller would report as peaks of any factor. Copy number: cancer cell lines (K562, HeLa, HepG2) have many amplifications; a 4-copy region gives twice as many reads in both ChIP and input; without the input every amplified region looks enriched. Mappability: repeats get no uniquely mapped reads in either; these gaps and the high-signal artefact regions are why we also use the blacklist. MACS uses the input to estimate a local background rate lambda in 1 kb, 5 kb and 10 kb windows around each candidate peak, which is how the input actually enters the statistics; that is covered in Peak calling. Match the control to the ChIP: same cells, same crosslinking and sonication, similar read length, sequenced at least as deep.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Input, IgG or no control


Input is the standard for ChIP-seq (ENCODE): cheap, complex, captures shearing, copy number and mappability.
IgG mimics the IP but recovers little DNA, so the library is often small and noisy.
ATAC-seq and CUT&Tag have no input: the background is estimated from the sample itself. Comparing conditions and replicates carries the weight instead.


Landt et al. describe both kinds of control and note that an IgG control must yield a library of complexity comparable to the ChIP, which often fails because a non-specific antibody pulls down very little DNA. In practice ENCODE uses inputs. For ATAC-seq there is no sensible control: naked genomic DNA tagmented by Tn5 would model Tn5’s sequence preference but nobody does it routinely. MACS then uses the genome-wide background of the sample, and a local lambda from the sample itself. CUT&Tag sometimes uses an IgG control, and its background is so low that the main concern is different (covered in CUT&RUN and CUT&Tag). Students should know that “no control” is normal for ATAC and a red flag for ChIP.

title: Experimental design and QC
section: Real data: CTCF ChIP and its input on chr21
text:
Real data: CTCF ChIP and its input on chr21


Left: reads per million in 1 kb bins over 400 kb. The ChIP has sharp peaks at the ENCODE peaks; the input is low, with small bumps at some of the same sites.
Right: 100 kb bins over all of chr21. ChIP and input rise and fall together (correlation 0.87): no reads on the unassembled short arm and the centromere, more reads in gene-dense regions. That is background, and the input measures it.


Real data from the exercise: GM12878 CTCF ChIP-seq (ENCODE ENCSR000DZN, replicate 1, 36 bp single-end reads from 2008) and its input (ENCSR000EYX), aligned to chr21, filtered, deduplicated and blacklist-filtered; about 200 000 ChIP and 108 000 input reads on chr21. Left: CTCF peaks are tall and narrow, and most bins between peaks have a few reads in both tracks. Look for the small input bumps under some CTCF peaks: input DNA is enriched at open chromatin, and many CTCF sites are open. Right: at 100 kb scale the ChIP looks almost like the input: 93 of 468 bins have no input reads (the first ~5 Mb of chr21 is the unassembled acrocentric short arm; the gap at 11-13 Mb is the centromere), and the gene-rich distal end of chr21 has more reads in both. This is the background that the peak caller must not report: it compares the ChIP with the local input level, not with the chromosome average. GM12878 has a near-normal karyotype; in a cancer cell line you would also see copy-number steps in both tracks.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Antibodies decide what you measure


A ChIP is only as specific as its antibody. Check: one main band on an immunoblot (ENCODE: at least 50% of the signal), and a second line of evidence: IP–mass spectrometry, a second antibody or an epitope tag, the expected motif, or loss of signal in a knockout or knockdown.
Histone-mark antibodies can cross-react with neighbouring states (H3K4me2 vs me3) or be blocked by a modification next door. Lots differ: record the lot number.


Landt et al. give the ENCODE antibody standards: a primary characterisation (immunoblot or immunofluorescence; on the blot the main band should hold at least 50% of the signal, ideally at the expected size) and one of several secondary characterisations: knockdown, a second antibody against another epitope or a complex member, an epitope-tagged construct, IP followed by mass spectrometry, or motif enrichment in the peaks. Histone antibodies are tested on peptide arrays or with modified nucleosomes. Egelhofer et al. 2011 tested more than 200 histone-modification antibodies and found that about a quarter failed specificity tests. The knockout control is the strongest: if the signal persists in cells lacking the protein, it was not the protein. When reading a paper, look for catalogue and lot numbers and some evidence of validation.

title: Experimental design and QC
section: Normalisation assumes the total does not change
text:
Normalisation assumes the total does not change


Standard normalisation (CPM, RPKM, DESeq2 size factors) makes every library the same total. Fine when most sites do not change.
An EZH2 inhibitor removes most H3K27me3 everywhere. The IP still returns DNA, the library is sequenced to the same depth, and after normalisation the tracks look unchanged.
To see a global change you need an external reference added in a known amount: a spike-in.


This is the same assumption students met with DESeq2 size factors: the median-of-ratios method assumes most genes do not change. In RNA-seq this fails for global transcriptional amplification (e.g. MYC); in epigenomics it fails whenever a drug or mutation changes the total amount of a mark: EZH2 inhibitors or EZH2 mutations (H3K27me3), the oncohistone H3K27M (loss of H3K27me3), BET inhibitors and HDAC inhibitors (acetylation), DOT1L inhibitors (H3K79me2). The IP always returns some DNA, library preparation adds PCR cycles until there is enough, and the sequencer gives each sample its 20 million reads. Information about the absolute amount is lost at every one of these steps. Normalising by read depth then redistributes the remaining signal, so a 4-fold global drop looks like no change, or even a gain at the strongest sites.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Spike-in normalisation (ChIP-Rx)


Add the same amount of foreign chromatin (e.g. Drosophila cells, or synthetic modified nucleosomes) to each sample before the IP. The antibody pulls down the fly mark too.
The fly reads measure how efficient the IP was in each sample. Scale each human signal by \alpha = 1/N_\text{fly} (fly reads, in millions).


Orlando et al. 2014 (ChIP-Rx, “reference exogenous genome”) added a fixed number of Drosophila S2 cells to a fixed number of human cells, did the ChIP with antibodies that recognise the conserved mark in both species, and aligned reads to a combined genome. Their normalisation factor was alpha = 1 / (million reads mapped to the fly genome). They showed that a DOT1L inhibitor reduced H3K79me2 globally, which standard normalisation hid. Variants: synthetic barcoded nucleosomes (SNAP-ChIP/ICeChIP), E. coli carry-over DNA in CUT&RUN, and spike-ins for ATAC-seq. Spike-ins add their own uncertainty: the ratio of cells must be accurate (count cells, check the fly fraction in the input), and the spike-in must be added before any step that loses material. When the total does not change, spike-in normalisation only adds noise.

CPM says nothing changed. The spike-in says the domain lost 1 - 400/1900 \approx 79% of its H3K27me3.
The inhibitor-treated IP pulled down less human DNA, so the same amount of fly chromatin made up a larger share of the library.


Go through the arithmetic slowly; a version of this is in the exercise and is a natural exam question. Both libraries were sequenced to 20 M reads. In the control, fly reads are 1 M (5%); in the treated sample 4 M (20%): the fly chromatin is the same amount, so a larger share means less human material was pulled down. CPM: 1900 / 19 = 100 and 1600 / 16 = 100, identical. Spike-in: alpha is 1/1 = 1 and 1/4 = 0.25, giving 1900 and 400, a 4.75-fold drop. Note that the CPM values are identical because the domain is a fixed fraction of the human reads; in real data the strongest domains often even appear to gain. In a full analysis the factor is also corrected for the fly fraction in each input (to account for small differences in how many cells were mixed), and DESeq2 can be given these factors as size factors instead of estimating its own.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Batches and confounding


Day of processing, antibody lot, sequencing run and operator all change the data. If they line up with the condition, the effect is not identifiable: no software can fix it.
Spread conditions across batches, record the batches, and put them in the model, ~ batch + condition, exactly as in DESeq2.


Students know design matrices from RNA-seq; the point here is that in epigenomic experiments batch effects are often larger than in RNA-seq, because the IP step adds variability: antibody lot, crosslinking time, sonication efficiency and IP efficiency all vary between days. In the confounded design, the batch2 column equals the treated column in every row, so the design matrix is rank-deficient and DESeq2 refuses to fit it; worse, if you drop batch from the model, it fits happily and attributes the day-2 effect to the treatment. Balanced design: process one control and one treated sample together each day. Also: randomise the order of samples on the sequencer, and use the same antibody lot for a whole study. A PCA of the samples (as in RNA-seq) shows whether samples cluster by batch.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Sequencing depth and saturation


Peaks called by MACS3 on random subsamples of the chr21 reads. CTCF saturates: about 500 peaks from half of the reads on. ATAC does not: weaker accessible sites keep appearing with depth.
ENCODE: 20 M usable fragments per replicate for TFs and narrow marks, 45 M for broad marks, 25 M non-duplicate, non-mitochondrial fragments for ATAC-seq. Depth cannot rescue a poor library: once every unique molecule has been read, more sequencing only adds duplicates.


How to read the figure: each point is a MACS3 run (q < 0.01) on a subsample, for CTCF with the input as control. The chr21 numbers correspond to roughly 70 times as many reads genome-wide: 200 000 CTCF reads on chr21 is about 15 M usable reads in total. CTCF is a strong factor with a long motif and high-occupancy sites, so most of its sites are found with a few million reads; the curve flattens at about 100 000 chr21 reads (some 7 M genome-wide). ATAC-seq measures a continuum of accessibility, and the number of peaks keeps growing; the same is true for weak TFs and for broad marks, where depth decides how much of each domain is called. Landt et al. 2012 (Fig. 3) showed the same for ENCODE TFs: peak numbers keep rising with depth for many factors, with the new peaks increasingly weak. The practical rules: plan depth from the standards, check saturation on your own data by subsampling, and remember that complexity, not depth, limits a poor library (next slide).

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Library complexity: NRF, PBC1, PBC2


Count reads by their start position and strand. A complex library has almost every read at its own position; a bottlenecked library (little starting DNA, too many PCR cycles) has the same molecules many times.
NRF = distinct positions / reads. PBC1 = positions with exactly one read / distinct positions. PBC2 = positions with one read / positions with two.


Definitions from the ENCODE data standards. They are computed on the filtered reads before duplicate removal. NRF is the fraction of reads that are not redundant. PBC1 asks: of the positions with any read, what fraction have exactly one? In a complex library sequenced to moderate depth almost all positions have one read, PBC1 close to 1. PBC2 is the ratio of singletons to doubletons; for a Poisson sample of a huge library, few positions get two reads and PBC2 is large; when a library is exhausted, positions with two, three, many reads become common and PBC2 drops towards 1. ENCODE ChIP-seq thresholds: NRF > 0.9, PBC1 > 0.9, PBC2 > 10 is ideal; NRF < 0.5, PBC1 < 0.5 or PBC2 < 1 is a severe bottleneck. ATAC-seq preferred values: NRF > 0.9, PBC1 > 0.9, PBC2 > 3. Note that all three depend on depth: the same library sequenced deeper looks less complex, and at very strong peaks, true independent fragments can share a start position (more so for single-end reads and narrow TF sites).

That is an artefact of our read selection (all chrM reads kept, but only chr21 of the nuclear genome); genome-wide, ENCODE reports 14% and 10% mitochondrial reads for the two ATAC replicates. Always compute complexity on the nuclear genome.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Fraction of reads in peaks (FRiP)


FRiP = reads overlapping peaks / all mapped (filtered) reads. A direct measure of how much of the library is signal.
Guides: ENCODE inspects TF ChIP with FRiP below 1%; for ATAC-seq FRiP should be > 0.3 (0.2 acceptable). Broad histone marks and good CUT&Tag reach much higher values.
FRiP depends on the peak caller and the number of peaks: compare samples only with the same peak set or the same caller and settings.


Landt et al. 2012: most of 1052 ENCODE TF datasets had FRiP of 1% or more with MACS default peaks, and ENCODE scrutinises experiments below 1%. That threshold suits factors with thousands to tens of thousands of sites; a factor with a few hundred sites can be a perfect experiment at 0.5%. ATAC-seq standard: FRiP > 0.3, values > 0.2 acceptable. FRiP correlates with the number of peaks, which is partly circular: a weak experiment gives fewer peaks and therefore lower FRiP. Computing FRiP against a fixed reference peak set (here the ENCODE peaks) makes samples comparable. For paired-end data, count fragments or reads, but say which.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Real data: FRiP


CTCF ChIP: 22% of reads in the 405 ENCODE CTCF peaks on chr21, which cover only 0.19% of the chromosome. ATAC: 59% and 50% of reads in ATAC peaks (1.5% of chr21). All far above the guidelines.
The input has 1.6% of its reads in CTCF peaks and 8.3% in ATAC peaks: 5–8 times more than uniform. Input DNA is enriched in open chromatin.


FRiP computed against ENCODE’s IDR-thresholded peaks with samtools view -c -L (exercise C3). The red marks show the fraction of chr21 covered by the peaks: what the FRiP would be if reads were spread uniformly. CTCF is a strong, high-quality ChIP: 22% is high for a TF (many good TF datasets are in the 1-10% range). ENCODE reports FRiPs of 46-60% for these ATAC replicates genome-wide, depending on the peak set, consistent with our chr21 values. The input result is the most instructive number on the slide: an input is supposed to be background, yet 8% of its reads fall into 1.5% of the chromosome where ATAC finds open chromatin. That is the sonication bias of slide “Why a control”: open chromatin shears more easily and is better represented in sequencing libraries. It is exactly why a ChIP peak at an open promoter is only meaningful when compared with the input.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
The fingerprint plot


Divide the genome into bins, count reads, sort the bins from fewest to most reads, and plot the cumulative fraction of reads (deepTools plotFingerprint, after the CHANCE method).
A uniform library (input) follows the diagonal. A good ChIP stays low and then rises steeply: a small fraction of the genome holds a large fraction of the reads.


The fingerprint plot is from Diaz et al. 2012 (CHANCE) and is implemented in deepTools plotFingerprint. It needs no peak calling, which makes it useful as a first check and for comparing ChIP with input directly. Read the plot from the right end: if the top 10% of bins (x from 0.9 to 1) hold 60% of the reads, the curve is at 0.4 at x = 0.9. Things to look for: the input should be close to the diagonal; a curve that rises steeply at the very end only (very few bins) can mean amplification artefacts or a few very high regions (blacklisted regions); a ChIP that looks like its input has failed. Broad marks (H3K27me3, H3K36me3) give a gentler bend than TFs, because the signal is spread over a larger part of the genome. With low coverage, many bins are empty, so the curve starts flat at zero for every sample: use bins large enough to have reads in most of them.

title: Experimental design and QC
section: Real data: fingerprint of CTCF ChIP and input
text:
Real data: fingerprint of CTCF ChIP and input





The input is closest to the diagonal; CTCF bends further; ATAC has the sharpest elbow.
Top 1% of 1 kb bins hold 8% of input reads, 30% of CTCF reads and 52% of ATAC reads.
All curves are flat up to 0.3–0.4: those bins have no reads at all (short arm, centromere, gaps). Only the rest of the chromosome is informative.



Computed from read 5’ ends in 1 kb bins over chr21 (make-design-figs.R); in the exercise students make the same plot with deepTools plotFingerprint. The input is not on the diagonal: partly because about 30% of the bins cannot receive reads at all, partly the open-chromatin bias from the FRiP slide. Compare like with like: the useful comparison is ChIP against its own input, made at the same bin size. The CTCF curve departs from the input mainly in the last 5% of bins: CTCF binds at a few hundred sites on chr21, each covering less than 1 kb. The ATAC curve bends earlier and harder: accessible sites are more numerous and the signal-to-noise of this ATAC library is excellent (FRiP 50-60%). deepTools also reports quality metrics derived from the curve, such as the elbow point and the Jensen-Shannon distance to the input (CHANCE, Diaz et al. 2012).

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Strand cross-correlation


Single-end reads come from the 5’ ends of fragments: around a bound site, + strand reads pile up to the left, − strand reads to the right, one fragment length apart.
Shift the − strand coverage by k bp and correlate it with the + strand: the correlation peaks at the fragment length. A second peak at the read length (“phantom”) comes from mappability, not from binding.
NSC = CC(fragment) / min(CC); RSC = (CC(fragment) − min) / (CC(read) − min). ENCODE repeats experiments with NSC < 1.05 and RSC < 0.8.


Kharchenko, Tolstorukov and Park 2008 introduced strand cross-correlation (in their SPP package) as a way to estimate the fragment length and the enrichment from single-end data without a peak caller. The phantom peak at the read length appears in every library, including the input: a position that is mappable on the + strand at x is also mappable on the − strand at x + read length, so the coverage of the two strands correlates at that shift for purely technical reasons. Good TF ChIP: the fragment peak is much higher than the phantom peak, RSC > 1. Input or failed ChIP: the phantom dominates, RSC well below 1. NSC compares the fragment peak with the background (the minimum of the curve), and is just above 1 for a weak experiment. Thresholds from Landt et al.: NSC < 1.05 and RSC < 0.8 lead ENCODE to repeat the experiment. Broad histone marks have flat profiles even when they are good, so these metrics are mostly for TFs and narrow marks. With paired-end data the fragment length is measured directly from the pairs.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Real data: CTCF cross-correlation


CTCF: a clear fragment-length peak at 93 bp (ENCODE: 90–95 bp). The read-length position (36 bp, dotted) lies on its rising flank. RSC 1.65 (ENCODE 1.69–1.86): passes.
Input: low, noisy, no fragment peak (RSC ≈ 1).
Our NSC (47) is far above ENCODE’s (4.9–10): NSC depends on how the background minimum is estimated. Compare it only between datasets computed the same way.


Computed in R in the exercise (R1): count the 5’ ends of + and - strand reads at every base of chr21, and correlate the + strand counts at x with the - strand counts at x + k for k from 0 to 1000. The y axes differ by a factor of 60. The CTCF fragments in this 2008 library are short (about 93 bp), so the phantom peak at the read length is not a separate peak but a shoulder on the fragment peak. RSC uses differences above the minimum and agrees well with ENCODE’s value from phantompeakqualtools on the whole genome. NSC divides by the minimum itself; our minimum is much lower than in ENCODE’s genome-wide computation (per-base vs binned counts, which chromosomes and repeats are included), so NSC comes out much higher. The lesson for reading papers: NSC and RSC from the standard tool (phantompeakqualtools, also in the ENCODE and nf-core pipelines) are comparable with the ENCODE thresholds; numbers from home-made implementations are not necessarily.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Replicate concordance


Count reads in bins (or peaks) in each replicate and correlate (deepTools multiBamSummary, plotCorrelation). ATAC rep1 vs rep2: r = 0.94 (log counts) in 10 kb bins, 0.99 in ENCODE peaks.
Smaller bins are noisier: 0.81 in 1 kb bins. Different assays correlate less: ATAC vs CTCF 0.65.
A high correlation is necessary, not sufficient: it is driven by shared background and the strongest regions.


Real data: the two ATAC replicates (ENCSR095QNB, about 480 000 reads each on chr21 after filtering). Bin-level correlation is the quickest check for a swapped or failed sample; plotCorrelation produces a heatmap of all pairwise correlations, and with many samples a PCA does the same job (as in RNA-seq). Use Spearman or Pearson on log counts: raw-count Pearson is dominated by the few largest bins. Why not sufficient: both replicates share the same mappability, GC and open-chromatin background, which alone produces correlation (ChIP and input correlate 0.87 at 100 kb, slide “Real data: CTCF ChIP and its input”). The question “are the same peaks found, and in the same order?” is what IDR answers (next slide). For differential analysis the relevant quantity is the dispersion between replicates in counts per peak, which DESeq2 estimates.

title: Experimental design and QC
section: IDR: are the same peaks found in both replicates?
text:
IDR: are the same peaks found in both replicates?


The irreproducible discovery rate (Li et al. 2011) compares the ranks of matched peaks in two replicates and keeps the peaks that are consistently strong. ENCODE’s TF and ATAC peak sets (including the ones we use) are IDR-thresholded.
ENCODE passes an experiment if the rescue and self-consistency ratios (true replicates vs pseudoreplicates) are both < 2. Details in Peak calling.


IDR is analogous to FDR, but for reproducibility rather than significance. The key idea: peaks that are real tend to be ranked high in both replicates, while noise peaks have uncorrelated ranks. The method fits a copula mixture model with a reproducible and an irreproducible component, and gives each peak pair a local IDR. The input to IDR must be a relaxed peak list (e.g. 300 000 peaks with a p-value threshold of 0.01), so that the noise component is represented; a stringent threshold before IDR breaks the method. The ratios: the self-consistency ratio compares the number of IDR peaks from the two pseudoreplicates of each replicate; the rescue ratio compares IDR on true replicates with IDR on pooled pseudoreplicates. Ratios above 2 mean the replicates disagree more than random halves of the data do. Students run IDR in Peak calling; here the concept is enough.

title: Experimental design and QC
section: ATAC-seq: fragment sizes and TSS enrichment
text:
ATAC-seq: fragment sizes and TSS enrichment


Fragment sizes: a nucleosome-free peak below 100 bp, then mono- and di-nucleosome humps (~200 and ~400 bp). ENCODE requires the NFR and mono-nucleosome peaks to be present.
TSS enrichment: Tn5 insertions at TSSs relative to 2 kb away. Here 33 (rep1) and 24 (rep2); ENCODE: > 7 ideal (GRCh38, RefSeq TSSs), and reports 28–30 and 22–23 for these replicates.
Also check the mitochondrial fraction (here 14% and 10% genome-wide) and FRiP. Details in ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder.


These two plots are the ATAC-specific QC; they replace the cross-correlation, which makes little sense for paired-end data where the fragment length is measured directly. The fragment-size ladder is the nucleosome signature: Tn5 cuts in linker DNA, so fragments that span one, two or three nucleosomes are enriched; a library with no ladder suggests over-digested or naked DNA. The TSS enrichment counts Tn5 insertion sites (read ends shifted +4/-5) in a window around all protein-coding TSSs on chr21 (602 TSSs), divided by the level 1900-2000 bp away, smoothed over 51 bp; the maximum is the score. It is the most robust single signal-to-noise metric for ATAC-seq: active promoters are open in almost every cell type. ENCODE’s thresholds depend on the TSS annotation (RefSeq vs GENCODE) and on the exact method, so compare like with like; our chr21 values are close to ENCODE’s genome-wide values for the same replicates. Rep2 has a lower TSS enrichment and FRiP than rep1 but higher complexity: no single metric decides.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Reading a MultiQC report


MultiQC collects the logs of fastp, Bowtie2, samtools, Picard, deepTools, MACS and many more into one HTML report, one row per sample. nf-core pipelines produce one at the end of every run.
Read it across samples: the bad sample is the one that differs from its replicates. Then open the plots behind the number (duplication curve, fingerprint, cross-correlation).


Ewels et al. 2016. The general statistics table is a summary; the value is in comparing samples side by side. In the schematic, rep3 has fewer reads, a lower alignment rate, 63% duplicates, NRF 0.37, FRiP of 0.04 and RSC 0.6, and its fingerprint looks halfway to an input: the IP worked poorly and the library was amplified from very little DNA. A defensible decision: exclude it and say so, or redo it. What is not defensible: keeping it in a differential analysis without comment, or dropping it silently. Show students an nf-core/chipseq or nf-core/atacseq MultiQC report in the browser if time allows; the course pipelines produce one.

From the ENCODE data standards pages (ChIP-seq TF, histone, ATAC-seq; current at the time of writing) and Landt et al. 2012. Thresholds are guides for flagging, not laws: a factor with few sites can have a low FRiP and be fine, broad marks have flat cross-correlation curves, and complexity metrics depend on depth. ENCODE itself marks data with coloured audit flags rather than rejecting them outright. The value of the table is as a reference point when you look at your own numbers or at a paper’s supplementary QC table. TSS enrichment thresholds depend on the TSS annotation and the exact method, so compare like with like.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Red flags in published data


No input for a ChIP-seq, or the same input reused for unrelated cell types. n = 1 with claims about differences between conditions.
FRiP of 1–2% for a histone mark, a fingerprint that looks like the input, duplication above 50% with no comment, fewer reads than the standard.
A global change (inhibitor, knockout of a writer) normalised by read depth. Conditions processed on different days. No antibody catalogue or lot number.


A checklist for reading methods sections and supplementary tables, and the core of the “judge the design” exam questions. Each flag is not automatically fatal, but each should be explained. Where to find the information: GEO entries often list the controls and the number of replicates; supplementary tables sometimes give FRiP and duplication. If the raw data are public, you can compute all of these metrics yourself in an hour, which is what the exercise does for an ENCODE dataset. Good practice to point out: ENCODE and the nf-core pipelines report all of these metrics by default, and the ENCODE portal flags experiments that fail them.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Summary

input for ChIP (shearing, copy number, mappability); IgG often too little DNA; ATAC has none

one main band, a second line of evidence, knockout loses the signal

ATAC

Students should leave able to compute NRF, PBC1, PBC2 and FRiP from counts, read a fingerprint and a cross-correlation plot, explain what an input corrects and why spike-ins are needed for global changes, and critique a study design. Next: the ATAC-seq block, where TSS enrichment and fragment sizes are covered properly, and the ChIP-seq block, where the input enters the peak caller.

title: Experimental design and QC
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Landt et al. 2012, Genome Res. ChIP-seq guidelines and practices of the ENCODE and modENCODE consortia. Where most of the metrics and thresholds in this lecture come from.
Kharchenko, Tolstorukov & Park 2008, Nat Biotechnol. Design and analysis of ChIP-seq experiments for DNA-binding proteins. Strand cross-correlation and the SPP peak caller.
Li, Brown, Huang & Bickel 2011, Ann Appl Stat. Measuring reproducibility of high-throughput experiments. The IDR method.
Orlando et al. 2014, Cell Rep. Quantitative ChIP-Seq normalization reveals global modulation of the epigenome. ChIP-Rx spike-in normalisation.
Diaz, Park, Lim & Song 2012, Stat Appl Genet Mol Biol. Normalization, bias correction, and peak calling for ChIP-seq. CHANCE and the fingerprint plot.
Ewels, Magnusson, Lundin & Käller 2016, Bioinformatics. MultiQC: summarize analysis results for multiple tools and samples in a single report.

title: Exercise: Experimental design and QC
text:
Background
Library complexity. Count the filtered reads (MAPQ ≥ 30, primary; duplicates not yet removed) by position: for single-end reads the 5’ end and strand, for paired-end reads the fragment’s start and end. With \(N\) reads, \(M_\text{distinct}\) distinct positions, \(M_1\) positions with exactly one read and \(M_2\) with exactly two:
\[\text{NRF} = \frac{M_\text{distinct}}{N}, \qquad \text{PBC1} = \frac{M_1}{M_\text{distinct}}, \qquad \text{PBC2} = \frac{M_1}{M_2}\]
ENCODE ChIP-seq: NRF > 0.9, PBC1 > 0.9, PBC2 > 10 is ideal; 0.8–0.9 (NRF “compliant”, PBC1 “mild”), PBC2 3–10 (“mild”); NRF or PBC1 below 0.5 or PBC2 below 1 is severe. ATAC-seq preferred values: NRF > 0.9, PBC1 > 0.9, PBC2 > 3.
FRiP = reads overlapping peaks / all filtered reads. ENCODE scrutinises TF ChIP-seq with FRiP below 1% (Landt et al. 2012); ATAC-seq should have FRiP > 0.3 (> 0.2 acceptable).
Fingerprint. Count reads in bins, sort the bins, plot the cumulative fraction of reads against the fraction of bins. Input ≈ diagonal; an enriched sample bends towards the lower right.
Strand cross-correlation \(CC(k)\): the correlation between + strand read 5’ ends at \(x\) and − strand read 5’ ends at \(x + k\). It peaks at the fragment length, with a “phantom” peak at the read length.
\[\text{NSC} = \frac{CC(\text{fragment})}{\min CC}, \qquad \text{RSC} = \frac{CC(\text{fragment}) - \min CC}{CC(\text{read length}) - \min CC}\]
ENCODE repeats experiments with NSC < 1.05 and RSC < 0.8.
Spike-in (ChIP-Rx). A fixed amount of fly chromatin is added to each sample before the IP. With \(N_\text{fly}\) the reads (in millions) on the fly genome, multiply the human signal by \(\alpha = 1/N_\text{fly}\).

title: Exercise: Experimental design and QC
text:
Data
The CTCF ChIP-seq of GM12878 (ENCODE ENCSR000DZN, replicate 1, single-end 36 bp, 2008-era Illumina reads with phred+64 qualities) and its input control (ENCSR000EYX, single-end 27–28 bp), and ATAC-seq of GM12878 in two biological replicates (ENCSR095QNB, paired-end 2 × 100 bp). For each library you get the original, untrimmed reads that ENCODE aligned to chr21 or chrM, plus a Bowtie2 index of chr21 + chrM, the ENCODE peaks (CTCF and ATAC, IDR-thresholded), the blacklist and the GENCODE annotation.
data/download.sh epigenomics-design      # about 1.5 GB
mkdir -p ~/epi/design && cd ~/epi/design
D=/path/to/course/data                   # where download.sh put the files
T=8                                      # threads
You need fastp, bowtie2, samtools (1.12 or newer), bedtools, deepTools and R with GenomicAlignments (see Install the software you need). The ChIP part runs in a minute; aligning the ATAC-seq reads takes about 10 minutes with 8 threads, so run it as a batch job on the cluster (wrap the alignment block in an sbatch script) and do the by-hand part meanwhile.






A shortcut to be aware of



The reads were selected because ENCODE aligned them to chr21 or chrM. Two consequences: the alignment rate is close to 100% (the reads that would not align were never selected), and the chrM fraction is hugely inflated (all mitochondrial reads were kept, but only 1/60 of the nuclear ones). We therefore compute every metric on chr21 only, where the reads are a faithful sample of the full library. The ENCODE values for the whole genome are given in the solutions for comparison.

By hand
Do these on paper.

Library 2 is sequenced again, to 40 M reads. Will NRF go up, stay the same or go down? Will the number of usable reads go up four-fold? Why?
Why must these metrics be computed before duplicate removal?

B2. FRiP. A CTCF ChIP-seq has 18 M filtered reads, of which 540 000 overlap the 45 000 called peaks. The peaks are on average 300 bp wide; the mappable genome is 2.7 Gb.

Compute FRiP. Does it pass the ENCODE guideline?
What FRiP would you expect if the reads were spread uniformly over the mappable genome? How many times more reads are in the peaks than expected?
The input of the same experiment has a FRiP of 0.4% in the same peaks. Why is that higher than your answer in (b)?
An ATAC-seq library has FRiP 0.15. What does ENCODE say? Name two things that could have gone wrong in the experiment.

B3. Read a fingerprint plot. The figure shows four samples, A–D, each with 1-kb bins over the genome.






Which curve is most likely an input? Which is a TF ChIP-seq with strong, sharp peaks? Which is a broad histone mark such as H3K27me3?
For curve B, read off the fraction of reads in the top 10% of bins.
Curve D follows the input until the last 1% of bins, which hold almost 30% of the reads. Is this a good ChIP? What could produce such a curve? (Think about the blacklist and about PCR.)
