title: Exercise: ATAC-seq
text:
In R
library(GenomicRanges); library(rtracklayer); library(ggplot2)
D <- "/path/to/course/data"
setwd("~/epi/atac")

R1 — The fragment-length distribution
fl <- read.table("rep1.fraglen.txt", col.names = c("len", "n"))
sum(fl$n)
ggplot(fl[fl$len <= 1000, ], aes(len, n)) + geom_line()
ggplot(fl[fl$len <= 1000, ], aes(len, n)) + geom_line() + scale_y_log10()
peak_in <- function(lo, hi) { x <- fl[fl$len >= lo & fl$len <= hi, ]; x$len[which.max(x$n)] }
c(nfr = peak_in(30, 120), mono = peak_in(150, 280), di = peak_in(300, 480))
c(nfr = sum(fl$n[fl$len < 100]), mono = sum(fl$n[fl$len >= 180 & fl$len <= 250])) / sum(fl$n)

Describe the plot. Where are the nucleosome-free, mono- and di-nucleosome peaks?
What can you see on the log scale that you cannot see on the linear one?
The raw counts are noisy at the di-nucleosome peak. Smooth them with a running mean over 11 bp, stats::filter(fl$n, rep(1/11, 11)), and find the peak again. Note: fl must have one row per length with no gaps for this to be correct; check with all(diff(fl$len) == 1) over the range you use.



R2 — The 10.5-bp periodicity
x <- merge(data.frame(len = 1:1000), fl, all.x = TRUE); x$n[is.na(x$n)] <- 0
x$trend <- as.numeric(stats::filter(x$n, rep(1/31, 31)))
p <- x[x$len >= 40 & x$len <= 150, ]
p$ratio <- p$n / p$trend
plot(p$len, p$ratio, type = "l"); abline(h = 1, col = "grey")
mx <- p$len[which(diff(sign(diff(p$ratio))) == -2) + 1]
mx; diff(mx); mean(diff(mx))

What do you see after dividing by the trend? At which lengths are the maxima, and what is their mean spacing?
Some maxima are spurious wiggles 1–3 bp apart. Look at diff(mx): how would you make the estimate more robust? (One option: keep only maxima that are the highest point within ±4 bp; another: spec.pgram() on p$ratio - 1 and take 1 / freq at the highest peak.)



R3 — TSS enrichment
gtf <- import(file.path(D, "gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz"))
tx  <- gtf[gtf$type == "transcript" & gtf$transcript_type == "protein_coding" & seqnames(gtf) == "chr21"]
tss <- unique(granges(resize(tx, width = 1, fix = "start")))
length(tss)

ins <- import("rep1.insertions.bed")                        # one base per insertion
win <- resize(tss, 4001, fix = "center")                     # ±2 kb
h   <- findOverlaps(ins, win, ignore.strand = TRUE)
d   <- start(ins)[queryHits(h)] - start(tss)[subjectHits(h)]
d   <- ifelse(as.character(strand(tss))[subjectHits(h)] == "-", -d, d)   # orient by strand
prof <- tabulate(d + 2001, 4001)                             # insertions at -2000 ... +2000

bg   <- mean(prof[c(1:100, 3902:4001)])                      # outer 100 bp at each end
norm <- prof / bg
bin10 <- tapply(norm, (seq_along(norm) - 1) %/% 10, mean)
c(background = bg, centre = mean(norm[2001 + (-5:5)]), tss_enrichment = max(bin10))
plot(-2000:2000, stats::filter(norm, rep(1/11, 11)), type = "l",
     xlab = "distance to TSS (bp)", ylab = "insertions / flank mean")
abline(h = c(1, 7), col = c("grey", "red"), lty = 2)

How many TSSs are used? What is the background (insertions per bp), and what is the TSS enrichment? How does it compare with ENCODE’s thresholds and with ENCODE’s own value for this library (29.6, genome-wide, RefSeq TSSs)?
Remove the line that orients by strand and recompute. What happens to the shape of the profile, and why?
The maximum is not exactly at 0. Where is it, and what lies on either side of it (think of the NDR and the +1 nucleosome)?
Why do we use unique() on the TSSs? What would happen to the score if a highly expressed gene with 12 transcripts starting at the same base were counted 12 times?



R4 — Nucleosome-free versus mono-nucleosome fragments
fr  <- import("rep1.fragments.bed")
mid <- (start(fr) + end(fr)) %/% 2
w   <- width(fr)
prof_mid <- function(pos, flank = 1000) {
  pts <- GRanges("chr21", IRanges(pos, width = 1))
  h <- findOverlaps(pts, resize(tss, 2 * flank + 1, fix = "center"), ignore.strand = TRUE)
  d <- pos[queryHits(h)] - start(tss)[subjectHits(h)]
  d <- ifelse(as.character(strand(tss))[subjectHits(h)] == "-", -d, d)
  p <- tabulate(d + flank + 1, 2 * flank + 1)
  p / mean(p[c(1:100, (2 * flank - 98):(2 * flank + 1))])
}
nfr  <- prof_mid(mid[w < 100])
mono <- prof_mid(mid[w >= 180 & w <= 250])
sm <- function(v) stats::filter(v, rep(1/21, 21))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(-1000:1000, sm(nfr),  type = "l", col = "darkgreen", main = "< 100 bp",   xlab = "distance to TSS", ylab = "relative")
plot(-1000:1000, sm(mono), type = "l", col = "steelblue", main = "180-250 bp", xlab = "distance to TSS", ylab = "relative")
which.max(sm(mono)[1001:2001]) - 1          # +1 nucleosome: distance of the downstream maximum

Describe the two profiles. Where is the +1 nucleosome, and where is the −1?
Why use the fragment centre here rather than the insertion sites?
If you had only single-end reads, could you make these plots? Why not?

title: Exercise: ATAC-seq
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — read positions and TLEN (B1, C4, C5)





SAM POS is the leftmost aligned base, 1-based, for reads on either strand. A − strand read’s 5’ end is its rightmost base: POS + aligned length − 1. TLEN is the distance from the leftmost to the rightmost aligned base of the pair, + for the leftmost mate. See the SAM specification (section 1.4) and samtools flags to decode flags.









Hint 2 — fragment classes and the ladder (B2, B6, R1, R2)





A fragment needs two insertions; Tn5 cannot insert into DNA wrapped on a nucleosome. Count how much DNA lies between two linkers separated by one, two or three nucleosomes. The 10.5-bp ripple is the helical repeat of DNA: Buenrostro et al. 2013, Fig. 2. For running means see stats::filter; for the periodogram spec.pgram.









Hint 3 — chrM (B3, C3)





If chr21 carries a fraction \(f\) of the nuclear reads, the full library had about \(n_{21} / f\) nuclear reads, and chrM fraction ≈ \(n_M / (n_M + n_{21}/f)\). samtools idxstats counts reads per reference sequence from the index; samtools view -c counts reads that pass filters.









Hint 4 — TSS enrichment (B4, R3)





Background = (sum of the two flank counts) / 200 bp. Enrichment = (count in the central bin / bin width) / background. ENCODE’s definition and thresholds are on the ATAC-seq standards page and the terms page. In R: resize, findOverlaps, tabulate.









Hint 5 — adapters and tools (B5, C1, C2)





Each end independently gets A or B. fastp detects adapters from the overlap of paired reads and from the sequence you give. bowtie2 manual: -X is the maximum fragment length for a valid paired-end alignment. samtools fixmate -m adds the mate tags that samtools markdup needs. bamCoverage with --extendReads fills in the whole fragment of a proper pair.
crumbs: ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder

title: Exercise: ATAC-seq
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) Read 1 is on the + strand, so its 5’ end is its POS: 33 500 101. Read 2 is on the − strand, so its 5’ end is its rightmost base: 33 500 247 + 100 − 1 = 33 500 346. (b) Fragment = 33 500 346 − 33 500 101 + 1 = 246 bp; TLEN = +246 for read 1 and −246 for read 2. (c) Mono-nucleosome size (180–250 bp): most likely two insertions in the linkers on either side of one nucleosome. (d) Both reads cover the same 62 bases: the fragment is 62 bp, nucleosome-free. The reads were 101 bp when sequenced, but after 62 bases they ran into the adapter of the other end, which fastp trimmed off.
B2. (a) Tn5 inserts only into DNA that is not wrapped on a nucleosome. Two insertions in the same open stretch (NDR or long linker) give a short fragment; any fragment that contains a nucleosome must be at least ~147 bp plus some linker, so lengths between ~100 and ~150 bp need an unusual geometry and are rarer. Fragments spanning one or two nucleosomes are ~one or two repeats long. (b) About 3 × 190 ≈ 570 bp (in our data a weak shoulder at 550–600 bp, visible only on the log scale). (c) The fragment contains the 147-bp core plus parts of the linkers on both sides, where Tn5 cut: 147 + two partial linkers ≈ 180–210 bp. (d) Very short fragments are lost in the cleanup (columns and beads do not keep them), cannot be amplified efficiently, and give reads too short to align uniquely (we also drop reads < 20 bp after trimming). Two Tn5 dimers also cannot insert right next to each other.
B3. (a) 12 / 40 = 30%; 28 M nuclear reads. (b) 25 / 0.70 = 35.7 M reads; with 3% chrM 25 / 0.97 = 25.8 M: Omni-ATAC saves about 10 M reads per sample. (c) 0.4 / 1.9 = 21% is the share of chrM among chr21 + chrM reads, not among all reads. The full library had about 1.5 M / 0.015 = 100 M nuclear reads, so chrM ≈ 0.4 / (0.4 + 100) ≈ 0.4%.
B4. (a) (1050 + 950) / 200 = 10 insertions per bp. (b) 2450 / 10 bp = 245 per bp; 245 / 10 = 24.5. (c) Yes, well above 7 (“ideal”). (d) 400 / 10 = 40 per bp; 40 / 10 = 4: “concerning”. Most insertions are background: dead or damaged cells, over-digestion, or a failed reaction (B6). (e) Total reads include chrM, peaks of every kind and background, and depend on depth; the flanks measure the background of this library at comparable positions, so the score is a pure signal-to-noise ratio that does not depend on sequencing depth.
B5. (a) \(2 \times 0.5 \times 0.5 =\) 50%. (b) \(2 \times 0.8 \times 0.2 =\) 32%. (c) Each fragment is usable with probability ½, so \(P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - 0.5^2 =\) 75%. A quarter of accessible sites are missed in a single nucleus by chemistry alone, before any losses in cleanup, PCR or sequencing: single-cell ATAC data are inherently sparse (mostly 0 or 1 fragment per site per cell).
B6. X: a good library: nucleosome-free peak, ladder, 10-bp ripple, high TSS enrichment. Use it. Y: over-tagmentation (too much Tn5 for the number of nuclei, or fewer nuclei than counted): the DNA is cut so often that nucleosomal fragments are rare; signal-to-noise is borderline (6). Usable for peaks with care; repeat with more nuclei if possible. Z: dead or dying cells. Apoptotic DNA is already cut into a nucleosome ladder, and DNA from damaged nuclei is tagmented everywhere, so the ladder is strong but there is almost no enrichment at TSSs (2.5, “concerning”). Do not use. The fragment-length plot alone would have made Z look like a fine library: always check the TSS profile too.
B7. (1) Cell composition: tumours contain different cells (tumour cells, immune infiltrate, stroma) than normal tissue; sites specific to a more abundant cell type gain signal in bulk without any chromatin change in any one cell. (2) Batch: all tumours were processed together and all normals months later, so processing day (Tn5 lot, cell viability, nuclei counting, sequencing run) is completely confounded with the condition. Also: tumour copy-number gains increase signal over amplified regions. Helps: process tumour and normal samples together in randomised batches; sort cell populations or use single-cell ATAC or deconvolution; check QC (TSS enrichment, fragment sizes) per group; account for copy number. “Epigenetic reprogramming” is a claim about mechanism that the data do not show.









Solutions — command line





Run times on a shared server with 8 threads: C1 24 s, C2 11.5 min (bowtie2 --very-sensitive is slow; on a quiet laptop with 8 cores expect 5–15 min), duplicate marking 24 s, C3–C6 a few seconds each.
C1. (a) 6 088 187 read pairs; 5 992 127 pairs (11 984 254 reads) pass the filters. Adapter was trimmed from 4 667 844 reads (38%): more than a third of the fragments are shorter than the 101-bp reads. fastp’s insert-size estimate peaks at 42 bp: the nucleosome-free peak again. (fastp reports a duplication rate of 56%, inflated by the many identical chrM fragments.) (b) Sequencing starts at one end of the fragment and continues for 101 cycles. If the fragment is only 60 bp, the last 41 cycles read the mosaic end and adapter on the other side. Untrimmed, those bases do not match the genome and the read fails end-to-end alignment.
C2. (a) 99.65% overall; 94.5% of pairs concordantly exactly once, 4.4% more than once (multi-mappers; MAPQ < 30 removes most of them). Very high because these reads were selected as ones ENCODE had aligned to chr21 or chrM. (b) -X 2000 sets the largest fragment that counts as a valid (“concordant”, properly paired) alignment. With the default of 500 bp, the tri-nucleosome fragments and part of the di-nucleosome fragments would not be flagged as proper pairs (flag 2), and -f 2 would remove them: the ladder would be cut off at 500 bp. (c) markdup flags 8 865 403 of 11 942 569 reads, 74%, almost all on chrM (C3c).
C3. (a) idxstats: chr21 1 111 555, chrM 10 831 014 mapped reads: 90.7% on chrM. (b) \(10.83 / (10.83 + 1.112 / 0.0151) = 10.83 / 84.6 =\) 12.8%, close to ENCODE’s 13.9% for the whole library. The assumption is rough (chr21 has an unmappable p-arm, and open chromatin is not uniform over chromosomes), but good enough. (c) After removing duplicates and MAPQ < 30: chr21 504 621, chrM 2 143 835 reads (81% chrM). On chr21, 20% of the reads were duplicates (632 859 → 504 621); on chrM, 80% (10.75 M → 2.14 M). chrM is only 16.6 kb and covered thousands of times, so two independent fragments with exactly the same two ends are common: many “duplicates” there are not PCR copies but saturation. (The same is true for very strong peaks in deep libraries.)
C4. (a) -f 66 = 2 + 64: properly paired and first in pair. Each fragment is counted once, and TLEN is taken with its absolute value because the first read can be either the left or the right mate. Taking column 9 from every read would count each fragment twice, and half the values would be negative. (b) 252 213 fragments; 28.7% shorter than 100 bp; the most common length is 45 bp (1 908 fragments).
C5. (a) For each first-in-pair read: L = |TLEN|; the fragment starts at the leftmost mate’s POS, which is the read’s own POS if TLEN > 0 and the mate’s position (PNEXT, column 8) if TLEN < 0. SAM positions are 1-based, BED starts are 0-based, hence s − 1; the BED end is start + length. (b) The first line is chr21  5032522  5032580  58: 5 032 580 − 5 032 522 = 58. (c) Over ±2 kb, a 4–5 bp offset is invisible (we even average over 10-bp bins). Footprints are dips of a few bp at a TF motif; there the exact position of each insertion matters, and the shift must be applied (ATAC-seq processing and peak calling).
C6. (3 s.) At ITGB2, ATAC peaks sit at the two promoters (44.921 and 44.929 Mb, both with H3K4me3 and H3K27ac) and at several sites in the gene body and upstream with H3K27ac but little H3K4me3 (candidate enhancers). The histone signal is broader than the ATAC peak and often highest on its flanks: the marks are on the nucleosomes next to the open DNA. The ATAC peak at 44.893 Mb has neither mark: load $D/gm12878_ctcf_peaks.bed.gz and you find a CTCF peak right on it (chr21:44 892 886–44 893 046), an insulator or loop anchor rather than a promoter or enhancer.









Solutions — R





R1. (a) A tall nucleosome-free peak at 45 bp with ripples, a broad mono-nucleosome peak near 200 bp and a weak di-nucleosome bump near 390 bp; 28.7% of fragments are < 100 bp and 16.1% are 180–250 bp. The raw which.max gives 45, 177 and 389 bp: the mono peak is flat-topped and noisy, so the raw maximum lands on one of the 10-bp spikes. (b) On the log scale the long tail is visible: the di-nucleosome bump, a weak shoulder at 550–600 bp (tri), and a smooth decay out to 1 kb. On the linear scale everything above 400 bp is squashed to the axis. (c) With an 11-bp running mean the peaks are at 45, 210 and 391 bp. fl has no gaps up to 700 bp (TRUE), so the running mean is over 11 consecutive lengths.
R2. (a) Below 150 bp the counts oscillate around the trend with maxima about every 10 bp (45, 54, 66, 75, 86, 95, 105, 115, 126 …), and the ripple continues into the mono-nucleosome peak (151, 167, 177, 187, 198 bp in the lecture figure). The naive maxima (mx) are 25 positions with a mean spacing of 4.3 bp: many are 2–4-bp noise wiggles. (b) Keeping only maxima that are the highest within ±4 bp leaves 45, 54, 66, 75, 86, 95, 105, 115, 126, 132, 138: spacing 10.1 bp between 45 and 126 (two spurious maxima at 132/138 drag the mean over all to 9.3). spec.pgram() puts the highest peak at a period of 10.0 bp (10.3 with pad = 9, a finer frequency grid). Expected: the helical repeat, ~10.5 bp. With 250 000 fragments from one chromosome, ±0.5 bp is as precise as it gets.
R3. (a) 602 TSSs; background 20.7 insertions per bp; centre (±5 bp) 33.1; TSS enrichment 34.0 (maximum of the 10-bp bins). Far above 7 (“ideal”), and close to ENCODE’s 29.6 for the full library (different TSS set, annotation and method; our chr21 subset is also small). (b) Without orientation the score is 32.8 and the profile becomes symmetric around 0: the upstream NDR peak of + strand genes and the downstream side of − strand genes are averaged, and the asymmetry (open upstream, +1 nucleosome downstream) disappears. (c) The highest 10-bp bin is at −140 bp (the 11-bp running mean peaks at −92 bp): the maximum is in the nucleosome-depleted region just upstream of the TSS, where TFs bind; downstream the signal drops where the +1 nucleosome sits. (d) A TSS shared by 12 transcripts would be counted 12 times: its insertions would weigh 12 times in the aggregate. Highly expressed genes tend to have many annotated transcripts and open promoters, so duplicates would inflate the score.
R4. (a) Nucleosome-free fragment centres peak at about −107 bp (15.8 × the flanks) and fall sharply downstream of the TSS. Mono-nucleosome fragment centres dip at the TSS (7.4 ×) and peak at +124 bp (the +1 nucleosome) and at −91 bp upstream (14.1 ×). The upstream peak is not a clean −1 nucleosome: in a highly accessible promoter, two insertions on either side of the whole NDR also make a ~200-bp fragment. (b) A nucleosome sits in the middle of a mono-nucleosome fragment, between the two insertions: the centre estimates the dyad. Insertions mark where the DNA was open, i.e. the linkers either side. (c) No: single-end reads give one insertion per fragment and no fragment length, so you can neither split fragments by size nor find their centres.

title: Exercise: ATAC-seq
text:
Where this leads

ATAC-seq processing and peak calling shifts the insertions by +4 / −5, calls peaks with MACS3 and builds consensus peaks across replicates.
Differential accessibility counts fragments in peaks across samples and uses DESeq2, as in RNA-seq.
Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting uses the insertion sites at base resolution, and has to deal with the Tn5 sequence bias.
Single-cell ATAC-seq uses the same fragments, one barcode per nucleus: the fragment-length and TSS-enrichment QC are computed per cell.

title: Quiz: ATAC-seq
text:
Short questions on Tn5, fragment lengths and ATAC-seq QC. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. What does ATAC-seq measure, and why does a peak of ATAC signal usually mark regulatory DNA?






Hint





Where can a large enzyme reach the DNA in a nucleus?









Answer





It measures where the Tn5 transposase could insert its adapters into the DNA of intact nuclei: accessibility. DNA wrapped on nucleosomes or packed in compact chromatin is protected. Active promoters, enhancers and insulators have a nucleosome-depleted region where transcription factors bind, so Tn5 inserts there often and the reads pile up into a peak.




Q2. “Tagmentation” combines two steps of ordinary library preparation. Which two, and what is the main practical advantage?






Answer





Fragmentation of the DNA and adapter ligation: Tn5 cuts the DNA and joins an adapter to each new end in one reaction. No sonication, end repair or ligation, so the protocol is fast (hours) and needs little material (hundreds to tens of thousands of cells), and it is done on native chromatin in the nucleus.




Q3. A read pair has read 1 on the + strand at POS 2 000 001 and read 2 on the − strand at POS 2 000 151; both reads are 100 bp. How long is the fragment, and at which positions did Tn5 insert (ignore the +4 / −5 shift)?






Hint





The 5’ end of a − strand read is its rightmost base.









Answer





Insertions at 2 000 001 (5’ end of read 1) and 2 000 250 (5’ end of read 2: 2 000 151 + 100 − 1). Fragment length 2 000 250 − 2 000 001 + 1 = 250 bp, TLEN = +250 for read 1 and −250 for read 2. A mono-nucleosome fragment.




Q4. Why do ATAC-seq fragment lengths show peaks below 100 bp, near 200 bp and near 400 bp?






Answer





Tn5 inserts into nucleosome-free DNA and linkers, not into DNA wrapped on a nucleosome. Two insertions in the same open region give a short (< 100 bp) fragment; two insertions in linkers on either side of one nucleosome give ~147 bp plus linker ≈ 200 bp; around two nucleosomes ≈ 400 bp. The steps are the nucleosome repeat length (~190 bp).




Q5. Tn5 is loaded with two adapter types, A and B, in equal amounts. What fraction of fragments can be amplified and sequenced? Why?






Answer





50%. Each end gets A or B at random, so fragments are A–B, B–A, A–A or B–B with probability ¼ each. PCR needs one primer site of each kind, and the sequencer reads from A and from B, so only A–B and B–A fragments (\(2 \times \tfrac12 \times \tfrac12\)) are amplified exponentially and sequenced.




Q6. A library has 30 M mapped reads, 9 M of them on chrM. What is the chrM fraction, why is it so high, and what protocol change would reduce it?






Answer





9 / 30 = 30%. Mitochondrial DNA has no nucleosomes (all of it is accessible) and is present in hundreds to thousands of copies per cell, so it attracts many Tn5 insertions once the lysis lets Tn5 into the mitochondria. Omni-ATAC (different detergents plus a wash step that removes much of the cytoplasm) typically brings it down to a few percent. Remove chrM reads before peak calling either way.




Q7. Insertions around 5000 TSSs are summed per bp over ±2 kb. The outer 100 bp at each end contain 600 and 400 insertions; the highest 10-bp bin near the TSS contains 1 200. Compute the TSS enrichment. Is the library acceptable by ENCODE’s GRCh38 thresholds?






Hint





Background = (600 + 400) / 200 insertions per bp.









Answer





Background = 1000 / 200 = 5 per bp. Central bin = 1200 / 10 = 120 per bp. TSS enrichment = 120 / 5 = 24: well above 7, “ideal” (ENCODE: < 5 concerning, 5–7 acceptable, > 7 ideal, for RefSeq TSSs on GRCh38).




Q8. Library P has a strong nucleosome ladder (peaks at ~200, ~400, ~600 bp, taller than the peak below 100 bp) and a TSS enrichment of 2. Library Q has almost only fragments shorter than 120 bp, no 200-bp peak, and a TSS enrichment of 6. What probably went wrong with each?






Answer





P: many dead or dying cells. Apoptotic DNA is cut between nucleosomes and gives a ladder by itself; the DNA of damaged nuclei is tagmented everywhere, so there is little enrichment at TSSs. The fragment plot alone would look fine; the TSS profile reveals the problem. Q: over-tagmentation: too much Tn5 for the number of nuclei (or too few nuclei counted), so fragments are short and the nucleosome information is lost; signal-to-noise is only borderline.




Q9. In the TSS-enrichment profile of a good library, short (< 100 bp) fragments peak right at the TSS, while mono-nucleosome (180–250 bp) fragment centres peak about 150 bp downstream and dip at the TSS. Explain.






Answer





Active promoters have a nucleosome-depleted region just upstream of and at the TSS: short fragments come from two insertions inside it. Mono-nucleosome fragments contain one nucleosome, so their centres mark nucleosome positions: the well-positioned +1 nucleosome just downstream of the TSS (and the −1 upstream), and a dip where there is no nucleosome.




Q10. A paper compares bulk ATAC-seq of whole blood from patients and healthy donors and concludes that “the disease rewires the epigenome of immune cells”. Which alternative explanation must be ruled out first?






Answer





A change in cell-type composition. Blood is a mixture (neutrophils, T cells, B cells, monocytes …), each with its own accessible sites. If patients have more of one cell type, its specific sites gain signal in bulk without any change of chromatin within a cell type. Sorted populations, deconvolution, or single-cell ATAC-seq address this. (Batch effects from processing patients and controls on different days are the second thing to check.)

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
text:
About this lecture
In ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder you saw what the assay measures. This lecture turns the reads into the things every downstream analysis starts from: peaks and a consensus peak set.

Reads to a clean BAM: trimming Nextera adapters, alignment with long fragments allowed, and five filters, each with a reason.
Tn5 insertion sites: the +4/−5 shift, and when to think in fragments or in cut sites.
Peak calling: what MACS3 computes (a local Poisson background), and the two ways to run it on ATAC-seq.
Replicates: naive overlap vs rank consistency (IDR) and pseudoreplicates.
Consensus peaks across samples, FRiP, comparison with ENCODE, and where the peaks sit.


The running example is real: ENCODE GM12878 ATAC-seq (experiment ENCSR095QNB), two biological replicates, paired-end 2 × 100 bp, restricted to the reads that ENCODE aligned to chromosome 21 or the mitochondrial genome. The reads are untouched, adapters and all, so every step in this lecture is one students run in the exercise, and every number on the slides comes from that run. The analysis continues in Differential accessibility, which starts from a count matrix over fixed-width 500-bp peaks: the consensus procedure at the end of this lecture is how such a matrix is built.

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
section: The ATAC-seq pipeline, end to end
text:
The ATAC-seq pipeline, end to end


Ten steps; each one answers a specific problem with the raw data. We go through them in order.
Production pipelines do exactly this: nf-core/atacseq (Nextflow) and the ENCODE ATAC-seq pipeline (WDL). Learn the steps on one sample by hand, then run the pipeline on all of them.


Top row: from FASTQ to a filtered BAM; bottom row: from the BAM to peaks and a peak set that can be counted. The QC line at the bottom lists what to look at along the way; the fragment-size distribution and TSS enrichment belong to the previous unit, FRiP and replicate agreement to this one. The two production pipelines differ in details (nf-core uses BWA by default and calls broad peaks on fragments by default; ENCODE uses Bowtie2, shifts reads, calls narrow peaks on insertion sites and runs IDR), but the logic is the same. nf-core is the easiest to run on an HPC cluster with SLURM; it is a single command with a sample sheet once Nextflow and a container engine are available. Point out the arrow from Shift to Signal track: most of the downstream work uses insertion sites rather than reads.

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
text:
Trim the adapters first


Tn5 loads the Nextera adapters. Both reads of a short fragment run into the adapter: CTGTCTCTTATACACATCT….
ATAC-seq is made of short fragments: in our data fastp trimmed adapter bases from 38% of the reads.
Untrimmed, these reads fail to align end to end or align with mismatches at the ends; trim with fastp, cutadapt or Trim Galore.


The sequence CTGTCTCTTATACACATCT is the reverse complement of the 19-bp Tn5 mosaic end; it is the same at both ends of every fragment, so R1 and R2 read into the same adapter sequence. In RNA-seq with TruSeq libraries and 300-bp inserts you could almost ignore adapters; in ATAC-seq the nucleosome-free fragments are often shorter than the read. fastp also detects adapters automatically from the overlap of R1 and R2, which works well for paired-end data; we give it the sequence explicitly to be sure. A minimum length (we use 20 bp) removes reads that are too short to align uniquely. The fraction quoted on the slide comes from the fastp report of replicate 1 (4.67 M of 12.18 M reads; replicate 2: 40%). fastp also reports an “insert size peak” of 42 bp for replicate 1: it can only estimate the insert size from pairs whose reads overlap, i.e. short fragments, so this is not the fragment-size mode.

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
section: Align with room for long fragments
text:
Align with room for long fragments
bowtie2 -p 8 --very-sensitive -X 2000 -x hg38_chr21_chrM \
        -1 rep1_R1.trim.fq.gz -2 rep1_R2.trim.fq.gz 2> rep1.bowtie2.log \
  | samtools fixmate -m -u - - | samtools sort -o rep1.raw.bam

-X 2000: pairs up to 2 kb count as concordant. The default (500) makes di- and tri-nucleosome fragments “improper”.
fixmate -m adds the mate tags that samtools markdup needs later.
Reference: chr21 + chrM only, an honest shortcut (see notes).


Bowtie2 in end-to-end mode is what the ENCODE pipeline uses (bowtie2 -X2000 –mm); nf-core/atacseq uses BWA-MEM by default. –very-sensitive is a common choice for short ATAC reads. Our reference is chr21 + chrM only: reads from other chromosomes are absent by construction, and with the whole genome you would also see reads that mis-align from elsewhere. The fragment-length ceiling matters because the next filter keeps only proper pairs (flag 0x2): with the default ceiling, every fragment longer than 500 bp would be thrown away, and with it the di-nucleosome peak of the ladder. In the exercise the alignment of one replicate takes a few minutes on 8 threads. Our reads are the ones ENCODE aligned to chr21 or chrM in the full genome, so almost all of them align again (99.6% overall, 98.9% of pairs concordantly with -X 2000; without -X 2000 only 94.7% of pairs are concordant, about 250 000 pairs fewer); a real sample aligned to the full genome typically aligns at over 95%.

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
text:
Five filters, five reasons


Keep a pair only if both mates pass: unique (MAPQ ≥ 30), properly paired, not chrM, not a duplicate.
Blacklisted regions (Amemiya et al. 2019) are removed from the insertion sites and from the peaks.


Each filter has a reason. Multi-mappers (low MAPQ) cannot be placed, and in repeats they create false peaks. Improper pairs are mostly artefacts (chimeras, rearrangements, a mate in another chromosome). Mitochondrial DNA has no nucleosomes and many copies per cell, so Tn5 loves it: chrM reads are often 20–50% of an ATAC library and would dominate every normalisation; the Omni-ATAC protocol reduced this, but it is still checked. Duplicates in ATAC-seq: a pair with the same start and the same end as another pair is almost always a PCR copy, because two independent Tn5 events would have to hit both exact ends. For paired-end data this is reliable; for single-end data it removes some real reads at very strong sites. The blacklist (ENCODE exclusion list) marks regions with artefactual high signal in every assay; ENCODE removes peaks there, nf-core removes reads. We filter reads by flags, then remove blacklisted insertion sites and peaks.

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
section: Real data: reads through the pipeline
text:
Real data: reads through the pipeline


GM12878 replicate 1: 6.1 M read pairs in, 0.25 M usable fragments on chr21 out.
Biggest losses: chrM (91% of our pairs; 14% of the whole library), MAPQ (43% of the chr21 pairs) and duplicates (20%).


Numbers from make-atacanalysis-figs.R (and the exercise). Our FASTQ files contain only the reads that ENCODE placed on chr21 or chrM: 6.09 M of the 38.2 M read pairs of the replicate-1 library. So 91% chrM is the fraction in our subset; in the whole library chrM is about 5.4 M of 38.2 M pairs, 14%, which is typical. The MAPQ filter removes 43% of the chr21 pairs: chr21 contains repeats and segments present twice in the reference, where a read cannot be placed uniquely (we come back to this when comparing with ENCODE). Duplicates: 63 852 of 316 329 filtered pairs (20%); the duplicate rate depends on library complexity and depth, and rises as you sequence deeper. ENCODE asks for 25 million non-duplicate, non-mitochondrial fragments per replicate genome-wide; chr21 is about 1.5% of the genome, so our 0.25 M chr21 fragments correspond to a library of roughly that size. Replicate 2: 4.1 M pairs in, 0.26 M fragments out.

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
section: Tn5 cuts the two strands 9 bp apart
text:
Tn5 cuts the two strands 9 bp apart


The Tn5 dimer joins adapters to the two strands 9 bp apart. Gap filling copies those 9 bp, so both fragments carry them.
The insertion “point” is the centre of the 9-bp duplication: +4 from a + read’s start, −5 from a − read’s end (BED coordinates).


Walk through the three rows. Row 1: the transposase dimer cuts the top strand before base 106 and the bottom strand after base 114 (0-based), a 9-bp stagger. Row 2 and 3: each piece gets an adapter on one 5’ end and has a 9-nt single-stranded gap on the other strand, which the polymerase fills in during the first PCR cycle (the 72 °C step). So the 9 bp 106–114 are now present on both fragments. A read on the right fragment starts at 106 on the + strand; a read on the left fragment ends at 114 on the − strand. The centre of the 9 bp is base 110: start + 4 for the + read, and BED end (115) − 5 for the − read. In 1-based coordinates the same rule is +4 and −4 (115 − 4 = 111, the 1-based number of base 110): the asymmetric −5 is only the half-open BED end. Buenrostro et al. 2013 introduced the +4/−5 offsets. The shift moves positions by only a few bases: it does not matter for 500-bp peaks, but it matters for TF footprints, where a few bp are the signal.

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
section: From a read pair to two insertion sites
text:
From a read pair to two insertion sites


Every properly paired fragment gives two insertion sites, one at each end.
In BED: + read start + 4, − read end − 5. Tools: awk on a BEDPE file, or alignmentSieve --ATACshift (deepTools).


A − strand read is stored in BAM by its leftmost base, but its 5’ end, where Tn5 cut, is its rightmost base: POS + aligned length − 1 in 1-based, which equals the BED end. This is the most common bug when people shift reads by hand: shifting the − strand read’s start instead of its end puts the insertion 100 bp off for a 100-bp read. In the exercise we convert the BAM to BEDPE with bedtools bamtobed -bedpe (one line per pair), take the leftmost start and the rightmost end, and apply +4 and −5. Single-cell ATAC “fragment files” (Cell Ranger ATAC, ArchR, Signac) store exactly such shifted fragments; their exact off-by-one conventions differ slightly between tools, which again only matters for footprinting.

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
text:
Fragments or insertion sites?


Fragment coverage counts the DNA between two cuts: smooth, but fragments that span a nucleosome fill it in.
Insertion sites count only where Tn5 cut: sharper, closer to “accessibility” in the strict sense.
Peaks, signal tracks and counts can use either. Be explicit about which.


Fragment coverage is what you would get from a ChIP-seq-style pileup; it answers “where was DNA released?”. Insertion counts answer “where could Tn5 reach the DNA?”, which is the definition of accessibility. Long fragments are the clearest case: a 350-bp fragment spanning a nucleosome is evidence of two accessible linkers, not of an accessible nucleosome. Most ATAC-specific tools (ENCODE pipeline, ArchR, chromVAR counting, footprinting) work on insertions; nf-core/atacseq and many papers call peaks on fragments. Both find the same strong peaks; they differ in peak width and in the weak, broad stuff.

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
section: Real data: insertions vs fragment coverage
text:
Real data: insertions vs fragment coverage


GM12878 replicate 1 at the SOD1 promoter (chr21). Same reads, two tracks, both CPM.
Insertions concentrate at the open sites; fragment coverage is broader and also covers the flanking nucleosomes.


At the SOD1 promoter the insertions are concentrated in a few hundred bp just upstream of the TSS, with the highest bins at the nucleosome-free region; the fragment coverage is a broad hump that extends about 1 kb into the gene, because fragments starting in the open region end in the flanking linkers. MACS3 calls a somewhat wider peak on fragments here (1183 vs 970 bp); across chr21 the median peak width is 611 bp with fragments and 290 bp with insertions. Both tracks are CPM-scaled (per million fragments or insertions), the same normalisation as the bigWigs students make.

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
text:
Signal tracks for the browser
# insertion sites (one line per cut), sorted, as bedGraph -> bigWig, CPM-scaled
sort -k1,1 -k2,2n rep1.ins.bed > rep1.ins.sorted.bed
n=$(wc -l < rep1.ins.sorted.bed)
bedtools genomecov -i rep1.ins.sorted.bed -g chrom.sizes -bg -scale $(echo "1000000 / $n" | bc -l) \
  > rep1.ins.cpm.bedGraph
bedGraphToBigWig rep1.ins.cpm.bedGraph chrom.sizes rep1.ins.cpm.bw

# or from the BAM with deepTools: fragment coverage, CPM
bamCoverage -b rep1.dedup.bam -o rep1.frag.cpm.bw --extendReads --normalizeUsing CPM -bs 10

CPM (counts per million) makes samples of different depth comparable on screen. It is a display normalisation, not the one for differential tests.


genomecov on a BED of single-base insertions gives the count of insertions per base; -scale multiplies by 10^6 / total insertions. Many people smooth insertions (for example a 150-bp window, like the MACS3 pileup) before display, otherwise the track is spiky at base resolution; IGV smooths automatically when zoomed out. bamCoverage with –extendReads on paired-end data fills in the whole fragment between the mates, which is the fragment-coverage track. bamCoverage also has –Offset and alignmentSieve has –ATACshift for insertion-based tracks. In Differential accessibility we come back to normalisation: CPM assumes the total amount of accessible chromatin is the same in all samples.

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
text:
What a peak caller does


Pile up the reads (or insertion windows) along the genome.
At each position compare the pileup k with the expected count \lambda under background: p = P(X \ge k), X \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda).
A peak is a run of positions below the cutoff; its summit is the highest point.


This is the MACS model (Zhang et al. 2008), which students will meet again in the ChIP-seq unit. A Poisson model for the number of reads landing in a window is reasonable if reads fall independently and uniformly under background; the real background is not uniform, which is why λ is estimated locally (next slide). MACS computes the p-value at every position of the pileup, joins adjacent positions passing the cutoff into peaks (gaps shorter than a small distance are bridged), and reports the summit. The narrowPeak columns are the peak’s fold enrichment at the summit, −log10 p and −log10 q at the summit, and the summit offset (see Genomic intervals).

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
section: The local λ: background is not uniform
text:
The local λ: background is not uniform


\lambda_\text{BG} = total reads × window / genome size. But open domains, copy-number gains and mappability make background vary.
MACS uses \lambda_\text{local} = \max(\lambda_\text{BG}, \lambda_\text{1k}, \lambda_\text{5k}, \lambda_\text{10k}): the largest estimate, the conservative choice.
Without a control (ATAC-seq), MACS3 uses \lambda_\text{BG} and the sample’s own 10-kb window.


All λ values are expected counts in a window of the same size as the one in which k is counted (MACS scales each window’s count to that size). In the original paper, the 1k, 5k and 10k windows were measured in the control (input DNA), and λBG from the genome-wide average. Taking the maximum protects against local biases: a region with high background everywhere does not get peaks just for being high. In MACS3 the defaults are –slocal 1000 and –llocal 10000. With no control, using the 1-kb window of the sample itself would include the peak and swallow it, so MACS3 skips it and uses only the 10-kb window and the genome background. Worked example on the slide: λBG = 3, λ1k = 8, λ5k = 7, λ10k = 6, so λlocal = 8, and the candidate with 25 reads gets p = P(X ≥ 25 | 8) ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻⁶ instead of 3 × 10⁻¹⁵ against the genome average. The exercise has a similar calculation by hand.

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
section: From counts to p-values and q-values
text:
From counts to p-values and q-values


The same 25 reads are extremely surprising against \lambda = 3 and much less so against \lambda = 8.
Millions of positions are tested, so MACS converts p to q-values (Benjamini–Hochberg FDR). -q 0.01: expect about 1% of called peaks to be false.


Read the figure: bars are the Poisson probabilities of each count under the two λ values; the shaded tail is P(X ≥ 25). Against the genome-wide background the tail is 3 × 10⁻¹⁵; against the local background 1.2 × 10⁻⁶. Students know the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure from RNA-seq; MACS applies it to the p-scores of the pileup. Two caveats worth saying: the Poisson model ignores overdispersion, so MACS p-values are too small in absolute terms and are best used to rank peaks; and the q-value is computed per position, not strictly per peak. That is one reason replicate-based methods (IDR) are used to choose the final number of peaks.

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
section: Two ways to run MACS3 on ATAC-seq
text:
Two ways to run MACS3 on ATAC-seq


A. -f BAMPE: the pileup is the real fragments, no model, no shift. Simple; nucleosome-spanning fragments widen the peaks.
B. Insertion sites as BED, --nomodel --shift -75 --extsize 150: every cut becomes a 150-bp window centred on it. Used by ENCODE and Corces et al. 2018.


MACS was written for ChIP-seq single-end reads, where it estimates the fragment size d from the shift between + and − strand peaks (the “model”) and extends each read by d. For ATAC-seq that model makes no sense, so it is always switched off (–nomodel). Mode A uses the fragments as measured. Mode B uses each insertion independently: –shift -75 moves the 5’ end 75 bp upstream and –extsize 150 extends it to 150 bp, so the window is centred on the cut. Our insertion BED has one line per cut with the strand set to +, so MACS treats the start as the 5’ end. Mode B counts both ends of every fragment and ignores what lies between them; this matches “insertion sites” in the previous slides. Other callers: Genrich (has an ATAC mode with replicates built in) and HMMRATAC (MACS3 hmmratac subcommand, models nucleosome-free and nucleosomal fragments with an HMM); neither is needed in this course.

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
text:
MACS3 in practice
# A: fragments
macs3 callpeak -t rep1.dedup.bam -f BAMPE -g 4.0e7 --keep-dup all -q 0.01 -n rep1_frag
# B: insertion sites
macs3 callpeak -t rep1.ins.bed -f BED --nomodel --shift -75 --extsize 150 \
               -g 4.0e7 --keep-dup all -q 0.01 -n rep1_cuts

-g: effective genome size, sets λBG (hs ≈ 2.7e9; here chr21 only, 4.0e7).
-q / -p: the cutoff; a lenient -p 0.01 when IDR chooses the final set.
--keep-dup all: duplicates were already removed. --call-summits: several summits per broad peak.


Flags are not examined; the logic is. -g matters here because our data come from one chromosome: telling MACS3 the genome is 2.7 Gb would make λBG about 70 times too small. It would not change the result much, because λlocal = max(…) is then dominated by the 10-kb window, but it is the kind of mistake that hides in a methods section. The default –keep-dup 1 keeps one read per position; after samtools markdup that is no longer needed, and for insertions it would wrongly collapse independent cuts at the same base. Outputs: _peaks.narrowPeak (the peaks), _summits.bed (one line per summit), _peaks.xls (a tab-separated table with a header of settings). On our chr21 data one MACS3 call takes about a second; on a full genome a few minutes.

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
text:
Real data: how many peaks?


Replicate 1, chr21, q < 0.01: 685 peaks with fragments (BAMPE), 1262 with insertion sites. ENCODE’s IDR set has 1784.
The number of peaks depends smoothly on the cutoff: there is no natural threshold. Weak peaks are a continuum, not a separate class.


Left: from p < 0.01 to q < 1e-10 the number of insertion-mode peaks falls from 1739 to 812, smoothly, without a plateau. Fragment mode gives about half as many, wider peaks at every cutoff: the pileup of whole fragments is smoother, and nearby sites merge into one peak. Right: the stricter the cutoff, the larger the fraction of peaks that ENCODE also has (insertion mode: 56% at p < 0.01, 74% at q < 0.01, 92% at q < 1e-10). Strict cutoffs give few, reliable peaks; lax cutoffs give more peaks and more noise. ENCODE has more peaks than we do at any cutoff partly because its pipeline pools deeper data and keeps multi-mapping reads (later slide). The point: “the number of peaks” is a choice, so two papers with different cutoffs report different numbers for the same cells, and replicates are the principled way to choose.

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
text:
Replicates: overlap vs rank consistency


Naive: call peaks in each replicate, keep those found in both. The answer depends on the cutoff, and a lax cutoff lets noise in.
IDR (Li et al. 2011) uses the ranks: real peaks rank similarly in both replicates, noise does not. It finds where the agreement breaks down.


IDR is to replicates what a q-value is to a single sample: a per-peak measure, estimated from the data, that lets you set a cutoff in terms of a rate. The model is a two-component copula mixture: a reproducible component in which the ranks are correlated and an irreproducible one in which they are independent. IDR needs many peaks including noise, so it is run on lenient calls (ENCODE: MACS2 -p 0.01, top 300 000 peaks per replicate), never on already-thresholded peaks. The output is the set of peaks with IDR below a threshold (ENCODE ATAC: 0.05). In the exercise we do not run the idr package; we plot the rank consistency ourselves, which shows the same thing.

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
text:
Pseudoreplicates and ENCODE’s peak sets


Pool the replicates, shuffle the reads, split in two: pseudoreplicates differ only by sampling.
If true replicates agree much less than pseudoreplicates (ratio > 2), the replicates differ in biology or quality, not just depth.


Pseudoreplicates answer: how many peaks would be reproducible if the two replicates were perfect copies of each other? Np (pooled pseudoreplicates) is usually somewhat larger than Nt (true replicates), because biological replicates also differ biologically. ENCODE reports both, the “rescue ratio” max(Np, Nt)/min(Np, Nt) and the “self-consistency ratio” between the two replicates’ self-pseudoreplicate counts N1 and N2; an experiment passes if both are below 2. Pseudoreplicates are also the way to get a reproducibility-filtered peak set from a single replicate, with the obvious caveat that they say nothing about biological variation. The file we compare with (gm12878_atac_peaks.bed.gz) is ENCODE’s IDR thresholded peak set from replicates 1 and 2.

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
section: Real data: do the replicates agree?
text:
Real data: do the replicates agree?


Left: −log10 p of matched peaks in replicate 1 vs 2. Right: of the top N peaks of replicate 1, the fraction also found in replicate 2.
The top 750 peaks: 99% found in replicate 2. Agreement stays ≥ 90% up to about 1450 peaks, then falls (82% for all 1739).


Peaks were called with a lenient cutoff (-p 0.01) in each replicate, as for IDR: 1739 and 1909 peaks. Matching is by overlap; unmatched peaks are drawn at the bottom of the left panel, and they are almost all weak. The Spearman correlation of matched scores is 0.82. The right panel is a “correspondence at the top” curve, the simple cousin of IDR: it stays flat while we add real peaks and bends down when we start adding noise, here somewhere around 1300–1500 peaks, close to the 1262 peaks at q < 0.01. ENCODE’s IDR set on chr21 is larger (1784) because it was made from deeper, pooled data and keeps multi-mapping reads.

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
section: Real data: our peaks and ENCODE’s
text:
Real data: our peaks and ENCODE’s


74% of our 1262 replicate-1 peaks are in ENCODE’s set; 89% of ENCODE’s 1784 chr21 peaks are in ours.
Left: 1680 read pairs but only 7 with MAPQ ≥ 30 (sequence present twice). We drop them; ENCODE keeps multi-mappers.


Locus: DNMT3L and AIRE (chr21:44.24–44.30 Mb). Where both replicates have signal, the three peak sets agree. On the left there are ENCODE peaks and no reads at all in our tracks: the reads are there in the raw BAM, but they align equally well to another place on chr21 (MAPQ ≈ 1), so our MAPQ ≥ 30 filter removes them. GRCh38 is known to contain falsely duplicated segments on chr21. The ENCODE ATAC-seq pipeline keeps reads with up to 4 alignments and assigns each to one of them at random (its multimapping = 4 setting), so it calls peaks in both copies. Most of the ENCODE peaks we miss are in such regions (43–44 Mb and 5–8 Mb). Neither choice is wrong: unique reads are conservative; random assignment recovers signal in duplicated regions at the price of not knowing which copy it came from. The other direction: 26% of our peaks are not in the ENCODE set; they are mostly weak peaks below ENCODE’s IDR threshold. Discussion: which set would you use for a motif analysis, and which for a differential analysis?

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
section: A consensus peak set across samples
text:
A consensus peak set across samples


To count reads per peak in many samples (Differential accessibility), every sample needs the same regions.
Merge (bedtools merge): simple, but overlaps chain into wide regions of very different widths.
Fixed width: summit ± 250 bp, overlaps resolved by significance. Every region is 500 bp, centred on a summit.


This is the step where ATAC-seq analysis differs most from RNA-seq: there the genes are given, here we make the features. nf-core/atacseq builds its consensus by merging the peaks of all samples (and requires a peak to be present in a minimum number of samples); DiffBind does something similar by default. Fixed-width peaks were introduced for large ATAC-seq atlases (Corces et al. 2016 and 2018; ArchR uses the same idea). Advantages: equal widths make counts comparable between regions (GC content, length effects), and adding a sample does not merge two elements into one. The 500-bp peaks of the Corces 2016 haematopoiesis count matrix used in Differential accessibility were built this way. On our data, with only two replicates, merging is harmless: 1442 merged regions, median 289 bp, the longest 1820 bp. The chaining problem grows with the number of samples, which is where fixed-width peaks pay off.

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
text:
Iterative overlap removal


Sort the 500-bp peaks by significance; keep the best; drop the peaks that overlap it; repeat with the next best that is left.
Across samples, first make the scores comparable (e.g. −log10 p divided by the sample’s total, “score per million”), then run the same procedure on all peaks together.


The subtle point is in step 3: peak 6 overlaps peak 10, but 10 was already removed by 15, so 6 is compared only with peaks that were kept and survives. The procedure therefore keeps local maxima of significance and removes their overlapping neighbours, without chaining. In Corces et al. 2018 this was done per sample, then on all samples together after normalising the peak scores to a score per million, and peaks had to be reproducible in at least two samples. In R it is a short loop over findOverlaps, which students write in the exercise. On our chr21 data: 1262 and 1323 peaks become 1116 and 1123 non-overlapping 500-bp peaks per replicate, 1286 in the joint consensus, and 958 of these are supported by both replicates.

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
section: FRiP: fraction of reads in peaks
text:
FRiP: fraction of reads in peaks


FRiP = insertions (or reads) in peaks / all. A signal-to-noise measure: how much of the library is in accessible sites?
Ours: 0.57 (replicate 1) and 0.48 (replicate 2), insertions in own q < 0.01 peaks. ENCODE standard for ATAC-seq: > 0.3, > 0.2 acceptable.


FRiP depends on the peak set: more lenient peaks give a higher FRiP, so compare FRiP between samples only with comparable peak calling (or with a fixed reference peak set). It is also lower in cell types with less open chromatin. In ATAC-seq a low FRiP usually means many reads from closed chromatin: over-digestion, dead cells (naked DNA), or too little nuclei clean-up. TSS enrichment, from the previous unit, is the other main signal-to-noise measure and does not need peaks at all. With ENCODE’s peaks instead of our own, replicate 1’s FRiP is 0.58.

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
text:
Where are the peaks?


Fraction of peaks within 1 kb of a protein-coding TSS, by peak strength (Genomic intervals).
Strongest 10% of consensus peaks: 70% at a promoter; the other deciles: 5–25%. Overall 17% (ours) and 26% (ENCODE).
Most peaks are distal: candidate enhancers and insulators.


The reproducible consensus has 958 peaks on chr21; 59% of the 602 distinct protein-coding TSS positions on chr21 have one within 1 kb, plausible since many genes are not expressed in a B-cell line. ENCODE’s set has a higher promoter fraction (26%) than ours because it reaches further into weak peaks in duplicated, gene-dense regions and because IDR keeps a different set of weak peaks. This is the same overlap logic as the genomic-intervals exercise, applied to our own peaks. The promoter fraction is a useful sanity check: an ATAC-seq peak set with very few promoter peaks suggests a problem, and a set with almost only promoter peaks suggests low sensitivity (only the strongest sites were found). The distal peaks are where cell-type-specific regulation lives, and the starting point for motif analysis (Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting).

Each row is something that has happened in published analyses. The chrM numbers come from calling peaks on the unfiltered replicate-1 BAM in make-atacanalysis-figs.R: 590 peaks, 8 of them on chrM (two among the top 20) and 7 in blacklisted regions, and fewer peaks on chr21 (582 vs 685), because the 5 M chrM fragments inflate the genome-wide background λ. A good habit: after peak calling, look at the number of peaks per chromosome and at the top 20 peaks in a browser; artefacts are usually at the top of the list.

Next: Differential accessibility, which starts from a count matrix over such a consensus set.

title: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Buenrostro et al. 2013, Nat Methods. Transposition of native chromatin for fast and sensitive epigenomic profiling of open chromatin, DNA-binding proteins and nucleosome position. The assay, and the +4/−5 shift.
Zhang et al. 2008, Genome Biol. Model-based Analysis of ChIP-Seq (MACS). The local-λ Poisson peak caller.
Li et al. 2011, Ann Appl Stat. Measuring reproducibility of high-throughput experiments. IDR.
Corces et al. 2018, Science. The chromatin accessibility landscape of primary human cancers. Fixed-width peaks and iterative overlap removal at scale.
Yan et al. 2020, Genome Biol. From reads to insight: a hitchhiker’s guide to ATAC-seq data analysis. A review of every step and the tools.
Ewels et al. 2020, Nat Biotechnol. The nf-core framework for community-curated bioinformatics pipelines. The pipeline framework behind nf-core/atacseq.

title: Exercise: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
text:
Background
Insertion sites. Tn5 cuts the two DNA strands 9 bp apart, and both resulting fragments carry a copy of those 9 bp. The insertion is taken as the centre of the 9 bp: in BED coordinates the start + 4 of a read on the + strand and the end − 5 of a read on the − strand. A properly paired fragment [s, e) therefore has insertion sites at bases s + 4 and e − 5.
Peak calling. MACS3 piles up reads (or windows around insertions) and, at each position, compares the pileup \(k\) with an expected count \(\lambda\) under background, \(p = P(X \ge k)\) for \(X \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)\). The expectation is local: \(\lambda_\text{local} = \max(\lambda_\text{BG}, \lambda_\text{1k}, \lambda_\text{5k}, \lambda_\text{10k})\), where each \(\lambda\) is the count in a window around the position, scaled to the size of the counting window. Without a control (ATAC-seq), MACS3 uses \(\lambda_\text{BG}\) and the 10-kb window of the sample itself. P-values are converted to q-values (Benjamini–Hochberg).
Replicates and consensus. Overlap between two replicates’ peak lists depends on the thresholds; IDR instead asks how far down the ranked lists the two replicates agree. To count reads in many samples you need one set of regions: either merged peaks or fixed-width peaks (summit ± 250 bp) where overlapping peaks are resolved by keeping the most significant one.

title: Exercise: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
text:
Data
ENCODE ATAC-seq of the lymphoblastoid cell line GM12878 (experiment ENCSR095QNB, GRCh38), two biological replicates, paired-end 2 × 100 bp. To keep the exercise small we use only the read pairs that ENCODE aligned to chromosome 21 or the mitochondrial genome; the reads themselves are the original, untrimmed reads. You also need the chr21 + chrM reference with its Bowtie2 index, ENCODE’s IDR peaks for the same experiment, the blacklist, the GENCODE annotation and chromosome sizes.



file
content




gm12878_atac_rep{1,2}_R{1,2}.fastq.gz
reads, replicate 1 (6.1 M pairs, 2 × 290 MB) and 2 (4.1 M pairs, 2 × 200 MB)


hg38_chr21_chrM.fa, bowtie2/hg38_chr21_chrM.*
reference and index


gm12878_atac_peaks.bed.gz
ENCODE IDR thresholded peaks, replicates 1 + 2 (ENCFF945SYZ)


hg38_blacklist.bed.gz, hg38.chrom.sizes, gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz
from Genomic intervals



data/download.sh atacseq-analysis     # peaks; the reads and index come with the course data
mkdir -p ~/epi/atac && cd ~/epi/atac
D=/path/to/course/data                # where the course data are
T=8                                   # threads
You need fastp, bowtie2, samtools (1.16 or later), bedtools, macs3 and, for the optional bigWig, bedGraphToBigWig (see Install the software you need). The whole command-line part takes 10–25 minutes with 8 threads, almost all of it alignment; on the cluster, put C1–C2 in an sbatch script with --cpus-per-task=8 --mem=8G.
Honest simplification: we align to chr21 + chrM only, so reads from other chromosomes cannot mis-align here, and the effective genome size we give MACS3 is that of chr21.

title: Exercise: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
text:
By hand
Do these on paper.
B1. Tn5 shift. A read pair, as shown by samtools view (1-based POS):
read 1   flag 99    chr21   POS 10001   CIGAR 50M   (+ strand)
read 2   flag 147   chr21   POS 10231   CIGAR 50M   (− strand)

Write both reads as BED intervals. How long is the fragment (TLEN)?
Give the two insertion sites as one-base BED intervals. How far apart are they?
After adapter trimming, a − strand read has POS 20001 and CIGAR 30M. Where is its insertion site?
A script shifts every − strand read by subtracting 5 from its start. Where would the insertion from read 2 end up, and how far is that from the correct site? What would it be for an untrimmed 100-bp read?
Why +4 but −5? What are the two offsets in 1-based coordinates?

B2. The genome-wide λ. After filtering, a sample has 2 000 000 insertion sites on chr21, whose mappable length is about 40 Mb. MACS3 replaces each insertion by a 150-bp window.

What is \(\lambda_\text{BG}\), the expected number of windows covering a position under uniform background?
What would \(\lambda_\text{BG}\) be if you forgot to set the genome size and MACS3 used the human genome (2.7 × 10⁹)?
Why does this mistake change the peaks less than you might expect? (Think about \(\lambda_\text{local}\).)

B3. Local λ and a Poisson p-value. At a candidate peak summit the pileup is \(k = 18\). \(\lambda_\text{BG} = 4.0\). The 10-kb window around the summit contains 600 insertions. A ChIP-seq-style control gives \(\lambda_\text{1k} = 6.0\) and \(\lambda_\text{5k} = 7.5\). Upper-tail Poisson probabilities \(P(X \ge k \mid \lambda)\):

Why does MACS take the maximum of the λ estimates, not the mean?

B4. p-values and q-values. MACS3 tests about 10⁶ independent windows on chr21. 2000 windows have \(p < 10^{-4}\).

How many windows would you expect below \(p < 10^{-4}\) if there were no real peaks at all?
Estimate the fraction of false discoveries among the 2000 (this is roughly the Benjamini–Hochberg q-value at that cutoff).
Why is -p 0.01 a bad final threshold, but a good input for IDR?

B5. FRiP. Replicate A: 3 100 000 insertions after filtering, 1 050 000 inside peaks.

Compute FRiP. Does it pass the ENCODE standard (> 0.3, > 0.2 acceptable)?
You call peaks again with -p 0.01 instead of -q 0.01; FRiP rises to 0.41. Is the library better now? What does this tell you about comparing FRiP between studies?

B6. Replicate overlap. Replicate 1 has 4000 peaks, replicate 2 has 5000. 3200 of replicate 1’s peaks overlap a replicate-2 peak; 3350 of replicate 2’s peaks overlap a replicate-1 peak.

Give the fraction reproduced in each direction. Why are 3200 and 3350 not the same number?
You lower the threshold in replicate 1 to get 8000 peaks; now 3900 of them overlap replicate 2. What happened to the fraction, and why?

B8. Judge the methods. A study merges the MACS3 peaks of 40 samples with bedtools merge and reports “120 000 accessible regions, median width 1.8 kb”. The peaks of each sample had a median width of 450 bp. What most likely happened, and what would you suggest?
B9. Read the figure.
