title: Exercise: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
text:
On the command line

C1 — Trim and align
The same block for both replicates (5–12 min per replicate with 8 threads, depending on the machine):
for r in rep1 rep2; do
  fastp -w $T -l 20 \
    -i $D/gm12878_atac_${r}_R1.fastq.gz -I $D/gm12878_atac_${r}_R2.fastq.gz \
    -o ${r}_R1.trim.fq.gz -O ${r}_R2.trim.fq.gz \
    --adapter_sequence CTGTCTCTTATACACATCT --adapter_sequence_r2 CTGTCTCTTATACACATCT \
    -j ${r}.fastp.json -h ${r}.fastp.html 2> ${r}.fastp.log
  bowtie2 -p $T --very-sensitive -X 2000 -x $D/bowtie2/hg38_chr21_chrM \
    -1 ${r}_R1.trim.fq.gz -2 ${r}_R2.trim.fq.gz 2> ${r}.bowtie2.log \
    | samtools fixmate -m -u - - | samtools sort -@ 4 -o ${r}.raw.bam
  samtools index ${r}.raw.bam
done

Open rep1.fastp.html (or read rep1.fastp.log). How many read pairs went in? What fraction of reads had adapter bases trimmed? fastp also reports an “insert size peak”: why is it so short?
From rep1.bowtie2.log: what fraction of pairs aligned concordantly exactly once, and overall?
Rerun the bowtie2 command for replicate 1 without -X 2000 (send the output to /dev/null, keep the log). How does the concordant fraction change? Which fragments are now discordant?



C2 — Filter
for r in rep1 rep2; do
  samtools idxstats ${r}.raw.bam | cut -f1,3          # mapped reads per chromosome
  samtools view -u -q 30 -f 2 -F 1804 ${r}.raw.bam chr21 \
    | samtools collate -u -O - | samtools fixmate -m -u - - \
    | samtools view -u -f 2 - | samtools sort -u - \
    | samtools markdup -r -s - ${r}.dedup.bam 2> ${r}.markdup.txt
  samtools index ${r}.dedup.bam
  echo $r $(samtools view -c -f 64 ${r}.dedup.bam) fragments
done

What fraction of mapped reads are on chrM in each replicate? Why so many (and why is this fraction inflated in our subset)?
Explain each part of the filter: -q 30, -f 2, -F 1804 (decode it with the flag explainer), the region chr21. Why collate + fixmate + view -f 2 again after the first filter?
From rep1.markdup.txt: what fraction of the filtered pairs were duplicates?
Fill in the read pairs per step for replicate 1: in → after trimming → properly paired → on chr21 → MAPQ ≥ 30 (both mates) → not duplicates. Where are the biggest losses?



C3 — Insertion sites
zcat $D/hg38_blacklist.bed.gz > blacklist.bed
for r in rep1 rep2; do
  samtools sort -n -u ${r}.dedup.bam | bedtools bamtobed -bedpe -i - 2> /dev/null \
    | awk -v OFS='\t' '{ s = ($2 < $5 ? $2 : $5); e = ($3 > $6 ? $3 : $6)
                         print $1, s + 4, s + 5, ".", ".", "+"
                         print $1, e - 5, e - 4, ".", ".", "+" }' \
    | bedtools intersect -v -a - -b blacklist.bed \
    | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n > ${r}.ins.bed
  wc -l ${r}.ins.bed
done
head -4 rep1.ins.bed

Explain the awk program. Why s + 4, s + 5 and e − 5, e − 4? Why is every line given the strand +?
How many insertion sites per replicate? Why is the number slightly less than twice the number of fragments?
Optional: make a CPM-scaled bigWig of the insertions and look at it in IGV with ENCODE’s peaks:

grep -w -e chr21 -e chrM $D/hg38.chrom.sizes > chrom.sizes
n=$(wc -l < rep1.ins.bed)
bedtools genomecov -i rep1.ins.bed -g chrom.sizes -bg -scale $(echo "1000000 / $n" | bc -l) > rep1.ins.cpm.bedGraph
bedGraphToBigWig rep1.ins.cpm.bedGraph chrom.sizes rep1.ins.cpm.bw


C4 — Call peaks in two modes
mkdir -p macs
for r in rep1 rep2; do
  macs3 callpeak -t ${r}.dedup.bam -f BAMPE -g 4.0e7 --keep-dup all -q 0.01 \
    -n ${r}_frag --outdir macs 2> ${r}_frag.macs.log
  macs3 callpeak -t ${r}.ins.bed -f BED --nomodel --shift -75 --extsize 150 \
    -g 4.0e7 --keep-dup all -q 0.01 -n ${r}_cuts --outdir macs 2> ${r}_cuts.macs.log
  macs3 callpeak -t ${r}.ins.bed -f BED --nomodel --shift -75 --extsize 150 \
    -g 4.0e7 --keep-dup all -p 0.01 -n ${r}_cuts_p01 --outdir macs 2> ${r}_cuts_p01.macs.log
done
wc -l macs/*_peaks.narrowPeak
for f in macs/*_peaks.narrowPeak; do
  echo $f $(awk '{ w += $3 - $2 } END { print w / NR }' $f) $(bedtools intersect -u -a $f -b blacklist.bed | wc -l)
done

How many peaks does each call give? Which mode gives more peaks at q < 0.01, and which gives wider peaks? Why?
How many peaks overlap the blacklist? (We removed blacklisted insertions, but not for the BAMPE call.)
In rep1_frag.macs.log, find the mean fragment size MACS3 reports in BAMPE mode and compare with the fragment-size distribution of ATAC-seq: Tn5, fragment sizes, nucleosome ladder. Find the line Range for calculating regional lambda: which window does MACS3 use, and why no 1-kb window?
How many peaks does the lenient -p 0.01 call give? Why would you never report this set as “the peaks”?



C5 — FRiP
for r in rep1 rep2; do
  n=$(wc -l < ${r}.ins.bed)
  k=$(bedtools intersect -u -a ${r}.ins.bed -b macs/${r}_cuts_peaks.narrowPeak | wc -l)
  echo $r $k $n $(echo "$k / $n" | bc -l)
done

What is FRiP in each replicate? Does it pass ENCODE’s standard?
Compute FRiP for replicate 1 with ENCODE’s peaks instead of your own. Why is it different?



C6 — Compare with ENCODE and between replicates
zcat $D/gm12878_atac_peaks.bed.gz | awk '$1 == "chr21"' | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n > encode_chr21.bed
wc -l encode_chr21.bed
for m in frag cuts; do
  for r in rep1 rep2; do
    p=macs/${r}_${m}_peaks.narrowPeak
    echo $r $m $(wc -l < $p) \
      $(bedtools intersect -u -a $p -b encode_chr21.bed | wc -l) \
      $(bedtools intersect -u -a encode_chr21.bed -b $p | wc -l)
  done
done
bedtools intersect -u -a macs/rep1_cuts_peaks.narrowPeak -b macs/rep2_cuts_peaks.narrowPeak | wc -l
bedtools intersect -u -a macs/rep2_cuts_peaks.narrowPeak -b macs/rep1_cuts_peaks.narrowPeak | wc -l

What fraction of your peaks overlap an ENCODE peak (precision-like), and what fraction of ENCODE’s chr21 peaks you recover (recall-like)? Which mode agrees better with ENCODE, and why might it?
What fraction of replicate 1’s peaks overlap replicate 2, and vice versa?



C7 — A naive consensus by merging
cat macs/rep1_cuts_peaks.narrowPeak macs/rep2_cuts_peaks.narrowPeak | cut -f1-3 \
  | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n | bedtools merge > merged.bed
wc -l merged.bed
awk '{ print $3 - $2 }' merged.bed | sort -n | awk '{ a[NR] = $1 } END { print "median", a[int(NR/2)], "max", a[NR] }'
How many merged regions, and what are their median and maximum width? Keep the numbers for R2.

title: Exercise: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
text:
In R
You need GenomicRanges, rtracklayer and ggplot2. Work in the same folder as the command-line part:
library(GenomicRanges); library(rtracklayer); library(ggplot2)
D <- "/path/to/course/data"
setwd("~/epi/atac")
np <- function(f) import(f, format = "narrowPeak")

R1 — Replicate consistency by rank
p1 <- np("macs/rep1_cuts_p01_peaks.narrowPeak"); p2 <- np("macs/rep2_cuts_p01_peaks.narrowPeak")
c(length(p1), length(p2))
p1 <- p1[order(-p1$pValue)]; p2 <- p2[order(-p2$pValue)]       # strongest first
# for each rep-1 peak: the best overlapping rep-2 peak (or NA)
h <- findOverlaps(p1, p2)
best <- tapply(subjectHits(h), queryHits(h), min)               # p2 is sorted, so min index = best
m <- data.frame(rank1 = seq_along(p1), p1 = p1$pValue, rank2 = NA, p2 = NA)
m$rank2[as.integer(names(best))] <- best
m$p2[as.integer(names(best))] <- p2$pValue[best]
# correspondence at the top: of the top N rep-1 peaks, what fraction is found in rep 2?
N <- c(250, 500, 750, 1000, 1250, 1500, nrow(m))
data.frame(N, found = sapply(N, function(n) mean(!is.na(m$rank2[1:n]))))
ggplot(m[!is.na(m$p2), ], aes(p1, p2)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.2, size = 0.6) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() + labs(x = "-log10 p, replicate 1", y = "-log10 p, replicate 2")
cor(m$p1, m$p2, use = "complete.obs", method = "spearman")

How many lenient peaks per replicate? What fraction of replicate 1’s top 1000, top 4000 and all peaks are found in replicate 2?
Where does the curve start to fall fast? Compare with your q < 0.01 peak count (C4) and with ENCODE’s chr21 IDR peaks.
What is the Spearman correlation of the matched scores? Why is it much lower than the agreement among the top peaks?



R2 — A fixed-width consensus with iterative overlap removal
fixed <- function(p, sample) {
  s <- GRanges(seqnames(p), IRanges(start(p) + p$peak, width = 1))   # summit base (1-based)
  w <- resize(s, 500, fix = "center")                                # 500 bp around it
  w$score <- p$pValue / sum(p$pValue) * 1e6                          # score per million
  w$sample <- sample
  w
}
keep_best <- function(gr) {
  gr <- gr[order(-gr$score)]
  ov <- as.list(findOverlaps(gr, gr))           # for each peak, the peaks it overlaps
  keep <- logical(length(gr)); gone <- logical(length(gr))
  for (i in seq_along(gr)) {
    if (gone[i]) next
    keep[i] <- TRUE
    gone[ov[[i]]] <- TRUE                       # itself and every overlapping peak
  }
  sort(gr[keep])
}
q1 <- np("macs/rep1_cuts_peaks.narrowPeak"); q2 <- np("macs/rep2_cuts_peaks.narrowPeak")
per_sample <- c(keep_best(fixed(q1, "rep1")), keep_best(fixed(q2, "rep2")))
cons <- keep_best(per_sample)
length(cons); table(width(cons))
# reproducible: overlapped by a fixed-width peak of both replicates
n_rep <- sapply(split(per_sample, per_sample$sample), function(x) overlapsAny(cons, x))
cons_rep <- cons[rowSums(n_rep) == 2]
length(cons_rep)
merged <- import("merged.bed")
c(merged = length(merged), median_width = median(width(merged)))
export(cons_rep, "consensus_500bp.bed")

Why does fixed() use start(p) + p$peak (check with Genomic intervals: is that the 1-based summit position)?
How many 500-bp peaks are kept per sample, in the consensus, and in the reproducible consensus? Compare with the merged set from C7 (number and widths).
Why is the score normalised per million before peaks from different samples are compared?
Check that no two peaks in cons overlap (last line of R3’s code, or run it now).



R3 — Where are the peaks?
gtf <- import(file.path(D, "gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz"))
tx  <- gtf[gtf$type == "transcript" & gtf$transcript_type == "protein_coding" & seqnames(gtf) == "chr21"]
tss <- unique(resize(tx, width = 1, fix = "start"))
d <- mcols(distanceToNearest(cons_rep, tss, ignore.strand = TRUE))$distance
mean(d <= 1000)
enc <- import(file.path(D, "gm12878_atac_peaks.bed.gz"), format = "narrowPeak")
enc <- enc[seqnames(enc) == "chr21"]
mean(mcols(distanceToNearest(enc, tss, ignore.strand = TRUE))$distance <= 1000)
# by strength: deciles of the consensus score
cons_rep$decile <- cut(rank(-cons_rep$score), 10, labels = 1:10)
tapply(d <= 1000, cons_rep$decile, mean)
c(length(tss), mean(overlapsAny(tss, cons_rep, maxgap = 1000)))
sum(countOverlaps(cons, cons) > 1)                # R2 (d)

What fraction of the reproducible consensus peaks lie within 1 kb of a protein-coding TSS? And of ENCODE’s chr21 peaks?
How does the promoter fraction change from the strongest to the weakest decile? What are the distal peaks likely to be?
What fraction of chr21 protein-coding TSSs (unique positions) have a consensus peak within 1 kb? GM12878 does not express every gene: is the answer plausible?

title: Exercise: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — the Tn5 shift (B1, C3)





SAM POS is 1-based: BED start = POS − 1. A read’s BED end = BED start + aligned length (sum of M, D, =, X in the CIGAR). On the + strand the 5’ end is the start, on the − strand the end. Insertion = start + 4 (+ strand) or end − 5 (− strand), written as a one-base BED interval [x, x + 1). See Buenrostro et al. 2013 and bedtools bamtobed -bedpe; the deepTools tool alignmentSieve --ATACshift does the same on a BAM.









Hint 2 — λ and Poisson (B2, B3, B4)





\(\lambda_\text{BG} = N \times w / G\) for \(N\) reads, window \(w\) and genome size \(G\). A count in a larger window \(W\) is scaled to \(w\): \(\lambda_W = n_W \times w / W\). \(\lambda_\text{local}\) is the maximum. Expected false positives at a cutoff = number of tests × cutoff. See the MACS3 callpeak documentation (--slocal, --llocal, -g) and Zhang et al. 2008.









Hint 3 — filters (C2)





samtools view -q 30 keeps MAPQ ≥ 30, -f 2 keeps proper pairs, -F 1804 removes unmapped (4), mate unmapped (8), secondary (256), QC-fail (512) and duplicates (1024). After filtering single reads, some pairs have lost a mate; samtools fixmate on name-grouped reads (collate) clears their proper-pair flag, so the second view -f 2 drops them. samtools markdup needs the MC/ms tags that fixmate -m adds and coordinate-sorted input; -r removes duplicates, -s prints statistics.









Hint 4 — MACS3 (C4)





-f BAMPE uses whole fragments from a paired-end BAM. For a BED of insertions, --nomodel --shift -75 --extsize 150 makes a 150-bp window centred on each line’s 5’ end (the start, for strand +). --keep-dup all because duplicates were removed already. -g is the effective genome size. Output formats are described under callpeak outputs; the narrowPeak columns in Genomic intervals.









Hint 5 — overlaps and FRiP (B5, B6, C5, C6)





Count each interval once with bedtools intersect -u. The two directions of an overlap differ because one peak can overlap several in the other set. FRiP is defined in the ENCODE ATAC-seq standards. IDR: Li et al. 2011 and the idr package.









Hint 6 — fixed-width peaks (B7, R2)





Sort by score; take the best; remove everything that overlaps it (findOverlaps of the set with itself); continue with the best peak not yet removed. resize(x, 500, fix = "center") makes the windows. Corces et al. 2018 (Methods, “peak calling”) describe the procedure.









Hint 7 — annotation (R3)





distanceToNearest gives 0 for overlaps. Build TSSs as in Genomic intervals (R2) and restrict to chr21, since our peaks are only there.

title: Exercise: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) Read 1: BED [10000, 10050); read 2: BED [10230, 10280). Fragment [10000, 10280), TLEN 280. (b) \(10000 + 4 = 10004\) → chr21 10004 10005; \(10280 - 5 = 10275\) → chr21 10275 10276; 271 bp apart. (c) BED [20000, 20030), insertion \(20030 - 5 = 20025\). (d) \(10230 - 5 = 10225\), 50 bp from the correct 10275: the error equals the read length, so 100 bp for an untrimmed 100-bp read. (e) The centre of the 9-bp duplication is 4 bases in from either end. From a BED start (the first of the 9 bases) that is +4; the BED end is the boundary after the last base, so the centre is end − 5. In 1-based closed coordinates: start + 4 and end − 4.
B2. (a) \(2\,000\,000 \times 150 / 4 \times 10^7 = 7.5\). (b) \(2\,000\,000 \times 150 / 2.7 \times 10^9 \approx 0.11\), about 70 times too small. (c) \(\lambda_\text{local}\) is the maximum of \(\lambda_\text{BG}\) and the 10-kb window of the sample; on chr21 the 10-kb window (and thus the data themselves) sets the background almost everywhere there are reads, so the too-small \(\lambda_\text{BG}\) rarely wins. It would matter in sparse regions, where weak noise would now pass the test.
B3. (a) \(600 \times 150 / 10\,000 = 9.0\). (b) With a control: \(\max(4.0, 6.0, 7.5, 9.0) = 9.0\). Without a control MACS3 uses \(\max(\lambda_\text{BG}, \lambda_\text{10k}) = 9.0\) too. (c) \(P(X \ge 18 \mid 9) = 0.0053\); against \(\lambda_\text{BG} = 4\) it would be \(2.5 \times 10^{-7}\). The peak sits in a region of high background; against its neighbourhood it is only weakly significant, and would not pass a cutoff of \(q < 0.01\) after testing millions of positions. (d) The maximum is conservative: if any scale shows high background (a broad open domain, a copy-number gain, a mappability artefact), the candidate must exceed it. A mean would let local biases through.
B4. (a) \(10^6 \times 10^{-4} = 100\). (b) About \(100 / 2000 = 0.05\), i.e. q ≈ 0.05: about 5% of these windows are expected to be noise. (c) At \(p < 0.01\) you expect \(10^4\) false windows on chr21 alone, so most of the peaks are noise. IDR needs exactly that: a long ranked list including noise, so that it can see where replicate agreement breaks down.
B5. (a) \(1\,050\,000 / 3\,100\,000 = 0.34\): passes (> 0.3). (b) No: the library is the same; more lenient peaks cover more of the genome and catch more insertions, so FRiP rises. FRiP is only comparable between samples with the same peak-calling settings, or when counted in one fixed reference peak set.
B6. (a) 3200/4000 = 80% of replicate 1, 3350/5000 = 67% of replicate 2. They differ because overlap is not one-to-one: one wide peak in one set can overlap two narrow peaks in the other, and the sets have different sizes. (b) 3900/8000 = 49%: the 4000 extra peaks are weaker and mostly noise or real but weak sites below replicate 2’s threshold, so the fraction falls. The overlap fraction measures the threshold as much as the data. (c) IDR ranks the peaks of both replicates (called leniently) and fits a mixture of a reproducible component, in which ranks are correlated, and an irreproducible one, in which they are not. Each peak gets the probability of being irreproducible, and the cutoff is set on that (e.g. IDR ≤ 0.05), independent of the original p-value thresholds.
B7. (a) S1: [750, 1250), [1100, 1600), [4750, 5250); S2: [950, 1450), [4450, 4950), [5350, 5850). (b) Order 40, 30, 25, 18, 12, 9. Keep 1000 (40); it overlaps 1200 (30) and 1350 (12): drop them. Keep 5000 (25); it overlaps 4700 (18): drop. 5600 (9) does not overlap 5000’s window (5350 > 5250): keep. Result: three windows, [750, 1250), [4750, 5250), [5350, 5850). (c) [750, 1600), [4450, 5250), [5350, 5850): also three regions here, but 850, 800 and 500 bp wide, and not centred on a summit. (d) Equal widths make counts comparable between regions and samples (no length effect); centring on the summit keeps the most informative part; overlapping peaks of different samples do not chain into long regions; adding samples does not change the existing regions’ boundaries.
B8. Chaining: with 40 samples, peaks of slightly different positions overlap each other in a chain, and merge joins neighbouring elements into long regions, so the “median width” is a property of the merging, not of the biology. Suggest fixed-width summit-centred peaks with iterative overlap removal (or at least requiring presence in several samples and splitting long regions).
B9. About 1450 peaks (the curve is 94% at 1250, 89% at 1500, 82% for all 1739). That is a little more than the 1262 peaks at q < 0.01 and fewer than ENCODE’s 1784 IDR peaks on chr21, which come from deeper, pooled data and include multi-mapping reads (see C6).









Solutions — command line





Numbers from our run (fastp 0.23.4, Bowtie2 2.4.4, samtools 1.21, bedtools 2.30.0, MACS3 3.1.0; 8 threads).
C1. (a) Replicate 1: 6 088 187 read pairs; fastp trimmed adapter bases from 4 667 844 of 12 176 374 reads (38%), and dropped 96 060 pairs (low quality, too short); 5 992 127 pairs remain. Replicate 2: 4 125 115 pairs, 40% of reads trimmed, 4 049 389 remain. The “insert size peak” (42 bp for replicate 1) is estimated only from pairs whose two reads overlap, i.e. from fragments shorter than about 200 bp (two 100-bp reads); it is not the mode of the fragment-size distribution. Runtime: fastp 15–25 s, Bowtie2 4–12 min per replicate on 8 threads (on a busy server). (b) Replicate 1: 94.5% concordantly exactly once, 4.4% more than once, 99.65% overall. (c) Without -X 2000: 90.8% + 4.0% = 94.7% concordant instead of 98.9%; about 250 000 more pairs are not concordant (most of them now align “discordantly”): the fragments longer than 500 bp, i.e. the di- and tri-nucleosome fragments.
C2. (a) Replicate 1: 10.83 M of 11.94 M mapped reads on chrM (91%); replicate 2: 7.05 M of 8.07 M (87%). mtDNA has no nucleosomes and many copies per cell. The fraction is inflated because our files contain only chr21 and chrM reads: in the whole replicate-1 library (38.2 M pairs) the 5.4 M chrM pairs are 14%. (b) -q 30: unique alignments; -f 2: proper pairs; -F 1804 = 4 + 8 + 256 + 512 + 1024: unmapped, mate unmapped, secondary, QC fail, duplicate; chr21: only reads on chr21 (drops chrM; needs the index). The first filter works read by read, so a pair can lose one mate (e.g. one mate has MAPQ < 30); collate brings mates together, fixmate marks a read without its mate as unpaired (flag 0x2 cleared) and refreshes the mate tags, and view -f 2 drops these orphans, so only complete pairs remain. (c) DUPLICATE PAIR: 127704 reads of 632 658, i.e. 63 852 of 316 329 pairs (20%). (d) Replicate 1: 6.09 M → 5.99 M after trimming → 5.93 M properly paired → 0.55 M on chr21 (5.38 M on chrM) → 0.32 M with MAPQ ≥ 30 for both mates → 0.25 M (252 477) non-duplicate fragments. Replicate 2: 4.13 M → 4.05 M → 4.01 M → 0.51 M → 0.29 M → 0.26 M (256 180). Largest losses: chrM, then MAPQ (43% of the chr21 pairs, from repeats and duplicated segments of chr21), then duplicates. C2 takes about 10 s.
C3. (a) bamtobed -bedpe writes one line per pair: chromosome, start and end of mate 1, then of mate 2 (BED coordinates). The fragment runs from the smaller start s to the larger end e. The + strand read’s 5’ end is s (insertion base s + 4, BED s+4 s+5); the − strand read’s 5’ end is the last base, e − 1, so the insertion is e − 5 (BED e−5 e−4). Strand + makes MACS3 treat each line’s start as the 5’ end in C4 (with --shift -75). (b) Replicate 1: 482 606 insertions from 252 477 fragments; replicate 2: 496 031 from 256 180. Slightly fewer than twice the fragments because insertions in blacklisted regions were removed. (c) The bigWig is about 2 MB; in IGV the insertion track looks spiky at base resolution and smooth when zoomed out.
C4. (a) q < 0.01: fragments (BAMPE) 685 (rep 1) and 697 (rep 2) peaks, mean width 741 and 791 bp; insertion sites 1262 and 1323 peaks, mean width 362 and 353 bp. Insertion mode gives about twice as many, narrower peaks: each cut contributes a 150-bp window centred on itself, so neighbouring sites stay separate, while whole fragments (mean 256 bp, some much longer) smear signal across neighbouring sites and merge them. Each MACS3 call takes about a second here. (b) 4 BAMPE peaks per replicate overlap the blacklist, but only 1–2 insertion-mode peaks (and those only partly). (c) “mean fragment size is determined as 255.6 bp” (replicate 1), larger than the nucleosome-free mode because the di- and tri-nucleosome fragments pull the mean up. “Range for calculating regional lambda is: 10000 bps”: without a control MACS3 uses only the 10-kb window of the sample (plus λBG); a 1-kb window around a peak measured in the sample itself would be dominated by the peak. (d) 1739 (rep 1) and 1909 (rep 2) peaks at p < 0.01. With roughly 106–107 positions tested, p < 0.01 lets through many false positives (B4); this set is only an input for IDR or rank analyses.
C5. (a) Replicate 1: 272 758 / 482 606 = 0.57; replicate 2: 237 863 / 496 031 = 0.48. Both pass the ENCODE standard (> 0.3). (b) With ENCODE’s chr21 peaks: 278 226 / 482 606 = 0.58 for replicate 1, slightly higher, because ENCODE’s set has more and wider peaks (median 891 bp vs 290 bp).
C6. (a) 1784 ENCODE peaks on chr21. Insertion mode: 932 of 1262 (74%) and 981 of 1323 (74%) of our peaks overlap an ENCODE peak; 1585 (89%) and 1572 (88%) of the ENCODE peaks overlap one of ours. Fragment mode: 580 of 685 (85%) and 576 of 697 (83%) of ours in ENCODE, but only 1477 (83%) and 1469 (82%) of ENCODE recovered. Fragment mode is more “precise” because it calls fewer, stronger peaks; insertion mode recovers more of ENCODE’s peaks, as expected since ENCODE also calls on insertions (shift −75, extsize 150). Most ENCODE peaks we miss lie at 43–44 Mb and 5–8 Mb, where chr21 sequence occurs more than once: we keep only uniquely aligned reads (MAPQ ≥ 30), ENCODE’s pipeline keeps reads with up to four alignments and assigns them at random. (b) 1081 of 1262 replicate-1 peaks (86%) overlap replicate 2; 1093 of 1323 replicate-2 peaks (83%) overlap replicate 1.
C7. 1442 merged regions, median width 289 bp, maximum 1820 bp. With two replicates of the same cell line, merging changes little; chaining becomes a problem with many samples (B8).









Solutions — R





R1. (a) 1739 and 1909 lenient peaks. Of replicate 1’s top 1000, 97.3% are found in replicate 2; top 1250: 93.8%; top 1500: 88.5%; all 1739: 82.2%; the top 750 are 99.3% reproduced. (b) The curve is flat to about 1000 peaks and drops faster after about 1300–1500, similar to the 1262 peaks at q < 0.01, and below ENCODE’s 1784 IDR peaks on chr21 (made from more reads, including multi-mappers). (c) Spearman correlation 0.82 among matched peaks. The correlation is computed over all matched peaks, including the many weak ones whose scores are mostly noise; agreement among the strongest peaks is near perfect. This is why IDR models the ranks as a mixture rather than using one correlation.
R2. (a) MACS3 writes the summit as an offset from the 0-based start; rtracklayer has added 1 to the start, so start(p) + p$peak is the 1-based position of the summit base (Genomic intervals, R1b). (b) 1262 and 1323 peaks become 1116 and 1123 non-overlapping 500-bp peaks per replicate (nearby peaks whose 500-bp windows overlap are resolved); the joint consensus has 1286 peaks, all 500 bp wide (table(width(cons))), and 958 of them overlap a peak from both replicates. The merged set (C7) has 1442 regions of variable width (median 289 bp, up to 1820 bp). (c) −log10 p grows with sequencing depth: a deeper sample would win every overlap. Dividing by the sample’s total score puts the samples on the same scale before they compete. (d) 0: no two consensus peaks overlap.
R3. (a) 17.3% of the 958 reproducible consensus peaks are within 1 kb of a protein-coding TSS; 25.8% of ENCODE’s chr21 peaks. (b) Strongest decile 70%, second 25%, the rest 5–15%: the strongest accessible sites are promoters, and the large majority of weaker peaks are distal: candidate enhancers, CTCF sites and other regulatory elements, plus some noise. (c) 59% of the 602 distinct protein-coding TSS positions on chr21 have a consensus peak within 1 kb. Plausible: a B-cell line expresses perhaps half to two thirds of protein-coding genes, and the rest have closed promoters; alternative TSSs of one gene are also counted separately. The R part runs in under a minute.

title: Exercise: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
text:
Where this leads

Differential accessibility starts from a count matrix over fixed-width 500-bp peaks like the consensus you built in R2 (the Corces et al. 2016 haematopoiesis data) and tests it with DESeq2.
Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting uses the summits and the base-resolution insertion sites: there the +4/−5 shift matters.
Peak calling (ChIP-seq) uses the same MACS3 model with an input control, where the 1-kb and 5-kb windows come from the control.

title: Exercise: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)

title: Quiz: ATAC-seq processing and peak calling
text:
Short questions on processing ATAC-seq reads, calling peaks and combining replicates. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A read pair from an ATAC-seq library aligns as read 1 on the + strand at BED [52 000, 52 100) and read 2 on the − strand at BED [52 310, 52 410). Give the fragment length and the two Tn5 insertion sites (BED, after the +4/−5 shift).






Hint





The + read’s 5’ end is its start; the − read’s 5’ end is its end.









Answer





Fragment [52 000, 52 410), 410 bp. Insertions at \(52\,000 + 4 = 52\,004\) and \(52\,410 - 5 = 52\,405\) (BED 52004 52005 and 52405 52406), 401 bp apart.




Q2. Why is the shift +4 on one strand and −5 on the other, when Tn5 cuts symmetrically?






Answer





Tn5 cuts the two strands 9 bp apart and both fragments keep a copy of those 9 bp. The insertion is the centre of the 9 bp: 4 bases in from either end. From a + read’s BED start (the first of the 9 bases) that is +4. A − read’s 5’ end is the last of the 9 bases, but BED stores the end as the boundary after it, so the centre is end − 5. In 1-based coordinates both are 4 bases (+4 and −4).




Q3. Bowtie2 is run with its default maximum fragment length (500 bp) and only properly paired reads are kept. Which part of the ATAC-seq fragment-size distribution is lost, and does it matter for peak calling?






Answer





Fragments longer than 500 bp, that is the di- and tri-nucleosome fragments, become “not concordant” and are removed. For peak calling on nucleosome-free regions it matters little (the short fragments carry most of the signal), but you lose part of the library and the nucleosome ladder, which is a QC readout and the input to nucleosome-positioning analyses. Use -X 2000.




Q4. In 10 kb around a candidate peak MACS3 counts 800 insertions. The window used for counting is 150 bp. The genome-wide expectation is \(\lambda_\text{BG} = 5\). There is no control. What is \(\lambda_\text{local}\)? The peak has \(k = 30\); is it more or less significant than it would be against \(\lambda_\text{BG}\)?






Hint





Scale the 10-kb count to 150 bp. Without a control MACS3 uses \(\lambda_\text{BG}\) and the 10-kb window.









Answer





\(\lambda_\text{10k} = 800 \times 150 / 10\,000 = 12\), so \(\lambda_\text{local} = \max(5, 12) = 12\). The peak is less significant than against \(\lambda_\text{BG}\): \(P(X \ge 30 \mid 12)\) is much larger than \(P(X \ge 30 \mid 5)\). The local background is high (an open region, an amplified segment); the peak must stand out from its neighbourhood, not from the genome average.




Q5. Two ways to call ATAC-seq peaks with MACS3 are -f BAMPE and a BED of insertion sites with --nomodel --shift -75 --extsize 150. In one sentence each, what is piled up?






Answer





BAMPE: whole fragments, from the start of one read to the end of its mate. Insertion mode: a 150-bp window centred on each Tn5 cut site (two per fragment), ignoring the DNA between the cuts.




Q6. After deduplicating with samtools markdup -r, a student calls peaks on insertion sites with MACS3’s default --keep-dup 1. What goes wrong?






Answer





--keep-dup 1 keeps one tag per position and strand. Insertion sites from different fragments often hit the same base at strong sites (Tn5 has sequence preferences), and they are all independent events, so the strongest peaks are flattened. Duplicates were already removed at the fragment level, where they can be recognised (same start and same end); use --keep-dup all.




Q7. Sample A has 20 million insertions after filtering, 7.2 million of them in peaks. Sample B, from the same cell type and with the same peak caller settings, has a FRiP of 0.11. Compute FRiP for A. What could explain B?






Answer





FRiP(A) = 7.2 / 20 = 0.36, above ENCODE’s 0.3. A FRiP of 0.11 means most of B’s insertions fall in closed chromatin: dead or damaged cells (naked DNA is accessible everywhere), over-transposition, or poor nuclei preparation. Check the fragment-size distribution and TSS enrichment for B before using it.




Q8. Replicate 1 has 50 000 peaks, replicate 2 has 30 000. 27 000 of replicate 2’s peaks overlap a replicate-1 peak. A colleague says “90% of peaks are reproducible”. Why is that a weak statement, and what is a better analysis?






Answer





The number depends on the thresholds and is asymmetric: 90% of replicate 2’s peaks overlap replicate 1, but at most 54% of replicate 1’s 50 000 peaks can overlap replicate 2. A lenient replicate 1 catches almost anything. Better: call both leniently, rank the peaks, and ask how far down the ranking the two replicates agree (IDR, or a rank-consistency curve); report the number of peaks that pass a reproducibility threshold.




Q9. Three samples have peaks with summits at positions 10 000 (score 22), 10 300 (score 35) and 10 650 (score 18). Build the fixed-width (500 bp) consensus with iterative overlap removal. How many peaks remain, and where are they?






Hint





Windows are summit ± 250. Start with the highest score; drop what overlaps it; continue with the next highest that is left.









Answer





Windows: [9750, 10250), [10050, 10550), [10400, 10900). Keep 10 300 (35); it overlaps both others, so both are dropped. One peak remains: [10050, 10550). (A plain bedtools merge would give one 1150-bp region [9750, 10900).)




Q10. A paper calls ATAC-seq peaks on the full BAM, without removing mitochondrial reads, and reports the 20 “most accessible regions” in the genome. What do you expect to find in that list?






Answer





The mitochondrial genome. mtDNA has no nucleosomes and many copies per cell, so its pileup is far above any nuclear region; the top peaks will all be on chrM (and possibly in blacklisted repeats). Remove chrM reads and blacklisted regions before peak calling, and look at the top of a peak list in a browser.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
About this lecture
ATAC-seq processing and peak calling ended with one set of peaks for all samples. Now we ask which of those regulatory elements are more open in one cell type (or condition) than in another. Most of the statistics is the DESeq2 you know from RNA-seq; this lecture spends its time on what is different.

From peaks and BAM files to a count matrix: consensus peaks, what to count.
The running example: B cells vs CD4 T cells from three donors (Corces et al. 2016), and why the design is paired.
Exploration: reads in peaks, PCA, sample correlation.
Normalisation, the central difference from RNA-seq: peaks, background, spike-ins, and what a global change does.
DESeq2 on peaks: dispersion, MA and volcano plots, shrinkage.
Interpretation: marker genes, nearest-gene caveats, agreement with RNA-seq.


Students have done a full DESeq2 analysis of RNA-seq. Say so at the start: the negative binomial model, the design formula, the Wald test and the multiple-testing correction are exactly what they know. The new ideas are where the rows of the matrix come from (peaks found in the data, not genes from an annotation), what normalisation assumes when the total amount of open chromatin can differ between samples, and how to turn a list of differential peaks into biology. The running example is real: the Corces et al. 2016 haematopoiesis atlas, 590 650 fixed-width peaks, which is exactly the kind of consensus peak set the previous unit ended with. The result of this unit (B-specific and T-specific peaks) is the input to Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
The question


Two cell types share most of their open chromatin (promoters of housekeeping genes), but each has its own enhancers.
Differential accessibility (DA): which peaks have more fragments in one group than in the other, more than donors differ among themselves?
Answers can be all-or-none (an enhancer open only in B cells) or quantitative (2.5-fold more open).


Walk through the four peaks: the first is shared (a promoter, open in both), the second is open only in B cells, the third only in T cells, the fourth is open in both but more in B cells. In counts, these become rows of a matrix: one row per peak, one column per sample. The question is the same as in RNA-seq, with peaks instead of genes. Note that the figure shows two donors per cell type: without replicates we could not say whether a difference is larger than the difference between two people. Typical applications: cell types (as here), treatment vs control, a knockout, a time course, disease vs healthy tissue.

title: Differential accessibility
section: What is the same as RNA-seq, and what is not
text:
What is the same as RNA-seq, and what is not


Same: a count matrix, the negative binomial GLM, the design formula, dispersion shrinkage, Wald test, Benjamini–Hochberg, fold-change shrinkage. DESeq2 or edgeR run unchanged.
Different: the rows are found in the data; the normalisation assumption (“most features do not change”) is shakier; the result is a list of regions, which needs annotation before it means anything.


This slide is the map of the lecture. Everything in grey is a recap; everything in red is new. A useful way to say it: DESeq2 does not know whether a row is a gene or a peak. It sees counts. All the epigenomics-specific decisions happen before (which regions, what to count, which normalisation) and after (what the regions are near, what binds there). That is also why published differential accessibility analyses differ so much: the statistics are standard, the choices around them are not.

title: Differential accessibility
section: One set of regions for all samples
text:
One set of regions for all samples


Every sample must be counted in the same regions. Peaks called per sample must be combined into a consensus set.
Union and merge (A) is simple, but nearby elements fuse into wide regions of unequal width.
Fixed-width peaks (B): extend each summit to 500 bp, keep the most significant, drop those that overlap it. Used by Corces et al. 2016 and by ArchR; DiffBind re-centres on summits (± 200 bp).
Keep only peaks found in at least k samples (DiffBind default: 2) or call peaks on pooled data per group, so one noisy sample does not add thousands of peaks.


The consensus step is a design choice with consequences. A merged region of 3 kb that contains a promoter and an enhancer will be counted as one feature: if the enhancer opens and the promoter does not, the change is diluted. Fixed-width peaks keep elements separate and make counts comparable between peaks (every peak is 500 bp, so count differences between peaks are not due to width). The iterative procedure in panel B is what Corces et al. describe: summits from MACS2 extended to 500 bp, ranked by significance, overlapping lower-ranked peaks removed. It is also the default in ArchR. Calling peaks on each group’s pooled reads (rather than per sample) is common too; the important thing is not to call peaks on one group only, which biases the test towards that group. The previous unit (ATAC-seq processing and peak calling) built such a consensus set; here we start from Corces’s.

title: Differential accessibility
section: What to count in a peak
text:
What to count in a peak


ATAC-seq measures Tn5 insertions: each fragment end is a cut site in open chromatin. Fragment 4 spans the peak without a single cut inside it.
Counting fragments that overlap the peak (featureCounts with pairs, bedtools multicov) is the common default; counting insertions (fragment ends, shifted +4/−5) is more precise and what ArchR and chromVAR use.
Either way: one number per peak per sample, integer counts, no normalisation yet.


For RNA-seq students counted reads per gene with featureCounts or salmon. Here it is the same, with peaks as features. Two subtleties. First, a long fragment spanning the peak (fragment 4) says that the DNA at both ends was accessible, not the peak itself; insertion counting does not count it. Second, with read counting (not fragment counting) a fragment with both ends in the peak counts twice, which breaks the Poisson assumptions mildly; count pairs (featureCounts -p –countReadPairs) or insertions. With 500-bp peaks and mostly short fragments the two methods give highly correlated counts; the choice matters more for nucleosome-scale questions. The Corces count matrix counts fragments per peak.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
Counting on the command line
# consensus peaks (BED) -> SAF, the simple annotation format of featureCounts
awk 'BEGIN { OFS = "\t"; print "GeneID", "Chr", "Start", "End", "Strand" }
     { print "peak" NR, $1, $2 + 1, $3, "." }' consensus.bed > consensus.saf

# count fragments (read pairs) per peak, all samples at once
featureCounts -F SAF -a consensus.saf -p --countReadPairs -B -C \
  -T 8 -o atac_counts.txt sample1.bam sample2.bam sample3.bam ...

# or, with bedtools: one column per BAM
bedtools multicov -bams sample1.bam sample2.bam -bed consensus.bed > atac_counts.bed

-p --countReadPairs: count fragments, not reads. -B -C: both ends aligned, on the same chromosome.
SAF is 1-based (start + 1), BED is 0-based: the boundary from Genomic intervals again.
The output is the matrix: peaks × samples. Corces et al. provide it, so the exercise starts there.


featureCounts is the same program students used for RNA-seq; with SAF they give it intervals instead of a GTF. By default featureCounts assigns a fragment that overlaps two features to neither (ambiguous); with non-overlapping fixed-width peaks this rarely matters, and –fracOverlap or -O change the behaviour. bedtools multicov is slower but transparent. A third route is csaw::windowCounts or DiffBind::dba.count in R, which read the BAMs directly. On the cluster, run featureCounts in an sbatch job with -T set to the number of cores requested. The matrix has one row per peak, an integer count per sample, and that is all DESeq2 needs.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
The dataset: Corces et al. 2016


ATAC-seq of 13 FACS-sorted blood cell types from 7 healthy donors (plus AML samples we ignore): 590 650 peaks (hg19) × 132 libraries, GEO GSE74912.
Our comparison: B cells vs CD4 T cells from the 3 donors with both (1022, 4983, 5483): 8 libraries.
Column names encode donor and cell type: Donor4983-CD4-9A-150120 = donor 4983, CD4 T cells (code 9), library A, run date. Early samples are just 4983-7A (code 7 = monocytes): decode from the GEO sample table, never guess.


Corces et al. sorted cells directly from bone marrow or blood of healthy donors and ran an optimised ATAC protocol (Fast-ATAC) on about 5000 cells each. The GEO series lists every library with its donor and cell type, which is how we decoded the numeric codes: 1 HSC, 2 MPP, 3 LMPP, 4 CMP, 5 GMP, 6 MEP, 7 monocytes, 9 CD4 T, 10 CD8 T, 11 NK, 13 B, 14 CLP, 15 erythroblasts. The design is unbalanced: progenitors come from donors 4983, 6792, 7256 and 2596, mature lymphocytes from 1022, 2596, 4983, 5483. Only three donors gave both B cells and CD4 T cells; donor 2596 has CD4 T cells but no B-cell library, so it cannot be paired and we leave it out (the exercise asks what including it would do). The peaks are on hg19; the course uses GRCh38, next slide.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
The peaks are hg19: liftOver
gr19 <- GRanges(atac$Chr, IRanges(atac$Start + 1, atac$End))   # 0-based starts in the file
lo   <- liftOver(gr19, import.chain("hg19ToHg38.over.chain"))  # a GRangesList: 0, 1 or more pieces
table(lengths(lo))



result of liftOver
peaks




no match in GRCh38 (deleted or rearranged)
159


split into ≥ 2 pieces
1 375


one piece, but not 500 bp or a different chromosome
46


one piece, 500 bp: kept
589 070 (99.7%)




Dropping 0.3% of the peaks is fine here. Better still, when you have the reads: re-align to GRCh38 and call peaks there.


This is the liftOver from Genomic intervals, now with real numbers. The file’s Start column is 0-based (End − Start = 500), so add 1 when building a GRanges. liftOver returns a list because one input range can map to zero, one or several pieces. A peak that is split, or whose lifted width is no longer 500 bp, spans a gap or rearrangement between the builds; we drop those rather than guess. We give each peak an ID from its row in the original file (peak000001…) so that hg19 and hg38 versions can always be matched. The counts do not change: liftOver moves the coordinates, not the reads. That is also the limitation: reads that would map differently in GRCh38 (new sequence, fixed errors) are not recovered.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
Technical and biological replicates


Biological replicates = independent donors. They carry the variation the test must beat.
Technical replicates (A, B) = two libraries from the same sorted cells. They measure library noise only: sum them (collapseReplicates), do not count them as extra samples.
8 libraries → 6 columns: 3 donors × 2 cell types.


Treating technical replicates as biological replicates is pseudo-replication: the model would think donor 5483 is two people and underestimate the variance between people, giving too many significant peaks. Summing counts is right because a technical replicate is just more sequencing of the same material (the two libraries correlate at r = 0.94 on log CPM in this dataset, against 0.77–0.93 between donors of the same cell type). DESeq2::collapseReplicates sums the columns that share a label. Sorting matters too: each population is FACS-sorted on surface markers (CD19 for B cells, CD4 for T helpers), so the purity of the sort is part of the biological sample.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
Why pair by donor?


If donors differ (genotype, age, sex, sample handling), each B-cell sample shares part of that difference with the T-cell sample from the same person.
~ donor + celltype compares every donor with itself: the donor effect is removed, and the celltype coefficient is the within-donor log fold change.
The cost: one coefficient per extra donor. With 6 samples, the residual degrees of freedom drop from 4 to 2.


The toy numbers are on the slide. Unpaired, the difference of 1.0 (log2 scale) is small against a within-group SD of about 2 (donors differ a lot), so nothing is significant. Paired, the three within-donor differences are 1.0, 1.2 and 0.8: a consistent increase. This is the paired t-test idea in a GLM, same as in RNA-seq experiments with patients. In DESeq2 the last term in the design is the one results() tests by default, so put the variable of interest last. Whether pairing pays off depends on how big the donor effect is compared with the cost in degrees of freedom; we will check that on the real data.

title: Differential accessibility
section: Exploration: reads in peaks per library
text:
Exploration: reads in peaks per library


Reads in peaks range from 0.6 to 25 million per library: a 40-fold range, partly sequencing depth and partly signal-to-noise (the fraction of reads in peaks, FRiP).
Erythroblasts are low in every donor (Corces et al. report poor replicate agreement for them, r ≈ 0.5). The B-cell library of donor 1022 has 4.6 M reads in peaks; the B cells of 4983 and 5483 have 17–18 M (5483: two libraries summed).


The count matrix only has reads in peaks, not total reads, so we cannot compute FRiP here; in your own data you have both (Experimental design and QC). Two libraries with the same depth can have very different counts in peaks if one is noisier (more reads in background, mitochondria, dead cells). For differential analysis this matters in two ways: low counts mean less power for that sample, and differences in FRiP feed directly into the normalisation question later. Erythroblasts are a hard sample (Corces et al. note R = 0.55 between technical replicates against 0.94 for other cell types), a reminder to look at QC per sample before a comparison.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
Signal-to-noise differs between libraries


Same depth, FRiP 40% vs 10%: a typical peak gets 4 times fewer fragments in library 2.
Normalising by total reads makes every peak “4-fold up” in library 1. Normalising within peaks says nothing changed.
Which one is right depends on why FRiP differs. A worse library? Then within-peak normalisation. Fewer or weaker open sites in the cells? Then the total-read answer may be the biology.


This is the first half of the normalisation story and the most important idea of the lecture. FRiP mixes technology (how many dead cells, how well transposition worked, how deep the library is relative to its complexity) and biology (how much of the genome is open). A cell type with fewer open sites (e.g. quiescent cells, or erythroblasts which compact their chromatin before enucleation) will have lower FRiP for biological reasons. The counts cannot distinguish the two; QC metrics (TSS enrichment, fragment-size distribution, mitochondrial fraction) and knowledge of the system can.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
PCA: cell type dominates


VST of 127 515 peaks with mean count ≥ 10, all 77 healthy libraries, the 10 000 most variable peaks.
Libraries cluster by cell type, not by donor (shape). PC1 runs from stem and progenitor cells (left) to mature cells (right); PC2 separates the erythroid branch (MEP → erythroblasts).


Exactly as in RNA-seq: variance-stabilising transformation (vst, blind = TRUE), then prcomp on the most variable rows. The picture follows the haematopoietic tree: HSC and MPP together, LMPP, CMP and GMP nearby; MEP on the way to erythroblasts (PC2); CLP between the progenitors and the mature lymphocytes; monocytes, B, NK and T cells are all mature and sit at the right of PC1, and separate from each other on later components. Erythroblasts spread out more than the others, matching their poor replicate agreement. Donor (point shape) adds little on top. Corces et al. made the same point more strongly: accessibility classifies cell types better than RNA does. For our test this is good news: the cell-type signal is large compared with donor variation.

title: Differential accessibility
section: The six samples of our comparison
text:
The six samples of our comparison


Pearson correlation of log2 CPM over 75 922 peaks (mean CPM ≥ 2), all 8 libraries.
Technical replicates: r = 0.94. Same cell type, other donor: 0.77–0.88 (B), 0.87–0.93 (CD4). B vs CD4: 0.19–0.37.
The 1022 B-cell library correlates least with its group: fewest reads in peaks (4.6 M).


Point out the block structure: B cells with B cells, T cells with T cells; inside each block, the technical replicates of 5483 are the most similar pair. This justifies summing technical replicates. Also note that 1022 B cells correlate less with the other B cells (0.77–0.84) than 4983 and 5483 do with each other (0.84–0.88): a lower-quality library (4.6 M reads in peaks) is noisier. With only 3 donors per group, one weaker sample matters; DESeq2’s dispersion estimates will absorb it, at a cost in power.

title: Differential accessibility
section: Normalisation: median of ratios, on peaks
text:
Normalisation: median of ratios, on peaks


DESeq2 size factor for sample j: s_j = \text{median}_i \, \dfrac{k_{ij}}{\left(\prod_{v} k_{iv}\right)^{1/m}}, the median over peaks of the count divided by the peak’s geometric mean.
The same as for genes. The assumption is too: the typical (median) peak does not change.
Here, for the 1022 B-cell library: size factor 0.46 from the median ratio, 0.35 from total counts in peaks.


Recap, students know this formula. Each peak votes with its ratio to a pseudo-reference sample; the median is robust to the minority of peaks that change. The histogram is the real distribution of log2 ratios for one sample. The two lines differ because the reads of 1022_Bcell are distributed differently across peaks: relatively fewer reads in the strongest peaks, consistent with a noisier library. Neither is “wrong”; they answer different questions. Total-count normalisation says “the same number of reads in peaks in every sample”; median ratio says “the typical peak is unchanged”. TMM (edgeR) makes the same assumption as the median ratio with a trimmed mean of log ratios, and gives similar factors.

title: Differential accessibility
section: When most peaks do change: a global opening
text:
When most peaks do change: a global opening


A treatment that opens chromatin everywhere (e.g. an HDAC inhibitor) gives more fragments in every peak. Sequenced to the same depth, the extra signal is diluted.
Peak-based size factors make the median peak unchanged: the global opening disappears, and only the relative change (p5) survives, at half its size.
Background bins (reads outside peaks) can recover it, if the background truly is constant.


Go through the numbers. Truth: all peaks double, p5 quadruples, background unchanged. The treated library has 1400 reads’ worth of material, but the sequencer gives 1000 reads, so everything is scaled by 1000/1400. The raw ratio is then 1.43 for most peaks. Median-of-ratios normalisation divides by 1.43: most peaks become 1.0 (no change) and p5 becomes 2.0. Normalising by the background (which went from 720 to 514 reads) divides by 0.71 and recovers 2 and 4. This is the same problem as the EZH2-inhibitor example in Experimental design and QC, now for accessibility. The by-hand exercise has a version of it. Note the symmetry: a global closing would be hidden in the same way.

title: Differential accessibility
section: Four ways to normalise, four assumptions
text:
Four ways to normalise, four assumptions


No method is assumption-free. Pick the one whose assumption you can defend for your experiment, and say it in the methods.
If two reasonable methods disagree, the disagreement is the result: report it (Reske et al. 2020 found the number and direction of DA peaks change with the method).


Library size: the total signal per cell is the same, fine when FRiP is similar across samples. Peak-based (median ratio, TMM): most peaks are unchanged, the default in DESeq2 and edgeR; wrong under global change. Background bins (csaw’s normFactors on 10-kb bins, Lun & Smyth): the reads outside peaks are noise at a constant rate per cell; wrong when signal-to-noise differs for technical reasons (a library with more dead cells has more background, and background normalisation then inflates its peaks). Spike-ins: add a fixed amount of foreign chromatin per cell (e.g. Drosophila nuclei) before transposition; for ATAC this is not yet routine. A fifth option is a set of reference peaks assumed constant (e.g. housekeeping promoters). Reske, Wilson & Chandler 2020 re-analysed an ATAC dataset with different normalisations and obtained different numbers of DA peaks and even different biological conclusions.

title: Differential accessibility
section: Real data: the choice changes the answer
text:
Real data: the choice changes the answer


DESeq2 and TMM factors agree within 10%; total counts differ by up to 25% (B cells of 1022 and 4983).
Same model, same data: 19 438 / 17 202 peaks up in B / up in T with DESeq2 factors, 18 342 / 19 074 with TMM, 23 703 / 13 540 with total counts.
Total counts shift all fold changes towards B (median log2 FC 0.52 vs 0.26 with DESeq2 factors): relative to the typical peak, the B-cell libraries have more reads in peaks.


Thresholds: padj < 0.05 and |MLE log2 fold change| > 1 for this comparison. Most of the strong cell-type-specific peaks are found by all three; the difference is in the hundreds to thousands of moderate peaks, and in the balance between “up” and “down”. The median log fold change over all tested peaks is a quick diagnostic: 0.26 with DESeq2 factors, 0.19 with TMM, 0.52 with total counts. (It is not exactly 0 even with peak-based factors, because the median is taken over many all-or-none peaks, and DESeq2 computes its factors only from peaks with no zero count.) Is the extra 0.26 with total counts real (B cells have more accessible chromatin) or technical (the B-cell libraries happen to have better signal-to-noise)? Without spike-ins or another external reference we cannot tell, and for a comparison of two cell types the conservative, conventional choice is peak-based. For a treatment expected to change chromatin globally, that default needs to be questioned.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
Tools: DiffBind and csaw


DiffBind: peak-based. Builds the consensus, counts, then calls DESeq2 or edgeR. What we do by hand in this unit.
csaw: window-based. No peak calling; counts in sliding windows, normalises on background bins, tests each window, merges windows into regions and controls the FDR over regions.
Neither is installed in this course: the exercise does the same steps with DESeq2 and edgeR directly.


DiffBind (Ross-Innes et al. 2012, Stark & Brown) was written for ChIP-seq of transcription factors (oestrogen receptor in breast cancer) and is widely used for ATAC too. Its defaults have changed between versions: since version 3 it normalises by full library size by default, and offers DESeq2/TMM/background options (dba.normalize). csaw (Lun & Smyth 2016) avoids the circularity of calling peaks and testing in the same data, handles regions of any width, and makes the FDR refer to regions rather than windows. For narrow, well-defined ATAC peaks the two approaches give similar answers; csaw shines for broad or shifting signals. The statistical core of both is the negative binomial GLM.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
DESeq2 on peaks
dds <- DESeqDataSet(se, design = ~ donor + celltype)       # se: peaks x 8 libraries, rowRanges in hg38
dds <- collapseReplicates(dds, groupby = dds$unit)         # 8 libraries -> 6 samples
dds <- dds[rowSums(counts(dds) >= 10) >= 3, ]              # 211 824 of 589 070 peaks
dds <- DESeq(dds)                                          # about 1 minute
res <- results(dds, name = "celltype_Bcell_vs_CD4", alpha = 0.05)
shr <- lfcShrink(dds, coef = "celltype_Bcell_vs_CD4", type = "apeglm")   # about 2 minutes

Exactly the RNA-seq workflow. Filter first: most of the 589 070 peaks were called in other cell types and have almost no reads in B or T cells.
celltype levels CD4, Bcell: positive log2 fold change = more open in B cells.


The filter keeps peaks with at least 10 fragments in at least 3 of the 6 samples (3 = the size of the smaller group, so a peak open in only one cell type is kept). Without it DESeq2 runs on 589 070 rows, most of them zeros, which costs time and multiple-testing burden; independent filtering in results() would remove many of them anyway. Factor levels: DESeq2 compares to the first level, so set CD4 first. The name of the coefficient is printed by resultsNames(dds). Run times are on one core of a server; on a laptop expect 2–4 minutes for DESeq() and a bit more for apeglm.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
Dispersion: paired or not


The familiar picture: noisy per-peak estimates, a fitted trend, shrunk final values. Typical dispersion ≈ 0.4 (coefficient of variation ≈ 60% between donors), higher than for genes.
Here the donor effect is small: only 47 peaks have a significant donor term (LRT). Pairing costs 2 degrees of freedom: 36 703 peaks at padj < 0.05 paired, 41 671 unpaired.


Dispersion is the squared coefficient of variation between biological replicates, beyond Poisson noise. ATAC peaks are noisier than genes: they are small (500 bp), counts are lower, and library quality varies. The dashed trend is the unpaired fit, lower because the residual degrees of freedom are 4 instead of 2 and the donor term absorbs little. This is a real, honest result: in this dataset of sorted cells from healthy adults, the donor effect is weak, and the paired model finds fewer peaks. Should we switch to the unpaired design because it gives more hits? No: choose the design from the structure of the experiment before looking at the number of hits. The paired design is the right one for a paired experiment; it protects against donor effects when they exist (e.g. patients with different genotypes or treatments), and the cost here is modest (most strong peaks are found by both).

title: Differential accessibility
text:
MA plot and fold-change shrinkage


Left: maximum-likelihood fold changes are huge and noisy for weak peaks (few reads: 0 vs 5 is “infinitely” open).
Right: apeglm shrinks uncertain fold changes towards 0 and leaves well-measured ones alone. Use shrunk values to rank and filter by effect size, and for plots.
Blue/orange: padj < 0.05 and |shrunk LFC| > 1. Where counts are high, the grey cloud of unchanged peaks sits on 0: the normalisation assumption holds for most peaks.


Same as for RNA-seq; students have probably used lfcShrink. Two things to read from an MA plot of peaks. First, the shape: a cell-type comparison gives many large fold changes (cell-type-specific enhancers are often all-or-none), so the plot looks more dramatic than a typical RNA-seq treatment. Second, the centre of the grey cloud: if it sat at +0.5 instead of 0, the normalisation would be suspect (or there is a global change). The p-values come from the unshrunk model; shrinkage changes the effect sizes, not which peaks are significant. Our definition of a differential peak uses both: padj < 0.05 from results(), |log2 fold change| > 1 from the shrunk estimate.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
Volcano plot


19 404 peaks more open in B cells and 16 897 more open in CD4 T cells (padj < 0.05, |shrunk log2 FC| > 1), out of 211 824 tested.
17% of tested peaks differ more than 2-fold: B and T cells are distinct lineages, so this is expected. A drug treatment typically moves hundreds, not tens of thousands.


The y axis is −log10 of the adjusted p-value, the x axis the shrunk log2 fold change. The two arms are roughly symmetric, a sign that the normalisation is not biased towards one side. These two lists are the result of the unit and the starting point of Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting, which asks which transcription factor motifs are enriched in B-specific vs T-specific peaks (expect EBF1, PAX5, PU.1/SPIB, OCT2 for B; TCF7/LEF1, RUNX, ETS, GATA3 for T). The exercise saves them as differential_peaks.tsv.

title: Differential accessibility
section: Do the peaks make sense? Marker loci
text:
Do the peaks make sense? Marker loci


Each bar is one peak (mean normalised count over 3 donors): blue = open in B, orange = open in T, grey = not differential.
PAX5 (B-cell identity factor): 31 peaks whose nearest TSS is PAX5 open in B, none in T. BCL11B (T-cell commitment): 58 open in T, 1 in B.
Other markers: CD79A, MS4A1, CD19, BLK, EBF1 (B); CD3E, TCF7, LEF1, GATA3, CD28 (T).


A sanity check every analysis should include: do the known marker genes come out on the right side? They do. Note how many peaks a single regulator gene has: PAX5 and BCL11B sit in large regulatory landscapes with dozens of enhancers, and the large intron of PAX5 is full of B-specific elements. Not every peak near a marker changes: promoters of these genes can be accessible (poised) in both cell types, and some elements near EBF1 open in T cells. A short table of counts per marker is in the exercise (R9).

title: Differential accessibility
section: From peaks to genes: the nearest-TSS caveat
text:
From peaks to genes: the nearest-TSS caveat


Only 8% of B-specific and 14% of T-specific peaks are within 1 kb of a protein-coding TSS (20% of all tested peaks): DA peaks are mostly distal.
Assigning each peak to its nearest gene is a first guess, right for perhaps half of enhancers. Better links use contacts or correlation (Linking regulatory elements to genes).


Promoters tend to be accessible in many cell types, enhancers are cell-type specific: that is why differential peaks are depleted at promoters. For the distal majority, the nearest gene is a convenient label, not a mechanism. The exercise annotates each peak with its nearest protein-coding TSS (GenomicRanges::distanceToNearest, as in Genomic intervals). Tools such as ChIPseeker or GREAT make this a one-liner and add rules (GREAT assigns a regulatory domain to each gene). Keep the distance in the table; a peak 400 kb from its “nearest gene” in a gene desert is not evidence about that gene.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
Does accessibility agree with expression?


RNA-seq from the same study (GSE74246), B vs CD4 T cells from 4 donors, DESeq2 ~ donor + celltype.
Genes near B-open peaks go up in B (median RNA log2 FC +0.5), near T-open peaks go up in T (−0.6). Promoter peaks agree well (Spearman 0.69), distal peaks less (0.42).


The RNA donors (1022, 2596, 5852, 7653) are only partly the same people as the ATAC donors, so this is a comparison of cell types, not of matched samples. The agreement is clear but far from perfect, for good reasons: a distal peak may not regulate its nearest gene; a gene can have several elements changing in opposite directions; accessibility can be primed before expression (or remain after it); and expression is also regulated after transcription. A promoter peak and its own gene are linked directly, which is why their correlation is higher. About two thirds of DA peaks (67% for B, 71% for T) have a nearest gene that changes in the same direction. This is the starting point of Linking regulatory elements to genes.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
The result to reuse
tab <- data.frame(peak_id = names(dds), chr = seqnames(dds), start = start(dds), end = end(dds),
                  baseMean = res$baseMean, log2FoldChange = shr$log2FoldChange, lfcSE = shr$lfcSE,
                  pvalue = res$pvalue, padj = res$padj, nearest_gene = ..., dist_to_tss = ...)
tab$class <- ifelse(tab$padj < 0.05 & tab$log2FoldChange >  1, "B_up",
             ifelse(tab$padj < 0.05 & tab$log2FoldChange < -1, "T_up", "ns"))
write.table(tab, "differential_peaks.tsv", sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)

Definition: differential = padj < 0.05 and |shrunken log2 FC| > 1; B_up = more open in B cells, T_up = more open in CD4 T cells. GRCh38, 1-based coordinates, 500 bp.
Keep all tested peaks (class ns included): motif enrichment needs a background.


This table is the hand-over to Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting. Two decisions are written into it and should be in any methods section: the thresholds (FDR 5%, at least 2-fold), and the background (all 211 824 peaks that passed the count filter, which are accessible in B or T cells; a better background for motifs than random genomic sequence, because it has the same GC and chromatin context). Coordinates are GRanges, 1-based closed; when writing BED from them, subtract 1 from start (Genomic intervals). A variant worth knowing: results(dds, lfcThreshold = 1) tests |LFC| > 1 directly instead of filtering afterwards, which is stricter (here 10 153 and 7 503 peaks).

title: Differential accessibility
text:
Limitations of this analysis

Sorted populations are still mixtures: a 2% contamination of T cells in the B-cell sort puts T-cell peaks into the B-cell counts. “Specific” means “much more”, not “only”. Single-cell ATAC avoids this, at the price of sparse counts.
Peaks lifted from hg19: 0.3% lost; reads were aligned to an older genome.
Fixed 500-bp peaks: good for TF sites and comparable counts, but a broad domain is cut into pieces or partly missed.
Peaks called in all 13 cell types: the set includes elements never open in B or T cells (filtered out), and misses none that are open in only one sample.
Three donors per group: dispersion estimates rely heavily on the trend; one weak library (1022) carries a lot of weight.
Normalisation: peak-based by choice. A real global difference in accessibility between B and T cells would be hidden.


These are the questions to ask of any differential accessibility paper, too. Mixtures: Corces et al. sorted with strict gates, but purity is never 100%, and for rare populations contamination can dominate. Peak set: calling peaks on all cell types together, then testing two of them, is fine (the consensus is not biased towards one of the two groups), which is a design point worth contrasting with calling peaks on one group only. Fixed width: some of the strongest B-cell elements are clusters of several peaks (super-enhancer-like), and counting them as independent peaks inflates the number of DA “elements”. A common follow-up is to merge DA peaks within a few kb before counting regions.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
Summary

normalisation

statistics

DA peaks are mostly distal; nearest gene is a guess; check markers and RNA


this dataset
211 824 peaks tested; 19 404 B_up, 16 897 T_up (padj < 0.05, |LFC| > 1)




Students should leave able to: compute a median-of-ratios size factor by hand; explain why a global change in accessibility is invisible to peak-based normalisation and what to do about it; write the design formula for a paired experiment and say what each coefficient means; read an MA and a volcano plot of peaks; and say what “nearest gene” can and cannot tell. Next: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting, which asks which transcription factors explain the B- and T-specific peaks.

title: Differential accessibility
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Corces et al. 2016, Nat Genet. Lineage-specific and single-cell chromatin accessibility charts human hematopoiesis and leukemia evolution. The dataset of this unit.
Love, Huber & Anders 2014, Genome Biol. Moderated estimation of fold change and dispersion for RNA-seq data with DESeq2. The model, unchanged for peaks.
Ross-Innes et al. 2012, Nature. Differential oestrogen receptor binding is associated with clinical outcome in breast cancer. The paper that introduced DiffBind.
Lun & Smyth 2016, Nucleic Acids Res. csaw: a Bioconductor package for differential binding analysis of ChIP-seq data using sliding windows. Windows, background normalisation, region-level FDR.
Robinson & Oshlack 2010, Genome Biol. A scaling normalization method for differential expression analysis of RNA-seq data. TMM, and why the total is not the right normaliser.
Reske, Wilson & Chandler 2020, Epigenetics Chromatin. ATAC-seq normalization method can significantly affect differential accessibility analysis and interpretation. The normalisation choice, on real data.

title: Exercise: Differential accessibility

After this exercise you will be able to:

title: Exercise: Differential accessibility
text:
Background
The count matrix. One row per peak (a consensus set shared by all samples), one column per library, integer counts of fragments in the peak. From here on the analysis is the RNA-seq one: DESeq2 or edgeR.
Size factors (DESeq2, median of ratios). For peak \(i\) and sample \(j\) with count \(k_{ij}\) and \(m\) samples:
\[ s_j = \operatorname{median}_i \frac{k_{ij}}{\left( \prod_{v=1}^{m} k_{iv} \right)^{1/m}} \]
Peaks with a zero in any sample are left out of the median. Normalised count = \(k_{ij} / s_j\). The assumption: the typical peak does not change. TMM (edgeR) makes the same assumption; normalising by total reads assumes the total signal per cell is the same; background-bin normalisation (csaw) assumes that reads outside peaks are constant.
Design. ~ donor + celltype fits one baseline per donor and one cell-type effect shared by all donors: the cell-type coefficient is the within-donor log2 fold change. ~ celltype ignores who is who.
FRiP (fraction of reads in peaks) = reads in peaks / all reads. Expected count in a peak ≈ depth × FRiP × (that peak’s share of the reads in peaks).
Our definition of a differential peak, used again in Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting: adjusted \(p\) < 0.05 and |shrunken log2 fold change| > 1. Positive = more open in B cells (B_up), negative = more open in CD4 T cells (T_up).

title: Exercise: Differential accessibility
text:
Data
ATAC-seq and RNA-seq count matrices from Corces et al. 2016 (GEO GSE74912 and GSE74246), the UCSC hg19 → hg38 liftOver chain, and the GENCODE v46 annotation. From the course repository:
data/download.sh differential-accessibility      # about 70 MB (plus the GTF, 40 MB)
mkdir -p ~/epi/diffacc && cd ~/epi/diffacc
D=/path/to/course/data                           # where download.sh put the files

corces2016_atac_counts.txt.gz: columns Chr Start End (hg19, 0-based starts, 590 650 peaks of 500 bp) followed by 132 libraries (77 from healthy donors, the rest from AML patients and bulk CD34+ cells).
corces2016_rna_counts.txt.gz: gene symbols × 81 RNA-seq libraries.

What the column names mean. From the GEO sample table of GSE74912 (each library is listed with its donor and cell type): Donor4983-CD4-9A-150120 is donor 4983, CD4 T cells, cell-type code 9, library A, sequenced on 2015-01-20. The early libraries have only donor and code: 4983-7A is donor 4983, code 7 (monocytes), library A. The codes are 1 HSC, 2 MPP, 3 LMPP, 4 CMP, 5 GMP, 6 MEP, 7 monocyte, 9 CD4 T cell, 10 CD8 T cell, 11 NK cell, 13 B cell, 14 CLP, 15 erythroblast. Libraries A, B (C) of the same donor and cell type are technical replicates (Corces et al. 2016, Supplementary Table 1).
Shortcuts, said plainly. We start from the authors’ count matrix, not from BAM files (counting is shown in the lecture and in ATAC-seq processing and peak calling), and the peaks were called on hg19 and are lifted to GRCh38 rather than re-called.
The R part runs in about 12 minutes in total and needs about 4 GB of memory. On the cluster, run the R part in an interactive job or wrap it in an sbatch script (Rscript diffacc.R).
