0.8
0.7
0.001


d
90
3.0
2.6
0.02




Which peaks are differential by our definition, and in which direction?
How many times more open is peak a in CD4 T cells than in B cells?
Peak c is significant but not differential by our definition. Is it “not changed”? What would you write about it?
Why is peak b’s MLE fold change so large, and why is it not significant?

B8. Judge the claim. A paper reports: “Peaks more open in B cells are near genes such as PAX5 and CD79A, so these peaks drive B-cell gene expression. Moreover, 30% of B-specific peaks are near genes that are not more expressed in B cells, showing that accessibility and expression are uncoupled.”
Give two reasons why the first sentence overstates what was shown, and two reasons why a B-specific peak can sit next to a gene that is not differentially expressed.

title: Exercise: Differential accessibility
text:
On the command line

C1 — Look at the count matrix
zcat $D/corces2016_atac_counts.txt.gz | head -1 | tr '\t' '\n' | head -30
zcat $D/corces2016_atac_counts.txt.gz | head -1 | tr '\t' '\n' | grep -c .
zcat $D/corces2016_atac_counts.txt.gz | head -1 | tr '\t' '\n' | grep -E -- '-(Bcell|CD4)-'
zcat $D/corces2016_atac_counts.txt.gz | head -3 | cut -f1-6
zcat $D/corces2016_atac_counts.txt.gz | tail -n +2 | awk '{ w[$3 - $2]++ } END { for (k in w) print k, w[k] }'
zcat $D/corces2016_atac_counts.txt.gz | tail -n +2 | cut -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr | head -25

How many columns, and how many libraries? Which B-cell and CD4 T-cell libraries are there, and from which donors? Which donors have both?
Are the coordinates 0-based or 1-based? (Use the widths.)
Which chromosomes are present? Which are absent, and what would that mean for comparing male and female donors?



C2 — Reads in peaks for one library, and the peaks as BED
zcat $D/corces2016_atac_counts.txt.gz | awk -F'\t' '
  NR == 1 { for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) if ($i == "Donor1022-Bcell-13-150120") c = i; next }
  { s += $c; if ($c == 0) z++ }
  END { print "column", c, "reads in peaks", s, "peaks with 0 reads", z }'
zcat $D/corces2016_atac_counts.txt.gz | tail -n +2 | cut -f1-3 > corces_hg19.bed
head -2 corces_hg19.bed

How many reads in peaks does the B-cell library of donor 1022 have, and in how many peaks does it have no read at all?
Why do so many peaks have zero reads in a B-cell library? (Where were the peaks called?)

title: Exercise: Differential accessibility
text:
In R
You need DESeq2, edgeR, apeglm, GenomicRanges, rtracklayer, data.table, ggplot2 and ggrepel (see Install the software you need).
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(data.table); library(GenomicRanges); library(rtracklayer)
  library(SummarizedExperiment); library(DESeq2); library(edgeR); library(ggplot2); library(ggrepel)
})
D <- "/path/to/course/data"

R1 — Load and decode the samples
atac <- fread(file.path(D, "corces2016_atac_counts.txt.gz"))        # about 5 s
dim(atac)
cn <- names(atac)[-(1:3)]
healthy <- grep("^(Donor)?[0-9]+-", cn, value = TRUE)
re <- "^(?:Donor)?([0-9]+)-(?:[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9]*-)?([0-9]+)([A-C]?)(?:-[0-9]+)?$"
m  <- regmatches(healthy, regexec(re, healthy, perl = TRUE))
code2type <- c(`1` = "HSC", `2` = "MPP", `3` = "LMPP", `4` = "CMP", `5` = "GMP", `6` = "MEP",
               `7` = "Mono", `9` = "CD4", `10` = "CD8", `11` = "NK", `13` = "Bcell",
               `14` = "CLP", `15` = "Ery")
samples <- data.frame(sample = healthy, donor = sapply(m, `[`, 2),
                      celltype = unname(code2type[sapply(m, `[`, 3)]), rep = sapply(m, `[`, 4))
table(samples$celltype, samples$donor)

Explain the regular expression piece by piece. Which part captures the donor, the cell-type code and the replicate letter? Why must the optional cell-type word start with a letter? (Try what happens to Donor7256-1A-110614 if it may start with a digit.)
How many healthy libraries, donors and cell types are there? Which donors have both B cells and CD4 T cells?
Which columns did grep leave out, and what are they?



R2 — Lift the peaks to GRCh38
gr19 <- GRanges(atac$Chr, IRanges(atac$Start + 1, atac$End))
chainf <- tempfile(fileext = ".chain")
writeLines(readLines(gzfile(file.path(D, "hg19ToHg38.over.chain.gz"))), chainf)
lo <- liftOver(gr19, import.chain(chainf))
table(pmin(lengths(lo), 2))                                     # 0, 1, 2 or more pieces
keep <- which(lengths(lo) == 1)
gr38 <- unlist(lo[keep])
ok <- width(gr38) == 500 & as.character(seqnames(gr38)) == as.character(seqnames(gr19)[keep])
sum(!ok)
keep <- keep[ok]; gr38 <- gr38[ok]
names(gr38) <- sprintf("peak%06d", keep)
length(gr38)

How many peaks fail, how many split into several pieces, and how many single pieces change width or chromosome? What fraction is kept?
Why atac$Start + 1?
Why name the peaks by their row number in the original file?



R3 — A SummarizedExperiment of the eight libraries
sel <- samples[samples$celltype %in% c("Bcell", "CD4") & samples$donor %in% c("1022", "4983", "5483"), ]
cnt <- as.matrix(atac[keep, sel$sample, with = FALSE])
rownames(cnt) <- names(gr38)
cd <- DataFrame(donor = factor(sel$donor), celltype = factor(sel$celltype, levels = c("CD4", "Bcell")),
                rep = sel$rep, row.names = sel$sample)
cd$unit <- paste(cd$donor, cd$celltype, sep = "_")
se <- SummarizedExperiment(assays = list(counts = cnt), rowRanges = gr38, colData = cd)
se
colSums(assay(se)) / 1e6
lcpm <- cpm(assay(se), log = TRUE, prior.count = 2)[rowMeans(cpm(assay(se))) >= 2, ]
round(cor(lcpm), 2)

How many reads in peaks does each library have? Which is the smallest?
What is the correlation between the technical replicates of donor 5483 (B cells; CD4 T cells)? Between the B-cell libraries of different donors? Between B and T cells?



R4 — PCA: all cell types, then our six samples
cnt_all <- as.matrix(atac[keep, samples$sample, with = FALSE])
use <- rowMeans(cnt_all) >= 10
dall <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(cnt_all[use, ], data.frame(samples[, 2:3], row.names = samples$sample), ~ 1)
vall <- vst(dall, blind = TRUE)                                  # a few seconds
plotPCA(vall, intgroup = "celltype", ntop = 10000)

dds <- DESeqDataSet(se, design = ~ donor + celltype)
dds <- collapseReplicates(dds, groupby = dds$unit)
colData(dds)
vsd <- vst(dds, blind = TRUE)
plotPCA(vsd, intgroup = c("celltype", "donor"))

In the PCA of all 77 libraries, which cell types group together? Is there a donor effect you can see?
After collapseReplicates, how many columns are there, and what are the counts of 5483_Bcell (compare with the two libraries in se)?
In the PCA of the six samples, what separates on PC1? On PC2?



R5 — DESeq2 with the paired design
dds <- dds[rowSums(counts(dds) >= 10) >= 3, ]
nrow(dds)
system.time(dds <- DESeq(dds))
resultsNames(dds)
plotDispEsts(dds)
res <- results(dds, name = "celltype_Bcell_vs_CD4", alpha = 0.05)
summary(res)

How many peaks pass the filter? Why “≥ 10 reads in ≥ 3 samples” and not “in all 6”?
How long does DESeq() take? What is the typical dispersion (median(dispersions(dds)))? What coefficient of variation between donors is that?
How many peaks have padj < 0.05, in each direction?



R6 — Fold-change shrinkage, MA and volcano plots
system.time(shr <- lfcShrink(dds, coef = "celltype_Bcell_vs_CD4", type = "apeglm"))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plotMA(res, ylim = c(-8, 8), main = "MLE")
plotMA(shr, ylim = c(-8, 8), main = "apeglm")
cls <- ifelse(!is.na(res$padj) & res$padj < 0.05 & shr$log2FoldChange >  1, "B_up",
       ifelse(!is.na(res$padj) & res$padj < 0.05 & shr$log2FoldChange < -1, "T_up", "ns"))
table(cls)
vol <- data.frame(lfc = shr$log2FoldChange, p = -log10(res$padj), cls = cls)
ggplot(vol[!is.na(vol$p), ], aes(lfc, p, colour = cls)) + geom_point(size = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(B_up = "#2a6f97", T_up = "#e67e22", ns = "grey70"))

How many B_up and T_up peaks are there?
Compare res$log2FoldChange and shr$log2FoldChange for the peaks with baseMean < 20. What does shrinkage do to them?
How many peaks would pass |MLE log2FC| > 1 instead? Why is the difference small here?



R7 — Three normalisations
tot <- colSums(counts(dds))
y <- normLibSizes(DGEList(counts(dds)))
eff <- y$samples$lib.size * y$samples$norm.factors
sf <- rbind(DESeq2 = sizeFactors(dds), TMM = eff / exp(mean(log(eff))), total = tot / exp(mean(log(tot))))
round(sf, 2)
dt <- dds
sizeFactors(dt) <- sf["total", ]
dt <- DESeq(dt, quiet = TRUE)
rt <- results(dt, name = "celltype_Bcell_vs_CD4", alpha = 0.05)
c(B_up = sum(rt$padj < 0.05 & rt$log2FoldChange > 1, na.rm = TRUE),
  T_up = sum(rt$padj < 0.05 & rt$log2FoldChange < -1, na.rm = TRUE))
c(DESeq2 = median(res$log2FoldChange, na.rm = TRUE), total = median(rt$log2FoldChange, na.rm = TRUE))

Compare the three rows of size factors. Which libraries differ most between the median-of-ratios and the total-count factors?
How many peaks are differential (here with the MLE fold change) with total-count normalisation? Compare with sum(res$padj < 0.05 & res$log2FoldChange > 1, na.rm = TRUE) and the same for < -1.
What is the median log2 fold change under each normalisation? What would have to be true for the total-count result to be the right one?



R8 — Paired vs unpaired
du <- dds
design(du) <- ~ celltype
du <- DESeq(du, quiet = TRUE)
ru <- results(du, name = "celltype_Bcell_vs_CD4", alpha = 0.05)
c(paired = sum(res$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE), unpaired = sum(ru$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
  both = sum(res$padj < 0.05 & ru$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE))
c(paired = median(dispersions(dds)), unpaired = median(dispersions(du)))
dl <- DESeq(dds, test = "LRT", reduced = ~ celltype, quiet = TRUE)
sum(results(dl)$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)

Which design finds more peaks? How much do the two lists overlap?
How many peaks have a significant donor effect (LRT)? Relate this to B3d.



R9 — Nearest gene and marker genes
gtf <- import(file.path(D, "gencode.v46.basic.annotation.gtf.gz"), feature.type = "transcript")
tss <- unique(resize(gtf[gtf$transcript_type == "protein_coding"], width = 1, fix = "start"))
mcols(tss) <- mcols(tss)["gene_name"]
dn <- distanceToNearest(rowRanges(dds), tss, ignore.strand = TRUE)
ann <- data.frame(peak = rownames(dds), gene = tss$gene_name[subjectHits(dn)], dist = mcols(dn)$distance,
                  lfc = shr$log2FoldChange, padj = res$padj, cls = cls)
tapply(ann$dist <= 1000, ann$cls, mean)
mk <- c("PAX5", "CD79A", "MS4A1", "CD19", "EBF1", "BLK", "CD3E", "BCL11B", "TCF7", "LEF1", "GATA3", "CD28")
t(sapply(mk, function(g) table(factor(ann$cls[ann$gene == g], levels = c("B_up", "T_up", "ns")))))
head(ann[order(ann$padj), ], 10)

What fraction of B_up, T_up and non-differential peaks lie within 1 kb of a protein-coding TSS? Why are differential peaks depleted at promoters?
Do the B-cell markers have B_up peaks and the T-cell markers T_up peaks? Which marker has peaks in both directions?
Look at the 10 most significant peaks. How far are they from their nearest TSS? Would you name these genes in a paper as “targets”?



R10 — Does it agree with RNA-seq?
rna <- fread(file.path(D, "corces2016_rna_counts.txt.gz"))
rc <- as.matrix(rna[, -1]); rownames(rc) <- rna[[1]]
rcol <- grep("-(Bcell|CD4Tcell)$", colnames(rc), value = TRUE)
rcd <- data.frame(donor = factor(sub("-.*", "", rcol)),
                  celltype = factor(ifelse(grepl("Bcell", rcol), "Bcell", "CD4"), levels = c("CD4", "Bcell")),
                  row.names = rcol)
ddr <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(rc[, rcol], rcd, ~ donor + celltype)
ddr <- DESeq(ddr[rowSums(counts(ddr) >= 10) >= 2, ], quiet = TRUE)
rr <- results(ddr, name = "celltype_Bcell_vs_CD4")
ann$rna <- rr$log2FoldChange[match(ann$gene, rownames(rr))]
tapply(ann$rna, ann$cls, median, na.rm = TRUE)
prom <- ann$cls != "ns" & ann$dist <= 1000 & !is.na(ann$rna)
dist <- ann$cls != "ns" & ann$dist >  1000 & !is.na(ann$rna)
c(promoter = cor(ann$lfc[prom], ann$rna[prom], method = "spearman"),
  distal   = cor(ann$lfc[dist], ann$rna[dist], method = "spearman"))
ggplot(ann[prom, ], aes(lfc, rna, colour = cls)) + geom_point(size = 0.6) +
  geom_text_repel(data = ann[prom & ann$gene %in% mk, ], aes(label = gene), colour = "black")

Which donors are in the RNA-seq comparison? Are they the same as in the ATAC comparison?
What is the median RNA log2 fold change of the genes nearest to B_up, T_up and non-differential peaks?
Why is the correlation higher for promoter peaks than for distal peaks?



R11 — Save the result
tab <- data.frame(peak_id = rownames(dds), chr = as.character(seqnames(dds)), start = start(dds), end = end(dds),
                  baseMean = res$baseMean, log2FoldChange = shr$log2FoldChange, lfcSE = shr$lfcSE,
                  log2FoldChange_mle = res$log2FoldChange, pvalue = res$pvalue, padj = res$padj,
                  nearest_gene = ann$gene, dist_to_tss = ann$dist, class = cls)
write.table(tab, "differential_peaks.tsv", sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)
table(tab$class)
The file has one row per tested peak (GRCh38, 1-based closed coordinates as in GRanges, 500 bp). Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting starts from it.

title: Exercise: Differential accessibility
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — size factors (B1, B2, R7)





Geometric mean of three numbers = cube root of their product. With two samples, the median of the per-peak ratios S2/S1 is the ratio of the two size factors. Normalised count = count / size factor. The DESeq2 vignette explains size factors; TMM is in normLibSizes (formerly calcNormFactors) and Robinson & Oshlack 2010; background bins in the csaw book.









Hint 2 — design matrices (B3, R5, R8)





model.matrix(~ donor + celltype, data) prints the matrix in R. Residual degrees of freedom = samples − columns. The intercept in ~ donor + celltype is the reference donor in the reference cell type. DESeq2 vignette: multi-factor designs; the likelihood ratio test compares a full and a reduced design.









Hint 3 — replicates (B4, R3, R4)





collapseReplicates sums the counts of columns with the same groupby value. A SummarizedExperiment holds the matrix, the row ranges and the sample table together (vignette); DESeqDataSet(se, design) turns it into a DESeq2 object.









Hint 4 — Poisson and depth (B5)





For a Poisson count with mean \(\lambda\) the standard deviation is \(\sqrt{\lambda}\), so the relative SD is \(1/\sqrt{\lambda}\). Real replicates add biological variation on top (the dispersion).









Hint 5 — MA plots, shrinkage and results (B6, B7, R6)





plotMA, lfcShrink with type = "apeglm" (Zhu et al. 2019). A log2 fold change of \(-2.3\) is a ratio of \(2^{-2.3}\). Shrinkage changes fold changes, not \(p\)-values.









Hint 6 — liftOver and annotation (R2, R9)





rtracklayer::liftOver returns a GRangesList; lengths() gives the number of pieces per peak. import.chain needs an uncompressed chain file. distanceToNearest gives the nearest TSS, as in Genomic intervals. The UCSC liftOver documentation explains the chain files.









Hint 7 — reading the data (C1, C2, R1)





The GEO sample list of GSE74912 gives donor and cell type for every library. data.table::fread reads gzipped files directly. In the regular expression, (?:...) is a group that is not captured, ? makes it optional; see ?regex in R.

title: Exercise: Differential accessibility
text:
Solutions






Solutions — by hand





B1. (a) p1: \((10^6)^{1/3} = 100\); p2: \((64\,000)^{1/3} = 40\); p3: \((2.7 \times 10^7)^{1/3} = 300\); p4: \((64\,000)^{1/3} = 40\). (b) Ratios S1: 1, 1, 1, 0.5 → median (of four: the mean of the middle two) 1. S2: 2, 2, 2, 8 → 2. S3: 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.25 → 0.5. (c) p4 normalised: 20, 160, 20. p4 is 8-fold more open in S2; p1–p3 are identical in all samples after normalisation. (d) Column sums 460, 1200, 230; geometric mean \((460 \cdot 1200 \cdot 230)^{1/3} \approx 503\); factors 0.92, 2.39, 0.46. S2’s total includes the extra reads in p4, so its factor is too large: p1–p3 in S2 become \(200/2.39 = 84\) instead of 100, a false 16% decrease, and p4’s increase shrinks from 8-fold to about 6.1-fold (21.9 in S1, 134 in S2). One strongly changing peak drags the total; the median ignores it.
B2. (a) Control FRiP \(500/1000 = 0.5\); drug \(800/1000 = 0.8\). (b) Per-peak ratios drug/control are all 1.6, so the size-factor ratio is 1.6, and every normalised fold change is 1: no differential peak. (c) Background ratio \(200/500 = 0.4\); normalised fold change \(1.6/0.4 =\) 4 for every peak: a global 4-fold opening. (d) Totals are equal (1000), so the fold change is the raw 1.6. (e) Biological: the drug opens chromatin everywhere (e.g. an HDAC inhibitor), so the true answer is close to (c). Technical: the control library has more background (more dead or damaged cells, worse transposition), so its peaks look weaker; then (b) is right and the “opening” is an artefact. To decide: QC per library (TSS enrichment, fragment-size distribution, mitochondrial fraction, FRiP across replicates), a spike-in (a fixed number of foreign nuclei per sample), or an orthogonal measurement (e.g. imaging of chromatin compaction, or a set of loci known not to change).
B3. (a)
     (Intercept) celltypeBcell
D1-T     1            0
D1-B     1            1
D2-T     1            0
D2-B     1            1
D3-T     1            0
D3-B     1            1



     (Intercept) donorD2 donorD3 celltypeBcell
D1-T     1          0       0         0
D1-B     1          0       0         1
D2-T     1          1       0         0
D2-B     1          1       0         1
D3-T     1          0       1         0
D3-B     1          0       1         1

\(6 - 2 = 4\) and \(6 - 4 = 2\). In (b) the intercept is the (log) level of donor D1’s CD4 T cells; donorD2 is how much D2 differs from D1 in both cell types; celltypeBcell is the B vs T log2 fold change within a donor.
Pairing removes donor-to-donor variation that both cell types share, but costs one parameter per extra donor. In this dataset (sorted cells from healthy adults) donors differ little, so the gain is small and the loss of 2 of 4 residual degrees of freedom dominates: fewer hits. Report the paired model: it is the design of the experiment, chosen before seeing results; choosing the model that gives more hits is a form of \(p\)-hacking. With patients or donors that differ more (genotype, age, treatment), pairing usually gains a lot.

B4. (a) \(120 + 80 = 200\). (b) Four B-cell “replicates” instead of three (the model thinks 5483 is two people). The variance between technical replicates is smaller than between people, so the dispersion is underestimated and the \(p\)-values are too small (pseudo-replication). Also, donor 5483 gets double weight.
B5. (a) \(40 \times 10^6 \times 0.25 / 10^5 = 100\). (b) \(10 \times 10^6 \times 0.4 / 10^5 = 40\). The first: depth beats FRiP here (100 vs 40 reads per peak), although the second library is cleaner. (c) \(1/\sqrt{5} \approx 0.45\): 45%. Between 5 and 20 the Poisson noise alone is large (and biological variation adds to it); a 4-fold difference between two single samples at this depth is weak evidence. This is what dispersion estimation and shrinkage handle.
B6. (a) Few reads: a peak with 0 vs 3 fragments has an MLE fold change that is huge and poorly determined. (b) apeglm shrinks in proportion to the uncertainty: weak peaks have large standard errors and are pulled to 0; strong peaks are well measured and keep their fold change. (c) At 0. A centre at +0.7 means the typical peak looks 1.6-fold more open in B cells: either a global difference (B cells more open overall) that peak-based normalisation should have removed (so check the normalisation), or a normalisation computed on a different set of peaks than the one plotted. (d) Few: a peak needs enough reads to reach |shrunk LFC| > 1 and padj < 0.05; weak peaks are shrunk below 1 or not significant.
B7. (a) a: T_up (padj tiny, shrunk −2.3); d: B_up (padj 0.02, shrunk 2.6). b and c are not. (b) \(2^{2.3} \approx 4.9\) times more open in CD4 T cells. (c) No: it is significantly more open in B cells, by about \(2^{0.7} \approx 1.6\)-fold. It fails only our effect-size threshold. Write “modestly more accessible (1.6-fold, padj 0.001)” if it matters; the threshold is a convention for making lists, not a test of “no change”. (d) baseMean 4: a few reads, so the MLE is noisy and huge; the standard error is also huge, so the Wald test is not significant and apeglm shrinks it to 0.4.
B8. First sentence: “near” a gene is not “regulating” it (the nearest gene is a guess, often wrong for distal elements); and correlation of accessibility and expression is not causation (“drive” needs perturbation, e.g. CRISPR deletion or inhibition of the element). A B-specific peak next to a non-DE gene: the peak regulates a different, more distant gene; the gene is expressed in both cell types from other elements; the element is primed (open before expression starts, or a repressor binds); or the gene is not expressed in either because another factor is missing. 30% non-concordance is therefore expected, not evidence of “uncoupling”.









Solutions — command line





C1. (a) 135 columns: Chr Start End and 132 libraries. B cells: Donor1022-Bcell-13-150120, Donor4983-Bcell-13A-150120, Donor5483-Bcell-13A-150305, Donor5483-Bcell-13B-150305. CD4 T cells: Donor1022-CD4-9-150120, Donor2596-CD4-9A-150303, Donor4983-CD4-9A-150120, Donor5483-CD4-9A-150305, Donor5483-CD4-9B-150305. Donors 1022, 4983 and 5483 have both; 2596 has CD4 T cells only. (b) Every peak has End − Start = 500 (590 650 peaks), so the file uses BED-style 0-based starts, from summit − 250 to summit + 250. (c) chr1–22 and chrX (chr1 has the most peaks, 51 405; chr21 the fewest, 6887). No chrY and no chrM: the authors removed them (chrM reads are a known ATAC artefact). Without chrY, male and female donors differ only on chrX, where one X is inactive in females; a donor’s sex can still create chrX differences, which the paired design absorbs.
C2. (a) Column 27; 4 650 539 reads in peaks; 46 335 peaks with no read at all. (b) The peaks were called on all 13 cell types (and AML samples) together, so many are elements open only in other cell types (e.g. erythroid or myeloid enhancers).









Solutions — R





Run times are from one server core; a laptop is 1.5–3 times slower.
R1. (a) ^(?:Donor)? an optional “Donor” prefix; ([0-9]+) the donor ID (group 1); -(?:[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9]*-)? an optional cell-type word such as CD4- or Erythroblast-; ([0-9]+) the cell-type code (group 2); ([A-C]?) the replicate letter (group 3, may be empty); (?:-[0-9]+)?$ an optional run date. If the word could start with a digit, in Donor7256-1A-110614 the regex would take 1A- as the word and 110614 as the code. (b) 77 libraries, 7 donors, 13 cell types; B cells and CD4 T cells both in donors 1022, 4983 and 5483. (c) The 52 AML columns (SU…: leukaemia, LSC and pre-leukaemic HSC samples) and the 3 bulk CD34+ samples (BM-CD34-1, BM-CD34-2, CB102-CD34-150627), whose names do not start with digits or Donor + digits.
R2. (a) 159 fail, 1375 split, 46 single pieces of the wrong width or on another chromosome; 589 070 kept (99.7%). (b) The file’s starts are 0-based (BED-like); GRanges is 1-based. (c) A stable ID that links the lifted peak back to the hg19 row (and to other analyses of the same file, such as Motifs), independent of filtering.
R3. (a) Reads in peaks after liftOver (millions): 1022 B 4.64, 1022 CD4 6.35, 4983 B 17.89, 4983 CD4 11.22, 5483 B 10.50 + 6.35, 5483 CD4 8.22 + 5.99. The smallest is the B-cell library of donor 1022. title: Exercise: Differential accessibility
text:
Where this leads

Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting reads differential_peaks.tsv, extracts the sequences of B_up and T_up peaks (GRCh38) and asks which transcription factor motifs are enriched, using the ns peaks as background.
Linking regulatory elements to genes replaces “nearest TSS” (R9) with contacts and activity, and returns to the RNA concordance (R10).
Experimental design and QC covers spike-ins and FRiP, the tools for deciding between the normalisations in B2 and R7.
Single-cell ATAC (ArchR, Signac) uses the same consensus peaks and counts, summed over cells of a type (“pseudobulk”) for differential tests.

title: Exercise: Differential accessibility
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined.

Corces et al. 2016, Nat Genet. Lineage-specific and single-cell chromatin accessibility charts human hematopoiesis and leukemia evolution.
Love, Huber & Anders 2014, Genome Biol. Moderated estimation of fold change and dispersion for RNA-seq data with DESeq2.
Ross-Innes et al. 2012, Nature. Differential oestrogen receptor binding is associated with clinical outcome in breast cancer.
Lun & Smyth 2016, Nucleic Acids Res. csaw: a Bioconductor package for differential binding analysis of ChIP-seq data using sliding windows.
Robinson & Oshlack 2010, Genome Biol. A scaling normalization method for differential expression analysis of RNA-seq data.
Reske, Wilson & Chandler 2020, Epigenetics Chromatin. ATAC-seq normalization method can significantly affect differential accessibility analysis and interpretation.

title: Quiz: differential accessibility
text:
Short questions on count matrices, normalisation, design and interpretation of differential accessibility. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. In RNA-seq the features to count come from a GTF file. Where do the features come from in a differential accessibility analysis, and why must all samples be counted in the same set?






Hint





Think about what happens to a peak that was called in sample 1 but not in sample 2.









Answer





From the data: peaks called in the samples and combined into one consensus set (merged, or fixed-width around summits). Every sample must be counted in the same regions, otherwise rows do not correspond: a peak missing from one sample’s own peak list still has reads there (maybe fewer), and those reads are exactly what the test needs. A peak “absent” from a sample’s peak calls is a low count, not a missing value.




Q2. Three samples have counts 30, 60 and 120 in peak A, and 10, 20 and 40 in peak B. Compute the geometric mean of each peak and the ratios of each count to it. If these were the only two peaks, what would the size factors be?






Hint





\(30 \cdot 60 \cdot 120 = 216\,000 = 60^3\).









Answer





Peak A: geometric mean 60, ratios 0.5, 1, 2. Peak B: \((8000)^{1/3} = 20\), ratios 0.5, 1, 2. The medians are 0.5, 1 and 2: these are the size factors. After normalisation both peaks are identical across samples (60 and 20).




Q3. A treatment opens chromatin at almost every peak by about 2-fold, and the libraries are sequenced to the same depth. You run DESeq2 with default size factors. What do you expect to see in the MA plot, and why?






Answer





A cloud centred at log2 fold change 0 and few differential peaks. The median-of-ratios size factors assume that the typical peak does not change, so they absorb the global 2-fold opening (the treated sample gets a larger size factor). Only peaks that change more or less than the typical peak appear as differential, and with a shrunken effect. To see the global change you need a reference that does not change with the treatment: background bins (if the background is constant), a spike-in, or known invariant regions.




Q4. Library 1 has 30 million fragments and FRiP 0.30; library 2 has 30 million fragments and FRiP 0.15. Both come from the same cell type. What is the expected ratio of counts in a typical peak? Would you normalise by total fragments or within peaks, and why?






Answer





\(30 \times 0.30 = 9\) M vs \(30 \times 0.15 = 4.5\) M fragments in peaks: a typical peak has 2 times more fragments in library 1. Same cell type, so the difference in FRiP is most likely technical (signal-to-noise of the library), and normalising within peaks (median of ratios, TMM, or reads in peaks) is right. Total-fragment normalisation would make every peak look 2-fold more open in library 1.




Q5. Three donors each give a treated and an untreated sample. Write the DESeq2 design formula. What is the meaning of the coefficient you test, and how many residual degrees of freedom are there?






Answer





~ donor + treatment (the variable of interest last). The treatment coefficient is the log2 fold change treated vs untreated within a donor, averaged over donors. Six samples, four coefficients (intercept, two donor terms, treatment): \(6 - 4 = 2\) residual degrees of freedom.




Q6. Donor 5483 has two B-cell ATAC libraries made from the same sorted cells (A and B). What should you do with them before DESeq2, and what goes wrong if you treat them as two biological replicates?






Answer





They are technical replicates: sum their counts into one sample (collapseReplicates). Treated as two donors, they make the variance between donors look smaller than it is (two libraries of one person agree better than two people do), so dispersions are underestimated and \(p\)-values too small: pseudo-replication. The donor also gets twice the weight.




Q7. A peak has baseMean 3, MLE log2 fold change 5.8 and padj 0.4; after apeglm shrinkage its log2 fold change is 0.3. Another has baseMean 900, log2 fold change −1.6 (shrunk −1.6), padj \(10^{-12}\). Interpret both.






Answer





The first has very few reads: the 5.8 is a noisy estimate (e.g. 0 vs 4 fragments), not significant, and shrinkage pulls it towards 0 because its standard error is large. No evidence of a difference. The second is well measured: \(2^{1.6} \approx 3\) times less accessible in the numerator group (more open in the reference group), highly significant; shrinkage does not change it. With the threshold padj < 0.05 and |LFC| > 1 it is differential.




Q8. In the B vs CD4 T-cell comparison, 8% of B-specific peaks but 20% of all tested peaks lie within 1 kb of a TSS. Explain the difference. What does it imply for linking differential peaks to genes?






Answer





Promoters tend to be accessible in many cell types (housekeeping and poised promoters), so they are less often differential; cell-type-specific regulation is mostly in distal enhancers. Most differential peaks therefore have no gene of their own: “nearest gene” is a guess, often tens or hundreds of kb away, and the true target may be a more distant gene contacted in 3D. Use the nearest gene as a label, not as a conclusion.




Q9. You use the Corces peaks, which were called on hg19, with a GRCh38 gene annotation. What must you do first, and what can go wrong?






Answer





Lift the peaks to GRCh38 with liftOver (chain file hg19ToHg38). Some peaks fail to map (deleted or rearranged regions: 159 of 590 650 here), some split into pieces (1375) or change width; drop those. Without lifting, bedtools or GenomicRanges would happily overlap hg19 peaks with hg38 genes and give wrong nearest genes, with no error message (Genomic intervals).




Q10. A study compares ATAC-seq of tumour and normal tissue from different patients, with tumours sequenced in 2019 and normal tissue in 2022. It reports 40 000 differential peaks with DESeq2 default normalisation. Name two problems with the design and one with the normalisation.






Answer





Design: (1) condition is confounded with batch (year of sequencing), so batch effects cannot be separated from tumour vs normal; (2) samples are unpaired (different patients) and tissues are mixtures of cell types: differences in cell-type composition (immune infiltration, stroma) appear as differential peaks. Normalisation: tumours often have different global accessibility and different signal-to-noise (FRiP) from normal tissue; peak-based size factors assume most peaks do not change, which may not hold, and a global difference would be hidden or distorted. Check FRiP and the MA plot, and compare with another normalisation.

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
About this lecture

Differential accessibility gave us thousands of peaks that are more open in B cells than in CD4 T cells, and the reverse. A list of peaks is not yet biology: which transcription factors (TFs) open these regions?

Motif enrichment: which TF motifs are over-represented in a set of peaks (a 2×2 test, and the choice of background).
chromVAR: how open the peaks with a given motif are, per sample (or per cell).
Footprinting: whether a TF actually sits on its site, from the pattern of Tn5 insertions.


This is the last unit of the ATAC-seq block. The running example continues from Differential accessibility: the Corces et al. 2016 haematopoiesis ATAC-seq data, B cells versus CD4 T cells from the same three donors. Of 211 824 peaks tested, 19 439 are more open in B cells (B-up) and 16 972 more open in CD4 T cells (T-up), at adjusted p below 0.05 and an absolute log2 fold change above 1. The question for this unit is which TFs are behind those differences. Three ideas, in increasing resolution: enrichment over a set of peaks, accessibility per sample, and protection of single sites. The motif sequences in the middle panel are real consensus sites (PU.1, OCT, IRF in blue; RUNX, TCF/LEF, ETS1 in orange); the lists on the right are what we actually find later in this lecture.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Recap: a PWM finds motif matches
text:
Recap: a PWM finds motif matches


A position weight matrix (PWM) gives a log-odds score for each base at each position (from Gene regulation). The score of a window is the sum; scan both strands.
A match is a window whose score is unlikely in random sequence: here p < 5 \times 10^{-5} (the motifmatchr default).
Short motifs match by chance everywhere. A 500-bp peak has ~1000 windows, so about 5% of peaks match any given motif by chance alone.


Only a recap: Gene regulation introduced counts, frequencies, log-odds and logos. What matters here is the threshold. Tools convert the score into a p-value: the probability that a random window with the background base composition scores at least this high. With p = 5e-5 and 1000 windows per peak, the expected number of chance matches is 0.05 per peak. In our 211 824 Corces peaks, the median JASPAR motif matches 6.4% of peaks, close to that expectation. This is why “my peak has a GATA motif” means very little on its own; the question is always whether there are more matches than expected.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Motif databases, and TF families


JASPAR 2024 (open, curated; 879 vertebrate CORE motifs), CIS-BP (motifs inferred for ~1600 human TFs), HOCOMOCO (from ChIP-seq). HOMER and MEME ship their own collections.
TFs of one family share a DNA-binding domain and bind almost the same motif. A motif hit names a family, not a TF.
Matrices for the same TF differ between databases and versions. JASPAR’s PAX5 matrix is only the 8-bp core; its PAX2 and PAX8 matrices are longer.


The logos are JASPAR 2024 matrices, aligned (RC = shown as reverse complement). PU.1 (SPI1) and SPIB are almost identical, and both share the GGAA core with ETS1 and GABPA; the flanks differ (an A-rich 5’ flank for PU.1/SPIB, CCGGAAGT for ETS1/GABPA), and this turns out to matter for B vs T cells. RUNX1, 2 and 3 all bind TGTGGT. TCF7, LEF1 and TCF7L2 all bind CTTTGAT. Humans have about 1600 TFs but only a few hundred distinct motifs, so a large motif collection is highly redundant: 28 of the 879 JASPAR motifs are ETS. Pick the TF within a family with other evidence: is it expressed (RNA-seq), is there ChIP-seq. The PAX example is real and will come back: a short matrix can fail where the family’s longer matrices work.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Motif enrichment is a 2×2 table


Count target and background peaks with and without a match. Effect size: the odds ratio; with 42% vs 20%, OR = 2.9.
p-value: Fisher’s exact test, which is the hypergeometric test: how surprising is it to draw this many motif peaks if the 19 439 B-up peaks were a random draw of all tested peaks?
Expected matches in B-up under the null: 19 439 × 47 509 / 211 824 = 4360. Observed: 8242.


The numbers are real: SPIB in B-up peaks. a = 8242 of 19 439 B-up peaks contain a SPIB match, against c = 39 267 of the 192 385 other tested peaks. The odds ratio (a·d)/(b·c) is 2.87. The one-sided hypergeometric p-value is about 10^-934, which R can only compute on the log scale. HOMER reports exactly this hypergeometric p-value (or a binomial approximation); MEME’s SEA uses Fisher’s exact test as well. Note the background here: all other tested peaks, i.e. regions that are open in at least some of the samples. Students did the same kind of 2×2 table for gene-set enrichment in RNA-seq; here genes are peaks and the gene set is “has a motif”.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Choosing the background


The background decides the question. For differential peaks the natural background is the other peaks you tested.
GC content is the classic confounder: motifs differ in GC, and so do peak sets (promoters are GC-rich, distal enhancers AT-richer).
The random-genome background is the motif version of the naive shuffle in Genomic intervals: it answers “open vs closed DNA”, not “B vs T”.


Three choices. (1) Other peaks: what distinguishes B-up regions from other open regions. Anything common to open chromatin cancels. (2) GC-matched: draw background regions with the same GC distribution as the target, so motifs that are GC-rich or AT-rich do not win simply because the target is GC-rich or AT-rich. HOMER does this by default, from random genomic regions (findMotifsGenome.pl), and normalises k-mer content as well. chromVAR, later, matches on both GC and average accessibility. (3) Random genome or shuffled sequence: the target is compared with closed, AT-rich DNA, so every motif of open chromatin looks enriched. Same lesson as the shuffle test in Genomic intervals: the null decides the answer. Shuffled sequences (preserving dinucleotide content) are what MEME tools use by default when no background is given.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Real data: the background changes the answer
text:
Real data: the background changes the answer


B-up peaks are AT-richer than other peaks (mean GC 0.48 vs 0.51) but GC-richer than random DNA (0.41).
Against other peaks, GC-rich motifs (SP1, KLF4, NRF1) look depleted; GC matching removes most of this. EBF1 (GC-rich) gains: OR 1.18 → 1.48.
Against random genome, SPIB looks twice as enriched (OR 5.1) and CTCF flips from depleted to enriched.


Real numbers from make-motifs-figs.R. For the GC-matched background, each B-up peak got one partner from the other tested peaks with GC content in the same 2% bin. For the random background, 19 439 random 500-bp windows from chr1–22 and X without Ns or blacklisted regions. Read the plot motif by motif. SPIB: enriched against any background, the robust finding. CTCF: depleted against peaks (CTCF sites are open in all cell types, so they are not B-specific), but enriched against random DNA (CTCF sites are open chromatin). SP1, KLF4, NRF1: their apparent depletion against other peaks is mostly GC: B-up peaks are distal, AT-richer elements, while the background contains GC-rich promoters. EBF1 is the reverse: its motif is GC-rich, so the AT-rich target hides its enrichment until GC is matched. Always report which background you used.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Real data: motifs in B-up and T-up peaks
text:
Real data: motifs in B-up and T-up peaks


B-up: PU.1 / SPIB / SPIC (ETS), IRF and STAT, OCT (POU2F2 = OCT2), IKZF1, MEF2, NF-κB. T-up: ETS1 / GABPA / ERG-type ETS, RUNX, TCF7/LEF1, BCL11B, GATA3 (OR 1.5).
EBF1 is only weakly enriched (OR 1.18) and PAX5’s JASPAR matrix not at all, although both are B-cell master regulators. EBF is clearly depleted in T-up peaks (OR 0.51).


Each point is one of 879 JASPAR motifs, B-up or T-up compared with all other tested peaks; the dashed line is the Bonferroni threshold. The B-cell list is textbook: PU.1 and SPIB, the ETS–IRF composite elements bound by PU.1 or SPIB with IRF4/IRF8, OCT2 with its coactivator OBF1, IKAROS, MEF2C, and NF-κB. The T-cell list: RUNX1/3 with CBFβ, TCF1 (TCF7) and LEF1, the ETS factors ETS1 and GABPA, BCL11B and GATA3. Where expectations fail is instructive. EBF1 is enriched only weakly with this matrix and background (better with GC matching, previous slide). PAX5, the B-cell identity factor, is not enriched with JASPAR MA0014.4, while the longer PAX2/PAX8 matrices give OR about 1.9: the PWM, not the biology, failed. And a motif being absent from the list does not mean the TF does not act there: TFs bind as partners, and many sites are weak matches below the threshold.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
One family, two lineages


Each point is a motif: enrichment in B-up (x) against enrichment in T-up (y).
The ETS family splits: PU.1/SPIB motifs (A-rich flank) go with B cells, ETS1/GABPA motifs (CCGGAAGT) with T cells. The flanks seen in the logos carry the lineage information.
CTCF and GC-rich promoter motifs (SP1, KLF4) are below 1 in both: constitutively open, not lineage-specific.


Points on the diagonal are enriched in both, points in the lower right only in B, upper left only in T. RUNX and TCF/LEF are T-specific, EBF is depleted in T-up, the POU and IRF motifs are positive in both sets (both are lymphoid, and the background contains everything that is open in either). This plot is a good way to see the redundancy problem: you cannot tell from the motif alone whether PU.1 or SPIB is the factor in B cells; both are expressed in B cells. To name the TF, combine motif enrichment with expression (RNA-seq of the same cells), with ChIP-seq, or with perturbation. This is the logic of Heinz et al. 2010 (key papers): a few lineage-determining TFs, PU.1 with C/EBP or with E2A/EBF/OCT, select the enhancers of a cell type.

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Hundreds of motifs: p-values and effect sizes
text:
Hundreds of motifs: p-values and effect sizes




B-up

enriched at BH FDR 5% (OR > 1)

With ~19 000 target peaks, tiny effects are significant. Half of all motifs pass FDR 5%; most are family members of a few real signals, or GC.
Correct for the number of motifs (BH or Bonferroni, as for genes in RNA-seq), then rank by effect size (odds ratio, or fraction of target vs background), and group motifs by family.
With few target peaks (say 200), the opposite problem: little power, and multiple testing matters more.


The multiple-testing part is the same as in RNA-seq: 879 tests, so a nominal p of 0.05 would give about 44 false positives. BH controls the false discovery rate; Bonferroni the family-wise error rate (threshold 0.05/879). But with nearly 20 000 peaks in the target set, statistical significance is almost guaranteed for any motif with even a few percent difference, as with a huge RNA-seq experiment where every gene is “significant”. So report the odds ratio and the two fractions (42% vs 20% for SPIB), not only −log10 p, and look at the top of the list by effect size. Correlated tests: motifs of the same family give nearly the same answer, so “474 significant motifs” is many fewer independent findings. For this reason many analyses first cluster similar motifs into non-redundant ‘archetypes’ and report one per cluster.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Known motifs vs de novo discovery
text:
Known motifs vs de novo discovery


Known-motif enrichment tests each database motif: fast, names come for free, but limited to the database and to the quality of each matrix (PAX5 above).
De novo discovery finds the words that best separate target from background, builds a PWM, then compares it with the database: “looks like EBF1”.
Both give a motif, not a TF: the family problem remains.


HOMER (Heinz et al. 2010) does both in one run: known motifs first, then de novo motifs of length 8, 10, 12, then matches each new motif to its database. The MEME suite (Bailey et al. 2015) has separate tools: SEA or AME for known motifs (enrichment), STREME and MEME for discovery, Tomtom for comparing a new motif with a database. De novo results are useful when the TF is unknown, when the cell type uses an unusual variant, or for composite elements such as the ETS–IRF composite in B cells, which appears as one longer motif. Newer approaches train a neural network on the sequence of peaks (chromBPNet) and extract the learned motifs (TF-MoDISco): see the machine-learning units.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: HOMER and MEME on the command line
text:
HOMER and MEME on the command line
# HOMER: known + de novo motifs, 200 bp at the peak centre,
# GC-matched random genomic background (default) ...
findMotifsGenome.pl b_up.bed hg38.fa homer_b_up/ -size 200 -p 8
# ... or the other tested peaks as background
findMotifsGenome.pl b_up.bed hg38.fa homer_bg/ -size 200 -bg tested.bed -p 8

# MEME suite: known motifs (SEA) and de novo (STREME) vs the other peaks
bedtools getfasta -fi hg38.fa -bed b_up.bed   > b_up.fa
bedtools getfasta -fi hg38.fa -bed tested.bed > tested.fa
sea    --p b_up.fa --n tested.fa --m JASPAR2024_CORE_vertebrates.meme
streme --p b_up.fa --n tested.fa --dna

Not installed in this course: the exercise does the known-motif test in R (motifmatchr + Fisher), which shows every step.


These are the commands a student would run on a cluster with HOMER or the MEME suite installed (both are in Bioconda). HOMER’s -size 200 uses 200 bp around the peak centre: for summit-centred TF peaks, a narrow window raises the signal-to-noise ratio, because the motif sits near the summit. Our Corces peaks are fixed 500-bp windows around summits. Without -bg, HOMER picks GC-matched random genomic regions as background, which is the “random genome” question with GC matching. With -bg tested.bed it asks the B-vs-other-peaks question. SEA wants a motif file in MEME format, which JASPAR provides for download. The output in each case is a ranked table like ours: motif, fraction of target and background with a match, p-value, q-value.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
chromVAR: motif accessibility per sample


Enrichment needs a set of peaks. chromVAR asks the question per sample: are the peaks with motif X more open in this sample than in the average sample?
Compare with background peaks matched for GC content and average accessibility, so technical differences between samples (GC bias, signal-to-noise) cancel.
Output: a deviation z-score per motif and sample, and the variability of each motif across samples.


chromVAR (Schep et al. 2017) starts from the peak-by-sample count matrix, the same matrix used for DESeq2. For each motif and sample: observed = reads in peaks with the motif divided by all reads in peaks; expected = the same fraction in the pooled data. The raw deviation is (observed − expected)/expected. The same is computed for many background peak sets: for each motif peak, a background peak with similar GC and similar mean accessibility, sampled 50 times. The z-score says how many standard deviations the motif’s deviation lies away from those background sets. It is robust to sample-level biases: if one library has more GC-rich fragments, all GC-rich peak sets go up, background included, so the z-score does not. Variability is the standard deviation of the z-scores across samples: high for motifs whose accessibility differs between cell types.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Real data: chromVAR across haematopoiesis


13 cell types, 47 donor × cell-type samples from Corces et al. 2016; the 100 000 most-read peaks; 879 JASPAR motifs.
Motifs of 26 known regulators. GATA in MEPs and erythroblasts (and rising from HSC to MPP to CMP); CEBP in GMPs and monocytes; PU.1/SPIB in LMPPs, GMPs, monocytes and B cells; EBF1 in CLPs (less in B cells); the E-box (TCF3, E2A) in LMPPs, CLPs, B and T cells; POU2F2 and NF-κB in B cells; TCF7/LEF1 in CD4 and CD8 T cells; T-box (TBX21, EOMES) and ETS1 in NK and CD8 T cells.
The motif called Gata3 behaves exactly like GATA1: it is highest in erythroid cells, not in T cells. Same family, same motif.


Each column is one donor and cell type (technical replicates summed), 47 columns over 13 cell types; z-scores capped at ±15 for colour. The data are the Corces et al. 2016 count matrix lifted to hg38, the 100 000 peaks with the most reads, 879 JASPAR motifs, 50 background iterations; the whole computation takes under a minute after motif matching. This is essentially the analysis of the chromVAR paper, which used the same haematopoiesis data. The picture recovers the textbook regulators of each lineage without any differential analysis: GATA1/TAL1 along the erythroid branch, C/EBP along the myeloid branch, PU.1 in myeloid and B cells, EBF in common lymphoid progenitors, E2A across lymphoid cells, TCF1/LEF1 in T cells, T-bet and Eomes in NK and CD8 T cells. Point at the Gata3 row: chromVAR cannot know that GATA3 is the T-cell GATA factor; the motif is the motif. HLF and HOXA9, HSC regulators, do not stand out here: their motifs are weak or shared with other factors. The z-scores of the same cell type from different donors agree well, which is what you want before trusting a difference.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Variability, and single cells


Variability ranks motifs by how much their accessibility differs between samples: an unsupervised way to find the TFs that distinguish cell types.
The top of the list is dominated by families, often under unexpected names: FIGLA, ASCL1, BHLHE22 are E-box motifs (E2A/TCF3 in lymphoid cells), TBR1 is a T-box motif (T-bet, Eomes), MAFG::NFE2L1 is the erythroid NFE2 motif.
chromVAR was built for single-cell ATAC-seq, where each cell has a few thousand fragments: no single peak is informative, but summed over the thousands of peaks with a motif, each cell gets a z-score (ArchR, Signac).


Left: the 15 most variable motifs, keeping one motif per group of motifs whose z-scores correlate above 0.9; the label in brackets says what kind of motif it is. GATA is far ahead (variability 33): erythroid and megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitors differ most from everything else. Right: one dot per donor for five motifs, along the haematopoietic tree. GATA1 rises from HSC (about 0) through MPP and CMP to MEP (about 65); PU.1 is high in LMPP, GMP, monocytes and B cells and negative in erythroid, T and NK cells; EBF1 peaks in CLPs, TCF7 in T cells, CEBPA in GMPs and monocytes. The names on the left are a lesson in the family problem: JASPAR names a matrix after the protein it was measured for, which is often not the factor active in blood. In single cells, chromVAR z-scores are used to cluster cells, to annotate clusters, and to follow TF activity along differentiation trajectories; the Schep et al. paper did this for single-cell ATAC-seq of the same haematopoietic populations.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Footprints: a bound TF protects its site
text:
Footprints: a bound TF protects its site


Tn5 cannot insert where a protein sits. A TF bound for long enough leaves a dip of insertions over its motif (the footprint), flanked by high insertion rates in the free DNA next to it.
Footprinting needs base-resolution insertion sites (the +4/−5 shifted read ends of ATAC-seq processing and peak calling), not coverage, and deep sequencing: ~10⁸ reads for single sites.


The idea is old: DNase I footprinting on gels since 1978, then genome-wide with DNase-seq, and with ATAC-seq: the first ATAC-seq paper (Buenrostro et al. 2013) already showed an aggregate CTCF footprint. The two features: the flanks are high because the TF keeps the neighbourhood free of nucleosomes, and the centre is low because the protein blocks Tn5. For a single site you need many insertions within ±100 bp, so footprinting individual sites requires very deep libraries; aggregating over thousands of sites of the same motif (next slide) works with ordinary depth.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: From reads to an aggregate footprint
text:
From reads to an aggregate footprint


Each read end is one Tn5 insertion: start + 4 for reads on +, end − 5 for reads on −.
Take every motif match, cut a window of ±100 bp around its centre, flip sites on the − strand, and average the insertion counts position by position.


The +4/−5 shift comes from the 9-bp duplication Tn5 creates when it inserts: the two strands are cut 9 bp apart, so the two read ends of a fragment are offset; shifting puts both on the centre of the insertion event (ATAC-seq processing unit). Orientation matters because motifs are not palindromic: the protein’s contacts, and Tn5’s sequence preference, are asymmetric relative to the motif. Without flipping, the footprint of a non-palindromic motif is smeared. In R this is coverage() on single-base GRanges, a Views/matrix of windows, and colMeans. deepTools computeMatrix on a bigWig of insertions does the same on the command line.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: Real data: CTCF footprint in GM12878
text:
Real data: CTCF footprint in GM12878


Bound sites (motif in a ChIP peak, n = 400): high flanks peaking at about −25 and +33 bp, and a dip over the motif. Open but unbound motif sites (n = 427): flat, no flanks, no dip. Closed sites: almost no insertions.
The narrow spike at the motif centre appears in bound and unbound sites: it is Tn5’s sequence preference, not protein.


Real data from the exercise: GM12878 ATAC-seq replicate 1, chr21 only, 505 000 insertions after removing duplicates. CTCF motif matches on chr21 at p < 1e-4 (JASPAR MA0139.2), oriented by motif strand, averaged per site; thin lines are 1-bp values, thick lines a 5-bp running mean. Bound sites: insertions rise to about 0.7 per site at the flanks and fall to about 0.2 on either side of the centre; averaged over ±10 bp the centre is 0.34 against 0.49 at 30–60 bp, a ratio of 0.7. Three lessons. The flanks: CTCF positions nucleosomes and keeps the neighbourhood open. The dip: the protein blocks Tn5 over roughly 20–40 bp, wider than the 19-bp motif because CTCF’s zinc fingers and the protein bulk cover more DNA. The spike at the centre: the unbound open sites have it too, so it comes from the motif sequence itself, which Tn5 prefers to cut (next slide). With one chromosome and 400 sites the profile is noisy; genome-wide it is very clean.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Tn5 has a sequence preference


Base composition around 200 000 insertion sites in the GM12878 reads, relative to the same reads 20–30 bp away. Within ±10 bp of the insertion, bases are up to 1.5-fold over- or under-represented, in a roughly symmetric pattern around the 9-bp duplication.
Tn5 does not cut at random: some sequences are cut more often whatever is bound. A motif has nearly the same sequence at every site, so this preference repeats at every site and does not average out.


The +4/−5 shift puts position 0 at the centre of the 9-bp target-site duplication. The pattern is a weak, roughly palindromic preference, as expected for an enzyme that binds DNA as a dimer. The same kind of bias exists for DNase I, MNase and the restriction enzymes: every enzyme has a sequence preference. Comparing with positions 20–30 bp away removes the general GC richness of open chromatin, which would otherwise dominate. The consequence for footprinting: averaged over thousands of copies of the same motif, Tn5’s preference for the motif’s own sequence produces a reproducible shape, a spike or a dip, that has nothing to do with binding. The central spike in the CTCF footprint is an example.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Correcting for Tn5 bias


Observed insertions = Tn5 sequence preference × protection. Inside a motif the sequence is the same at every site, so the bias is the same at every site and adds up in the aggregate: it can create a fake footprint, or hide a real one.
Correct by comparing with insertions expected from sequence alone: Tn5 on naked DNA, a k-mer model (TOBIAS ATACorrect), or a neural network bias model (chromBPNet).


Sung et al. 2014 showed for DNase-seq that much of the fine structure inside “footprints” comes from the enzyme’s sequence preference, not from protein contacts; Tn5 has the same problem. TOBIAS (Bentsen et al. 2020) estimates Tn5’s preference from the data with a position-weight model around insertion sites, computes the expected insertions at every position, and subtracts them (ATACorrect); then it scores footprints (ScoreBigwig) and compares conditions per site (BINDetect). chromBPNet (Kundaje lab) trains a small network on insertions in closed regions to learn the bias, and a second network for the rest; the bias-corrected predictions show footprints. Commands in the exercise “Where this leads”. The key point for the exam: an aggregate dip is evidence of binding only after bias correction, or with a control set of unbound sites with the same motif.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Which TFs leave footprints?


Footprint depth reflects how long the TF stays on DNA (residence time), not just whether it binds.
CTCF (minutes) footprints well. Many TFs exchange within seconds and leave little or no footprint even where ChIP-seq shows binding (Sung et al. 2014).
“No footprint” is therefore not evidence of no binding; compare conditions (TOBIAS BINDetect) rather than reading single sites.


Live-cell imaging measures residence times: about 10 seconds for the glucocorticoid receptor, two orders of magnitude longer for CTCF. Sung et al. 2014 compared DNase-seq footprints with these kinetics: GR and SOX2 showed little or no protection at sites bound in ChIP-seq, AP-1 and CREB1 were intermediate, CTCF strong; the same logic applies to Tn5. In a 30-minute tagmentation, a site with a short residence time is free most of the time, so Tn5 cuts it almost as often as the flanks. The TF still opens the chromatin (high flanks), but leaves no dip. This is why footprinting works beautifully for CTCF and a few others, and poorly for many important regulators. A practical consequence: compare the same motif between conditions (B vs T), where bias and residence time cancel, rather than claiming binding at individual sites.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
section: A motif is not a binding event
text:
A motif is not a binding event


Of 15 684 CTCF motif matches on chr21, only 400 (2.6%) lie in a CTCF ChIP-seq peak; 95% are in closed chromatin. Conversely, 82% of the 405 chr21 CTCF ChIP peaks contain a match.
CTCF has one of the longest, most informative motifs. For short motifs (GATA: WGATAR) the fraction bound is far smaller. A match says where a TF could bind; chromatin and partners decide where it does (Gene regulation).


Real numbers from the exercise. Motif matches at p < 1e-4 on chr21, after removing blacklisted regions; ChIP peaks are the ENCODE conservative IDR peaks for GM12878 CTCF. Even for CTCF, which binds a long motif with high specificity and is bound at about 44 000 sites in this GM12878 ChIP-seq experiment (all chromosomes), the vast majority of motif matches in the genome are not bound: most lie in closed chromatin, in DNA methylated at the motif’s CpGs, or are weak matches. The 18% of ChIP peaks without a match are weaker motifs below the threshold, indirect binding, or noise. This is why enrichment, chromVAR and footprinting all restrict motif analysis to open chromatin, and why the step from motif to binding needs direct evidence. The 427 open but unbound sites in the previous figure show no footprint: being in open chromatin is not enough either.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Three questions, three tools


Enrichment for a set of peaks (differential peaks, a cluster); chromVAR for samples or single cells; footprinting for sites, with deep data and bias correction.
All three start from motifs, so all three inherit the motif’s limits: family redundancy, imperfect matrices, and motif ≠ binding.


A map for choosing. If you have a list of differential peaks: enrichment. If you have many samples or cells and want a per-sample activity score, for clustering or for plotting along a trajectory: chromVAR. If you want to know which sites are occupied, or how occupancy changes between conditions: footprinting, with deep data and a bias-corrected tool. Each answer is still about a motif, and naming the TF needs other evidence: expression, ChIP or CUT&RUN for the candidate TF, or perturbation. The ChIP and CUT&RUN units come next.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Summary







idea
key fact




motif match
PWM log-odds score above a p-value threshold; ~5% of 500-bp peaks match any motif by chance


databases
JASPAR, CIS-BP, HOCOMOCO; families share motifs, so a motif names a family


enrichment
2×2 table: target vs background × match vs no match; odds ratio; Fisher = hypergeometric


background
decides the question; other peaks for differential sets; match GC; random genome inflates


multiple testing
~900 motifs: BH or Bonferroni, then rank by effect size and group by family


de novo
find enriched words, build a PWM, compare with the database (HOMER, STREME, Tomtom)


chromVAR
per-sample deviation of motif peaks vs GC/accessibility-matched background; z-score; variability; single cells


footprint
dip of Tn5 insertions at a bound motif, high flanks; aggregate over oriented sites


caveats
Tn5 sequence bias makes fake footprints (correct: TOBIAS, chromBPNet); short residence time leaves none




Students should leave able to fill in and evaluate a 2×2 motif table by hand, explain why the background matters, read a chromVAR heatmap, read an aggregate footprint and say what the flanks and the dip mean, and explain why neither a motif match nor a missing footprint settles whether a TF binds. Next: ChIP-seq, which measures the binding of one TF directly.

title: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Key papers (optional further reading)
Not required reading and not examined. For those who want the primary literature.

Heinz et al. 2010, Mol Cell. Simple combinations of lineage-determining transcription factors prime cis-regulatory elements required for macrophage and B cell identities. HOMER, and PU.1 with partners selecting cell-type enhancers.
Bailey et al. 2015, Nucleic Acids Res. The MEME Suite. The other standard motif toolkit (MEME, STREME, SEA, Tomtom).
Rauluseviciute et al. 2024, Nucleic Acids Res. JASPAR 2024: 20th anniversary of the open-access database of transcription factor binding profiles. The motif database we use.
Schep et al. 2017, Nat Methods. chromVAR: inferring transcription-factor-associated accessibility from single-cell epigenomic data. chromVAR, demonstrated on the same Corces haematopoiesis data.
Sung et al. 2014, Mol Cell. DNase footprint signatures are dictated by factor dynamics and DNA sequence. Why many bound TFs leave no footprint, and why enzyme bias shapes the ones you see.
Bentsen et al. 2020, Nat Commun. ATAC-seq footprinting unravels kinetics of transcription factor binding during zygotic genome activation. TOBIAS: bias correction and differential footprinting.

title: Exercise: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Background
Motif matches. A position weight matrix (PWM, from Gene regulation) gives each window of DNA a log-odds score; a window is a match when its score would be reached by chance with probability below a threshold \(p\) (motifmatchr uses \(p < 5 \times 10^{-5}\)). A region of length \(L\) has about \(2L\) windows (both strands), so it contains on average \(2Lp\) chance matches.
Enrichment. For a target set of peaks (for example B-up) and a background set (the other tested peaks):




with match
without




target
\(a\)
\(b\)


background
\(c\)
\(d\)



Odds ratio \(\mathrm{OR} = ad / bc\). Under the null, the target is a random draw of \(a + b\) peaks from all \(N = a + b + c + d\) peaks, of which \(K = a + c\) have a match; the expected number in the target is \((a+b)K/N\). The one-sided p-value is the hypergeometric upper tail \(P(X \ge a)\), which equals the one-sided Fisher’s exact test.
Multiple testing. With \(m\) motifs, Bonferroni rejects when \(p < 0.05/m\). Benjamini–Hochberg (BH): sort the p-values, find the largest \(i\) with \(p_{(i)} \le 0.05\, i/m\), and reject the \(i\) smallest.
chromVAR computes, for each motif and sample, the fraction of reads in peaks with the motif, compares it with the expected fraction (all samples pooled), and standardises it against background peak sets matched for GC content and average accessibility: a deviation z-score. Variability is the standard deviation of a motif’s z-scores across samples.
Footprints. Each read end marks one Tn5 insertion: read start + 4 on the + strand, read end − 5 on the − strand. Averaging insertions around many motif sites, oriented by motif strand, gives an aggregate footprint: a dip where the bound protein blocks Tn5, flanked by high insertion rates in the open DNA next to it.
crumbs: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting

title: Exercise: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
Data

Corces et al. 2016 haematopoiesis ATAC-seq (GEO GSE74912): read counts in 590 650 fixed 500-bp peaks (hg19) for 132 samples. The 77 samples from healthy donors cover 13 cell types; the sample names encode donor and cell type (decoded below from the GEO sample table). The same file as in Differential accessibility, with the UCSC hg19 → hg38 chain file.
hg38 genome as a bgzip-compressed, indexed FASTA (hg38.fa.bgz, .fai, .gzi), so R can read any region quickly.
GM12878 ATAC-seq, ENCODE ENCSR095QNB replicate 1, paired-end 2 × 100: the 6.1 million read pairs that ENCODE aligned to chr21 or chrM, as raw FASTQ, and a bowtie2 index of chr21 + chrM. Plus the ENCODE GM12878 ATAC peaks and CTCF ChIP-seq peaks (from Genomic intervals).

data/download.sh motifs-footprinting      # about 2 GB, mostly the hg38 genome and the reads
D=/path/to/course/data                    # where download.sh put the files
mkdir -p ~/epi/motifs && cd ~/epi/motifs
# only if your data folder has hg38.fa.gz but not hg38.fa.bgz:
# zcat $D/hg38.fa.gz | bgzip -@ 4 > $D/hg38.fa.bgz && samtools faidx $D/hg38.fa.bgz
Shortcuts, said plainly. The footprint uses one chromosome (chr21) of one replicate: aggregate footprints work at this depth, single-site footprints do not. chromVAR uses the 100 000 most-read peaks rather than all 589 000, and sums technical replicates per donor. Motif enrichment is done in R with motifmatchr; HOMER and the MEME suite, the usual command-line tools, are shown in the lecture and under Where this leads but not installed in this course.
You need fastp, bowtie2 and samtools (≥ 1.10) on the command line, and the R packages listed in Install the software you need, including JASPAR2024, TFBSTools, motifmatchr, chromVAR and universalmotif. Total running time on a laptop with 4–8 cores: about 25 minutes, most of it alignment, motif matching and DESeq2.

title: Exercise: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
By hand
Do these on paper.
B1. Chance matches. You scan 300-bp peaks with a motif at threshold \(p = 10^{-4}\).

How many windows does one peak have (both strands, ignore the ends)? How many chance matches do you expect per peak?
In 50 000 peaks, how many chance matches do you expect in total?
Chance matches are rare events, so the number per peak is roughly Poisson. What fraction of peaks has at least one chance match? (\(P(\ge 1) = 1 - e^{-\lambda}\).)
A paper reports “a GATA motif in 25% of our peaks”. What do you need to know before this means anything?

B2. A 2×2 table. 400 target peaks, 120 with a match to motif M. 9600 background peaks, 1440 with a match.

Write the 2×2 table and the fraction with a match in each group.
Compute the odds ratio.
How many target peaks would you expect to have a match if the target were a random draw from all 10 000 peaks? Is the observation higher or lower?
In the real data, an EBF1 match is in 2724 of 19 439 B-up peaks and in 23 440 of 192 385 other tested peaks; \(p \approx 4 \times 10^{-13}\). Compute the two fractions and the odds ratio. Is EBF1 “the TF that drives B-cell chromatin”? What else would you look at?

B3. Many motifs. You test 800 motifs. The eight smallest p-values are
\(1\times10^{-40}\), \(3\times10^{-12}\), \(2\times10^{-6}\), \(4\times10^{-5}\), \(9\times10^{-5}\), \(1.5\times10^{-4}\), \(2.5\times10^{-4}\), \(6\times10^{-4}\).

What is the Bonferroni threshold at 5%, and how many of these motifs pass?
Apply Benjamini–Hochberg at FDR 5%. How many pass?
If none of the 800 motifs were truly enriched, how many would you expect below \(p = 0.05\)?
The top 30 motifs include 12 ETS motifs (ELF1, ELF3, ETV1, GABPA, …). How many independent findings is that?

B4. Background and GC. Your target peaks are promoters (mean GC 0.62). You compare them with (i) random 500-bp windows of the genome (mean GC 0.41) and (ii) GC-matched peaks from the same cells.

With background (i), which kinds of motifs will look enriched only because of base composition? Give an example.
Why does the comparison with (ii) answer a more useful question?
In the real B-up peaks (mean GC 0.48, other peaks 0.51), the SP1 motif has OR 0.60 against the other peaks and 0.93 against GC-matched peaks. Which number would you report, and what do you conclude about SP1?

B5. One motif, many TFs. In B-up peaks the three most enriched motifs are SPIB (OR 2.87), SPI1 (PU.1, OR 2.58) and SPIC (OR 2.80).

Can you tell from these numbers which of the three TFs binds the B-cell peaks? Why not?
Name two kinds of data that would help.
In T-up peaks, ETS1 has OR 2.67 but SPI1 only 1.18. How can two ETS motifs behave so differently? (Hint: look at the logos in the lecture.)

For each motif, name the cell types where peaks with the motif are more accessible than expected.
What does a z-score of −22 for GATA1::TAL1 in monocytes mean? Does it mean GATA1 represses those peaks in monocytes?
chromVAR reports a motif named “GATA3” with almost the same z-scores as GATA1::TAL1, highest in MEPs and erythroblasts, although GATA3 is a T-cell factor. Explain.

B7. Read an aggregate footprint. Mean Tn5 insertions per site around 1000 CTCF motif sites inside CTCF ChIP peaks: about 0.70 at ±30–60 bp from the motif centre, 0.25 within ±10 bp of the centre, and 0.30 at ±100 bp.

Compute the ratio centre/flank. What would it be for a motif without any protection?

A colleague finds no footprint for the glucocorticoid receptor at its ChIP-seq peaks and concludes that it does not bind there. What is wrong with this conclusion?
An aggregate footprint of motif X shows a sharp 3-bp dip at the same position in cells with and without the TF. What is the likely explanation, and how would you correct for it?

B8. Judge the claim. “Peaks gained after stimulation are enriched for AP-1 motifs (p < 10⁻¹⁰⁰ against random genomic regions), so AP-1 opens these regions.” List three problems or missing controls.

title: Exercise: Motifs, motif enrichment and TF footprinting
text:
On the command line

C1 — Trim and align the GM12878 ATAC-seq reads
This is the pipeline of ATAC-seq processing and peak calling, run on the chr21 + chrM subset. It keeps properly paired fragments with MAPQ ≥ 30 and removes duplicates.
fastp -i $D/gm12878_atac_rep1_R1.fastq.gz -I $D/gm12878_atac_rep1_R2.fastq.gz \
  -o R1.trim.fq.gz -O R2.trim.fq.gz --detect_adapter_for_pe -w 4 -j fastp.json -h fastp.html

bowtie2 -p 4 -X 2000 --very-sensitive -x $D/bowtie2/hg38_chr21_chrM \
    -1 R1.trim.fq.gz -2 R2.trim.fq.gz 2> bowtie2.log \
  | samtools fixmate -m -u - - \
  | samtools view -u -f 2 -q 30 - \
  | samtools sort -u - \
  | samtools markdup -r -s - gm12878_atac_rep1.bam 2> markdup.log
samtools index gm12878_atac_rep1.bam
tail -1 bowtie2.log
samtools idxstats gm12878_atac_rep1.bam

What fraction of the read pairs aligned? How many reads are left on chr21 and on chrM after filtering?
What fraction of the filtered reads is on chrM? Why is it so high in ATAC-seq, and why does it not matter for footprinting on chr21?
markdup.log reports the duplicates removed. Why are duplicates a particular problem when you count insertions at single bases?
